itineraries.title: Dodecanese Circuit: Patmos, Leros & Karpathos
itineraries.subtitle: From the sacred island of Saint John to the volcanoes of Nisyros—a journey through the hidden Dodecanese, far from the crowds.
itineraries.climate: Best period: April-June and September-October, temperatures 22-28°C, calm sea and pleasant weather. Avoid July-August (intense heat 30-35°C, strong meltemi winds, overcrowding). Mild winter (12-16°C) but windy, rainy with limited ferry services.
specialties: Traditional Doric costumes still worn daily in Olympos
Byzantine manuscript illumination at Patmos monastery

map_keywords: Monastery of Saint John the Theologian Patmos

visits.text: The Monastery of Saint John the Theologian has commanded the heights above Chora since 1088—the year monk Christodoulos, commissioned by Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, laid the first stones atop the ruins of an Artemis temple. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999, the complex resembles a fortress from the outside—high grey walls, corner towers—but the interior holds a revelation: a library housing 4,000 documents including the celebrated Codex Purpureus, Saint Mark's Gospel inscribed in silver letters on purple-dyed parchment, one of the world's oldest illuminated manuscripts. Allow at least 90 minutes to explore the museum and central courtyard. In high season, arrive at opening to beat the tour groups.

Halfway between Skala port and Chora, the Cave of the Apocalypse is carved into living rock—this is where Saint John, exiled to the island by Emperor Domitian around AD 95, supposedly dictated Revelation to his disciple Prochoros. Look closely at the wall: a three-lobed fissure in the stone symbolizes, according to tradition, the voice of the Trinity. The atmosphere is otherworldly—cool and silent even in peak crowds—contrasting sharply with the island's blazing white sunlight. Plan for 45 minutes on site.

Chora, the medieval village that grew around the monastery starting in 1138, is one of the rare Greek settlements to have evolved continuously since the 12th century—UNESCO cites this unbroken lineage as a criterion for World Heritage status in its own right. Lose yourself in its cobbled lanes between whitewashed houses with wooden balconies: several mansions once belonged to wealthy Aegean sea captains and bear witness to past prosperity. In the evening, this is one of the island's finest spots to watch golden light settle over the rooftops.

Skala, Patmos's main port, is the island's beating heart: fishing boats, inter-island catamarans, waterfront tavernas and colorful shops. This is where you'll take the pulse of daily life—far removed from the monastery's contemplative atmosphere. If you're here on a Sunday, you'll often encounter pilgrims in traditional dress disembarking for Holy Thursday Mass, when the abbot reenacts the washing of the feet in the monastery courtyard.

In Chora's lanes, push open the doors to the Zoodochos Pigi monastery, founded in 1607, and the Annunciation (Evangelismos), founded in 1937—two active convents of nuns that prove Patmos remains a living religious center, extending well beyond the main monastery alone. The sisters receive visitors discreetly but genuinely: dress respectfully.

activities.text: Walk from Skala to Chora on the flagstone path that winds between fig trees and dry-stone walls—about 40 minutes. It's the same route pilgrims have followed for centuries. The panorama over the island's bays widens at every turn. If you prefer to drive, note that Chora's parking is tiny and fills quickly in July-August.

Take a day trip to Patmos's southern beaches—Psili Ammos is accessible only by boat or via a 45-minute hiking trail from Diakofti. The sand is fine and the bay sheltered, yielding water of rare calm. Water taxis depart from Skala throughout the morning.

'Pouggia,' small cakes filled with almonds and cinnamon, are Patmos's signature sweet, tied to monastic tradition. Look for them in Skala bakeries—available year-round, but especially tender when they emerge from the oven in the morning. 'Revithia fournou,' chickpeas baked slowly overnight with olive oil and herbs, appear on most Chora taverna menus on weekends.

In Skala, stop at Sarampelou Café Wine Bar, which stocks wines from the Patoinos estate. Ask which local bottles are available, then examine the three styles produced on the island: white Assyrtiko, red Mavrothiriko and orange Assyrtiko. As production is limited, choose the wine with the staff rather than relying on a specific label. This half-hour stop allows you to buy wine genuinely made on Patmos. A visit to the Patoinos estate itself requires advance booking.

visits.text: The Kastro of Panagia, perched on Apityki hill 200 meters above the sea, is visible from the ferry long before you dock at Leros. Built by the Byzantines in the 11th century and reinforced by the Knights of Rhodes in the 15th, it shelters the miraculous icon of the Virgin who, according to legend, emerged from the sea of her own accord before being installed in the powder magazine chapel. Climb the 300 steps from Platanos—the view of Agia Marina and Panteli bays spreading on either side of the hill is one of the Dodecanese's finest. The 1745 iconostasis and the bronze-and-silver bell cast by Russian artisans are worth the ascent.

Platanos, Leros's former capital, is a quiet village squeezed between two hills, with sand-colored neoclassical houses and small squares shaded by plane trees. This is where the island's administrative heart beats, far from the port bustle. Take time to wander its lanes—several buildings date from the 19th century, when local shipowners were at the height of their prosperity.

Lakki is one of Greece's most bizarre architectural curiosities. Founded in the 1930s by the Italians under the name Porto Lago, this port was designed from scratch according to fascist rationalist principles: wide boulevards, buildings with rounded facades, a cinema and town hall resembling beached ocean liners. Lakki Bay is one of the Mediterranean's largest natural harbors. It's hard not to feel disoriented strolling these nearly deserted streets off-season—like wandering a forgotten 1930s film set.

The War Museum, installed in an authentic underground tunnel at Merikia, is unique in Greece. The Italians excavated it as a munitions depot; in 1943, the Battle of Leros left scars here when the Germans bombarded for 42 days before seizing the island from the British, Greeks and Italians. The museum, opened in 2005, preserves weapons, uniforms, munitions and maps from the 1912-1943 period. Allow 45 minutes.

Alinda's Belleni Tower, built between 1925 and 1927 by expatriate Parisi Belleni, is a neo-Gothic turreted stone building that now houses the island's folklore museum. Exhibits include the watch from the destroyer 'Queen Olga,' sunk in the harbor during the 1943 battle, and artwork painted by political prisoners interned on Leros under Greece's dictatorship (1967-1974).

activities.text: Leros's beaches are perfect for families: Alinda, the longest, is lined with tamarisks and its shallow waters suit children. Vromolithos offers a beach bar and crystalline water. Panteli, at the castle's foot, is the ideal spot in late afternoon when light settles on the ruined windmills along the ridge. For diving, Xirokampos in the south is renowned for its World War II wrecks—a good dozen ships and planes rest at 10 to 30 meters depth.

'Koukouvadès,' fish marinated with rosemary, are Leros's signature seafood specialty. 'Pitakia,' pies stuffed with fava beans, and 'Kakavia,' bouillabaisse prepared with fish pulled from caïques that very morning, are essential at tavernas in Panteli or Agia Marina. For dessert, 'Melopita'—honey-and-mizithra-cheese cake—is the local sweet touch.

Ride a scooter (ideal for this reasonably sized island) up to the castle at sunset, when the last visitors have left and bats begin circling the battlements. The panorama of both bays in orange light is one of the Dodecanese's most memorable views. Scooter rentals are available at Agia Marina and Lakki ports.

visits.text: Olympos is arguably the Dodecanese's most spellbinding village. Founded between the 7th and 9th centuries on the heights of Mount Profitis Ilias to escape Saracen raiders, it remained cut off from the rest of the island for centuries—the paved road only opened in 2011. The result: women still wear traditional embroidered costumes daily (not for tourists), the local dialect preserves Doric Greek phrasings, and single-room houses are built in intact medieval architecture. The 75 windmills along the ridge, many still operational, are the island's symbol. Plan a full day.

Pigadia, Karpathos's capital and main port, is the island's logistical hub. Its natural semicircular harbor is one of the Dodecanese's most sheltered. Take time to visit the archaeological museum housed in the Prefecture Palace: Mycenaean ceramics, ancient coins, Roman statues—the collection documents 3,000 years of human presence on the island.

Aperi, Karpathos's former capital until the 19th century, clings to the hillside with stone houses and flower-filled courtyards. The village is famous for its grand 19th-century mansions built by wealthy shipowners—some feature neoclassical facades that seem transported from another Mediterranean entirely. It's also one of the island's best-maintained villages.

Menetes, at 350 meters elevation in the southern hinterland, is the birthplace of the Karpathos lyre—the traditional stringed instrument that has accompanied dances for centuries. The Church of the Dormition of the Mother of God is considered the island's most beautiful. The view across the sea from the village edge at sunset alone justifies the detour.

At Apella, the beach combines pale sand and pebbles beneath red cliffs, in a bay of turquoise water. The paved but winding road descends to the beach; parking quickly becomes difficult in summer. Part of the shore then offers sunbeds and umbrellas for rent, while a taverna a few metres above serves food and drinks. Enter the water carefully, as it deepens quickly, then follow the rocks with a mask if the sea is calm.

activities.text: If you're in Olympos on August 15th, don't leave under any circumstances: the Feast of the Dormition of the Virgin is celebrated here with epic songs transmitted orally for generations, costumed dances, and music played on lyre and tsambouna (local bagpipe) until dawn. Diaspora residents return from abroad just for this.

The hike between Olympos and the port of Diafani descends about 8 km via a mountain trail that overlooks the sea. The view is vertiginous and the vegetation changes at every elevation. Count on 2.5 to 3 hours of walking. Boats connect Diafani to Pigadia for the return journey.

'Makarounes' are Olympos's signature handmade pasta: shaped by hand through rolling between the palms, they're served with melted butter, fried onions and grated mizithra. You'll find them in Olympos tavernas—one of the rare places where they're still made fresh on site every morning. 'Kserotigana,' ribbons of fried dough drizzled with honey, are served at festivals.

visits.text: Astypalea's Chora is a cascade of cubic white houses tumbling down a rocky hillside to the old port of Pera Gialos. At the summit looms Querini Castle, built of dark stone by the eponymous Venetian family after 1413—contrasting spectacularly with the village's white walls below. The ramparts once served as exterior walls for three-story houses built against them inside. The 1956 earthquake left ruins within, but the monumental entrance remains intact and the view from the top over the two bays forming the island's isthmus is extraordinary. Free admission.

The eight windmills aligned along the ridge of Chora, between the village and the castle, are Astypalea's symbol. Their position allowed them to capture north and south winds interchangeably according to season. One has been converted into the municipal library, another into a shop. In the evening, this is the locals' meeting point before descending to the tavernas.

Pera Gialos, the old port at Chora's foot, is Astypalea's most authentic spot: painted wooden fishing boats, tavernas with plastic tables facing the sea, fish market in the morning. This is where the island truly lives, far from the tourist animation of Chora. Stroll the quay in late afternoon when fishermen return.

The Church of Panagia Portaïtissa (18th century), just below the castle, is considered one of the Dodecanese's most beautiful: its carved and gilded wooden iconostasis was built over nine years by Agios Anthimos of Cephalonia, who was blind according to tradition. A copy of the Panagia Portaïtissa icon was brought from Mount Athos.

Pera Gialos's archaeological museum sits directly on the old port waterfront. It houses finds ranging from prehistory to the medieval era, including pieces from the Kylindra necropolis—a unique burial site where 2,700 infant skeletons interred in jars were discovered on the castle hill's flank, spanning a thousand-year period. A local cult whose significance archaeologists still debate. The museum is small but dense: allow 30 to 40 minutes.

activities.text: From Pera Gialos, drive or ride a scooter to Livadi, an organized beach below Chora, then continue for about 5 km to Agios Konstantinos. The final kilometre follows a passable dirt road. There, alternate swimming with a walk to the small chapel overlooking the cove and a break beneath the tamarisks or in the serviced area. The beach combines sand and pebbles, facing Chora and Querini Castle. On the way back, stop at Livadi to see Chora's white silhouette again from the other side of the bay.

Reserve half a day to reach Vathy by water taxi from Pera Gialos. This natural fjord on the island's east—accessible only by sea or via a poor-condition track—is one of the Dodecanese's most timeless atmospheres: a silent fishing village at the end of a narrow sea arm surrounded by arid hills. A single taverna serves the morning's catch. Boats generally depart late morning.

Have a drink in front of Chora's windmills at sunset—it's the locals' gathering spot. Illuminated Chora gives the impression the village is either climbing the mountain or suspended in the void, depending on the viewing angle. The atmosphere shifts dramatically once night falls.

Astypalea's 'Kopanisti' is a pungent, fermented soft-paste cheese served as mezze. The local 'Pouggia' are filled with almonds and mastiha (mastic resin), a perfumed variation on the specialty you may have tasted in Patmos. Ask for them in Pera Gialos pastry shops.

visits.text: Stefanos Crater, at the center of Nisyros's caldera, is one of the Aegean's most striking geological experiences. The caldera measures 4 km in diameter and Stefanos itself spans 300 meters across and 30 meters deep. The last phreatic eruption occurred in 1888, but hydrothermal activity is very present: sulfur fumaroles, ground hot and yellow underfoot, bubbling mud pots—all with a frank rotten-egg odor. Arrive before 9 am: in peak season, up to 1,000 day-trippers from Kos land in the morning. Closed shoes mandatory—the ground burns in places.

Mandraki, Nisyros's capital, is a compact village with white houses and lanes paved with pebble mosaics—a technique you'll find in squares and even private courtyards. The archaeological museum covers more than 3,000 years of island history, from the Neolithic to the Byzantine era. The waterfront with its tavernas comes alive in the evening, when the day-trippers have departed and the island regains its calm.

The Monastery of Panagia Spiliani—'Our Lady of the Cave'—is built directly inside the ruins of the Knights of Saint John castle, on a 30-meter rock above Mandraki. Access is via a staircase of more than 130 steps. The monastery is partly carved into natural rock: the atmosphere inside the cave-sanctuary, cool and dark, contrasts with the blinding whiteness of the Aegean. The 1725 iconostasis and library preserve manuscripts and liturgical objects of great value. From August 6-15, celebrations for the Dormition of the Virgin draw pilgrims from across the Dodecanese.

Nikia, perched on the caldera's rim, is one of Greece's most photogenic villages. Its central square is entirely paved with pebble mosaics, bordered by colorful-shuttered houses. From here, the plunging view onto Stefanos Crater below is vertiginous—this is the ideal spot to grasp the volcano's scale. Two small tavernas serve on the square.

Paleokastro, Mandraki's ancient acropolis, is remarkably well-preserved from the Classical era (6th-4th century BC). Its black volcanic stone walls run nearly 2 km in perimeter and some blocks weigh several tons. From the ramparts, the view embraces the port, the sea and neighboring islands. The climb takes about twenty minutes from Mandraki.

activities.text: Hike between Nikia and the caldera on the trail that descends from the village rim to the crater floor—about 45 minutes down on a marked path that crosses landscapes of yellow sulfur and black rock. You transition from a white village with colored shutters to a near-lunar landscape in under an hour. The ascent is strenuous: count on 1 hour and bring water.

From Mandraki, walk to Chochlaki Beach, very close to the village. Its name comes from the large, smooth, black volcanic pebbles that also cover the entrance to the water. Follow the shore to the cavity carved into the rocks at one end, then return along the same beach. Bring water shoes: entering the sea is awkward over the large pebbles. Swim only when the sea is calm; if it is rough, stay ashore to observe the rocks and the coast of Nisyros.

'Soumada,' a beverage made from bitter almond extract mixed with cold water, is Nisyros's signature non-alcoholic specialty—refreshing and fragrant. 'Pitia,' focaccia topped with tomatoes, onions, olives and herbs, is sold in Mandraki bakeries from morning. For a heartier meal, 'Bogana' (lamb braised with garlic and potatoes) and 'Kapamas' (goat stuffed with rice and cooked in tomato sauce) are the island's two traditional main dishes.

Emborios, semi-abandoned on the caldera rim, has been reinventing itself in recent years: ruined houses are being restored one by one by artists and Athenians. A small café terrace overlooks the volcano directly—it's one of the island's most dramatic viewpoints. Come in the evening when raking light makes the fumaroles smoke.

seo.h1_title: Dodecanese Circuit: Patmos, Leros & Karpathos
seo.intro_paragraph: Patmos, where Saint John wrote Revelation around AD 95, sets the tone: this circuit isn't just another beach tour. At Leros, you encounter an art deco port designed by Italians in the 1930s and a Byzantine castle erupting from nowhere on its hill. At Karpathos, the village of Olympos didn't open its first paved road until 2011—women there still wear embroidered costumes daily. Then Astypalea, the butterfly-shaped island with Cycladic architecture lost in the Dodecanese, and Nisyros, whose active 4-km-wide caldera reminds you that the Aegean is still being formed.
seo.seo_hook: From Patmos, the sacred island, to the craters of Nisyros: art deco architecture, timeless villages. Hidden Dodecanese, far from the crowds.
featured_list: Patmos: the island where Saint John wrote Revelation
Leros: unique art deco architecture in Greece
Olympos: living medieval village with Doric traditions
Astypalea: the butterfly island between Dodecanese and Cyclades
Nisyros: walk inside an active volcanic caldera

Saint John the Theologian Monastery at Patmos and its Codex Purpureus, Saint Mark's Gospel on purple parchment
Olympos village in Karpathos, the only place in Greece where women still wear traditional costume daily
Italian rationalist architecture of Lakki in Leros, utterly unique in the Greek landscape

itineraries.title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages
itineraries.subtitle: From the thermally-rich north to the megalithic south: 6 days traversing Greece's second-largest island end to end.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October, temperatures 20-28°C, pleasant sea. Avoid July-August (intense heat 32-38°C, thermal baths hardly bearable). Mild winter (12-16°C) but rainy, frequent Meltemi winds in summer.

visits.text: Édipsos' thermal springs have risen from the depths of the earth for 20,000 years, welling up from 3,000 meters below. More than 80 springs dot the municipality—the largest concentration anywhere in Greece. The waters reach 70 to 84°C at the Damaria source, cooling to 40 to 50°C at the beach springs. The ancients knew these waters well: Plutarch, Aristotle, and Strabo all documented them as the "Springs of Heracles." Legend has it that after each of his Twelve Labors, Heracles himself soaked in these waters to recover. The Roman general Sulla, plagued by a mysterious skin condition, came here and departed healed—a victory that cemented Édipsos' reputation among the empire's elite.

Along the central beach, Roman bathing pools carved directly from the rock still feed from natural 38°C springs. You can dip your feet for free—search the rocky outcrops north of the waterfront for telltale steam rising from the stones. It's an extraordinary sensation: sulfur-tinged air, steam rising, the Aegean Sea just meters away. History hovers here too: Aristotle, whose family hailed from Chalcis, reportedly visited to study the region. Later arrivals included Winston Churchill, Greta Garbo, Maria Callas, and Omar Sharif, all seeking the waters' restorative magic.

Modern thermal facilities offer medically supervised treatments: thermal baths, hydrotherapy, mineral mud wraps, and programs for rheumatoid conditions. Recognized therapeutic applications include arthritis, sciatica, and circulatory disorders. If you're not taking a formal cure, you can access outdoor thermal pools on a day-visit basis—though advance booking is wise during peak season, as capacity is limited.

Édipsos' waterfront stretches several hundred meters along the North Euboean Gulf. Stroll it at late afternoon when the light rakes across the continental mountains across the strait—the panorama is particularly stunning at that golden hour. Tavernas, cafés, and small shops selling local produce line the promenade, where the pace slows to that of a quiet Greek seaside town.

activities.text: Thermal bathing or a structured cure: both are available. A medical cure lasting several days is recommended for rheumatism, arthritis, or sciatica—it requires a local doctor's prescription. For a shorter visit, stick to the outdoor pools or natural beach basins. Water temperatures of 28–34°C are considered optimal for therapeutic benefit.

practical_info.duration: 1 hour to several days depending on program

activities.text: Half-day excursion to northern Euboean villages: Istiaia and the small port of Oreoi, 20 km to the east. Istiaia is an animated market town; Oreoi has a picturesque jetty and waterfront tavernas beloved by locals. Plan roughly an hour's drive from Édipsos along the coast.

Taste kolokythokeftedes—herb-stuffed zucchini fritters fried golden in olive oil. It's the emblematic vegetarian mezze of the Greek summer, served everywhere along the waterfront. Pair them with local Savatiano, a crisp dry white produced on the island, which cuts beautifully through the richness of fried vegetables and grilled fish.

In the evening, order galaktoboureko: creamed semolina wrapped in crispy phyllo leaves, drenched in warm lemon syrup. It's the ultimate comfort dessert of this region—more tender than baklava, less aggressively sweet, often served still warm.

visits.text: Stop at the historic sliding bridge in the city's heart: you're standing at the narrowest point of the Euripus Strait, where just 38 meters separate island from mainland. Watch the water for a few minutes—the current reverses approximately every six hours, building to speeds of 12 km/h, then achieving eight minutes of eerie stillness before reversing again. This phenomenon, governed by lunar cycles, has mystified scientists since antiquity. Aristotle, whose ancestors hailed from Chalcis, came here to study what seemed to defy the laws of nature. A wooden bridge already spanned this strait in 411 BCE; the current structure dates to 1962.

Karababa Castle towers over the city from the opposite hillside. Constructed by the Ottomans in 1686—just years after they conquered Chalcis from the Venetians—it commands a spectacular vantage over the strait, the bridge, and the terracotta rooftops below. The climb from the center takes about 20 minutes on foot. It's the finest spot for photographing the current phenomenon from above.

Agia Paraskevi Church in the old town is among Greece's rarest surviving examples of Gothic Dominican architecture. Begun around 1250, it housed one of the earliest two Dominican priories approved in the Greek province. The central vault and carved stone sculptures in the southern chapel rank among the finest examples of Italian Gothic in Greece. Don't miss the central arch above the iconostasis.

Chalcis Archaeological Museum holds regional finds: geometric and archaic ceramics, Hellenistic sculpture, and domestic objects from local excavations. The Euboean pottery collection is especially rewarding for understanding Chalcis' pivotal role in Greek colonization. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, Chalcidian colonists founded roughly thirty cities on the Chalcidice peninsula and several in Magna Graecia, including Cumae in Italy.

The historic quarter of Chalcis blends Ottoman lanes, Venetian traces and an old Jewish quarter. The synagogue of Chalcis bears witness to a continuous Jewish presence since Antiquity, one of the oldest in Europe. Stroll through the small streets behind the seafront to find the most distinctive facades.

activities.text: Claim a terrace table facing the old bridge and observe the current shift. Locals do the same—it's free theater and genuinely hypnotic. On "chaotic" days—about 6–7 per lunar month—the current can reverse up to 14 times instead of the usual four. If you hit one of those days, you'll understand why the ancients spoke of Chalcis' "wild waters."

Taste syglino, Euboean smoked pork cured in fat—a highland specialty. Served on local bread with olives, it's the quintessential savory mezze of the region. Pair it with Euboean retsina, that resinous white wine of ancient tradition, here produced locally and superb alongside charcuterie and cheese.

As evening descends, Chalcis' waterfront comes alive. Residents gather at waterfront cafés and tavernas overlooking the strait. Order loukoumades—small fried pastries drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon—and watch pleasure boats navigate against the current.

visits.text: Eretria's archaeological site spreads beneath the modern town—you'll circulate among open-air ruins with a map available at the museum (€5). At the site's heart stands the Temple of Apollo Daphnephoros: its earliest phases date to the late 8th century BCE, with the Doric version of 520–490 BCE destroyed by the Persians during the 490 BCE sack. Foundation stones and sculptured pediment fragments remain. Bring water and a hat in summer—the site offers no shade.

The House of the Mosaics, dated to the 4th century BCE, stands among Greece's finest preserved Hellenistic dwellings. Its floors showcase pebble mosaics depicting mythological scenes—Nereids astride sea creatures, griffins, panthers. Check before visiting: travelers report it's occasionally closed early despite posted hours.

Eretria Archaeological Museum, founded in 1960 and expanded by the Swiss School of Archaeology in Greece (excavating since 1964), displays remarkable finds. Don't miss the sculptured group of Theseus and Antiope, attributed to the Athenian sculptor Antenor (circa 510 BCE), and a black-figure funerary amphora dated 560 BCE depicting Heracles battling Centaurs. Labels appear in Greek and French.

Eretria's ancient theater, with earliest phases from the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, is remarkable for an underground tunnel still visible—actors vanished through it for stage effects, a rarity of ancient theatrical machinery. Climb to the acropolis in the north for a commanding overview of the site and the coastline.

The Persians destroyed Eretria in 490 BCE—Darius sought vengeance for the city's aid to the Ionian Revolt. The male population was slaughtered; women and children were enslaved and deported to Persia. The city rebuilt swiftly, sent 600 hoplites to the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE, flourished in the 4th century, then fell to the Romans in 198 BCE and was finally abandoned after 87 BCE. Marshland reclaimed it until 1824, when refugees from Psara resettled the site.

activities.text: Swimming along Eretria and Amarynthos beaches—a neighboring village to the east celebrated for seafood tavernas and grilled shellfish spreads. Waters here are calm and shallow, ideal for children. If you're motoring about, Amarynthos merits a detour for dinner: locals prefer its fish freshness to Eretria.

Sample fava: a creamy yellow-pea purée dressed with excellent olive oil, capers, and lemon juice. It's among Greece's finest yet most underappreciated mezzes. Pair it with local Savatiano white—a dry, fruity Euboean varietal that harmonizes beautifully with legumes.

Pasteli—sesame bars bound with thick honey—sells in waterfront shops and groceries. It's one of Greece's oldest candies, energy-dense and nourishing, perfect to carry for tomorrow's hike to Kymi or Karystos.

visits.text: Kymi perches 200 meters above the Aegean Sea, hidden behind forested hills—locals call it "the Balcony of the Aegean." Shipowner mansions from the 19th century, when Kymi commanded 400 sailing vessels and ranked second only to Chalcis in island prominence, lend the center a rare architectural character. Climb to the main square for vistas across the open sea. A statue in the square commemorates the town's most celebrated son.

Kymi's folk museum gathers embroidered costumes, maritime documents, traditional tools, and daily-life artifacts chronicling this sailors' town. It also houses archives connected to Dr. George Papanicolaou, born here May 13, 1883. This Greek physician, who emigrated to the United States in 1913, developed the cytological test known as the "Pap smear"—a screening method for early cervical cancer detection that has saved millions of lives worldwide. His birthhouse is visible nearby.

Descend the serpentine 5-km road to Paralia Kymis at the clifftop's base. This is where ferries depart for Skyros, Skopelos, and Alonissos. The atmosphere is that of an animated fishing harbor: seaside tavernas line the quay, blue-and-white boats bob at anchor, nets dry in the sun. If timing allows, dine here rather than in the upper town.

The Monastery of the Transfiguration (Metamorphosis), founded in the 16th century by monks from Mount Athos, nestles in greenery along the route between Kymi and the sea. It's a peaceful sanctuary with characteristic monastic architecture and small-batch honey production sold on-site. The nuns who inhabit it today welcome visitors outside service hours—dress appropriately.

activities.text: Kymi's dried figs are among Euboean products most prized: fumigated with sulfur by the local cooperative, they acquire a pale hue and slightly tart edge distinguishing them from standard dried figs. Search for them in central-town groceries—they're the edible souvenir worth bringing home.
Hike to Maniakiatis Falls: the Maniakiatis River originates on Mount Kserovouni. A 50-minute trail leads to a 15-meter waterfall amid lush vegetation. Start early to enjoy the cool morning air.
Savor Kymi's baklava: the local pastry craft is celebrated for its quality, crafted with Euboean walnuts and honey. Pair it with amygdalota—tender almond cakes found in every pastry shop in town.

visits.text: Bourtzi Castle stands harborside in Karystos, steps from waterfront cafés—a two-story, horseshoe-shaped hexagonal Venetian fortress from 1350 built partly with marble salvaged from a nearby Roman mausoleum. It's among southern Euboea's finest-preserved fortifications. In summer, the courtyard hosts concerts and exhibitions. Entry is free.

From town, gaze toward the heights 4 km away: Castello Rosso (Kokkino Kastro) crowns a rocky spur. Early Byzantine fortifications date to 1030. The Lombard baron Ravano dalle Carceri rebuilt the castle between 1209 and 1216. It later passed to Franks, Venetians, and Ottomans before 1470. A ten-minute car journey from the center rewards you with vistas spanning the bay and surrounding mountains.

Karystos Archaeological Museum, housed in the Yokaleio Cultural Foundation, presents local excavation finds including ceramic sherds recovered in 1959 during Professor Moutsopoulos' excavation of the Drakospito on Mount Ochi. Pieces related to ancient quarries and maritime history appear as well. Small but well-documented.

About 4 km north of Karystos, above the village of Myloi, you'll find the ancient quarries known as "Kolones": monolithic columns of green cipollino marble (marmor Carystium), some reaching 12 meters in length, abandoned in situ two millennia ago before they could be shipped out. This veined green marble, quarried since the 1st century BCE, was exported as far as Rome for the imperial forums, temples, and baths. Columns from Karystos still adorn Hadrian's Library in Athens. The site is accessible on foot from Myloi.

The Drakospita—Dragon Houses—rank among Euboea's most enigmatic monuments. Twenty-three exist across southern Euboea; the largest and best-preserved crowns Mount Ochi's 1,389-meter summit. These megalithic structures, raised without mortar from slabs weighing up to 10 tons, likely date to the Classical or Proto-Classical period (5th–4th centuries BCE). Their purpose remains baffling: temple to Zeus and Hera? Watchtower? Quarryman's lodge? Astronomical observatory? One doorway slab measures 4 meters long, 2 meters wide, yet weighs 10 tons. Their first scholarly mention came October 21, 1797, when British geologist John Hawkins ascended Mount Ochi and documented what he found.

activities.text: Hike up Mount Ochi to reach the Drakospito at the summit: this is the big excursion of the day. Start from the parking area above the village of Myloi (via the forest road that climbs up from the national road), pass the refuge at 1,050 meters and reach the Profitis Ilias chapel. The Dragon House is just a few meters from the summit. Allow about 7 hours there and back, start early, and bring water and a jacket—the wind can be strong at the summit even in summer. The trail crosses the Kastanologos chestnut grove, a haven of rare vegetation.

Visit the Myloi quarries (alternative to the Ochi hike or complementary short excursion): chisel marks in living rock, abandoned columns, and ancient transport systems remain perfectly legible. The open-air, unfenced site commands spectacular vistas over Karystos Bay and the Aegean.

Taste matsata—homemade Karystos pasta served in sauce with braised cock and tomato: this is the town's festive specialty, rustic and generous. Seek it in central tavernas, preferably at dinner. Wash it down with Karistia Gi white, a local blend of Savatiano, Malagouzia, and Assyrtiko.

Before departing toward Rafina or Athens via ferry from Marmari (10 km from Karystos, regular service to Rafina in 1h15), take one last café on the waterfront facing Bourtzi. This ranks among the island's most tranquil waterfronts—fishermen, a handful of pleasure boats, waves lapping stone beaches. The whistled language of nearby Antia village (10 km away) is one of the world's last remaining systems of long-distance vocal communication: a detour there is delightfully offbeat if time permits.

seo.h1_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: Immerse yourself in Édipsos and its 80 thermal springs—waters frequented by Aristotle and Roman generals alike—then traverse Chalcis and its beguiling strait whose currents reverse every six hours. Climb toward Eretria, the mighty ancient city razed by the Persians in 490 BCE, and Kymi, the "Balcony of the Aegean" and birthplace of Dr. Papanicolaou. Close in Karystos, where green marble columns await shipment to Rome and megalithic stone houses continue to defy explanation.
seo.seo_hook: Thermal springs since Aristotle, a strait with reversing currents, Persian-razed city, megalithic mysteries. Euboea: Greece's overlooked island.
featured_list: Édipsos: Heracles' thermal springs where Churchill sought healing
Chalcis: the Mediterranean's strangest strait
Eretria: the ancient powerhouse razed by Darius in 490 BCE
Kymi: the Balcony of the Aegean, birthplace of the Pap test
Karystos: cipollino marble, megalithic dragons, and ferry gateway to Athens

The extraordinary tidal phenomenon of the Euripus Strait at Chalcis
