seo_keywords: mainland greece off the beaten path

highlights: Delphi: 'navel of the world' in antiquity, Temple of Apollo and Pythia's oracle, UNESCO site
Osios Loukas: finest Byzantine monastery on mainland Greece, 11th-century golden mosaics, UNESCO-listed
Nafpaktos: Venetian port encircled by ramparts where the Battle of Lepanto took place (1571) – Cervantes lost the use of one hand there
Messolonghi: city of Greek independence heroes (1821-1826), Kleisova Lagoon and Garden of Heroes
Thermos: sanctuary of the Aetolian League with one of Greece's oldest Doric temples (630-610 BC)

itineraries.title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves
itineraries.subtitle: 19 sailing stages in a loop from Paros, from the Lesser Cyclades to the volcanic southern islands
itineraries.notes: Itinerary designed for a loop sailing cruise from Paros. All legs are by boat. Actual duration: 19 sailing days.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 24-28°C, sea at 22-24°C, comfortable sailing. Avoid July-August (heat 30-35°C, strong Meltemi winds complicating crossings, overtourism). Mild winter but windy, rough seas, many businesses closed.

visits.text: Parikia's old harbor greets you on arrival with its white windmills on the breakwater—a quintessential Cycladic postcard scene. Behind the ferries and bustling quays, the old town winds through pebble-paved lanes around a Venetian kastro built in 1260 from marble blocks taken from a nearby Temple of Athena: look carefully and you'll still spot ancient columns embedded in the walls. The old market follows the main street to the kastro and brims with tavernas, bakeries, and little boutiques. Get lost in this maze—the late afternoon light on the white facades is worth more than any guidebook.

The Panagia Ekatontapiliani basilica—“the church of a hundred doors”—ranks as Greece's third-largest early Christian sanctuary. Its foundation dates to the 4th century, traditionally attributed to Saint Helena, mother of Constantine the Great; the present building dates from the 6th century and was restored under Justinian. The complex is enclosed by a 252-meter wall and houses a main church measuring 40 by 25 meters, flanked by the oldest baptistery in the Christian East. Legend holds that the hundredth door is invisible and will open only when Constantinople is reconquered. Visit early in the morning—the filtered light in the nave, the Doric columns salvaged from a Roman gymnasium, and the 15th-century iconostasis are worth the stop. It's also a major pilgrimage site for the Assumption, almost on a par with Tinos.

activities.text: Swim at Livadia Beach, the most accessible beach from the port - a 10-minute walk away. Fine sand and shallow water, ideal for a first dip after the crossing.
Sheltered anchorage available at Krios Beach depending on conditions, just across from Parikia harbor—dinghy shuttle, good holding on sandy bottom.

visits.text: Naoussa brings together Paros's charm in one village. The fishing harbor is ringed by whitewashed lanes climbing toward the Kastro—a partially submerged 15th-century Venetian fortification whose round tower still stands at the harbor entrance. The old Venetian warehouses have become elegant restaurants serving the morning catch. Naoussa actually boasts the largest fishing fleet in all the Cyclades: watch fishermen mending their nets early in the morning before the terraces fill. Come evening, the Kastro lanes turn into an open-air lounge.

Kolymbithres, 4 km northwest of Naoussa, is Paros's most photographed spot. Giant granite boulders, polished by millennia of wind and sea waves, have formed natural basins filled with translucent saltwater—somewhere between swimming pools and stone sculptures. The water is often less than a meter deep and takes on milky-blue reflections against the pearl-gray stone. In July–August, the pools fill with people as early as 11 a.m.: arrive before 10 a.m. to be among the first or come late in the day. Caiques make the trip from Naoussa harbor.

activities.text: Anchorage at Naoussa marina or Ormos Plastira depending on conditions—good holding on sandy bottom, sheltered from the north.
Snorkeling in the coves of Kolymbithres: the granite formations create tunnels and underwater cavities accessible with just a mask. Colorful fish guaranteed.

visits.text: The Portara greets you at the entrance to Naxos harbor—this monumental white marble gateway standing 6 meters tall is all that remains of a temple dedicated to Apollo, whose construction began around 530 BC under the tyrant Lygdamis. The building was never completed, and the Venetians carted off all the blocks to build the kastro, except these four blocks weighing 20 tonnes each, too heavy to move. The Portara faces toward Delos, Apollo's birthplace, and legend places Theseus's abandonment of Ariadne here. Sunset from the causeway is a popular classic—for crowd-free photos, go early in the morning.

The Kastro of Naxos Chora was built in 1207 by Marco Sanudo, nephew of the Doge of Venice, after the Fourth Crusade. He moved the island's capital down from the heights to the coast. The inner enclosure, entered through just two gates - one with its original 13th-century wooden door - contains noble residences with Venetian coats of arms carved in stone, the Catholic cathedral and almost deserted vaulted lanes. A journey through time, a 15-minute walk from the port.

The Bourgos quarter, between the harbor and the Kastro, is full of artisan shops, marble workshops, tavernas, and galleries. Naxos has been an island of marble since antiquity—the kouros statues abandoned in the quarries during the Archaic period still bear witness. Push open the shop doors: sculptors still work the local white stone.

activities.text: Sunset facing the Portara from anchorage or the islet causeway—the white marble turns amber, the sea turns gold. One of the Aegean's most photographed spectacles.

Waterfront stroll and provisioning at the harbor market: Naxos is the largest island in the Cyclades and its hinterland produces renowned cheeses, honey, lemons, and potatoes. The market is well stocked.

visits.text: Welcome to the Lesser Cyclades. Iraklia has just 150 permanent residents across 18 km² and electricity only arrived in 1982. The port of Agios Georgios is endearing: the entire village comes down to greet the ferry, collect deliveries, and chat under the tamarisks. Livadi beach, 1.5 km from the port, is the island's finest—a long crescent of golden sand with turquoise water where you'll find space even in the middle of August. No umbrellas are available to rent on site; bring your own.

activities.text: Snorkeling and swimming in Livadi bay: the crystalline waters let you spot fish, sea urchins, and if you're lucky, sea turtles that regularly visit the bay.

Hike to the village of Panagia (Chora), 4 km from the port via a marked trail. This inland hamlet is the island's traditional capital, with its Cycladic stone houses and whitewashed church. Those with energy left can continue to the Agios Ioannis cave, considered the largest in the Cyclades with 2 km of stalactite-adorned galleries—bring a flashlight and closed-toe shoes.

practical_info.duration: ~1h30 round trip to Panagia, 3h to the cave

visits.text: Schinoussa is even smaller than Iraklia—8 km², fewer than 300 residents. Its main village, Chora (or Panagia), perches 1.5 km from Mersini port: a single street you can walk down in 5 minutes, lined with family tavernas and geranium-draped houses. Here, everyone knows everyone and newcomers quickly blend in. Come evening, Chora comes alive on the central square: locals and the Greek vacationers who make up most of the island's clientele gather over a warm rakomelo. Push open the door of kafeneio Xara—an institution.

Tsigouri beach is Schinoussa's most accessible beach, 600 m from Chora along a paved road. Golden sand, shallow water and tamarisk trees for shade. A beach bar serves drinks and mezedes. For a wilder experience, Psili Ammos beach is worth the 45-minute walk from Chora: an unspoiled bay with water of unreal clarity and no facilities. Arrive early in summer.

activities.text: Swimming and lounging at Tsigouri—or swim out to the small islet 200 meters offshore for absolute solitude.
A short coastal hike to Livadi or Aligaria beach: Schinoussa's paths connect the beaches, all less than a 40-minute walk from Chora.

visits.text: Koufonissia—actually two islands, Ano and Kato Koufonissi—is the rising star of the Lesser Cyclades. Ano Koufonissi's Chora, the only inhabited village, sprawls around a colorful harbor dominated by the church of Agios Georgios. But what makes the island unique is its southeastern coast: a 45-minute coastal path from Chora links the beaches of Finikas, Fanos, and Italida—surreal turquoise waters on golden sand—before reaching Pori, the archipelago's finest beach. At Pori's northern tip, the Ksilobatis caves offer limestone arches bathed in emerald water. Budget 3 hours round trip for the full circuit from Chora, no shade along the way: leave early and pack water.
Gala Beach is a hidden cove whose Greek name means 'milk' - the foam of the waves in the cave does indeed give the water a distinctive milky hue.

activities.text: Sea kayaking from Ammos beach toward the cliffs of Kato Koufonissi: paddling along the sheer walls reveals arches and coves invisible from land. Kayaks are for rent at the main beach. Check the wind (meltemi) before setting out.
Anchorage in Pori bay: sandy bottom, good holding depending on conditions. Water taxis from Chora make 4 runs per day—handy for alternating between swimming and exploring Chora.

visits.text: Katapola, one of Amorgos's two ports, opens onto spectacular mountain scenery. Amorgos Chora, at an elevation of 320 meters, is linked to the port by a winding road—take the municipal bus or walk for 45 minutes along the switchback trail. At the top, white windmills keep watch over the village from a ridge exposed to the wind, and Venetian coats of arms still adorn the doors of old houses.

The Panagia Hozoviotissa monastery is one of the Aegean's marvels. Founded in the 11th century by Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos to shelter a miraculous icon from Palestine, it's built literally into a cliff face 300 meters above the sea. The building stands 40 meters tall yet only 5 meters wide in places—8 floors carved into rock, a labyrinth of small rooms and narrow staircases. You'll need to climb about 300 steps to reach it from the road. The monks (3 or 4 remain) welcome visitors with Amorgian raki, loukoumi, and Greek coffee. Modest dress required—garments are loaned at the entrance. Luc Besson filmed scenes from The Big Blue here in 1987.

Agia Anna beach lies below the monastery at the foot of the cliffs. Turquoise water, pebbly bottom, access via stairs from the road. This is where the monastery's icon supposedly washed ashore mysteriously on a boat from Palestine. Open sea, sometimes with swell.

activities.text: Waterfront stroll at Katapola and provisioning: Amorgos is known for its honey, local wine, and sun-dried octopus. The harbor market is modest but authentic.
Easy hike between Chora and the windmills for panoramas over the archipelago—on clear days, the view reaches Naxos and Paros.
Swimming at Agia Anna (open sea, possible swell)—diving from the rocks is an island classic.

visits.text: Ios has a dual identity that you will grasp as soon as you arrive: Chora, perched on its hill, is an authentic Cycladic maze of whitewashed lanes adorned with bougainvillea and 12 windmills - but after dark, the bars take over, and for more than 40 years the island has been a major party destination in the Aegean Sea. If you are looking for peace, go up to Chora early and come back down before noon. History lovers can visit the prehistoric site of Skarkos, 10 minutes from Chora. The hill where Homer's tomb is believed to stand can be reached via paths in the north of the island.

Mylopotas is Ios's largest beach—a crescent of sand over 1 km long facing due west, with Blue Flag status and crystal-clear water. It's also the liveliest: beach clubs, wakeboarding, diving, evening concerts. The eastern part of the beach is calmer than the western end, where nightlife is concentrated. The bay offers an anchorage with good holding on a sandy bottom, but it is very busy in July–August.

activities.text: Swimming and paddleboarding in Mylopotas bay—SUP and canoe rental on the beach. Waters stay shallow for 5 to 10 meters from shore.
Anchorage in the bay (good holding on sand, heavy seasonal traffic). In season, it's best to arrive early in the morning to drop anchor.

visits.text: Santorini—the caldera and its hilltop villages seen from the sea offer one of the Mediterranean's most spectacular arrivals by sea. Vlychada harbor on the south coast is calmer than the crowded caldera and ringed by white cliffs with lunar shapes. It's the best overnight anchorage. The volcanic sand beach of Perissa and Perivolos stretches 7 km: burning-hot black sand (bring sandals), crystal-clear water, and a gently sloping sandy bottom. In high season, it's one of the island's liveliest.

The Akrotiri archaeological site is Santorini's equivalent of Pompeii—a Minoan city buried under meters of volcanic ash during the catastrophic eruption around 1500 BC. Excavations began in 1967 under Spyridon Marinatos. Beneath a massive protective dome, you wander the ancient city streets: two-story houses with sewer systems, murals depicting daily life, pottery, tools. No bodies were found, suggesting inhabitants fled before the eruption.

At Red Beach, a blood-red cliff plunges vertically into the sea, creating a striking contrast with the blue water. The beach is narrow and busy; access is restricted because of rockfall risks. Enjoy it from the sea.

activities.text: Swimming on the volcanic beach of Perissa or Perivolos—the black sand absorbs heat, consider water shoes. Water is deep and clear.

Wine tasting in Santorini—the island's vineyards produce assyrtiko, a mineral white wine unique in the world, with vines trained into baskets (kouloura) on volcanic soil. Several estates are accessible from the anchorage or by road.

visits.text: Folegandros is an island of character—lashed by the meltemi, with 300-meter cliffs plunging into intense blue sea, and a Chora perched on a vertiginous ledge that long served as a place of political exile (until 1969). The main village is entirely pedestrian: three beautiful squares lined up and shaded by plane trees, stone-paved lanes, an inhabited Venetian kastro, and the persistent feeling that time passes differently here. From Chora, the switchback trail (20-30 min) leads to the Panagia church on its promontory—the view over the Aegean and neighboring islands at sunset ranks among the Cyclades' most spectacular.

Agkali (or Angali) beach on the south coast is accessible by car or bus from Chora. Pebble bottom sheltered by a cliff, deep blue water, two tavernas under the tamarisks. No natural shade except at the cliff base—bring an umbrella. From there, a 30-minute coastal trail leads to the wild cove of Agios Nikolaos, a favorite among island regulars.

activities.text: Swimming and snorkeling at Agkali: the rocky seabed shelters varied marine life. The cove is sheltered enough to be pleasant even in moderate wind.
Sunset from anchorage or Panagia church—the golden light on Folegandros's white cliffs is a spectacle that regulars return for every summer.

visits.text: Sikinos is the least visited of the inhabited Cyclades—300 residents, little infrastructure, no hotel chains. Alopronia port is a peaceful fishing village with a small, calm sandy beach. Then take the road (or better, the paved mule path) climbing 4 km to the Kastro and Chora, perched at 280 meters—two quarters facing each other, the first lively with cafés and the town hall, the second a labyrinth of white lanes bordered by bougainvillea. Three windmills watch over both quarters from the cliff edge, facing the sea.

activities.text: Climb to Zoodochou Pigi monastery, built in 1690 atop the Kastro: panoramic view over the archipelago and beyond. The island's most astonishing monument, however, is Episkopi—a 3rd-century Roman mausoleum converted to a Christian temple in the 17th century, accessible via trail from the Kastro. The place radiates a particular energy.
Swimming on Alopronia beach below the port—fine sand, calm water, and tamarisks. It's the island's most accessible beach, perfect for a pause before continuing your journey.

visits.text: Milos is the quintessential volcanic island—more than 70 beaches, each different in the color of its sand and the shape of its cliffs. Kleftiko, on the southwest coast, is the highlight: ancient white limestone formations pierced by sea caves, accessible by sea. It was a hideout for Saracen pirates, as its name recalls (kleftiko = place of bandits). Today, boat excursions leave Adamas every morning. The caves can be reached by swimming from the boat—light filtering underwater creates captivating shades of blue and green. Dolphins, turtles and seals frequent the area.

Adamas, Milos's main port, sits on one of the Mediterranean's largest natural bays. The waterfront is lively and well supplied. From the port, boat excursions take you to Kleftiko, Sarakiniko (the lunar scenery of the north), and the syrmata—boat garages carved into the colorful shoreline rocks, a symbol of Milos.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Kleftiko: the sea caves can be reached by swimming from excursion boats. Bring a mask and fins. Don't go ashore from your sailboat, as access is regulated—daytime anchorage only.

visits.text: Kimolos takes its name from the Greek 'kimolia'—chalk—and its houses are indeed whiter than white. The island covers just 36 km² and is easily explored on foot or by scooter from Psathi port. The village of Chorio, perched on a hill 2 km from the port, is dominated by a 14th-century Venetian kastro, some of whose houses are still inhabited. The metropolitan church of Panagia Odigitria (1592) is its religious heart. Wandering Chorio, look for the syrmata at tiny Goupa beach: these are former boat garages carved into rock, intact maritime heritage.

Prassa beach (also called Agios Georgios) is unanimously considered Kimolos's finest—some even say the finest in all the Cyclades. Almost surreal white sand, turquoise water of exceptional clarity. A beach bar, sun loungers, and sea caves within swimming distance with fins. Near Prassa, natural hot springs with reddish waters are said by locals to have healing properties. It's not uncommon to spot a monk seal in the neighboring waters.
The Skiadi rock is worth the 20-30-minute walk from the main road: erosion has sculpted a formation shaped like a giant mushroom. Look for the marked path between Chorio and the west coast.

activities.text: Swimming at Prassa and snorkeling around the rock formations: corals, sea urchins, and colorful reef fish in remarkably clear water. The nearby Vromolini sea caves will please freedivers.

visits.text: Sifnos is the Cyclades' island of ceramics and gastronomy. Since at least the 9th century BC, the island has exported utilitarian pottery throughout the Mediterranean—Sifnos clay is rich in feldspars that speed vitrification. In the 18th and 19th centuries, about a hundred workshops ran at full tilt. Today a handful of potters perpetuate the tradition: at Platys Gialos and Vathy, you'll still see the old pottery buildings recognizable by their curved roof and elongated shape. Several workshops welcome visitors.

Platys Gialos is Sifnos's largest sandy beach - a long, well-exposed bay with a Blue Flag, waterfront tavernas and a convenient anchorage on the left side of the bay. The White Tower stands 1.5 km to the northeast. A 2 km walk takes you to Chryssopigi beach, the island's most iconic, with its small white monastery perched on a rocky spur - one of the most photographed sights on Sifnos.

activities.text: Swimming and paddleboarding at Platys Gialos: wide sheltered bay, shallow water, fine sand. SUP rental on the beach.

visits.text: Ormos Vathy is one of the Cyclades' finest anchorages—a perfectly sheltered horseshoe bay with a small fishing village at the back. On nearby Tsopos beach, the Atsonios pottery has operated for 4 generations: it's one of the last workshops set up the old way, right on the beach, with wood-fired kilns and drying tables. Watch the potter work before choosing from the utilitarian ceramics and artisan pieces on display.

Apollonia, Sifnos's capital, perches in the hills at the island's center. It's a maze of paved lanes where you'll happily get lost among artisan shops, traditional tavernas, and small flower-filled squares. It was founded in the 6th century BC and bears the god Apollo's name. Come evening, it's the island's liveliest spot—open terraces, Greek music, warm ambiance without Mykonos excess.

activities.text: From Vathy, travel to Faros by road for this walk: the fishing hamlet borders a small sheltered beach. Walk along the waterfront, then follow the coastal path toward Glyfo beach; it follows the shoreline and lets you explore the coves on foot.

visits.text: Megalo Livadi is a timeless village in southwest Serifos, a 30-minute drive along winding roads from the port. This is where the island's major industrial history unfolded—until 1963, Serifos's iron mines (worked since antiquity, reopened on a large scale in 1880 by a Franco-German company) loaded their ore from this quay onto cargo ships bound for Europe. The rusted metal loading bridge is still there, bulky and poetic. In 1916, a miners' strike led to a bloody confrontation with the gendarmerie—4 miners were killed. It's considered the first bloody labor strike in modern Greek history. A memorial on the quay commemorates this episode.

activities.text: Sunset from anchorage or the surrounding hills—Megalo Livadi bay is well sheltered and faces west. A small waterfront taverna serves good fresh fish.

visits.text: Kolona is one of the Cyclades' great surprises. A narrow sand tombolo—a natural spit barely a few meters wide—connects the main island to the islet of Agios Loukas, creating two back-to-back beaches with different water temperatures: the one on the right is slightly warmer because hot springs emerge nearby. It's rare to find such a formation in the Mediterranean. Access is via a dirt track (the water taxi from Merichas is preferable, 15 min)—there's no shade on the beach, so bring sun protection.

Dryopida, Kythnos's second village, deserves a 20-minute detour from Kolona. Its red-tiled lanes break from the usual Cycladic white—this is where the island's characteristic tiles have been made for centuries. Katafyki cave, beneath the village, sheltered residents during World War II. It's open in season.

activities.text: Swimming between two seas: swim on one side then the other of the tombolo to feel the temperature difference. Snorkeling possible around the islet's rocks.

visits.text: Despotiko is an uninhabited islet 700 meters southwest of Antiparos, and it's one of recent decades' archaeological revelations in the Cyclades. Systematic excavations led since 2001 by archaeologist Yannos Kouragios have unearthed a sanctuary of Apollo dating from the 8th century BC—20 buildings, over 70 fragments of archaic marble kouroi, inscribed pottery shards bearing Apollo's name. Like Delos, the island was a pilgrimage site attracting visitors from across the Aegean. The temple's Doric columns are under restoration. Access only by sea from Antiparos.

activities.text: Swimming and snorkeling around Despotiko: the crystal-clear waters, with few visitors, let you observe unspoiled marine life. Anchorage on a sandy bottom in the small bay of Livadi.

visits.text: Return along the west coast of Paros from Antiparos - a quiet passage between the two islands. Finding Parikia again feels almost like a relief after the wild stops of the past few days: Wi-Fi, fresh water, fresh provisions, and lively Chora for a final dinner facing the sea.

activities.text: Final quick swim depending on timing and weather—Krios beach, dinghy-accessible from anchorage, is perfect for a farewell plunge in still-turquoise water.

seo.h1_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves
seo.intro_paragraph: Sail in a loop from Paros, between the Byzantine church of a hundred doors and the granite formations of Kolymbithres, before diving into the unspoiled Lesser Cyclades of Iraklia, Schinoussa, and Koufonissia. Travel across Amorgos and visit its cliffside monastery, experience the contrasting energy of Ios, then head north to Milos and its pirate caves before completing the loop via Sifnos and Antiparos.
seo.seo_hook: A 16-day sailing cruise through the Cyclades: from wild coves to cliffside monasteries, from unspoiled villages to volcanic beaches with lunar landscapes.
featured_list: Paros: harbor and 4th-century early Christian basilica
Lesser Cyclades: timeless Iraklia, Schinoussa, Koufonissia
Amorgos: monastery clinging to a 300-meter cliff
Santorini: Minoan city of Akrotiri and volcanic beaches
Milos: Kleftiko and its pirate caves
Despotiko: archaic sanctuary of Apollo under excavation

Unspoiled Lesser Cyclades: Iraklia, Schinoussa, Koufonissia
Hozoviotissa Monastery clinging to a 300-meter cliff on Amorgos
Akrotiri archaeological site, Greece's Pompeii, on Santorini

itineraries.title: Ionian Islands Road Trip: Corfu, Paxos & Lefkada
itineraries.subtitle: From Corfu's UNESCO-listed Venetian old town to the white cliffs of Lefkada, a journey through history, turquoise coves and the Ionian Sea.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May-June and September-October, temperatures 22-28°C, pleasant sea. Avoid July-August (intense heat 32-38°C, crowded beaches) and November-March (heavy rainfall—the Ionian Islands are Greece's rainiest region).
specialties: olive oil from centuries-old Venetian groves

map_keywords: Palace of St Michael and St George Corfu

visits.text: Corfu's old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007 — a maze of narrow cobblestone lanes known as kantounia, lined with neoclassical facades in pastel hues inherited from centuries of Venetian rule. Venice held the island almost uninterrupted from 1386 to 1797, and it's the Republic that shaped this unique urban fabric, which neither the French nor the British managed to erase. Get up early: the lanes are stunning before 9am, empty and gilded by the morning light.

The Old Fortress (Palaio Frourio) sits on a rocky headland separated from the town by a sea moat — the Contrafossa — which the Venetians dug to turn the citadel into an artificial island. It successfully repelled three major Ottoman sieges: 1537, 1571 and 1716. Inside, don't miss the Church of St George, whose golden facade resembles an ancient temple — the contrast is striking. Climb to the lighthouse at the top for the best panoramic view over the sea and the town.

The New Fortress (Fortezza Nuova), built by the Venetians from 1577 on the hill overlooking the harbour, draws fewer visitors than the Old one — take advantage of that. Its underground galleries, bastions and tunnels carved into the rock form a fascinating labyrinth. The view over the harbour and the Ionian Sea from the battlements alone makes it worth the visit.

The Palace of St Michael and St George, built by the British between 1819 and 1824 in neoclassical style, now houses the Museum of Asian Art — a collection of 11,000 pieces from China, Japan and India, bequeathed by a Greek diplomat. An unexpected combination for a Greek island. The entrance from the People's Garden also offers a fine angle on the Spianada.

The Spianada Esplanade is the largest green public square in Greece. The arcaded Liston that lines its western edge was built during the French occupation, directly inspired by the Rue de Rivoli in Paris. This is where the Corfiots still play cricket, a tradition inherited from the British — one of the few places in Greece where the sport is practised. Late in the afternoon, grab a table on the terrace and watch local life unfold.

activities.text: Lose yourself in the Campiello, the oldest neighbourhood in the old town, north of the Old Fortress. It's a tangle of kantounia so narrow that two people can barely pass, with carved Venetian wells popping up in tiny squares. Laundry dries between buildings, bougainvillea spills over ochre walls — the atmosphere is light-years away from mass tourism.

On Orthodox Holy Saturday (in April or early May depending on the year), the people of Corfu celebrate the Resurrection by throwing ceramic jars out of their windows at exactly 11 a.m. - a noisy, festive spectacle unique in Greece. If you are not there for Easter, the religious processions carrying the relics of Saint Spyridon, the island's patron saint, also take place on 11 August and the first Sunday of November, and their atmosphere is worth stopping for.

Pastitsada is Corfu's signature dish: rooster (or veal) braised in a tomato sauce with Venetian spices, served over thick macaroni. The recipe is a direct trace of four centuries of Italian influence. Try it in an old-town taverna — the spots around the Campiello are the most authentic.

Bourdeto is Corfu's other pride: fish (scorpionfish by preference) cooked in a tomato sauce fired up with hot paprika. It's a fisherman's recipe — rustic and bold. Pair it with a glass of Robola, the dry, mineral white from neighbouring Cephalonia, which cuts through the acidity of the sauce.

visits.text: The Achilleion is one of the most romantic — and most tragic — palaces in the Mediterranean. Sisi had it built between 1889 and 1891 in a neo-Pompeian style, 10 km south of the capital, on a 200,000 m² plot overlooking the Ionian Sea. She had taught herself Ancient Greek to read Homer in the original and wanted to pay tribute to Achilles, whom she saw as the embodiment of the Greek soul. After her assassination by an anarchist in 1898, Kaiser Wilhelm II bought the palace in 1907 and spent every spring there until World War I. In 1981, the first floor served as the casino set for the James Bond film For Your Eyes Only. Allow at least 1h30 for the gardens and the apartments.

The peninsula of Kanoni, 4 km south of the capital, offers Corfu's most iconic view: in the foreground, Vlacherna Monastery perched on its tiny islet connected to the shore by a causeway, and behind it, the islet of Pontikonisi ('Mouse Island') crowned with dark cypresses. Homeric legend says it's the Phaeacian ship turned to stone by Poseidon after bringing Odysseus home to Ithaca. Arrive in the late afternoon for the best light.

Paleokastritsa, 25 km to the northwest, is one of the most beautiful natural sites in the Ionian Islands: six interlocking bays, crystal-clear turquoise waters and limestone cliffs rising 30 to 50 metres. The Monastery of Panagia Theotokos, founded in 1225 on a rocky headland above the main bay, was according to tradition established after the discovery of an icon of the Virgin. The present buildings date from the 18th century. Modest dress is required to enter — cover-up garments are provided at the door. The view from the monastery gardens over the sea is among the finest on the island.

The hilltop villages of Lakones and Makrades, above Paleokastritsa, offer plunging views over the six coves of the bay - a panorama the locals call the “balcony of Corfu”. These villages of centuries-old olive groves have kept their traditional architecture and their unpretentious tavernas. Plan a day trip from Corfu Town, combined with Paleokastritsa. Stop there for a coffee or a simple lunch on a terrace.

Corfu's Archaeological Museum, in town, houses the pediment of the Artemision, a 6th-century BC temple of Artemis discovered on the island: the central Gorgon stands nearly 3 metres tall and ranks among the best-preserved archaic sculptures in Greece. Allow about 45 minutes.

activities.text: Book a boat trip from Paleokastritsa to explore the sea caves along the northwest coast. Small boats slip into limestone cavities where sunlight creates blue and green reflections on the water — local guides call one of them the “Blue Light Cave”. The experience is at its best in the morning, when the sea is calm.

Take a dip in Agios Spyridon bay at Paleokastritsa — it's the most accessible beach in the resort, a mix of sand and pebbles with shallow waters. Several outfitters rent sea kayaks to explore the coves that can't be reached on foot. Expect to pay around €25–35 for a half-day kayak rental.

Sofrito is Corfu's quintessential Venetian dish: thin slices of veal pan-fried in a sauce of garlic, parsley, white wine and vinegar. The recipe dates back to 16th-century Venetian cooks. Pair it with a glass of Verdea, the dry white from Zakynthos — slightly oxidised and full-bodied, it holds its own against the bold flavours of the sauce.

Mantolato, a hard nougat made with roasted almonds and thyme honey, is Corfu's traditional confection — old-town delicatessens have stocked it since the 19th century. It's the ideal edible souvenir to bring home: it travels well and keeps for several weeks.

visits.text: Gaios, the capital of Paxos, stretches along a natural channel sheltered by two islets: Agios Nikolaos, which bears the ruins of a Venetian fortress built between 1424 and 1510, and Panagia, home to a small monastery. The pastel-coloured waterfront with its Venetian-influenced buildings is one of the most charming in the Ionian Islands. According to Greek mythology, Poseidon struck off the tip of Corfu with his trident to create Paxos as a love retreat for himself and Amphitrite. Standing here, you can believe it.

The blue caves along Paxos' west coast are accessible only by sea — no road, no stairway. Local boats depart from Gaios or Lakka to cruise along the limestone cliffs, where sunlight filtered through the water casts blue and green reflections inside the cavities. Set aside half a day for the excursion and book ahead in July–August.

Lakka, at the northern tip of the island, nestles at the head of a horseshoe-shaped bay with perfectly still waters — sailing boats moor here by the dozen in summer. The village is tiny (a handful of tavernas, flower-lined lanes) but the waterfront atmosphere at sunset is hard to beat. If you have access to a small boat, rent one and explore the pebble beaches along the north coast, unreachable any other way.

Loggos is the most discreet of Paxos' three villages — a fishing port of a few dozen houses, with tavernas right on the water. It's the best address for a lunch of grilled fish in an authentic setting, well away from the organised excursions that flood Lakka in high season.

The Tripitos arch, on the west coast of Paxos, is a natural limestone arch several metres high rising sheer above the sea. It can be reached on a short walk from the village of Ozias. Few tourists make this detour - it is one of the most spectacular landscapes on the island.

activities.text: Book a boat trip to Antipaxos as soon as you arrive — the little sister island sits just 15 minutes to the south. Its beaches of Vrika and Voutoumi regularly rank among the finest in the Mediterranean — fine white sand and turquoise water that could pass for the Caribbean. The excursion typically takes a full day and includes a stop at the blue caves.

Set off on the footpaths that wind through the centuries-old olive groves in the island's interior. The Republic of Venice actively promoted olive cultivation on Paxos from the 15th century to secure its oil supply — the gnarled trees you'll see are often several hundred years old. The coastal trail from Loggos to Lakka (roughly 2 hours) offers magnificent views.

Paxos' bourdeto is a local twist on the Corfu classic: fish (scorpionfish or gurnard) simmered in a spicy tomato sauce, with a more pronounced kick than the Corfu version. Enjoy it at a harbour-side taverna in Gaios with a glass of tsipouro, the anise-scented grape marc spirit of the Ionians, served ice-cold.

Amygdalota from Paxos are small, soft almond-and-icing-sugar biscuits traditionally baked in the island's monasteries for religious feast days. You'll find them in the artisanal grocery shops of Gaios — pick up a box for the ferry ride the next day.

visits.text: The castle of Agia Mavra (Santa Maura), standing at the edge of the channel that separates the island from the mainland, is the first thing you'll see as you cross the bridge. Built in the 14th century by the Orsini counts, it gave its medieval name to the entire island — Lefkada was known as Santa Maura until the 19th century. The Turks held it from 1479 to 1684, before the Venetians took it back. The grounds are freely accessible and the view over the lagoon and salt flats is beautiful in the late afternoon.

Cape Lefkatas, at the south-western tip of the island, is one of the sites most steeped in mythology in all of Greece. Plan a day trip from Lefkada Town. The white cliff drops 72 metres into the Ionian Sea. In Antiquity, according to tradition, those suffering from an impossible love came to throw themselves into the sea from this headland - surviving the leap meant being cured of one's passion. The poet Sappho (c. 630-580 BC) is said to have died here for Phaon, according to legend. A lighthouse built in 1913 now stands on the site of the ancient temple of Apollo. On a clear day the view reaches as far as the coasts of Epirus.

Nydri, on the east coast, is the launching pad for boat trips to the small islands of the archipelago: Meganisi, Madouri, Sparti and, most famously, Skorpios — formerly owned by Aristotle Onassis, where he married Jackie Kennedy in 1968. Water taxis and organised excursions leave from the harbour throughout the day in summer. The marina is lively, with plenty of waterfront tavernas.

The Faneromeni monastery, perched on a wooded hill 3 km from the capital, offers the finest view down over Lefkada Town and the channel separating it from the mainland. The current buildings date from the 17th-18th centuries. Allow 20 minutes' walk from the car park.

The town of Lefkada itself is worth an hour's wander through its lanes: the facades are built of painted corrugated iron on wooden frames — an earthquake-resistant technique honed over centuries of seismic experience, which gives the houses a Caribbean feel unique in the Ionians. The archaeological museum, in town, displays finds from the excavations of Dörpfeld, the German archaeologist who came here searching for the homeland of Odysseus.

activities.text: Rent a boat from Nydri and explore the islets off the east coast at your own pace. Skorpios remains private property, but you can anchor nearby; Meganisi has several superb coves accessible only by sea. The east coast of Lefkada is sheltered from the prevailing winds — ideal for a relaxed day on the water, even without sailing experience.

Eglouvi lentils are Lefkada's most prized agricultural product — this small mountain village at 700 metres altitude grows tiny, flavourful lentils that carry a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). In soup with local olive oil or as a cold salad, they're simple and outstanding. Look for them in the grocery shops of the capital.

Ladopita is a rustic Lefkadian cake made with olive oil, flour and raisins — no butter, no milk. It's a Lenten recipe handed down from the Venetian centuries. Dense and mildly sweet, it pairs perfectly with a Greek coffee on a terrace. You'll find it in the traditional bakeries of the old town.

Agios Nikitas, 12 km northwest of the capital, is the most charming seaside village on the coast: its pedestrian lanes lead straight down to a small sandy beach, the tavernas sit at the water's edge and the crowds are more manageable than in Nydri. It's a good option for dinner or a late-afternoon swim.

visits.text: Porto Katsiki ('Goat Port') is one of the most photographed beaches in the Mediterranean. A concave limestone cliff drops sheer onto a strip of white pebbles and sand, lapped by water of an almost unreal blue-turquoise hue — locals attribute the colour to the geological composition of the seabed. From the car park at the top of the cliff, roughly a hundred steps cut into the rock lead down to the beach. Arrive before 10am in July–August: after that, the beach fills quickly and the staircase becomes a queue.

Egremni, a few kilometres north of Porto Katsiki, stretches for almost 2.5 km of golden pebbles at the foot of 150-metre-high cliffs. The earthquake of 17 November 2015 destroyed the old staircase of 347 steps and buried part of the beach under a landslide. A new staircase was built in 2021, but the municipality closed land access in 2025 because of ground instability, and the February 2026 storms damaged the steps: the beach is reached by boat from Vassiliki, which keeps it wilder and less crowded than Porto Katsiki. The waves can be powerful: take care with children.

Vassiliki is a world-class windsurfing destination — the reliable afternoon thermals that blow across the bay from the open sea draw competitors and enthusiasts from around the globe. In the morning, the bay is a mirror-flat playground for beginners; from 2pm, the wind picks up and sails multiply. Dozens of windsurf and kitesurf schools cater to all levels.

Karya, a mountain village in the centre of the island at 550 metres above sea level, is famous throughout Greece for its handmade embroidery - the village women carry on a tradition dating from the 19th century with intricate floral patterns. Plan a day trip from Vassiliki. The local folklore museum traces this history. In summer, an artisans' market livens up the central square. The view from the heights takes in both coasts of the island.

Kathisma beach, halfway between the capital and Porto Katsiki on the west coast, is the largest organised beach on the island: golden sand, sun loungers, beach bars and sometimes paragliding sessions from the nearby hill. Plan a day trip from Vassiliki. If Porto Katsiki feels too chaotic, Kathisma offers the same turquoise water with a little more comfort.

activities.text: Take a windsurfing lesson in Vassiliki — it's one of Europe's most renowned spots to learn or improve. Conditions are close to ideal: calm mornings for the basics, steady thermal winds in the afternoon for practice. Book your slot the day before — schools fill up fast in high season.

Head out early by boat from Vassiliki to Egremni and Porto Katsiki — the perspective from the sea on those white cliffs plunging straight down is completely different from the view at the top. Water taxis and small excursion boats leave from the harbour from 9am.

Savoro is a traditional preservation dish of Corfiot and Lefkadian fishermen: fish (sardines, mackerel) is fried, then marinated in vinegar, raisins and rosemary. The result is a surprisingly tangy-sweet preparation served cold — perfect for a light lunch after the beach.

Pasteli, a sesame-and-honey bar, is the traditional beach snack of the Ionian Islands — people have been eating it since ancient Greece. Simple, energising and utterly unprocessed. Pick up a few from a grocery shop in Vassiliki before heading down to Porto Katsiki: you'll need the fuel for the climb back up.

seo.h1_title: Ionian Islands Road Trip: Corfu, Paxos & Lefkada
seo.intro_paragraph: Corfu unfolds four centuries of Venetian architecture through its labyrinthine UNESCO-listed lanes, before the ferries carry you to Paxos — a 25 km² island blanketed in olive groves and carved into coves accessible only by sea. Lefkada rounds off the journey with its 72-metre white cliffs plunging into impossibly blue water, and Vassiliki where windsurfing sails fill the bay every afternoon.
seo.seo_hook: UNESCO Venetian lanes in Corfu, Paxos coves accessible only by boat, Lefkada's white cliffs. A journey through Ionian islands of singular beauty.
featured_list: Corfu: UNESCO-listed Venetian old town since 2007
Paxos: turquoise coves and blue caves reachable only by boat
Lefkada: limestone cliffs and the legend of Sappho
Vassiliki: world-renowned windsurfing spot

places_taglines.GR::paxos: A pocket-sized island of twisted olive groves and turquoise coves that no road can reach
places_taglines.GR::corfu: Where Venetian kantounia, British cricket and Ottoman-defying fortresses share one spellbinding UNESCO old town
places_taglines.GR::lefkada: Where Sappho leapt and white cliffs drop 72 metres into impossible shades of blue
places_taglines.GR::vasiliki: Morning glass, afternoon thermals: the bay where Europe comes to windsurf beneath Lefkada's cliffs

highlights: Corfu's UNESCO-listed old town with its Venetian fortresses and labyrinthine lanes
Blue caves of Paxos and Antipaxos beaches accessible only by boat
Porto Katsiki and Egremni cliffs, ranked among the most beautiful beaches in the Mediterranean
Vassiliki, a European benchmark for windsurfing and kitesurfing

itineraries.title: Kefalonia and Zakynthos Tour: Caves and Beaches
itineraries.subtitle: From the underground lakes of Kefalonia to the cliffs of Zakynthos, via the island of Odysseus – 6 days in the wildest Ionian Islands.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with temperatures of 24–29°C, pleasant sea temperatures and fewer visitors at the sights. Avoid July–August (intense heat of 30–35°C, crowded beaches) and November–March (frequent rain, many services closed). Sea caves are best visited outside peak season.
specialties: Ladotyri cheese aged in olive oil (Zakynthos PDO)

visits.text: Argostoli has been the capital of Kefalonia since 1757 — before that, the population sheltered inside the Venetian fortress of San Giorgio as protection against pirates. The town thrived as one of the busiest ports in the Greek islands, until the earthquake of 12 August 1953 levelled it entirely. What you see today is therefore a rebuilt city, but it has held on to an authentic Mediterranean character with its palm-lined waterfront and the lively Vallianos Square, which comes alive every evening.

The De Bosset Bridge — also called the Drapano Bridge — is the longest stone bridge over the sea in the world, stretching 700 metres. Originally built in wood in 1813 by Swiss engineer Charles-Philippe de Bosset in British service, it was entirely reconstructed in stone a few decades later. Almost halfway across, you'll come upon an obelisk erected by the British to commemorate their presence — the original plaque reading “To the glory of the British Empire” was destroyed in 1865, one year after the island was united with Greece. The bridge marks the edge of the Koutavos Lagoon, where you can spot Caretta caretta turtles swimming freely.

The archaeological museum of Argostoli, inaugurated in 1960 (architect Pátroklos Karantinós), is closed to the public and its reconstruction is unfinished. Do not plan to visit its collections from Samé, Kranioi, Pronnoi and Paléis. In Argostoli, head instead to Vallianos Square to discover the town rebuilt after the 1953 earthquake, then walk along pedestrian Lithostroto Street, lined with shops and cafés. Finish on the waterfront, where you can walk along the harbour.

The Korgialenios Historical and Folklore Museum, founded in 1963 on the ground floor of the library bearing the same name, traces the history of Kefalonia from the Venetian period through to the 1953 earthquake. You'll find antique furniture, silverware, household tools, traditional costumes and close to 3,000 photographs — a tangible way to understand what the town looked like before it was completely destroyed. The entrance is through the library, which also holds 50,000 rare books and manuscripts.

Saint Theodore Lighthouse, locally known as Fanari (“the lighthouse”), is a neoclassical circular structure with 20 Doric columns, built in 1829 during the British occupation to plans drawn by J.P. Kennedy. Its lantern sits 11 metres above the Bay of Argostoli. Destroyed in the 1953 earthquake, it was rebuilt to the original design in 1960. Come here in the late afternoon: the sun sinking behind the Paliki peninsula on the far side of the bay paints the sea orange — one of the finest sunsets on the island.

The Katavothres are one of the strangest geological phenomena in the Mediterranean: seawater rushes into cracks in the limestone, vanishes underground, crosses the entire island — roughly 15 km — and resurfaces in the Bay of Sami, on the eastern coast, fourteen days later. In 1963, Austrian hydrogeologists Maurin and Zoetl poured 160 kg of fluorescent green dye (uranine) into the sinkholes — and detected it again in the underground lake at Melissani and the springs at Karavomilos. The process remains partly unexplained. As far back as 1835, a British tax collector had the idea of harnessing the current to power corn mills — the ruins of those mills are still visible on site.

activities.text: Lithostroto, the main pedestrian street of Argostoli, is where locals gather every evening for the ritual stroll. Shops, cafés, the Catholic church, the clock tower rebuilt in 1985 — everything is packed into a few hundred metres. Keep walking to Vallianos Square, the large central square, for a Greek coffee facing the palm trees. It's quiet during the day, crowded and lively in the evening.

The Koutavos Lagoon, once a mosquito-infested swamp and a hotbed of malaria, is now a bird sanctuary where migratory species nest. Caretta caretta turtles feed here regularly. You can walk the coastal path or rent an electric boat to get a closer look at the wildlife. Morning is the ideal time — peace and quiet, soft light, and often a few fishermen by the harbour.

Kreatopita is the quintessential Kefalonian pie: puff pastry filled with a mixture of meats (lamb, pork, beef), rice and spices, baked in the oven. It's a festive dish that families still prepare for special occasions. Find it in the bakeries and tavernas around the market — it's the best quick lunch in town.

Robola of Kefalonia is one of Greece's most acclaimed white wines. This ancient grape variety grows on the Omala plateau at an altitude of 700 metres and has AOC status. The wine is dry, mineral and taut, with fine acidity — nothing like the rounded whites from the rest of Greece. Ask for it at any taverna by the harbour: it pairs perfectly with grilled fish and mezze.

visits.text: Melissani Cave — also known as the 'Cave of the Nymphs' — is a limestone cenote whose ceiling collapsed during the 1953 earthquake, allowing sunlight to pour directly onto the underground lake. The lake stretches roughly 160 metres long and reaches depths of 30 to 40 metres; its surface sits one metre above sea level, fed by water that has travelled 15 km underground from the Katavothres in Argostoli. Archaeological excavations in 1962 uncovered a sanctuary dedicated to the god Pan on a small central islet, along with clay figurines and oil lamps dating from the 3rd–4th centuries BC. Plan your visit between 11 am and 1 pm: that's when the sun strikes the opening directly and transforms the water into a kaleidoscope of blues and violets. The tour is by rowboat and lasts 10 to 15 minutes.

Drogarati Cave, 5 km from Sami, was discovered around 300 years ago when an earthquake caused its entrance to collapse. It measures 65 metres long, 45 metres wide and 20 metres high, with a steady temperature of 18°C — a relief in summer. The stalactites and stalagmites, some of which resemble dolphins according to speleologists, have formed over roughly 100 million years. The main chamber, known as the “Hall of Apotheosis”, has such remarkable acoustics that it has hosted concerts — including, in 2014, a performance by the Bavarian Philharmonic, which arrived on a cruise ship docked at Argostoli. Bring a jumper even in summer, and wear sturdy shoes for the slippery steps.

Sami's harbour is Kefalonia's main ferry port, with connections to Patras and Ithaca. The town itself is modest but pleasant, with a handful of tavernas and cafés along the waterfront. Just next door lies Karavomylos, the village where the resurgent springs from the Katavothres emerge — the seawater that entered the ground in Argostoli reappears here, slightly brackish, after its 14-day underground journey.

Antisamos Beach, 4 km from Sami, is one of the most beautiful on Kefalonia: a long sweep of white pebbles framed by pine forest that tumbles down to the shore, with deep turquoise water. Several scenes from the 2001 film 'Captain Corelli's Mandolin' were shot right here. The beach is lifeguarded in summer but never overcrowded — the winding access road from the main highway puts off the lazier crowd. Bring your snorkelling mask: the seabed is rich.

activities.text: A combined visit to both caves (Melissani + Drogarati) works best as a half-day outing. Start early in the morning with Drogarati to beat the cruise-ship coaches, then head to Melissani around 11:30 am to catch the peak sunlight. Allow about an hour at each cave, including queuing time in high season.

After the caves, head to Antisamos for a swim. The water is crystal-clear and less crowded than at the southern beaches. If you have a mask, dip your head below the surface and look around — the visibility is exceptional.

Riganada is dried bread (a rustic rusk) rubbed with fresh tomato, drizzled with olive oil, topped with feta and sprinkled with dried oregano — a Greek summer classic across the Ionian Islands. Very simple, very good. Order some with a well-chilled glass of white Robola at a taverna by Sami harbour at the end of the day.

map_keywords: Cave of the Nymphs Vathy Ithaca

visits.text: Vathy, the capital of Ithaca, is a small town of 1,700 people tucked at the end of a horseshoe-shaped gulf — one of the best-sheltered natural anchorages in the Ionian Sea. Most of the Venetian-style buildings were rebuilt to their original designs after the 1953 earthquake; one of the painter El Greco's earliest works is said to be in the local cathedral. Stroll along the harbour, stop at one of the quayside tavernas — the atmosphere is gentle, far from mass tourism.

The Archaeological Museum of Vathy holds over 1,000 objects unearthed on the island, covering the Mycenaean through Roman periods. The star exhibit is a pottery fragment inscribed with the name “Odysseus”, found during excavations at the Alalkomenes site. There is also a small bronze sculpture that some identify as depicting Odysseus himself, along with Mycenaean votive tripods. Admission is free. The museum is closed on Tuesdays.

Aetos Hill, 4 km from Vathy, rises to 380 metres. From the church of Aï Giorgios, a steep trail climbs in 20 minutes to the ruins of the ancient city of Alalkomenes — this is where Heinrich Schliemann dug in 1868 and 1878, convinced he had found the palace of Odysseus. Modern archaeologists are more cautious: the fortifications date from the 7th century BC, after the events of the Odyssey. But the view from the top, over both coasts of the island and Kefalonia across the water, is worth the trip on its own.

Kathara Monastery stands at around 600 metres above sea level, on the mountain Homer called Nirito. Founded in the late 17th century, it offers a 360° panorama of Vathy, the southern part of the island and Kefalonia. Allow for a return drive from Vathy for this visit. Even if the monastery itself does not interest you, make the trip for the view - it is among the most beautiful in all the Ionian Islands.

The Cave of the Nymphs, known locally as Marmarospilia, lies a few kilometres north of Vathy. According to the Odyssey, this is where Odysseus hid the gifts of the Phaeacians on his return. Its interior is closed to the public: do not plan to enter to see the stalactites or the ancient altar. To explore Vathy's links with the Odyssey without relying on this access, walk along the harbour and visit the archaeological museum of Vathy, which displays finds from the island.

activities.text: Ithaca is tailor-made for gentle hiking. Signposted trails connect the villages through olive groves and scrubland of kermes oak. The island is home to just 3,000 people, and the paths are often deserted — one of the most authentic experiences in the Ionians. Ask in Vathy for details on the marked routes.

Revithokeftedes are chickpea fritters laced with fresh herbs, typical of the Ionian Islands. In Ithaca, they're usually served with yoghurt or skordalia (garlic mash). A simple, delicious vegetarian starter — one of the best things to order in a harbourside taverna in Vathy.

The village of Stavros, in northern Ithaca, is worth a stop: its central square has a bust of Odysseus and a model of his “idealised” castle, while a small archaeological museum displays finds from excavations conducted by the British School of Archaeology in the 1930s. Allow for a return drive from Vathy for this visit. Do not confuse it with the museum in Vathy - this one focuses on the north of the island and its connections with the Odyssey.

visits.text: Zakynthos Town — dubbed “the Flower of the East” (Il Fiore di Levante) by the Venetians — was completely destroyed in the 1953 earthquake and rebuilt in a neo-Venetian style with arcades and colonnaded façades. Solomos Square, the largest in town, opens directly onto the Ionian Sea. Here you'll find the Byzantine Museum, a statue of the poet Dionysios Solomos (who penned the Greek national anthem in 1823), and the town hall. This is where the action is in the morning; in the evening, head up to Bohali.

The Church of Agios Dionysios is dedicated to the island's patron saint. Founded in 1708, it houses his relics in a silver reliquary and features a gilded carved iconostasis along with fine Byzantine frescoes restored after 1953. The bell tower overlooking the harbour is one of the defining landmarks of Zakynthos. Every year on 24 August and 17 December, thousands of worshippers gather here for the saint's feast days.

The Byzantine Museum of Zakynthos, on Solomos Square, is one of the richest in the Ionians. It brings together carved wooden Byzantine icons, original frescoes from the 15th to 17th centuries rescued from churches destroyed in 1953, and 18th-century paintings by artists of the Ionian School such as Doxaras, Koutouzis and Kandounis. Some canvases depict the town before the earthquake — a striking comparison with what it looks like today. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

The Venetian Castle of Bohali, perched on the hill above the town, was built in the 15th century by the Venetians on even older foundations. The enclosure among the pines overlooks the harbour from 150 metres — from the ruined ramparts you can take in the entire bay, the port and the mountains of the hinterland in a single glance. Drive up or walk (25 minutes from Solomos Square). At sunset, locals from the village of Bohali settle on terraces with a drink — join them.

Zakynthos National Marine Park (NMPZ), created to protect Caretta caretta turtles, encompasses Laganas Bay and the nesting beaches in the south of the island. The turtles lay their eggs on these beaches between May and August - access is regulated, but glass-bottom boat excursions allow you to observe them in their natural habitat without disturbing them. If you visit in summer, do not miss a trip out to sea.

activities.text: Roma Street, the main pedestrian thoroughfare leading off Saint Mark's Square, is lined with local shops where you can pick up mandolato nougat (almonds, honey, egg white — the island's signature sweet), ladotyri (a hard cheese aged in olive oil, Zakynthos PDO) and olive-oil products. It's also the place for evening outings — the tavernas come alive from 8 pm.

Facing Saint Mark's Square stands the Solomos and Kalvos Museum, housed in the island's former casino and open since 1968. On the ground floor lie the tombs of the two poets — Dionysios Solomos, author of the national anthem, and Andreas Kalvos. Upstairs: manuscripts, personal belongings and period documents. A must for anyone interested in Greek literature.

Fritoura is a traditional sweet from Zakynthos: a thick mixture of semolina and water, cooled, cut into pieces, fried and sprinkled with sugar and cinnamon. You can taste it from vendors who prepare it, especially during the island's festivals. In Zakynthos, look for the kiosk in front of Saint Dionysios Church to discover this speciality, served warm and crisp on the outside, with a soft centre.

Verdea is Zakynthos's AOC white wine, made from local grape varieties (pavlos, goustolidi). Dry, with lively acidity and a slightly bitter finish - it contrasts with the rounded whites of most islands. Ask for it at the taverna with local cheeses.

visits.text: Navagio Bay - also known as “Smugglers' Bay” - is the most photographed image in all of Greece. It takes its name from the wreck of the cargo ship Panagiotis, which ran aground here on the night of 2 October 1980 after being chased by the Greek navy during a storm. The ship had left Argostoli carrying contraband goods. The white limestone cliffs rise more than 200 metres above the white-sand beach and turquoise water. Warning: landing on the beach and swimming in the bay are prohibited because of rockfall risks. Viewing from a boat remains subject to access restrictions. For the view from above, allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town, via Anafonitria or Volimes, to the clifftop viewpoint, subject to permitted access conditions.

The Blue Caves are a series of arches and tunnels carved by the sea into white limestone cliffs in the north of the island, between Agios Nikolaos harbour and Cape Skinari. Their name comes from the electric colour of the water inside, caused by sunlight reflecting off submerged limestone - a phenomenon very similar to the Blue Grotto on Capri. The walls and even your body underwater take on a vivid blue hue. They can only be reached by small boat (maximum 50 passengers to enter the arches). From Zakynthos town, allow for a return road trip to Agios Nikolaos harbour or Cape Skinari, followed by the boat visit.

Cape Skinari is the northern tip of Zakynthos, facing Kefalonia - on clear days, Mount Ainos on the neighbouring island is clearly visible. The lighthouse dates from 1897 and stands 9.5 metres tall. This is a departure point for boat excursions to the Blue Caves and Navagio Bay. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach the cape. The cape's characteristic windmills have become one of the island's symbols.

Anafonitria Monastery, inland in the northwest, dates from the 15th century. It is one of the island's oldest and is famous for having welcomed Saint Dionysios as a monk before he became the patron saint of Zakynthos. It is surrounded by groves of century-old olive trees and a medieval defensive tower that still stands. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town for this visit. The atmosphere is peaceful, far from the beaches.

Xigia Beach is a natural curiosity: sulphur springs emerge directly into the sea from the rocks, giving the water a milky hue and a faint characteristic smell. The therapeutic properties of these sulphurous waters have long been known locally. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach Xigia. The beach is small, wild and lightly visited - a good alternative to Navagio for those who want a different bathing experience.

activities.text: The ideal plan for this last day: leave early in the morning for Cape Skinari and board a small boat to the Blue Caves (allow 2 hours). Then head inland to Volimes and Anafonitria, passing through olive groves and mountain villages. In the afternoon, make the detour to the Navagio viewpoint for the photo, then finish at Xigia Beach for a dip in the sulphurous waters before returning to Zakynthos Town.

The hill village of Volimes is known for its textile artisans - rugs, embroidery and lace are displayed in the small shops along the main street. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach Volimes. This is also where the best local products are sold: mountain honey, olive oil and handmade mandolato. The sellers are often the producers themselves.

The boat excursion combining the Blue Caves and Navagio Bay (viewed from offshore) lasts between 3 and 4 hours, depending on the option chosen. Boats depart from Agios Nikolaos harbour or Zakynthos's main port. For a departure from Agios Nikolaos, allow for a return road trip from Zakynthos town to this harbour in the north of the island. Book the day before in summer - places sell out quickly. Small boats carrying 12 to 50 passengers can enter the caves; larger ones can only pass around them.

practical_info.departure: Port of Agios Nikolaos or Zakynthos Town port

activities.text: Ladotyri is the AOC cheese of Zakynthos: a hard cheese made from sheep's and goat's milk, aged in olive oil — hence the name (lado = oil, tyri = cheese). It has a firm texture, a dark rind and a powerful, slightly fruity flavour. It is eaten at the end of a meal with local honey, or diced with an aperitif.

seo.h1_title: Kefalonia and Zakynthos Tour: Caves and Beaches
seo.intro_paragraph: Step inside Melissani Cave on Kefalonia, with its unearthly blue underground lake lit from above, then cross to Ithaca and its echoes of the Odyssey. Continue to Zakynthos to watch Caretta caretta turtles and finish beneath the dizzying cliffs of Navagio. 6 days of mythology, geology and unspoilt shores.
seo.seo_hook: Melissani and its underground lakes, Ithaca, the island of Odysseus, Caretta turtles and the Navagio shipwreck: 6 mythical days in the Ionian Islands.
featured_list: Melissani: underground lake and midday light
Ithaca: the island of Odysseus and its wild trails
Zakynthos: a paradise for Caretta caretta turtles
Navagio: a shipwreck beneath 200-metre cliffs

places_taglines.GR::argostoli: A capital reborn after 1953, where a 700-metre stone bridge spans a lagoon full of sea turtles
places_taglines.GR::sami: Ferry port and launchpad for the two most spectacular caves on Kefalonia
places_taglines.GR::zakynthos: Venetian grace, nesting sea turtles, the Navagio shipwreck and glowing Blue Caves
places_taglines.GR::ithaca: A 96 km² island forever tied to Odysseus's homecoming in Homer's epic

highlights: Melissani underground lake: visit between 11 am and 1 pm for the light show
Drogarati Cave: outstanding acoustics, steady temperature of 18°C all year round
Navagio: view from the clifftop platform or boat trip from Agios Nikolaos
Caretta caretta turtles: glass-bottom boat observation in the Zakynthos Marine Park

itineraries.title: Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi
itineraries.subtitle: From Kavala's Ottoman fortress to Europe's first Christian site, via the colourful lanes of Xanthi.
itineraries.notes: Thasos is only accessible by ferry from Keramoti (35 min) or Kavala (75 min). Visiting the Evros Delta requires a military permit that must be requested in advance.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: April–June and September–October, with temperatures of 20–28°C and pleasant sea temperatures. Avoid July–August (intense heat of 35–40°C, crowded beaches) and December–February (frequent rain). Thasos benefits from a refreshing sea breeze.

visits.text: The fortress of Kavala commands the entire peninsula from the summit of Panagia hill. Its current form dates from the first quarter of the 15th century, though it rests on Byzantine foundations subsequently reworked by the Venetians and the Ottomans. Climb up to the outer walls for the view: at your feet, the red-tiled roofs of the old town, the turquoise harbour, and in the distance the silhouette of Thasos on the horizon. The open-air theatre nestled within the walls hosts performances in summer — check the programme if you're here in July or August.

The Kamares Aqueduct is the most photographed monument in the city, and it deserves every shot. This double-tiered structure — 11 large arches below, narrower arches above — stretches 270 metres long and stands 25 metres high. It was built between 1520 and 1536 on the orders of Ibrahim Pasha, Grand Vizier to Suleiman the Magnificent, after the city was destroyed in 1391. Made of local granite with Ottoman brick detailing, it supplied Kavala with water from Mount Pangaion until 1911. The best angle for a photo: from Lahana Street in the late afternoon, when the golden light brings out the stone.

In the old quarter of Panagia, look for the house of Mehmet Ali (1769–1849) — the founder of the last dynasty to rule Egypt, born right here in this modest cantilevered stone building. The house is preserved as a museum and gives a good sense of Ottoman domestic architecture of the era. Across from it, the square bearing his name features an equestrian statue of the pasha — one of the rare depictions of a human figure tolerated within Islamic tradition.

The Panagia quarter, perched on the peninsula between the fortress and the sea, is the historic heart of Kavala. Its cobbled alleyways, colourful houses with cantilevered balconies (sachnisia), and hidden courtyards make it one of the best-preserved Ottoman neighbourhoods in northern Greece. Don't miss the Halil Bey Mosque, built on the foundations of an early Christian basilica — during the population exchange of 1922–1923, it served as temporary shelter for Greek refugee families.

The Imaret, on the western flank of the Panagia peninsula, is one of the largest Islamic complexes from the Ottoman era still standing in Europe. Built in the early 19th century by Mehmet Ali to serve as a soup kitchen, madrasa and mosque, it combines Ottoman arches and slender columns in a remarkable inner courtyard. The interior is now privately managed, but the exterior can be viewed from the lane.

activities.text: Stroll along the Kavala waterfront down to the fishing harbour: the blue-and-white boats, nets drying on the quay, and fish tavernas lined up along the water give the city the feel of an authentic Greek port, well away from the mass-tourism circuit. This is where Saint Paul landed on his first journey to Europe — a commemorative plaque near the harbour marks the event.

Sample sardeles pastes: salted, dried and pressed sardines are Kavala's signature culinary speciality, going back centuries. They're eaten on toasted bread, simply drizzled with lemon juice, alongside a glass of Macedonian tsipouro without anise — the local spirit served chilled with olives and feta. The tavernas along the harbour serve both without ceremony.

In the evening, order a saganaki: a slice of graviera cheese, breaded and fried in olive oil, served still crisp with a wedge of lemon. Simple, no-nonsense, and far better than it looks — it's the essential meze to start a meal across the entire region.

visits.text: The site of Philippi has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016 — the 18th Greek site to join the list. Founded in 360 BC by colonists from Thasos under the name Krenides, the city was conquered in 356 BC by Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, who gave it his name. Allow at least two hours to cross the entire site — it covers 67 hectares, slightly larger than Pompeii.

The theatre of Philippi was built by Philip II in the mid-4th century BC and remodelled under the Romans in the 2nd century AD into a theatre with a monumental three-storey stage façade. In the 3rd century it was converted into an arena for gladiatorial combat: the wild animal pit beneath the orchestra is still visible. Since 1957 it has hosted the Philippi Festival every summer — one of the oldest ancient-theatre festivals in Greece.

The Roman forum of Philippi is one of the best-documented in the eastern provinces of the Empire: a vast square surrounded by temples, shops, the orators' tribune, and a meeting hall for the decurions. A monumental inscription at least 20 metres long, with metal letters 62 cm high set into the paving, honoured the flamen of the divine Augustus. Look for the ruts left by chariots on the Via Egnatia — they're still visible in the stone.

The early Christian basilicas of Philippi are among the most impressive in Greece. Basilica A (late 5th century) measured 130 by 50 metres, with a transept, galleries and atrium. The Octagon, an episcopal complex built on the presumed site of Saint Paul's house of prayer, went through three construction phases from the 4th to the 6th century. It was here, in AD 49–50, that the Apostle Paul founded Europe's first Christian community — and was briefly imprisoned in a Roman cistern traditionally identified as the 'Prison of Paul'.

The Archaeological Museum of Philippi, spread over two floors, presents the site's collections chronologically: sculptures, vases, coins and gold jewellery from prehistoric through Roman times on the ground floor, Christian heritage and the city's decline upstairs. Allow 45 minutes to an hour — the Macedonian jewellery and coins from the era of Philip II are particularly worth your time.

activities.text: Side trip to the Baptistery of Saint Lydia, a few hundred metres from the archaeological site, on the bank of the Zygaktis River. Lydia, a wealthy purple-cloth merchant from Thyatira, was the first European baptised by Paul in AD 49–50 in this river. The modern octagonal baptistery dates from 1974, but an open-air baptism ceremony takes place every 20 May — if you happen to be here on that date, you can attend.

Try kavourmas: pork or veal slow-cooked in its own fat with spices — a traditional Macedonian winter preservation method you'll find in tavernas around the Kavala area, served as a hot or cold meze. Pair it with an assyrtiko from Drama: this mineral white wine, produced in the highland vineyards to the west, is dry, bright and sharply acidic.

The evening drive back to Kavala follows the Philippi plain, dominated by Mount Pangaion to the south-west — it was from its gold and silver mines that Philip II bankrolled his conquests. If you have time, stop at Krinides, the small modern village on the site of ancient Krenides, to see the remains of the Hellenistic city walls on the outskirts of the UNESCO site.

visits.text: To reach Thasos, take the ferry from Keramoti, 35 km south-east of Kavala — the crossing takes just 35 minutes and departures run every 30 minutes in season. It's by far the quickest and cheapest option. Once in Limenas, the capital, head down to the ancient agora: it sits right in the heart of the modern town, surrounded by the ruins of sanctuaries dedicated to Heracles, Dionysus, Artemis and Poseidon, with a medieval tower occupying one corner. Information panels at the entrance show a reconstruction of what the square once looked like — helpful for grasping the scale.

The ancient theatre of Thasos, built into a natural hollow in the hillside north-east of town, dates in its earliest phases from the late 4th century BC. In the 1st century AD it was converted into an arena for gladiatorial combat. It has been fully restored in recent years using white marble from Thasos — the same stone used in antiquity, quarried on the island. The view from the upper tiers over the harbour of Limenas and the Aegean is one of the finest on the island.

The Archaeological Museum of Thasos, founded in 1935 and renovated between 1989 and 2000, is the oldest museum in the Eastern Macedonia and Thrace region. Its centrepiece is the Kouros of Thasos: an archaic statue standing 3.5 metres tall, depicting a young man carrying a ram — a masterpiece of the 6th century BC discovered in 1911 in five pieces inside a Byzantine wall, where it had been reused as building material. The museum also holds a fine head of Alexander the Great and an Aphrodite with a Dolphin regularly lent to major international exhibitions.

The acropolis of Thasos dominates the town from its rocky spur. Climb up from the theatre along the signposted path: you'll pass the sanctuaries of Apollo and Athena, then the Sanctuary of Pan carved directly into the rock face. Along the way, look for the Cyclopean ramparts of white marble — some blocks are fitted so precisely that you still can't slide a credit card between them. The view from the top sweeps across the entire northern coastline of the island.

activities.text: Swim at Makryammos, 2 km east of Limenas: a crescent-shaped cove with fine sand, emerald-green waters and maritime pines reaching down to the sea. This is the picture-postcard image of Thasos - the blend of dense vegetation and clear sea that earned the island its nickname, “the Emerald Island”.

In the evening, settle into a café on the harbour at Limenas and order a local retsina — the resinated white wine produced on the island, slightly bitter, served chilled with olives and goat's cheese. It's here that you understand why ancient Greece regulated its wine production by law: Thasian amphorae bearing inspection seals have been found across the entire Mediterranean basin.

visits.text: The village of Panagia, perched in the mountains 10 km south of Limenas, is one of the most beautiful on the island: stone fountains, century-old plane trees, tile-roofed houses and cobbled lanes on the hillside. It's the birthplace of the local dance and one of the best-preserved villages in Eastern Macedonia. Arrive on a Sunday morning to see the locals in traditional dress after Mass.

The village of Theologos, which calls for a day trip from Limenas, was the island's medieval capital under Genoese and Turkish rule. This is where the population took refuge to escape pirates. Its narrow lanes, stone houses with enclosed gardens and old fountains distinguish it from the modernised coastal villages. Allow 45 minutes to walk around the whole village.

The marble quarries of Alyki, on the cape of the same name 32 km south-east of Limenas, are an exceptional archaeological site: the extraction of Thasian white marble — one of the most prized in antiquity — is documented here from the Archaic period through to Byzantine times. Half-cut blocks have been waiting in the rock for twenty centuries. This white marble with its glittering crystals was used, among other things, to build the Arch of Galerius in Thessaloniki. From the beach at Alyki, submerged blocks are visible beneath the water.

activities.text: Drive around the island: the coastal road covers 95 km and can be comfortably done in a day with stops. Don't miss Golden Beach (Chrisi Amoudia) on the east coast — a long beach of golden sand with deep-blue water, considered one of the most beautiful in the northern Aegean. Behind the beach, archaeologists uncovered a well dating from the 3rd century BC, and on the headland above, the ruins of a 4th-century BC lighthouse.

Sample roast goat with mountain herbs at a taverna in Theologos or Panagia: it's the island's traditional festive dish, oven-roasted or spit-roasted with wild herbs gathered from the slopes of Mount Ipsarion. The mountain-village tavernas are cheaper and more authentic than those on the beaches.

visits.text: The old town of Xanthi (Palia Poli) is one of the largest preserved traditional settlements in Greece: 380,000 m² declared a protected zone in 1976, with over 1,200 buildings listed as monuments. It was rebuilt after two devastating earthquakes in 1829 and reached its zenith between 1880 and 1925 thanks to basma tobacco — an exceptional aromatic variety that supplied imperial courts and European markets. The Epirote and Macedonian craftsmen who built it blended Baroque, Neoclassical, Romanesque and Ottoman elements into a result the Greeks then nicknamed “Little Paris”.

Walk up the main street to Demokratias Square to see the clock tower, erected in 1870 by the Pomak Hadji Emin Aga. The Greek authorities wanted to demolish it in 1972 — protests by Muslim residents forced a reversal.
