seo.seo_hook: Byzantine frescoes at Mystras, the legendary plains of Sparta, the stone towers of the Mani and the rock of Monemvasia. Laconia reveals its little-known corner of the Peloponnese.
featured_list: Mystras: UNESCO Byzantine capital with 14th-century frescoes
Sparta: the bust of Leonidas and the Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia
Gytheio: the island of Paris and Helen, gateway to the Mani
Monemvasia: medieval fortress on a rock and Malvasia wine

places_taglines.GR::kalamata: Where ancient olive groves meet the shimmering Messenian Gulf
places_taglines.GR::mystras: A Byzantine ghost city draped across the flanks of Taygetus
places_taglines.GR::gytheio: Sparta's harbour where Helen and Paris sparked a ten-year war
places_taglines.GR::monemvasia: A medieval fortress carved from a sea-battered rock, reached by a single causeway
places_taglines.GR::sparta: The warrior city that needed no walls — only courage and legend

highlights: Mystras, a UNESCO Byzantine city with 14th-century frescoes on the slopes of Taygetus
The bust of Leonidas and the votive masks of Artemis Orthia at Sparta's archaeological museum
Gytheio and the Mani coastal road with its villages of stone towers
Monemvasia and its medieval lanes on the rock, birthplace of the Malvasia grape

itineraries.title: Western Peloponnese: Olympia, Three Venetian Fortresses and the Wild Mani
itineraries.subtitle: A 7-day road trip from the port of Patras to Aréopoli, through the birthplace of the Olympic Games, a coast lined with Venetian fortresses, and the Mani peninsula — Greece at its most rugged and most beautiful.
itineraries.notes: This itinerary works as a loop: fly into Patras (Araxos airport, 45 min away) or Kalamata (KLX international airport). The Mani is a region of mountains and narrow roads — a compact car is recommended. In summer, book Diros Caves tickets in advance (limited availability).
itineraries.climate: Best period: April-May and September-October, temperatures 20-26°C, swimmable sea. Avoid July-August (scorching heat 35-40°C, very dry) and November-March (frequent rain). The Mani remains arid year-round.

visits.text: The Kastro of Patras has crowned its hilltop since the 6th century — Emperor Justinian had it built on the site of the ancient Greek acropolis, and Venetians, Turks and Byzantines all left their mark. Head up in the late afternoon: the views over the Gulf of Patras and the Ionian Sea are breathtaking, and the raking light turns the whole scene into something spectacular. Just steps from the castle stands the well-preserved 2nd-century Roman odeon, which still hosts concerts in summer.

The Cathedral of Saint Andrew is the largest church in Greece — 12 domes surrounding a central dome that rises to 50 metres, built from 1908 and inaugurated in 1974. It houses what tradition holds to be part of the skull of the Apostle Andrew, the first disciple of Christ, who according to legend was crucified in Patras. The cathedral seats 5,500 people — step inside to admire the mosaics and the massive wooden chandelier.

activities.text: The Archaeological Museum of Patras, opened in 2009, is the second largest in Greece after the Acropolis Museum: 8,000 m² covering prehistory through the late Byzantine period. Its collection of Roman mosaics from the Achaea region is particularly outstanding. If you only have an hour, spend it on those mosaics and the statues from the Sanctuary of Artemis Laphria.

practical_info.tip: Closed on Tuesdays.

activities.text: In the evening, the old upper town is worth a stroll: narrow cobbled lanes, Venetian mansions, café terraces. Patras is a lively university city. Riga Fereou Street and the area around Georgiou Square are the hubs of nightlife. Try loukoumades (honey fritters) in one of the many bakeries of the lower town.

visits.text: The archaeological site of Olympia is the birthplace of the Olympic Games — held every four years from 776 BC to 393 AD, spanning over 1,100 years. The Temple of Zeus, built between 470 and 456 BC, was the largest temple in the Peloponnese. Inside stood the chryselephantine statue of Zeus by Phidias — 12.75 metres tall, its body carved in ivory, its drapery plated in gold — one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, now lost. The ancient stadium, however, is intact: its terraces once held 45,000 spectators. Arrive at opening, before 9:30 am — the heat and the tour groups show up together after that.

The Archaeological Museum of Olympia is essential after exploring the site. Its two masterpieces are the Hermes of Praxiteles (c. 343 BC), one of the rare surviving original Greek sculptures, and the Nike of Paionios, carved around 420 BC — a winged victory surging forward through the air. The reconstructed pediments from the Temple of Zeus depict the preparations for the chariot race of Pelops and the battle of the Lapiths against the Centaurs.

activities.text: The Museum of the History of the Ancient Olympic Games, separate from the archaeological museum, tells you what these games were really like — and they were nothing like their modern counterpart. Athletes competed naked, women were barred from the events (though not from the stands), and winners received nothing more than a wreath of wild olive. The museum displays objects that belonged to the athletes: jumping weights for the long jump, discuses, and weapons used in the race in armour.

practical_info.tip: The combined ticket for the site + archaeological museum + Games museum is the best deal.

visits.text: The fortress of Niokastro commands Pylos from a headland overlooking the Bay of Navarino. Built by the Ottomans from 1573 — two years after their defeat at Lepanto — to secure the entrance to the bay, it forms an irregular triangle with a perimeter of 1,566 metres. Inside you'll find a star-shaped citadel with five bastions built by the Venetians, a mosque converted into a church, ramparts with magnificent views over the bay and the island of Sphacteria, and four museums including one devoted to underwater archaeology with headless Hellenistic statues recovered from the sea.

Voidokilia beach is one of the most perfect in the Mediterranean: an almost geometric omega (Ω) shape drawn by nature, fine sand, turquoise water, and the ruins of the Frankish Paleokastro perched on the cliff behind. The Gialova lagoon alongside it is home to 254 bird species — including flamingos depending on the season. To get there, drive around the lagoon from Gialova (5 km), leave the car and walk down to the beach.

activities.text: The Bay of Navarino is where, on 20 October 1827, 27 Allied warships (British, French and Russian) trapped and destroyed an Ottoman fleet of 80 to 90 vessels without losing a single ship. This victory forced Ibrahim Pasha to withdraw from the Peloponnese and made Greek independence inevitable. Local operators run boat trips around the bay to see the memorials on the island of Sphacteria and the wooden wrecks of Ottoman ships, still visible in calm weather.

practical_info.tip: Boat trips depart from Pylos harbour. Check availability on the spot.

activities.text: Three Admirals Square in the heart of Pylos, shaded by centuries-old plane trees, is the centre of local life. The marble stele and period cannons honour the faces of Codrington, De Rigny and Hayden — the three Allied commanders at the battle. It's the perfect spot for an outdoor dinner with views of the lit-up harbour and the silhouette of Niokastro.

visits.text: The citadel of Methoni is one of the finest fortresses in Greece — 9.3 hectares on a peninsula surrounded by the sea on three sides, cut off from the mainland by an artificial moat. The Venetians built it from 1209 after seizing it from Geoffrey de Villehardouin, turned it into a vital staging post on the route to the East, and held it until 1500 when the Ottomans took it after a bloody siege. At the end of a 70-metre causeway, the octagonal Ottoman Bourtzi tower — topped with a dome — offers stunning views of the sea at sunset. Chateaubriand landed here on 10 August 1806 for his only journey to Greece. Allow at least 2 hours.

The castle of Koroni, 35 km to the east, spreads across 62,000 m² on a low peninsula overlooking the Gulf of Messenia. It's one of the rare medieval castles in Greece that is still inhabited: a few families live inside, olive trees grow within its walls, and the Timios Prodromos convent occupies the original Byzantine acropolis. The church of Agia Sophia, built on the ruins of a temple of Apollo and an early Christian basilica, carries within it every layer of the site's history. The view from the ramparts over the Gulf of Messenia with the snow-capped peaks of Mount Taygetus behind is magnificent.

activities.text: Methoni's beach, east of the castle, is a long strip of fine sand at the foot of the ramparts. The water is clear and shallow. The evening is ideal for a swim facing the illuminated fortress walls — one of the most photographed sunsets in the Peloponnese.

visits.text: Kalamata's kastro, built in the early 13th century by the Byzantines and later completed by Geoffroi de Villehardouin, overlooks the old town from its hill. It helped give the city its present name: excavations there uncovered a church dedicated to the Virgin “Kalomata” - with the beautiful dark eyes. At the foot of the castle, to the south-east, stands the Kalograion monastery, an Orthodox convent for women founded in the late 18th century, famous for its silk-weaving workshop where traditional looms are still in use.

The ancient site of Messene, 30 km from Kalamata, is one of the best-preserved archaeological sites in Greece — founded in 369 BC by the Theban general Epaminondas to free Messenia from Spartan rule. The 9-kilometre circuit wall and the remains of the stadium, baths, theatre and Sanctuary of Asclepius paint a vivid picture of life in a 4th-century Greek city. The site sees few visitors and is often entirely empty of tourists.

activities.text: Kalamata's open-air market, held on Wednesday and Saturday mornings, is the perfect place to stock up on local flavours. Kalamata olives hold PDO status — plump, purple-black, with a fruity and slightly tart flavour — and the region's olive oil ranks among the best in Greece. The area produces some 45,000 tonnes of olive oil per year from over 40 million olive trees. Try the pastéli (sesame and honey bars) and the dried figs, two more local specialities.

practical_info.tip: Market runs Wednesday and Saturday mornings until 1 pm. Pack olive oil in your checked luggage — not carry-on.

activities.text: Kalamata's seafront runs along the town beach. In the evening, the promenade is lined with fish restaurants, bars and cafés. Don't miss the street murals in the town centre, including a huge 115 m² portrait of Maria Callas, commissioned as part of the “Kalamata 2030” initiative.

visits.text: Aréopoli — 'the city of Ares' — is the gateway to the Deep Mani. Its former name was Tsimova; it was renamed in honour of Petros Mavromichalis, the last bey of the Mani, who set out from here on 17 March 1821 at the head of 300 Maniots to liberate Kalamata — two days before the official start of the War of Independence. His statue stands in the main square. The Church of the Taxiarches (Archangels), built in the second half of the 18th century, has the tallest bell tower in the Mani — a multi-tiered structure decorated with relief carvings and zodiac symbols on its façade, a testament to the Maniots' peculiar bond with Antiquity.

The Diros Caves, 11 km from Aréopoli, are explored by boat on an underground river — one of the most extraordinary experiences in the Peloponnese. A boatman rows you through 1,200 metres of flooded galleries, past stalactites skimming the water's surface, before a final 300-metre stretch on foot. The total mapped network exceeds 14,700 metres, reaching a maximum depth of 80 metres. Speleologists Ioannis and Anna Petrochilos first explored the caves in 1949; they've been open to the public since 1967. Bones of panther, hyena, lion and the largest hippopotamus bone deposit in Europe have been found inside.

activities.text: The tower houses of the Mani are the emblem of the peninsula: each clan built a stone tower to dominate its neighbours and defend itself during the vendettas that plagued the region for centuries. Around 800 of them still stand. Wander through the alleyways of Aréopoli to spot the Kapetanakos tower and the fortified Koutrakos residence — used in 1826 to resist Ibrahim Pasha's landing at the neighbouring village. Afterwards, drive down to the tiny harbour of Limeni (5 minutes by car): tower houses plunge straight into an emerald cove.

visits.text: Vathia is the ghost village of the Deep Mani: a collective fortress perched on a hill, made of stone towers packed so tightly that they form a continuous rampart against neighbouring clans. Allow a return day trip from Aréopoli. Vathia had up to 200 inhabitants in the 19th century; today a few houses have been restored, but the abandoned part is the most fascinating. Wander the deserted lanes without entering the towers, whose floors are in danger of collapsing. A striking atmosphere, between beauty and melancholy.

Cape Tainaron (or Matapan) is the southernmost point of mainland Greece. It can be reached by car as a day trip from Aréopoli. Leave the car at the car park and walk 45 minutes along a coastal path between two seas: the Ionian Sea to the west and the Aegean Sea to the east merge here into the Mediterranean. The Ancients regarded this cape as one of the gates of the Underworld - a local cave was said to lead straight to the realm of Hades. Near the car park, at the start of the path, lie the ruins of a 4th-century BC temple of Poseidon and a small chapel built on its foundations. The white lighthouse stands 41 metres above the sea.

activities.text: The road through the Deep Mani is the spectacle in itself: landscapes growing ever more barren and lunar, stone towers rising from hilltops, blue sea on both sides. After Vathia, stop for lunch in Gérolimenas — one of the Mani's few harbours, whose name means 'old port'. Waterside tavernas serve fried calamari and shrimp saganaki practically at the water's edge. Continue on to Porto Kagio, the southernmost village on the peninsula, for a swim in a quiet little cove before heading back toward the cape.

practical_info.tip: Leave early — the heat at Cape Tainaron is stifling after 11 am. Bring at least 2L of water for the hike.

visits.text: Kardamyli is the most appealing village of the Outer Mani - Homer mentions it in the Iliad as one of the seven cities offered by Agamemnon to Achilles. Allow a return day trip by car from Aréopoli. The writer and traveller Patrick Leigh Fermor settled here in the late 1960s, and it was here that he wrote “Mani”, the book that revealed this peninsula to the world. Stroll through Kardamyli's old town with its stone houses, and climb up to the church of Saint Spyridon, whose ornate bell tower dominates the village. The path to the Viros gorge, below, is one of the finest hikes in the Mani.

activities.text: The coast between Kardamyli and Stoupa offers a string of quiet little coves - some of fine sand, others of pebbles, all with remarkably clear water. It can be reached by car as a day trip from Aréopoli. Stoupa, the most developed resort on the west coast of the Mani, has sunloungers and seaside tavernas. For something wilder, look for the coves north of Kardamyli, reached by paths from the road.

The hike through the Viros gorge, starting from Kardamyli, is a 3 to 4-hour loop through a canyon covered in plane trees. The trailhead is reached by car from Aréopoli: set aside the whole day. The path is waymarked and accessible. If you don't have time for the full loop, the first hour of walking is enough to feel the beauty of the place.

practical_info.tip: Walking shoes are essential. Bring water.

seo.h1_title: Western Peloponnese: Olympia, Three Venetian Fortresses and the Wild Mani
seo.intro_paragraph: The western Peloponnese is the ideal itinerary for travellers who want it all: the site of the ancient Olympic Games, three of the finest Venetian fortresses in the Mediterranean, the Bay of Navarino where Greek independence was sealed in 1827, and the Mani — Greece's wildest peninsula, with its stone villages, tower houses and the southernmost cape on the mainland.
seo.seo_hook: Olympia, Methoni, the Battle of Navarino and Cape Tainaron: 7 days in the Greece the guidebooks don't show you.
featured_list: Olympia: birthplace of the Olympic Games since 776 BC, with a 64-metre-long Temple of Zeus and an outstanding museum
Methoni and Koroni: twin Venetian sea fortresses, built after 1209
Pylos and the Battle of Navarino: 27 Allied warships crushed the Ottoman fleet on 20 October 1827
Cape Tainaron: the southernmost point of mainland Greece, ancient gateway to the Underworld, ruins of a Temple of Poseidon

places_taglines.GR::patras: The Peloponnese's gateway port, home to Greece's largest cathedral and a Byzantine fortress from the 6th century.
places_taglines.GR::pylos: A harbour town tucked into the Mediterranean's largest natural bay, where a naval battle sealed a nation's freedom.
places_taglines.GR::methoni: A 9.3-hectare Venetian fortress rising from the sea, with an Ottoman tower standing guard on its own tiny island.
places_taglines.GR::kalamata: Capital of Messenia and the first city freed in 1821, world-famous for its PDO olives.
places_taglines.GR::areopoli: Gateway to the Deep Mani, where Petros Mavromichalis launched the War of Independence on 17 March 1821.
places_taglines.GR::olympia: Where the Olympic flame was first lit in 776 BC, beneath the shadow of one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

highlights: Olympia: site of the first known Olympic Games (776 BC), with a 64-metre Temple of Zeus and a chryselephantine statue — one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World
Methoni: a 9.3-hectare Venetian fortress built after 1209, with the Ottoman Bourtzi tower standing on a tiny island facing the sea
Battle of Navarino (1827): 27 Allied warships destroyed 80–90 Ottoman vessels in the Bay of Pylos — the turning point of Greek independence
Diros Caves: 14,700 m of mapped galleries, a boat ride along an underground river, stalactites reaching 71 m below the surface
Cape Tainaron: the southernmost point of mainland Greece, ancient gateway to the Underworld, ruins of a Temple of Poseidon

itineraries.title: Sporades Trip: Skiathos, Skopelos and Alonissos
itineraries.subtitle: From the beaches of Skiathos to the Mamma Mia filming locations on Skopelos, and on to the Alonissos marine park, home to Mediterranean monk seals - 6 days in the unspoilt Sporades.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with temperatures of 22–28°C and pleasant sea temperatures. Avoid July–August (intense heat of 30–35°C, crowds) and November–March (frequent rain, closures). Refreshing meltemi winds in summer.
specialties: Astakomakaronada — lobster spaghetti in fresh tomato sauce
Skopelos plums — PDO-recognised, sun-dried or preserved in syrup
Tsipouro — grape-marc spirit, the Sporades' drink of choice
Tyrokafteri — spicy whipped feta with roasted red peppers
Monk-produced wine, olive oil and honey from Evangelistria monastery

visits.text: Skiathos town is a lively little capital whose cobbled lanes wind their way down to the double harbour. It's the most tourist-oriented island in the Sporades — in summer the atmosphere is cosmopolitan and the nightlife is intense, with bars open until dawn on Papadiamanti Street. If you prefer peace and quiet, avoid July–August or arrive in the morning to see the sights before the influx of cruise ships.

The Bourtzi peninsula, linked to the old harbour by a short footbridge, holds a 13th-century Venetian fortification built by the Ghisi brothers to defend the island from pirates. Century-old trees cover the headland, making it a pleasant spot in the evening — concerts are sometimes held here in summer. The view across both harbours of Skiathos from the tip of the peninsula is one of the most photogenic on the island.

Evangelistria Monastery, founded in the 18th century on a hillside 4 km above town, is the most historically charged site on Skiathos. It was here, in September 1807, that the first Greek flag — a white cross on a blue field — was designed, woven, blessed and raised in the presence of the revolutionary hero Theodoros Kolokotronis. The monks who still live in the monastery produce wine, olive oil and honey. The museum housed in the old olive press displays the loom that, according to tradition, was used to weave that first flag. Take the marked trail from town rather than the road — it's more enjoyable and shorter.

Kastro is the former fortified capital of Skiathos, perched on a rocky headland in the north of the island. The inhabitants took refuge here in the 14th century to escape pirate raids and only moved back down to the coast after Greek independence, in 1829. A few churches still cling to the cliffs, including the chapel of the Nativity of Christ, along with a striking view over the Aegean Sea. It can be reached on foot (3 km of track, then a path) or by boat from the port. By car from the overnight stop, the road ends before the site: the last stretch is done on foot.

The Papadiamantis Museum, at number 12 on the street of the same name near the port, occupies the birthplace of Alexandros Papadiamantis, Greece's greatest 19th-century novelist, born on Skiathos in 1851. The two-storey house retains its period interior virtually intact: original furniture, personal library, everyday objects. The cave known as the 'Murderess's Cave' near Lalaria takes its name from one of Papadiamantis's short stories. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30 am to 1:30 pm and 5:15 pm to 8 pm.

activities.text: Papadiamanti Street, the main artery of Skiathos town, is the hub of local life in the evening: craft shops, tavernas with outdoor tables, and ouzo bars. Stroll along it from 7 pm when the locals start to come out — the summer crowds don't descend until after 9 pm. It's also the best spot to order a mezze platter: taramosalata, tyrokafteri, grilled octopus.

Astakomakaronada, the signature dish of the Sporades, is spaghetti with fresh lobster in a lightly spiced tomato sauce. You'll find it at almost every taverna along Skiathos's old harbour — ask whether the lobster was caught that day, as the fishermen deliver directly in the morning. It's one of the island's best combinations of quality and freshness.

Tsipouro, a Greek spirit distilled from grape pomace, is the Sporades' drink of choice. On Skiathos it's served cold, in small glasses, alongside mezze — grilled octopus, feta, marinated olives. The monks at Evangelistria produce an artisanal version available from the monastery shop.

visits.text: Koukounaries, around twenty minutes' drive from the overnight stop, is the picture-postcard beach of Skiathos - ranked among the most beautiful in Greece, with 1,200 metres of fine golden sand edged by an Aleppo pine forest protected under Greek law. Behind the beach lies the wetland of Lake Strofilia, a refuge for rare migratory bird species such as swans and herons. In high season, sunbeds are snapped up early in the morning - arrive before 9am or come in the late afternoon.

Lalaria is Skiathos's show-stopping beach: reachable only by boat from the old harbour, it curves in a half-moon of round white pebbles beneath sheer limestone cliffs that plunge into water of an almost unreal blue-green. A natural arch carved into the rock is the focal point of every photograph of the island. Boats run daily from the port, but if the northerly winds pick up the crossing is cancelled. Bring water and food — there's nothing on site.

The sea caves near Lalaria are every bit as worthwhile as the beach itself. The Blue Cave (Galazia) owes its name to the extraordinary colour of the water inside when the sun hits — reflections off the limestone walls produce an almost supernatural blue glow. The Dark Cave (Skotini), roughly 20 metres long, can only be entered by small boat because the opening is so narrow. Most excursions to Lalaria include a visit to these caves.

Troulos, 8 km west of town, is a family-friendly beach with shallow water and a quiet atmosphere. Pines reach down to the sand, and a few tavernas serve grilled fish. Facing it is the cluster of Troulonisia islets. It's the ideal beach with children if Koukounaries feels too crowded.

activities.text: Book a half-day boat trip from Skiathos old harbour to Lalaria and the sea caves — it's the simplest and most enjoyable way to get there. Departures are usually at 9 am or 10 am. In July–August, book the day before: places sell out fast. Options include swimming and snorkelling stops in coves that are impossible to reach on foot.

Revithada, a thick soup of chickpeas slow-baked with olive oil, onion and herbs, is a vegetarian dish from the Sporades often served on Sundays in tavernas. It's a reheated winter dish, though some inns keep it on the menu year-round. With country bread and olives on the side, it makes a complete and very inexpensive lunch.

Retsina is a Greek white wine infused with resin, made according to a tradition stretching back millennia — pine resin once prevented oxidation in amphorae. Its distinctive, slightly terpenic taste pairs perfectly with grilled fish and mezze. It's the cheapest and most authentic bottle you'll be served in the tavernas of the Sporades.

visits.text: Skopelos town is built amphitheatre-style around a deep bay — white houses with red-brown tile roofs tumble down toward the harbour in a setting the filming of Mamma Mia made famous worldwide. The town alone counts 123 Orthodox churches and chapels — nearly as many as days in the year — some dating back to the Byzantine era. Wander the cobbled alleys of the upper town: no two facades are alike.

The Kastro of Skopelos, on the hill above the harbour, is the highest point in town. The Venetian and Byzantine ruins here offer the best panoramic view over the bay, the ferries coming and going, and, on a clear day, the outline of Alonissos on the horizon. Head up towards the end of the day: the light is ideal and the atmosphere calmer than at midday.

The chapel of Agios Ioannis Kastri is perched on top of a sheer rock that drops into the sea, in the north of the island of Skopelos, near the village of Glossa, around 30 km from the overnight stop, a 45-minute drive. To reach it from the car park below, you have to climb 106 steps cut into the rock. This is where the outdoor wedding scenes of the film Mamma Mia were shot in 2007. Arrive early in the morning or after 5pm to avoid the groups of fans who turn up all day long in summer. The view over the Aegean Sea and Alonissos is worth the detour even if you have never seen the film.

The village of Glossa, perched in the hills of Skopelos, around 24 km from the overnight stop, a 40-minute drive, is one of the best-preserved mountain villages in the Sporades. Its Macedonian architecture - overhanging roofs, stone houses, a square shaded by plane trees - contrasts with the white Cycladic houses of the rest of the island. The inhabitants still grow olive and plum trees here. The central square with its cafés is an ideal place to stop on the way to the chapel of Agios Ioannis.

activities.text: The kalderimi trails — old paved paths that once linked Skopelos's monasteries — are the best way to explore the island's wooded interior. The route to the 18th-century Evangelismos Monastery on Mount Palouki passes through a pine forest with panoramic sea views. Set off in the morning to avoid the heat and bring water.

The tyropita on Skopelos is different from the one you know: here, local cheese — a fresh, lightly salted sheep's-milk cheese — is wrapped in homemade puff pastry, not industrially produced filo. It's the island's breakfast speciality, sold in bakeries from 7 am. Don't leave without eating one hot, straight from the oven.

Skopelos plums are recognised for their geographical origin and are the island's agricultural pride. Family orchards produce plums preserved in syrup, sun-dried, or turned into liqueur. You'll find these products in the shops around town — they're the best edible souvenir to bring home from Skopelos.

visits.text: Panormos is a sheltered seaside village tucked into a natural bay, with a fine-sand beach fringed by pines. It's a very pleasant stop for recreational boaters, and its waterfront tavernas serve fresh fish in a peaceful setting. Less crowded than the beaches in the south of the island, it's the perfect spot for lunch by the water.

The beaches of Kastani and Milia are two of the most recognisable Mamma Mia filming locations. Kastani, in particular, hosted the longest scene in the film. These two coves - pebbles or sand depending on the spot, turquoise water, a pine forest running down to the shore - are among the most beautiful on Skopelos, quite apart from their cinematic fame. Milia is windier and ideal for snorkelling. Kastani lies around 15 km from the overnight stop, a 25-minute drive, and Milia just before it on the same road.

The Sendoukia are an archaeological mystery in the hills of Skopelos: four large sarcophagi cut straight into the rock at the top of a hill, linked by local legend to the Greek pirate Glaucus, who is said to have ruled these seas. Their dating and exact purpose are still debated by archaeologists. You drive up from the overnight stop, the last part on a dirt track, to the start of the path, then it is around a 15-minute walk along a waymarked trail. The view from the site alone is worth the effort.

activities.text: The ideal day on the west coast of Skopelos: set off by car in the morning for Panormos and a coffee by the sea, head down to Milia for a swim, then on to Kastani for the afternoon. Finish at the small cove of Hovolo, around thirty minutes' drive from the overnight stop, which is less crowded, with flat rocks perfect for snorkelling. Boat hire companies in Skopelos town also offer small motorboats for exploring these coves on your own.

practical_info.advice: Pack a picnic for Hovolo — there's no taverna on site

activities.text: Astakos — lobster simply grilled with lemon and olive oil — is served at the fishermen's tavernas in Panormos and at small harbours like Agnontas. Ask whether it was caught that morning: Skopelos fishermen have a reputation for delivering straight to the local tavernas. Pair it with garlic-rubbed toasted bread.

Loukoumades — small, light doughnuts fried to order, drizzled with honey and sprinkled with walnuts and cinnamon — are the street dessert of the Sporades. You'll find them at the kiosks on Skopelos town's harbour from 6 pm. They're hot, crisp on the outside and airy inside. Eat them standing up with sticky fingers, the way the locals do.

visits.text: Patitiri, the port of Alonissos, takes its name (“wine press”) from the island's viticultural past. Rebuilt after the 1965 earthquake, it's a functional and endearing town with a paved waterfront, a few seafood tavernas, and above all the MOm Information Centre on the Mediterranean monk seal — a small educational centre with videos and infographics about the species and the challenges facing the marine park. Don't miss it if you have children or want to understand what you'll see on boat excursions.

The Chora — also known as Palia Alonissos or the Old Village — sits at 200 metres above sea level on a ridge overlooking the entire island. Abandoned after the 1965 earthquake that partly destroyed it, it was gradually restored from the 1970s onward by artists and lovers of authenticity. Today its cobbled lanes lined with whitewashed, blue-shuttered houses, cascading bougainvillea and 360° panoramas over the Aegean make it the most captivating spot on Alonissos. Come in the late afternoon for sunset from the taverna terraces — it's one of the quietest spectacles in all the Sporades.

The Alonissos National Marine Park, established in 1992, is Greece's first marine park and one of the largest in Europe, covering 251,440 hectares encompassing Alonissos, six smaller islands and 22 islets. It was created to protect the Mediterranean monk seal (Monachus monachus), the most endangered seal species on earth. The park's colony numbers between 50 and 60 individuals — roughly 10% of the 500 to 600 still alive worldwide. The core zone around the island of Piperi is strictly off-limits to visitors in order to safeguard breeding sites. The areas accessible on excursions, however, offer the chance to spot dolphins, sea turtles, and more than 300 fish species.

Kokkinokastro is a striking spot on the east coast of Alonissos: a pebble beach in shades of rust and ochre beneath cliffs of the same hue, coloured by oxidised iron in the rock. Remains of an ancient settlement and traces of Neolithic occupation have been found here. The colour of the soil makes a dramatic contrast against the blue of the sea — it's one of the most visually arresting sights on the island.

activities.text: The boat excursion through the marine park is the centrepiece of any visit to Alonissos. Departures are from Patitiri, with several options: a full-park trip (6 to 8 hours) taking in the islands of Kyra Panagia and Peristera, swimming stops in exceptionally clear water, and sometimes dolphin sightings. Spotting a monk seal remains rare and depends on luck — but even without one, the quality of the water and the beauty of the deserted islets make the trip more than worthwhile. Book ahead in July–August.

Since 2015, Alonissos has banned single-use plastic bags across the whole island - a pioneering decision in Greece that reflects the eco-minded identity of its people. If you want to find out more about this commitment and about the protection of the monk seal, drop into the information centre run by the organisation MOm in Patitiri: the team and volunteers explain the threats facing the species and the marine environment, and what can be done to help protect them.

Tyrokafteri is a dip of crushed feta blended with spicy red peppers and olive oil — creamy, punchy, with a hint of sweetness. On Alonissos it's served as a starter with slices of toasted bread to open every taverna meal. Order it with a glass of ice-cold tsipouro and olives marinated in the island's wild herbs for an aperitif that's thoroughly local.

seo.h1_title: Sporades Trip: Skiathos, Skopelos and Alonissos
seo.intro_paragraph: Start with Skiathos and its 60 beaches - Koukounaries with its golden sand beneath the pines, Lalaria with its white pebbles below limestone cliffs, reachable only by boat. Cross over to Skopelos to climb the 106 steps to the chapel of Agios Ioannis, the iconic Mamma Mia setting, and discover the mountain villages known for their PDO plums. End on Alonissos, the wildest island in the Sporades, where 50 Mediterranean monk seals live in the marine park.
seo.seo_hook: Sixty pine-backed beaches on Skiathos, Mamma Mia scenery on Skopelos, monk seals in the marine park of Alonissos — the Sporades in 6 days.
featured_list: Skiathos: Lalaria and its blue caves, accessible by boat
Evangelistria Monastery: where the first Greek flag was raised
Skopelos: the chapel of Agios Ioannis and its 106 rock-cut steps
Alonissos: a 251,000-hectare marine park, a refuge for monk seals

places_taglines.GR::skiathos: Sixty beaches under the pines, where nightlife and history share one small island
places_taglines.GR::skopelos: The greenest island in the Sporades, famed for Mamma Mia and its 300 whitewashed chapels
places_taglines.GR::alonissos: A wild island at the heart of Europe's largest marine park, where monk seals still roam

highlights: Lalaria, Skiathos: boat-access only — arrive early or in the late afternoon
Evangelistria Monastery: birthplace of the first Greek flag (1807), monk-produced wine
Agios Ioannis Kastri: 106 rock-cut steps — beat the midday crowds in summer
Alonissos Marine Park: 6–8 hr excursion from Patitiri, booking essential in high season

itineraries.title: Thessaly & Meteora
itineraries.subtitle: From Volos and the Pelion peninsula to the cliff-hanging monasteries of Meteora, this 6-day circuit crosses Thessaly from the Aegean coast to the inland plains — through mountain villages, rock pillars, and a hidden lake.
itineraries.notes: This itinerary requires a car — Pelion is poorly served by public transport. Expect winding roads through the Pelion massif and around Lake Plastiras. Strict dress code at the Meteora monasteries: shoulders and knees must be covered.
itineraries.climate: Best period: April-May and September-October, temperatures 18-26°C, ideal for visiting Meteora. Avoid July-August: scorching heat in the Thessalian plain (35-40°C) and in Kalambaka makes monastery visits exhausting. Winter can bring cold and snow to Meteora.

visits.text: Volos stretches between the sea and the first slopes of Pelion - a setting that gives it a character of its own in Greece. Start with the Athanasakeion Archaeological Museum, built in 1909 thanks to the fortune of Alexios Athanasakis, a Pelion merchant who made his money in Egypt. The collection will surprise you: the painted funerary stelae of ancient Demetrias, their colours still vivid, are an absolute rarity in Greece - the pigments survived because the stelae were buried. You will also see Neolithic pieces from the sites of Dimini and Sesklo, located less than 15 km from the town.

The old Palia quarter, a former Byzantine fortress fortified in the 4th century, grew around the port from the 19th century onwards. The Ottomans held it from 1423 until the liberation of Volos in 1881 — nearly 460 years. Behind the train station, the Volos City Museum occupies the former Papantou tobacco warehouse (1920), restored in 2014: the glass floor on the first level reveals 6th–7th-century water channels beneath your feet. The building alone is worth a visit for its industrial architecture.

activities.text: In the evening, Volos reveals its true self through its tsipouradika — tsipouro bars, named after the local grape spirit, where you eat mezze while sipping slowly. It's an institution here: Volos is widely regarded as the Greek capital of tsipouro. The waterfront (Argonauts' promenade) is packed with these places, at their best around aperitif hour. The city owes its mythological name to Iolcos, from where Jason and the Argonauts are said to have set sail in search of the Golden Fleece — a myth that looms over the entire region.

practical_info.tip: Tsipouradika serve free mezze with each glass of tsipouro — the tradition is that you don't order food separately. Arrive early to grab a seaside terrace table

visits.text: Portaria, 13 km from Volos, is the first village on western Pelion — its nickname "lady of welcome" is well earned: centuries-old plane trees, fountains, stone houses with carved wooden balconies. During Ottoman rule (15th–19th c.), Pelion was a refuge for Greek intellectuals fleeing Constantinople and for merchants who traded freely with Europe. That era left behind exceptional architecture, libraries, and secret schools in every village.

Makrinitsa - “the balcony of Pelion” - lives up to its reputation. At 650 m above sea level, its cobbled lanes open onto a main square with a view over Volos, the Pagasetic Gulf and, on clear days, the Sporades islands. The 18th-century houses of local stone, with projecting upper floors in carved wood, are among the best preserved in Greece. On the square stands the church of Agios Ioannis Prodromos (St John the Baptist). The fountain with four lion heads from 1809, known as the “Spring of Immortal Water”, still flows. Allow at least 2 hours to wander.

The Topali house museum, built in 1844 and now the Folklore Museum, is a dive into the bourgeois life of Pelion: furniture, jewellery, costumes, weapons and mountain utensils. Take the opportunity to also visit the church of Agia Magdalini (1737) with its icons and wall paintings - the interior is unexpectedly rich for such a small village.

activities.text: The shops of Makrinitsa sell local produce from Pelion - mountain herbs, honey, preserves of local fruit (apples, chestnuts), liqueurs, handmade pasta. Try the spicy Pelion sausage and mountain tea (tsai tou vounou) in a taverna with a view over the bay. It is a distinctly Thessalian food experience - far removed from the tourist spots of the islands.

practical_info.tip: Cars aren't allowed into Makrinitsa — park at the large car park at the village entrance (5 min walk). The village is pedestrian out of necessity, not as a tourist gimmick

visits.text: Tsagarada, on Pelion's east side facing the Aegean, is one of the most beautiful villages on the peninsula. Its central square is dominated by a plane tree that locals say is over 1,000 years old — its circumference exceeds 14 m and its shade covers half the square. It was under this tree that villagers gathered for centuries to hold the agora, settle village affairs, and debate politics. Have your morning coffee here, facing the Aegean Sea glimpsed between the trees — it's one of the finest terraces in Greece.

Damouchari, below Tsagarada, is one of those tiny Pelion harbours that look like a postcard of the ideal Mediterranean: a bay split in two by a headland topped with the ruins of a medieval castle, fish tavernas right on the jetty, water so clear you can see the bottom at 5 metres. Several scenes from the film "Mamma Mia" were shot here — the producers didn't have to look far.

activities.text: Mylopotamos beach, reached from Tsagarada via 7 km of side road followed by a 15–20 minute walk along a forest trail, is one of the most beautiful on the Greek mainland: white sand, rocks splitting the beach into two coves, turquoise water, and pine trees reaching down to the shore. The walk through Pelion's dense forest is as good as the beach itself. Plan on spending the afternoon — the descent is easy, the climb back takes a good 30 minutes of effort.

practical_info.tip: Bring water and food — there's nothing at the beach off-season. In July–August, sunbed vendors set up on the sand

activities.text: The inter-village trails of Pelion (monopatia) are paved with grey schist slabs and date largely from the Ottoman period — they connected villages when there were no roads. The Damouchari–Tsagarada section (roughly 45 minutes one way) is one of the finest: dense forest, waterfalls, and sea views. The trail is waymarked and manageable for everyone.

practical_info.tip: Closed shoes recommended — the slabs can be slippery in wet weather

visits.text: Arriving in Kalambaka from the Thessalian plain, the Meteora pillars appear without warning — conglomerate columns rising 400 m above the town, as if the ground had been punched upward from below. These geological formations took shape during the Tertiary period: a river flowing into the Thessalian sea deposited pebbles cemented by sand over millions of years, creating these “pudding stones” later sculpted by erosion. The first hermits took refuge on them in the 10th century. The Great Meteoron, the first monastery built in 1382 by the monk Athanasios, is also the largest: it has never been empty since its founding. Before going in, look at the pulley systems still in place — until the early 20th century, monks were hauled up in nets by hand. Allow 30 minutes to climb the 200 steps carved into the rock.

The Monastery of Varlaam, founded in 1517, is often the favourite of returning visitors: more intimate than the Great Meteoron, it offers spectacular valley views from its terraces and houses an impressive capstan system with a still-visible storage net. Note the 16th-century frescoes in the main church — the martyrdom scenes display a level of anatomical precision that's unsettling for the era.

Roussanou is a convent of the Météores, perched on a 60 m rock pillar and linked to the cliff by a footbridge. Founded in the 16th century, it was restored and reoccupied by nuns in 1988. The interior is very beautiful: 16th-century frescoes in the main church, a flower garden hanging over the void. If you only visit three, make them the Grand Météore, Varlaam and Roussanou.

activities.text: Stay in Kastraki rather than Kalambaka for the night — this tiny village sits 2 km from the monasteries, right at the foot of the pillars. Sunset from the viewpoints above Kastraki paints the rocks orange and pink — it's one of the most photographed sights in Greece, and it's free. Stay until nightfall if you can.

practical_info.tip: Strict dress code at all monasteries: shoulders and knees must be covered. Cover-up garments are sometimes lent at the entrance, but don't count on it. Bring cash for admission fees

visits.text: The Monastery of the Holy Trinity (Agias Triados) is the most dramatically positioned of all: it rises on a completely isolated pillar, reachable only by 140 steps carved through a tunnel in the rock. This is where the final scene of "For Your Eyes Only" (James Bond, 1981) was filmed — the producers needed a location impossible to access from below, and they found it. The view from the terrace spans the entire Pinios valley.

Agios Stefanos is the most accessible monastery - no steps, just a footbridge. For this reason, it often welcomes visitors with reduced mobility. Its museum houses a collection of liturgical embroidery and vestments from the 14th to the 19th century, remarkably well preserved.

The monastery of Agios Nikolaos Anapafsas, founded in the 15th century, preserves outstanding frescoes by Theophanes the Cretan (1527), one of the great masters of late Byzantine painting. If you can only visit one monastery for its frescoes, come here.

activities.text: A day on foot is the other way to experience Meteora. The Kalambaka–Great Meteoron–Varlaam circuit takes about 3 hours of walking and passes through forest at the base of the cliffs, with constantly shifting views of the pillars. The trails (monopatia) are waymarked from the village of Kastraki — far less busy than the paved roads between the monasteries. Bring plenty of water in summer.

practical_info.tip: Set off early in the morning — tour groups arrive between 9 and 11 am. At dawn, mist sometimes clings to the pillars for a one-of-a-kind spectacle

visits.text: Trikala is little known to foreign travellers — which makes it one of the best "real" towns in Thessaly. The Byzantine fortress on the hill above the city has ancient origins: this is the site of the Sanctuary of Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine whose mythical birthplace was Trikala. The current fortress dates from the 4th century, with later Byzantine and Ottoman modifications. The Ottoman clock tower, still standing at the eastern corner, has become the symbol of the city.

The Varousi quarter, at the foot of the fortress, is the old Ottoman neighbourhood with its narrow lanes, overhanging houses, and old churches. The Asclepieion of Trikala — the remains of the ancient healing sanctuary dedicated to Asclepius — is visible in the park below the fortress. The Koursoum Mosque (16th c.), one of the best preserved in Greece, stands in the lower town — it's no longer active but its Ottoman architecture is remarkable.

On the banks of the Litheos river, the Matsopoulos mill (19th century) is a singular industrial monument: built of imposing stone, it is still standing. The footbridge across the Litheos opposite the mill is the locals' favourite meeting place in the evening - with views of the water and the lights of the old town.

activities.text: Trikala is known for its spiced sausage (loukaniko Trikalinon) seasoned with herbs from nearby Mount Koziakas, its mountain feta cheese, and its tsipouro. The tavernas in the centre are affordable and packed with locals — a welcome break after the tourist prices of Kalambaka. The Tuesday morning market in the lower town draws producers from across the region.

practical_info.tip: Trikala is 20 km from Kalambaka and deserves a proper half-day. It's often overlooked in favour of Meteora, but its lively centre and Ottoman quarter are the real deal

visits.text: Lake Plastiras — a 25 km² artificial lake created in the 1950s by damming the Tavropos river — has every appearance of a natural Alpine lake: clear blue water, fir and oak forests along the banks, the Agrafa mountains as a backdrop. The 70 km loop road around the lake connects villages perched between 850 and 1,000 m altitude. Neochori, the largest (500 inhabitants), offers a spectacular lake view from its belvedere — and a few decent tavernas.

The Monastery of Panagia Pelekiti is one of the strangest attractions in the area: it's literally carved into the vertical cliff face overlooking the lake. Construction began in the late 15th century and was completed in 1529. Its vertiginous position is comparable to the Meteora monasteries — only much smaller and far less visited. The access path winds along the rocks above the lake.

Morfovouni, a mountain village built like an amphitheatre north of the lake, is home to a small museum dedicated to General Nikolaos Plastiras - the man who commissioned the construction of the dam in the 1950s and after whom the lake is named. Plastiras was born in this village in 1883 and wanted to protect his native region from seasonal floods.

activities.text: The lake is ideal for kayaking and canoeing — calm waters and wooded banks. Local operators rent out boats from the lakeside villages, particularly Kalyvia Pezoula. The atmosphere is a world away from the coastal beaches: quiet, uncrowded, with nothing but wind in the fir trees for company. If you're here in spring, the seasonal waterfalls in the Megalo Rema gorge are worth a detour.

practical_info.tip: The best time for Lake Plastiras is spring (April–May) and autumn (October) — in summer the water warms up and the level drops. Some hotels close off-season

visits.text: Messenikolas, nicknamed "the balcony of Thessaly", is built in an amphitheatre on a promontory with views in two directions: on one side Lake Plastiras, on the other the Thessalian plain. With fewer than 500 inhabitants, the village has kept its traditional stone houses and an end-of-the-world atmosphere. It's also the starting point for the Megalo Rema gorge, a moderate-level hike through a narrow ravine.

Fylakti, a viewpoint village on the southern shore, offers one of the finest panoramas on the circuit. From its square, the winding dam road is visible below — a 1950s structure that's still impressive, passable by car in a single lane. The Tavropos Dam is the engineering feat that created this entire landscape: 82 m high, 275 m long.

activities.text: Drive the full loop around the lake (70 km) at your own pace, stopping at the viewpoints and villages that appeal to you. Morning is the best time - the low light on the lake is perfect and the roads are empty. Finish in Karditsa for lunch: the town is a lively farming market, and its tavernas serve game from the Agrafa mountains - wild boar, roe deer - depending on the season. From Karditsa, the road to Volos (1.5 hours) makes for an easy return to the airport.

practical_info.tip: Volos is 100 km from Karditsa (1h30). Larissa also has an airport and is 65 km away (45 min). Both are connected by expressway

seo.h1_title: Thessaly & Meteora
seo.intro_paragraph: This 6-day circuit through Thessaly starts in Volos, a port city at the foot of Mount Pelion, climbs through the peninsula's stone villages to the turquoise beaches of the east coast, then cuts across the plain to Meteora. The Byzantine monasteries suspended on their 400 m rock pillars, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, rank among the most striking sights on the Greek mainland. The trip ends around Lake Plastiras, an artificial lake ringed by fir forests and hilltop villages untouched by mass tourism.
seo.seo_hook: Pelion + UNESCO Meteora + Lake Plastiras: deep Thessaly, between sea, mountains, and suspended monasteries.
featured_list: Meteora: 6 active monasteries on 400 m rock pillars, the first founded in 1382, UNESCO-listed since 1988
Makrinitsa: the "balcony of Pelion", a stone village at 650 m with views over the Pagasetic Gulf
Tsagarada: a 1,000-year-old plane tree with a 14 m girth on the village's central square
Lake Plastiras: a 25 km² artificial lake created in the 1950s, surrounded by villages perched at 850–1,000 m

places_taglines.GR::volos: A Thessalian port at the foot of Mount Pelion, where the Argonauts are said to have set sail.
places_taglines.GR::makrinitsa: A stone village perched 650 m above the Pagasetic Gulf, known as the balcony of Thessaly.
places_taglines.GR::tsagarada: A Pelion village facing the Aegean, famous for its millennial plane tree and hidden coves below.
places_taglines.GR::kalambaka: A town dwarfed by the rock pillars of Meteora, gateway to the UNESCO Byzantine monasteries.
places_taglines.GR::trikala: A Thessalian riverside town, mythical birthplace of Asclepius the god of medicine.
places_taglines.GR::karditsa: A Thessalian market town, launching point for Lake Plastiras and the villages of Agrafa.

highlights: Meteora: 6 active Byzantine monasteries perched on 400 m rock pillars, UNESCO-listed since 1988
Pelion: 24 traditional stone villages with carved balconies, mythical home of the Centaurs, turquoise beaches accessible on foot
Volos: archaeological museum with the painted funerary stelae of Demetrias, unique in Greece
Lake Plastiras: 25 km² artificial lake nestled among the Agrafa mountains, villages perched at 850–1,000 m

itineraries.title: Epirus & Zagori: Gorges, Stone Villages and the River of the Underworld
itineraries.subtitle: A 6-day circuit through the heart of Epirus, taking in the Ottoman citadel of Ioannina, the 46 stone villages of Zagori, Vikos Canyon and the mythological Acheron River.
itineraries.notes: Zagori is a mountain region: winding roads, snow possible from October to May. Some villages (Vradeto, Papigo) are isolated—check road conditions in winter. Vikos Gorge is accessible from April to November.
itineraries.climate: Best time: May–June and September–October, 15 to 25°C in the mountains, ideal for hiking. Avoid July–August (scorching heat in Ioannina, up to 35°C) and November–April (snow in Zagori, mountain roads closed or difficult to navigate). Spring: spectacular flowering in the gorges.

visits.text: The Kastro of Ioannina is one of the few Byzantine fortresses in Greece still inhabited today. Originally built by Emperor Justinian in the 6th century on a rocky promontory overlooking Lake Pamvotis, it has been extensively remodeled by successive rulers—Byzantines, Normans, Serbs, Venetians, and Ottomans. Enter through the Agios Georgios gate, redesigned by the Ottomans in 1843; to your left stands Bohemond of Taranto's tower, built by the Norman crusader in 1082. Allow at least two hours to lose yourself in the cobbled lanes.

Inside the Its Kale citadel, the Fethiye Mosque (“of the Conquest”) was built when the Ottomans captured Ioannina in 1430, then renovated by Ali Pasha in 1795. Next to it stands the tomb of Ali Pasha, a tyrant as charismatic as he was formidable, who ruled an independent quasi-state covering much of Greece and Albania from 1787 to 1822—and who was assassinated by the sultan himself. Macabre detail: only his body is buried here; his severed head was sent to Constantinople as proof of his death.

The Aslan Pasha Mosque, built in 1618 by an Albanian pasha, has housed the Ethnographic Museum of Ioannina since 1933. For centuries, Jews, Christians, and Muslims coexisted in Ioannina—the city's Romaniote Jewish community was one of the oldest in Greece. The museum presents artifacts from these communities, including liturgical objects from the nearby synagogue, almost entirely destroyed during the Occupation.

activities.text: From the quay at Mavili Square, ferries depart every 15 minutes to Nissi, the lake island (10-minute crossing). Walk through its peaceful lanes lined with tavernas serving lake trout, then visit the Agios Panteleimon monastery where Ali Pasha met his death in 1822—the monks had hidden him in his ground-floor room when the sultan's troops surrounded the island. The adjacent museum reconstructs his life and death.

practical_info.tip: Ferries run every 15 min from 8am to midnight in summer. Try the lake trout in the island tavernas.

activities.text: In the evening, stroll through the shopping streets of the old town around the Kastro: Ioannina has been the capital of Epirote gold- and silversmithing for centuries—this is where Sotirios Voulgaris, founder of Bulgari, was born. Silver shops still line the alleyways. End the evening on the lakeside terraces, with views of the illuminated Kastro and its reflections in the water.

visits.text: The site of Dodona lies 22 km south of Ioannina and is well worth the drive. It's one of the oldest oracular sanctuaries in Greece, dedicated to Zeus and the mother goddess Dione—its oracle was renowned throughout the Greek world as early as the 6th century BC, long before Delphi. Priests interpreted the will of the gods through the rustling leaves of a sacred oak tree. The theater, which could seat 25,000 spectators, is one of the largest in Greece. The site is remarkably uncrowded—you'll likely have it to yourself outside July-August.

Perama Cave, 4 km from central Ioannina, was discovered by chance in 1940 by locals seeking shelter during the bombings. It extends for 1 km in length over an area of 14,800 m², with chambers whose ceilings are covered in stalactites and stalagmites formed over 1.5 million years. The bones of a cave bear from the Pleistocene era were found inside.

activities.text: The Archaeological Museum of Ioannina, housed in Litharitsia Park, presents a collection covering all of Epirus from prehistory to the Roman era. Don't miss the objects from Dodona—bronze tablets engraved with questions posed to the oracle, votive figurines, and coins from the time of Pyrrhus, the king of Epirus whose costly victories against Rome gave the expression “Pyrrhic victory” its meaning.

practical_info.tip: Closed on Tuesdays.

activities.text: In the evening, enjoy the buzz of Ioannina: the city is home to several universities whose medical and humanities faculties rank among the best in Greece. The streets of Anexartisias and Kallari, between the old Bazaar quarter and the lake shores, come alive after 9 pm. Sample Ioannina's baklava—the city is one of the Greek capitals of this pastry made with phyllo dough and pistachios.

visits.text: Monodendri perches at 1,060 meters altitude at the southern entrance to the Vikos Gorge. The Agia Paraskevi monastery, clinging to the cliff face 800 m from the village via a paved path, was built in 1412 by local lord Michael Therianos in gratitude to the saint for curing his daughter. From its terraces, the gorge floor—900 meters below—stares straight back at you. Take care: there's no guardrail at the precipice edge.

The Oxia viewpoint, 7.5 km north of the village via a drivable track, offers the best view of the gorge from the Monodendri side. On the way, you pass through the 'stone forest'—a field of limestone columns eroded over millennia, some reaching several meters high. Once at the viewpoint, you gaze straight down into the vertiginous chasm: the narrowest point of the gorge is barely a few hundred meters wide and over 1,000 m deep.

activities.text: For a first look at the gorge without crossing it in full, follow the trail down from Monodendri to the floor of Vikos Gorge along the old kalderimi (paved path). The descent takes 1 hour 30 minutes and lets you see the limestone walls from the bottom of the canyon. Returning by the same path is more demanding: save some energy for the climb back to Monodendri. The turquoise Voidomatis springs are not halfway down this short descent, but toward the village of Vikos.

practical_info.tip: Bring water. No mobile signal at the canyon floor.

activities.text: Late in the day, wander the lanes of Monodendri and neighboring villages Vitsa and Ano Pedina. All houses are built from local stone and roofed with stone slabs—Zagori's designation as a national historical monument prohibits any other materials. Tavernas serve pites (savory pies) with wild mountain mushrooms and grilled local lamb.

visits.text: Vikos Gorge is listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the world's deepest canyon relative to its width: 20 km long, with walls reaching 1,000 meters and a width sometimes reduced to a few hundred meters. The classic trail descends from Monodendri to the village of Vikos—allow 5 to 7 hours depending on your pace. Vikos-Aoos National Park, which encompasses it, is a UNESCO geopark home to more than 1,800 plant species and 186 bird species, including golden eagles and griffon vultures.

The Vradeto steps, starting from Kapesovo, are a masterpiece of engineering: roughly 1,100 steps carved into the cliff face of the Mezaria canyon over a 400-meter elevation gain. Until 1970, this was the only access to the village of Vradeto, perched at 1,340 meters—the highest village in Zagori. The ascent takes 45 minutes to an hour and offers increasingly spectacular views of the gorge.

activities.text: The full crossing of Vikos Gorge from Monodendri to the village of Vikos is one of Greece's great hikes. The O12 trail is marked but requires good physical fitness and hiking boots. Once on the gorge floor, you walk between forest-covered limestone walls. Stop at the karst springs of the Voidomatis: the water emerges from the limestone in an unreal shade of turquoise blue. A return transfer can be arranged from the village of Vikos.

practical_info.tip: Bring minimum 2L of water. No mobile signal in the canyon. Arrange return from Vikos (transfer or taxi).

visits.text: Megalo Papigo and Mikro Papigo are the two most photographed villages in Zagori, separated by 3 km along a hiking trail. Their cobbled lanes, houses built of stone and roofed with stone slabs, and century-old plane trees on the central square are perfect examples of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Epirote architecture. Look up and you'll see the Astraka Towers dominating the landscape—vertical limestone columns connecting the summit of Mount Tymfi (2,497 m) to Vikos Gorge.

Near Kipi, the Kalogeriko (or Plakidas) Bridge is Zagori's emblematic three-arched bridge; plan a day trip from Papigo. Built in 1814 by Abbot Seraphim of the local monastery to replace a wooden bridge, it spans the watercourse over a length of 56 meters and a height of 6.7 meters. Seen from the surrounding hills, its three successive arches resemble a moving caterpillar—a nickname that has stuck. A few minutes away, Kokkoris Bridge, built in 1750, is framed by two sheer rock faces: the region's most spectacular setting.

activities.text: Between Megalo and Mikro Papigo, the trail connecting the two villages passes by the Ovires (or Kolymbithres)—natural pools carved into the limestone rock by the Rogovo River. Legend has it that Ali Pasha himself came here to bathe. In summer, the water is cool and the cascading pools offer a unique swim. The trail makes an easy loop through both villages in 2 hours.

practical_info.tip: The pools are well-filled in spring and early June. In summer, water levels can be low—morning is best.

activities.text: For this excursion, plan a day trip there and back from Papigo to Kipi, then walk the bridge circuit (10 km, 3 hours) to discover six arched bridges in a single outing. The Kipi and Koukouli area has the highest concentration of stone bridges in all of Zagori - every configuration is represented: one, two and three arches. These bridges were the only connection between the villages until the first paved roads arrived in the 1950s.

practical_info.tip: Easy and well-marked. Bring water, limited shade on some sections.

visits.text: Konitsa is built amphitheater-style on a Pindus slope, overlooking the confluence of the Aoos and Voidomatis rivers. Its stone bridge is one of the largest single-arch bridges in the Balkans: 20 meters high, with a span of nearly 40 meters, built between 1823 and 1871 by master mason Zioga Frontzo from the village of Pyrsoyianni. Cross it on foot—the wind blows hard at the arch's summit, and the masons hung a small bell underneath to keep rhythm during construction.

Panagia Stomiou Monastery lies upstream of Konitsa Bridge, clinging to the rock face at an altitude of 650 meters and accessible on foot along the Aoos Gorge trail. Built in 1774, it was inhabited for several decades by the monk Paisios, who lived there as a hermit before moving to Mount Athos. The trail leading to it follows the turquoise river through a magnificent setting—swimmers bathe there in summer; the water is icy and the current strong.

activities.text: The Aoos River below Konitsa is one of Europe's last wild rivers: clear water, a pebble bed and steep-sided gorges. From Konitsa's stone bridge, set out on foot along the trail entering the gorge toward Panagia Stomiou Monastery. The path lets you observe the cliffs, pebbles and riverside vegetation as you follow the river. Return along the same route to the bridge, choosing your turnaround point according to your fitness.

practical_info.tip: Booking recommended in July-August.

visits.text: The Acheron is one of the five rivers of the Underworld in Greek mythology and actually rises in Epirus. For the ancient Greeks, this river, which plunged into karst chasms before reappearing near the Ionian Sea, could only be the boundary between the world of the living and that of the dead. In the Odyssey, Homer sends Odysseus to consult it and question the seer Tiresias. The village of Glyki is the starting point for activities on the river; plan a day trip from Preveza.

At Mesopotamos, the ruins of the Necromanteion of Ephyra stand on a hill; plan a day trip from Preveza. Since 1958, the site has been identified as the oracle of the dead described by Homer in the Odyssey, although this identification remains disputed among archaeologists. According to this interpretation of the site, pilgrims descended into an underground labyrinth after purification rituals and sacrifices to “receive” the souls of their dead. The ruins from the 4th century BC are worth a visit, whatever interpretation is given to them.

activities.text: The hike through the Acheron Gorge starting from Glyki is one of Greece's most beautiful river hikes; plan a day trip from Preveza to reach Glyki. The trail follows the river for an 8 km round trip between limestone walls covered with plane trees and oleanders. The water is clear and cool—swimming is possible in the natural pools along the way. Operators also offer canoe descents from Glyki, which are less physically demanding and just as spectacular.

practical_info.tip: Bring a swimsuit—the pools in the gorge are perfect for swimming. Hiking shoes essential, the trail is wet in places.

visits.text: Nikopolis—“the city of victory”—was founded in 31 BC by Octavian Augustus on the very hill where he had pitched his camp during the naval Battle of Actium against Mark Antony and Cleopatra. It's the largest ancient city in Greece, covering 900 hectares. Its Victory Monument still bears anchor-shaped notches where bronze rams from ships captured from the enemy were set—it is said to have had 36 in all. This is also where Epictetus, the slave-philosopher founder of Stoicism, taught until AD 125.

The Archaeological Museum of Nikopolis, inaugurated in 2009, is an essential introduction before exploring the site. It presents collections chronologically: from the Battle of Actium to the city's abandonment. Don't miss the early Christian mosaics from the basilicas—some are of exceptional quality and exceptionally well preserved—and fragments of Augustus's votive inscription, 54 meters long.

activities.text: Preveza, 7 km south of Nikopolis, is a quietly charming Ionian port town. In the evening, the pedestrian Spiliadou street comes alive around its fish and seafood tavernas—the Ambracian Gulf before you is the same one where the fate of the Roman world was decided on September 2, 31 BC. Aktion airport is 20 km away, across the strait.

practical_info.tip: Aktion airport (PVK) serves several European cities in summer. Check schedules in advance.

seo.h1_title: Epirus & Zagori: Gorges, Stone Villages and the River of the Underworld
seo.intro_paragraph: Epirus is the Greece nobody knows: no islands, no postcard beaches, but breathtaking gorges, UNESCO-listed stone villages, a lake haunted by Ali Pasha, and the real River of the Underworld from Greek mythology. This 6-day route connects Ioannina to Preveza via Zagori and Vikos Gorge—listed in the Guinness Book as the world's deepest canyon relative to its width—before ending at the ruins of Nikopolis, the city founded by Augustus after his victory over Mark Antony.
seo.seo_hook: Ioannina, Vikos Gorge, the Acheron River and Nikopolis: 6 days in Epirus, the Greece nobody knows.
featured_list: Vikos Gorge: listed in the Guinness Book as the world's deepest canyon relative to its width
Ioannina: inhabited Byzantine citadel, lake island and the legend of Ali Pasha
Acheron: the mythological river of Hades that actually rises in Epirus
Nikopolis: founded by Augustus in 31 BC after his victory over Mark Antony, Greece's largest ancient city
