itineraries.title: Chios in 4 Days: Mastic Villages, Anavatos, and Nea Moni
itineraries.subtitle: Spend 4 days exploring from Chios Town to Nea Moni, Anavatos, the fortified mastic villages, and Volissos.
itineraries.notes: The Ottoman baths, Byzantine Museum, Mastic Museum, and Nea Moni museum are closed on Tuesdays, while Olympi Cave is closed on Mondays: start on a Wednesday or Thursday instead. The cave can only be visited from early May through late September.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with average highs of 20 to 26 °C and sea temperatures of 18 to 22 °C. In July–August, highs reach 28 °C: visit the mastic villages early in the morning and save the afternoon for the beach. From November to March, expect 11 to 16 °C and 8 to 12 rainy days per month.

visits.text: The most beautiful neighborhood in Chios Town is still inhabited behind its ramparts. The Kastro, a Byzantine citadel remodeled by the Genoese and then the Ottomans, is still home to about 650 residents, an Ottoman cemetery, and the tomb of Kara Ali Pasha, whose flagship Kanaris set ablaze in 1822. Enter through Porta Maggiore to the south, then look for the “dark dungeon” where seventy prominent citizens were held before their execution. Come in the morning, when the narrow streets are still shaded.

Circles of light fall from the dome onto marble benches: the Ottoman baths in the Kastro have retained the dim atmosphere of a hammam. Dating to the 18th century, they form the citadel’s largest hammam, with ten rooms covering 365 m², and their restoration was completed in 2012; the foundations still reveal how hot air circulated. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. except Tuesdays: stop by before lunch.

Orthodox icons beneath the dome of a mosque: the Byzantine Museum of Chios occupies the former Mecidiye Mosque on Vounaki Square. Built in the 19th century under Sultan Abdülmecid I, it traces the island’s history from early Christian times, with Genoese and Ottoman artifacts and sculptures in the courtyard. The icons from Panagia Krina catch the eye. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

One hundred thirty thousand volumes downstairs, a 19th-century birthing chair upstairs: the Korais Library brings together an eclectic mix. Founded in 1792 thanks to the scholar Adamantios Korais, it preserves medical texts from the 15th century. Upstairs, the Philip Argenti Museum brings together traditional costumes, embroidery, shepherds’ tools, and portraits of the wealthy Argenti family. Come on a weekday morning: closing time is around 3 p.m.

The Chios Maritime Museum tells the story of an island of shipowners, in a house in the town center donated by the heirs of the Patera family. Paintings of sailing ships and steamships by Aristides Glykas, a native of Vrontados, sit alongside models and photographs; one section explores the Liberty ships that fueled the growth of the Greek fleet after the war. Check the seasonal hours: 9 a.m.–2 p.m. from May to October, 9 a.m.–1 p.m. in winter, and closed Sundays except in August.

activities.text: Stroll along Aplotaria Street, Chios Town’s pedestrian shopping thoroughfare, for clothing, souvenirs, and island products. Then head to the harbor, lined with cafés and restaurants that bustle day and night. Look for mastiha, a mastic liqueur protected by a designation of origin in the European Union, to take home rather than drink in direct sunlight. Save this walk for late afternoon, after the museums.

practical_info.tip: The museums in Chios Town close in the early afternoon: save Aplotaria Street and the harbor for the end of the day.

visits.text: The gold of the mosaics begins to glow as your eyes adjust to the dim light inside the katholikon of Nea Moni. Created under Constantine IX Monomachos in the mid-11th century, they are among the three surviving Middle Byzantine mosaic ensembles in Greece inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1990. Look for the Washing of the Feet in the narthex. Arrive before 1 p.m.: the monastery closes for a long break in the afternoon.

In April 1822, Ottoman troops stormed Nea Moni, where nearly 2,000 people had taken refuge. Near the gate, the small Chapel of the Holy Cross holds the bones of the massacre’s victims in a display case. In the northwest corner of the enclosure, a defensive tower is a reminder that the monastery also needed to protect itself. Keep your voice low: a community of nuns lives here.

Finish with the small Nea Moni museum, housed within the monastery. It brings together silverwork from the 18th and 19th centuries, icons, and 11th-century sculptures from the katholikon. It opens from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., except Tuesdays: a good reason to start your day here.

Nicknamed the “Mystras of the Aegean,” Anavatos clings to a granite outcrop at the top of a cliff in central Chios. Abandoned after the massacre of 1822 and then the earthquake of 1881, the village still has some 400 stone buildings. Climb the paved path and stay on it: signs warn of the danger posed by the ruins. Sturdy shoes are essential.

The Church of the Taxiarchs in Anavatos deserves a stop before the climb. It stands near the small square where the path to the ruins begins. Take the opportunity to stop at the only café in the area, a welcome respite in hot weather.

Explore Avgonyma on foot, from its narrow lanes to the paved square where a medieval tower faces the Church of Saint George. Almost abandoned in the 1960s, this village perched at an elevation of about 475 m has since been extensively restored in the traditional style, centered on its cube-shaped stone houses. Allow 30 minutes, ideally before lunch.

activities.text: On a clear day, the view from Avgonyma stretches across the Aegean Sea to the island of Psara. Tradition attributes the village’s founding to workers from Nea Moni in the 11th century, although no documents substantiate this. Have lunch here overlooking the open sea before descending to the west coast via Elinta and Lithi.

practical_info.tip: The road to Mesta via Elinta and Lithi is winding: allow nearly 1 hour for the drive.

to_next_leg.road_type: West coast via Elinta and Lithi

visits.text: Mesta was designed to confuse pirates. Its tightly packed houses form a pentagonal defensive wall with just two gates, and its vaulted alleys create a maze that slowed raiders on their way to the center. The Genoese strengthened these defenses between 1346 and 1566. Feel free to get lost, then ask for directions to the central square, lined with tavernas and cafés.

Where Mesta’s circular tower once stood, the large Church of the Taxiarchs now dominates the village center. More understated, the Old Taxiarch Church, a single-nave Byzantine basilica, remains Mesta’s oldest monument: traces of frescoes survive inside, largely covered over. Enter quietly if a service is underway.

activities.text: The scent of warm honey and the clink of glasses: in the evening, Mesta’s central square comes alive around the tables. The tavernas serve souma, a fig brandy, village wine, and loukoumades, honey-covered doughnuts. Settle in after the day-trippers have left and save the souma for the end of the meal: it is strong.

practical_info.tip: Souma is a strong brandy: try it as a digestif, in moderation if you will be driving the next morning.

visits.text: Olympi is clenched like a fist: its interconnected houses form the defensive wall, a single central gate provides access, and only half of the defensive tower remains standing. On the square, the small Church of Agia Paraskevi houses an 18th-century carved wooden iconostasis. Stop by around 10:30 a.m., before the nearby cave opens.

If you visit between early May and late September, descend into Olympi Cave at Sykia, about 5 km from the village. The cave reaches 52 m underground and stays around 18 °C year-round; some stalactites lean, shaped by air currents, and clay stains the walls ocher. Guided tours run from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on Mondays.

The climb to the acropolis of Emporios is worth the effort. On Prophet Elijah Hill, the chief’s megaron and the altar of a temple of Athena survive above an excavated town dating to the early 8th century BC; the view stretches toward Asia Minor, Samos, and Ikaria. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.: climb before your swim, during the cooler hours in summer.

activities.text: The black pebbles of Mavra Volia crunch underfoot and grow hot in the afternoon sun. This beach beside the port of Emporios owes its color to ancient volcanic activity and stretches across three successive bays with deep, dark blue waters. There is no lifeguard: swim carefully, as the seabed drops away quickly, and bring water shoes.

practical_info.tip: The beach has no lifeguard or facilities, just a basic snack bar: bring water and water shoes.

visits.text: In 2014, UNESCO inscribed Chios mastic cultivation on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list; the Chios Mastic Museum, which opened near Pyrgi in 2016, traces every stage. Incisions in the bark starting in July, resin “tears” sorted by women, cooperatives: the exhibits continue outdoors among the mastic trees. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes; closed on Tuesdays, open until 6 p.m. in season.

Pyrgi deserves its nickname, the “painted village.” On the facades, xysta—black-and-white geometric patterns scratched into the plaster—recall Italian sgraffito; in the center, an 18 m tower rises above the island’s largest medieval village. Return to the alleys in the late afternoon, when the low-angle light brings out the patterns.

Step inside the Church of Agioi Apostoloi in the heart of Pyrgi. Modeled on the katholikon of Nea Moni, seen the day before, it is covered with frescoes painted in 1665 by the Cretan Antonios Domestichos. If it is closed, its very well-preserved exterior alone makes the detour worthwhile.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Chios (overnight), then the road northwest

visits.text: Few walls remain standing, but what a view: the foundations and a few ruined towers of Volissos Castle crown the village. Tradition attributes it to the 6th-century general Belisarius; research instead dates it to the 11th century, before a Genoese restoration in the mid-15th century. Admission is free: climb the path that starts near the church.

For the July 22 feast day, many pilgrims from Chios walk to the Monastery of Agia Markella from Vrontados, 50 km away. Built beside the beach, 8 km from Volissos, it honors the island’s patron saint, who was born in that village and, according to tradition, martyred by her own father. Avoid this date if you are looking for peace and quiet.

activities.text: Follow the path at the end of Agia Markella Beach to the site of the martyrdom, where a warm spring flows into the sea. The sand-and-pebble beach faces Psara; the water here stays cool and deep. There is no lifeguard or beach equipment, but a nearby taverna serves lunch.

practical_info.tip: Avoid July 22, the feast day when pilgrims flock to the monastery and beach.

visits.text: The Citrus Museum on the Perivoli estate occupies a house dating to 1742 in the heart of Kampos. Maps, photographs, tools, and packaging tell the story of the citrus cultivation and trade that brought prosperity to the plain, supplemented by a short documentary. Admission is free; check the estate’s hours before visiting and leave some time to try its jams.

It is tempting to believe the legend of Daskalopetra in Vrontados: Homer is said to have taught his students on this rock near the sea. Archaeologists instead interpret it as a rock sanctuary of Cybele dating to the late 6th or early 5th century BC. Access is free; late in the day is the best time to visit.

activities.text: Hop on a bike or walk through the lanes of Kampos, south of Chios Town, between high walls of reddish Thymiana stone. Behind the gates, two- and three-story mansions, most dating from the Genoese period, watch over groves of mandarin, orange, and lemon trees, once irrigated by waterwheels known as manganas. Stay on the lanes: most estates are private.

practical_info.tip: Kampos is about 7 km from the port of Chios, roughly ten minutes by car.

seo.h1_title: Chios in 4 Days: Mastic Villages, Anavatos, and Nea Moni
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary starts in Chios Town and its inhabited Kastro, climbs to the mosaics of Nea Moni and the ruins of Anavatos, then passes through the fortified mastic villages, from Mesta to Pyrgi. It ends with Volissos Castle, Agia Markella Beach, and the orchards of Kampos.
seo.seo_hook: Chios in 4 days: the Kastro of Chios Town, the mosaics of Nea Moni, the ruins of Anavatos, the maze of Mesta, and the etched facades of Pyrgi.
featured_list: Chios Town: a Kastro still home to around 650 people
Nea Moni: 11th-century mosaics added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1990
Anavatos: some 400 stone buildings on a granite outcrop
Mesta: a pentagonal defensive wall with just two gates
Olympi: a cave 52 m underground, open from May to September
Emporios: the volcanic pebbles of Mavra Volia
Pyrgi: xysta facades and the Mastic Museum
Volissos: a medieval castle and Agia Markella Monastery

places_taglines.GR::chios: An inhabited Kastro, museums, and a lively port.
places_taglines.GR::nea-moni: An 11th-century monastery with gold-background mosaics, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
places_taglines.GR::anavatos: An abandoned stone village perched on a granite outcrop.
places_taglines.GR::avgonyma: Cube-shaped stone houses and sea views stretching to Psara.
places_taglines.GR::mesta: A fortress village with a pentagonal layout and vaulted lanes.
places_taglines.GR::olympi: A fortified mastic village and a cave with colorful stalactites.
places_taglines.GR::emporios: A southern port, an ancient acropolis, and a black pebble beach.
places_taglines.GR::pyrgi: The painted village with its xysta facades and Mastic Museum.
places_taglines.GR::volissos: Medieval castle above the village and Agia Markella Beach.

highlights: Nea Moni: mid-11th-century mosaics, a World Heritage Site since 1990
Mesta: a fortified village with a pentagonal layout, accessible through two gates
Pyrgi: xysta facades and the Mastic Museum, which opened in 2016
Anavatos: some 400 buildings abandoned after 1822 and the earthquake of 1881
Chios Town: inhabited Kastro, Ottoman baths, and Byzantine Museum
Emporios: the acropolis of Prophet Elijah and the volcanic pebbles of Mavra Volia

itineraries.title: Syros, Tinos, and Andros in 7 Days: Marble and Springs
itineraries.subtitle: In 7 days, travel by ferry between neoclassical Ermoupoli, the marble villages of Tinos, and the springs of Andros.
itineraries.notes: Several museums close on Tuesdays, and some sites, such as the Museum of Contemporary Art on Andros, open only during the warmer months: check opening hours before planning your days. From mid-May to mid-September, the meltemi can delay ferries, so allow extra time before your flight.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May–June and September–October: on Tinos, average highs hover around 22 to 26 °C, compared with 28 °C in July–August. From mid-May to mid-September, the meltemi blows mainly in the afternoon, sometimes reaching force 7 to 8, and can prevent ferries from departing: do not schedule a flight on the day of your final crossing. In winter, several ancient sites are closed to visitors, and ferry services become less frequent.

visits.text: A square worthy of a capital on an island of 83.6 km²: Ermoupoli’s Miaouli Square is quite a surprise, paved with marble and planted with tall palm trees. The town hall designed by Ernst Ziller, whose construction began in 1876, overlooks it, while the statue of Admiral Andreas Miaoulis has stood watch since 1889. Return after dark to see the town hall’s illuminated facade.

Behind the town hall’s formal facade lies the Archaeological Museum of Syros, established in 1889. An entire room displays finds from Kastri and Chalandriani, prehistoric sites in the north of the island, while the final room explores the excavations of Christos Tsountas, complete with notebooks. Admission is €5; in summer, the museum closes on Tuesdays but stays open until 9 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays.

Velvet seats and a ceiling adorned with portraits of poets and composers: Ermoupoli’s Apollon Theater has all the features of a miniature La Scala. Italian architect Pietro Sampò designed it, and the auditorium opened on April 20, 1864; now restored, it seats 350 spectators. Check the schedule before you visit: the theater hosts operas and concerts, especially in summer, and attending a performance remains the finest way to experience it.

Agios Nikolaos Church marks Ermoupoli’s skyline with its brilliant blue dome: it is one of the two churches visible from the ferry. Built around 1870 with the support of Queen Olga, it houses a marble templon and throne carved in 1899 by Georgios Vitalis, an artist from Tinos. Remember his name: you will encounter his work again at the Museum of Tinian Artists in Pyrgos.

Next, walk along Vaporia, the neighborhood stretching behind Agios Nikolaos, where the shipowners and captains of Syros built neoclassical homes that seem to rest on the water. Some conceal frescoed ceilings and walls; several have been restored and turned into guesthouses. Walk here in the late afternoon, when the low sunlight illuminates the facades facing the sea.

The Industrial Museum of Ermoupoli is the most unexpected visit on Syros. Opened in 2000 in an 1888 building that first housed a lead shot foundry and then a paint factory from 1909, it tells the story of the island’s industrial past, when Ermoupoli, home to the Hellenic Steam Navigation Company founded in 1856, had yet to be eclipsed by Piraeus. Look for the first electric car built in Greece, and visit in the morning: the museum closes at 3:30 p.m. most days.

activities.text: Head down for a swim at Asteria, below Vaporia, when the heat rises. There is not a grain of sand: a concrete platform and a ladder leading into the sea, with lounge chairs, umbrellas, and bars, make this one of the city’s liveliest swimming spots. Combine it with your neighborhood walk, wearing your swimsuit under your clothes.

practical_info.tip: A platform with no sand: water shoes make it easier to reach the ladder.

activities.text: In Ermoupoli, no one leaves the island without a box of loukoumi: vendors even board the ferries to sell it. The first cauldron is said to have arrived on Syros in 1832 with artisans from Chios who came via Constantinople, and mastic was added to the recipe. Try halvadopita, another island sweet, too, and shop at the city’s long-established producers.

practical_info.tip: Loukoumi travels well: buy it at the end of your stay on Syros, before taking the ferry to Tinos.

to_next_leg.justification: Ce parcours se fait à pied par les cheminements locaux ; le routeur automobile produit un détour ou une valeur nulle inadaptée.

visits.text: You’ll climb the whitewashed steps to the top of Ano Syros, where the Catholic Cathedral of Saint George overlooks Ermoupoli. First built in 1208, destroyed three times, and rebuilt, it recalls the medieval origins of this town, founded around 1200. Head up early: there’s still shade, and the views stretch to the neighboring islands.

Founded in 1637, the Capuchin monastery is a reminder that Ano Syros is still home to Catholic Greeks, a legacy of centuries of Latin rule on Syros. Enter quietly if a service is underway, then continue through the narrow streets to the tunnel-like gateway marking the entrance to town.

A ring, a watch, shoes, a small pair of pliers: the Markos Vamvakaris Museum displays everyday belongings of the rebetiko musician, born in Ano Syros in 1905. His family donated them, along with his passport, manuscripts, and photographs, to this two-story stone house. In summer, it’s open from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. and from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.; off-season visits are by appointment.

activities.text: You’ll then wander without a set route through the narrow streets of Ano Syros, past white houses and courtyards overflowing with bougainvillea, to the square named after Markos Vamvakaris. The slopes are steep, and there are plenty of steps. Leave time for a drink on a terrace overlooking Ermoupoli and the neighboring islands.

practical_info.tip: Flat shoes and water are essential: getting around town mostly involves stairs.

visits.text: Posidonia, also known as Della Grazia after the Catholic church of Santa Maria della Grazia, was a vacation retreat for wealthy Ermoupoli families in the 19th century. Their houses and neoclassical mansions still line the streets of the village in the southwest of the island. Park near the church and take a short loop walk.

Galissas is the busiest beach on Syros, and it’s easy to see why: a U-shaped cove, fine sand, and shallow water awarded Blue Flag status. The best view, though, is from above, at Agia Pakou Chapel, overlooking the entire bay. Bring a mask and snorkel to explore the cove.

activities.text: You’ll then head to Agathopes Beach, near Posidonia: sand, shallow water, and families with young children. The sea daffodils growing in the sand are protected, so don’t step on them. Offshore, the islets of Strongylo and Schinonisi mark the horizon; lounge chairs and a ramp into the sea make swimming easier.

practical_info.tip: Swim in the early afternoon to leave enough time to reach Kini before sunset.

activities.text: The sun sinks into the sea opposite Kini’s small harbor, 9 km from Ermoupoli, silhouetting the boats moored in the bay. The village viewpoint is an excellent spot for sunset, near the bronze mermaid on the shore. Stay for dinner: tavernas known for their fish line the waterfront.

practical_info.tip: During the day, boats leave Kini for the bays of Grammata and Varvarousa; at Grammata, sailors carved prayers into the rock.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Galissas → Ermoupoli → Tinos port → Volax
to_next_leg.justification: Route de Galissas au port d’Ermoupoli, ferry vers Tinos puis route intérieure jusqu’au village de Volax.

visits.text: “The debris from an ancient cannonball battle between Titans”: that’s the explanation Discover Greece offers for the rocks of Volax. These almost perfectly spherical gray granite boulders dot the plateau around a village with 51 residents recorded in the 2011 census. Walk the trail winding between the boulders early in the morning, before the stone heats up.

Until 1715, the Venetians controlled Tinos from Exomvourgo, a 641 m peak they called Castello di Santa Elena. The commander eventually negotiated its surrender to the Ottomans, who dismantled the fortress; only ruins remain, perched above the plateau. Allow about twenty minutes for the climb from the Iera Kardia Iisou sanctuary, and wear hiking shoes.

Kechrovouni Monastery is worth a detour for one particular room: the cell of Sister Pelagia, the nun who, according to tradition, was guided by a vision to the icon of the Evangelistria. Dedicated to the Dormition, it is said to have been founded in the 10th or 11th century by three daughters of a wealthy family. Wear clothes that keep you covered and combine your visit with Exomvourgo on the same morning.

Built for pigeons, tended like manor houses: Tinos is said to have around a thousand dovecotes. The Tarampados valley brings together several of the best-preserved examples, restored and connected by trails; the first written mention of these two-story stone towers dates to 1726. Leave your car in the village and walk down into the valley.

activities.text: In the narrow streets of Volax, you’ll find the workshops of basket weavers who preserve a long tradition of woven baskets. The village also has a small stone open-air theater and a folklore museum. Buy directly from a workshop: it’s a chance to exchange a few words with the artisan.

practical_info.tip: The open-air theater in Volax hosts cultural events in summer: check the poster in the village.

map_keywords: Museum of Marble Crafts Pyrgos Tinos

visits.text: The Museum of Marble Crafts in Pyrgos recreates a quarry, a stonecutting workshop, and the assembly of a bishop’s throne, complete with quarrying and sculpting tools; a lifting crane is displayed outside. Opened in 2008, it welcomes visitors every day except Tuesday, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., from March to mid-October. Admission is €8, free for ages 17 and under.

The most famous work by a native of Pyrgos is elsewhere: Sleeping Girl by Yannoulis Chalepas, born here in 1851, rests in the First Cemetery of Athens. His house museum displays a copy in the courtyard, next to the Museum of Tinian Artists, founded in 1930, where you will encounter Georgios Vitalis again. A combined ticket covers both; closed Mondays.

The coolness beneath a large plane tree above a marble fountain: the square in Pyrgos, Tinos’s largest village and a protected traditional settlement, invites you to take a break. Cafés and shops surround it. Walk on to the cemetery to see its marble sculptures, remaining discreet: this is first and foremost a place for quiet reflection.

activities.text: Next, head down to Panormos, the port of Pyrgos, tucked into a naturally sheltered bay where seafood tavernas and boats line the quay. For swimming, Stafida is the nearest beach, while Rochari has a beach bar. At Kavalourko, you can swim to the islet of Planitis when the sea is calm.

practical_info.tip: Do not attempt to swim to Planitis in rough seas.

map_keywords: Sanctuary of Poseidon and Amphitrite Kionia

visits.text: On January 30, 1823, residents of Falatados clearing foundations struck an icon: the Panagia Evangelistria of Tinos grew out of this discovery, which tradition links to a vision of Sister Pelagia. The icon measures just 20 by 30 cm, but the three-aisled church, completed around 1830, overflows with gold and silver votive offerings, including a fleet of ships donated by sailors from all over Greece. Come early in the morning, before the tour groups.

The museums surrounding the Evangelistria deserve almost as much attention as the church itself. Seven museums and galleries surround the church, featuring Byzantine icons, 19th-century religious art, sculpture, and a small archaeological collection. A chapel commemorates the torpedoing of the cruiser Elli in the harbor on August 15, 1940, by an Italian submarine: nine sailors died. Allow 1 hour to explore them.

Large jars covered with reliefs depicting scenes from the Theogony greet visitors at the Archaeological Museum of Tinos, on the avenue leading up from the port to the Evangelistria. The centerpiece is a multifaceted sundial signed by Andronicus of Cyrrhus in the 1st century BC, sometimes presented as a precursor to the Antikythera mechanism. Admission is €5; open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

If you visit between April and October, head to Kionia, 3 km west of town: the sanctuary of Poseidon and Amphitrite was founded here in the late 4th century BC. Excavated by the Belgians Demoulin and Graindor beginning in 1902, it features a Doric temple built of local marble, a fountain, an altar, and a large portico. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

activities.text: From the quay, walk up Megalocharis Avenue: an 800 m route that pilgrims still follow on their knees to the church. The contrast between the docking ferries and this slow progress is striking. At the top, a mosaic courtyard made with stones from Tinos and Paros leads to the church. Set out early in the morning, before the heat, and always leave room for those ascending on their knees.

practical_info.tip: On August 15 and March 25, major feast days, the avenue and town are packed: avoid these dates if you can.

activities.text: An ancient temple on one side, beach towels on the other: Kionia Beach, a few steps from the sanctuary of Poseidon, rounds out your visit with a swim. The temple’s sculptures depicted dolphins and tridents, a nod to the god of the sea. Go in the late morning, after visiting the site, and bring sun protection.

practical_info.tip: The nearby sanctuary is open from April to October, except Tuesdays, from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Tinos port → Gavrio → Batsi → Palaiopoli
to_next_leg.justification: Traversée en ferry de Tinos à Gavrio sur Andros, puis route par Batsi jusqu’à Palaiopoli.

visits.text: Batsi rises in tiers like an amphitheater above its golden-sand bay, 8 km from the port of Gavrio and along your route south. A seaside resort since the 1970s, the village retains the Piso Vrisi spring, whose water flows down to the harbor alongside a lovely path. Follow it to stretch your legs after the ferry.

The small Archaeological Museum of Palaiopolis surprises visitors with the quality of its pieces: a Pegasus carved in the 6th–5th centuries BC, a funerary lion from the 4th century BC, and a hymn to Isis engraved in marble. Housed since 2003 in a building donated by the Goulandris Foundation, it opens in summer only on Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

activities.text: Next, descend the 1,039 steps leading from the road to the site of ancient Palaiopolis, the capital of Andros in the Classical period. At the bottom are sections of defensive walls and ruins along the shore; the agora and ancient harbor lie beneath the sea. Bring water and save your strength: the climb back up takes effort.

practical_info.tip: In summer, on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays, the Museum of Palaiopolis is closed, but the site of Ypsili, toward Aprovatou, is open from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.

visits.text: Water flows beneath the greenery in Menites, a lush village 6 km from Chora: the springs of Dionysus gush from fountains decorated with lion heads. The wine god’s name suits this cool, shady spot. Walk around the fountains during the hottest hours, when the shade is welcome.

According to legend, General Nikephoros Phokas, emperor from 963 to 969, promised to fund Panachrantou Monastery if he won his battle on the way to Crete. Clinging to Mount Katafygio, this 10th-century monastery holds the skull of Saint Panteleimon and offers sweeping views of Chora. Wear clothes that keep you covered and allow time to enjoy the panorama.

Legend has it that a pasha from Euboea lost his fez in a stream on his island, and the hat resurfaced in this fountain: hence the name of the Sariza spring in Apoikia. Built in 1787, the fountain pours water through a carved lion head, and a nearby plant bottles it. Drink straight from the fountain: the water is safe to drink.

A factory in the heart of a stone village: in Stenies, water flowing down from Pythara powered a large mill, the Fabrica, from 1863 to 1936. This industrial past comes as a surprise on the greenest island in the Cyclades. Stop at the Stenies spring, a drinking-water source on Trail 8, before heading down toward the coast.

activities.text: From Apoikia, follow marked Trail 2a to the Pythara waterfalls, about ten minutes from the road, deep in a lush green valley. The stream rises on Mount Petalo and ends its journey at Gialia Beach. Shoes with grippy soles are recommended: the rocks near the falls are often wet.

practical_info.tip: Trail 2a is short and rated easy, but it becomes slippery after rain.

activities.text: If the heat catches up with you, head down to Gialia Beach, where the Pythara stream reaches the sea through a small wetland. The setting remains peaceful, with places to grab a bite above Piso Gialia. Pack a towel in the morning: a swim is a fitting end to a day exploring the springs.

practical_info.tip: Feel like walking farther? Trail 8 connects Apoikia to Nimporio over 3.8 km; allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours.

map_keywords: Tis Grias to Pidima Beach Andros

visits.text: Tis Grias to Pidima, “the old woman’s leap,” is Andros’s most famous beach, north of the Gulf of Korthi, watched over by an isolated 21 m rock. Legend has it that an old woman opened the gate of the nearby castle to the Turks, then threw herself into the sea in shame. The steep trail takes five minutes to descend: leave your flip-flops in the car.

The lapping waters of the bay set the pace in Ormos Korthiou, a quiet town at the head of its gulf in southeastern Andros. Three sandy beaches surround it, and the neighboring village of Aidonia preserves an old spring and fortified tower houses. Stroll along the waterfront in the late afternoon before driving back to Chora.

activities.text: You can also try windsurfing at Mylos Beach, very close to Ormos Korthiou, where there is a windsurfing school. For a calmer swim, Vitsi-Agia Aikaterini Beach has a beach bar and a nearby taverna. Book your lesson the day before, especially during peak season.

practical_info.tip: Tis Grias to Pidima can also be reached on foot from Gialos via Agia Ekaterini, or by boat.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: Standing 2.19 m tall, the Hermes of Andros is a Roman copy carved from Parian marble, based on a fourth-century BC type attributed to Praxiteles. It is the star attraction at Chora’s Archaeological Museum, which opened in 1981 in a building donated by the Goulandris Foundation. Upstairs, finds from Zagora, a Geometric-period settlement, include scarabs that reveal contacts with Egypt. In summer, the museum is open from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., except Tuesdays; admission is €5.

The Goulandris Foundation’s Museum of Contemporary Art alone is reason enough to spend time on Andros in summer. Established in 1979, the foundation presents a temporary exhibition here each summer; in 2026, it was devoted to sculptor Germaine Richier. The museum opens only during the warmer months, from June 14 to September 27 in 2026: 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. and 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday, and 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. on Monday. The old wing is accessible only by stairs.

Kairi Square is Chora’s living room, with cafés and ouzo bars beneath the plane trees, the Kambanis marble wall fountain dating from 1818, and a bust of Theophilos Kairis installed in 1912. Steps lead down from the square to Paraporti Beach. Settle in at an outdoor table in the morning, while the square is still quiet.

A Venetian castle reduced to a few sections of wall, a bronze sailor looking out to sea: Riva Square, at the tip of Chora’s peninsula, captures the history of Andros. The Unknown Sailor by Michail Tombros, erected in 1959, faces the islet of Kastro, which was dynamited in 1943 and is connected to the mainland by the Kamara arch, built under the Dandolo family in the 13th century.

A lighthouse that seems to rest on the waves at the harbor entrance: Tourlitis is one of the few lighthouses in Europe built this way on a rock out at sea. Destroyed during World War II, it was rebuilt to match the original and returned to service in 1994 thanks to Alexandros and Marieta Goulandris, in memory of their daughter Violanda; it was Greece’s first automated lighthouse.

If you wonder where the wealth behind Chora’s homes came from, the Andros Maritime Museum has the answer: in 1914, the fleet registered on the island ranked second in Greece by tonnage. Founded in 1972, the museum brings together models of schooners and oil tankers, uniforms, logbooks, and insurance policies. Hours vary by season: check locally the day before.

activities.text: End the day at Paraporti Beach, a long stretch of shore reached by steps from Kairi Square. After the museums, you can swim just steps from Chora’s lanes, without getting back in the car. If the wind is strong, check the sea conditions before entering the water.

practical_info.tip: The Archaeological Museum and the Museum of Contemporary Art are closed on Tuesdays: schedule your day in Chora for another day.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Andros Chora → Gavrio → Rafina
to_next_leg.justification: Trajet routier depuis la ville d’Andros jusqu’au port de Gavrio, puis ferry vers Rafina.

activities.text: The port of Rafina, on the east coast of Attica, 25 km from central Athens, welcomes your ferry from Gavrio after a crossing of 50 minutes to 2 hours, depending on the vessel. Rafina serves most of the Cyclades and southern Euboea. Allow about 40 minutes by taxi or 50 minutes by bus to reach Athens Airport.

practical_info.tip: In summer, up to eleven daily crossings connect Andros to Rafina: choose a departure that leaves plenty of time before your flight.

seo.h1_title: Syros, Tinos, and Andros in 7 Days: Marble and Springs
seo.intro_paragraph: This 7-day itinerary links three islands in the northern Cyclades, connected by ferry crossings lasting 15 minutes to 2 hours. You travel from Ermoupoli’s neoclassical mansions to the dovecotes and marble workshops of Tinos, then on to the springs, marked trails, and museums of Andros before heading to Rafina.
seo.seo_hook: Syros, Tinos, and Andros in 7 days: Ermoupoli’s Apollon Theater, the marble villages of Tinos, the Pythara waterfalls, and the museums of Chora on Andros.
featured_list: Ermoupoli: the 350-seat Apollon Theater, opened in 1864
Ano Syros: Saint George’s Cathedral, first built in 1208
Tinos: the Evangelistria icon, discovered on January 30, 1823
Pyrgos: the Museum of Marble Crafts, inaugurated in 2008
Exomvourgo: a Venetian fortress surrendered to the Ottomans in 1715
Palaiopolis: 1,039 steps to the ancient capital of Andros
Chora on Andros: the 2.19 m Hermes at the archaeological museum

places_taglines.GR::ermoupoli: The neoclassical capital of the Cyclades, between Miaouli Square and the Vaporia district.
places_taglines.GR::ano-syros: A medieval Catholic town perched above Ermoupoli, with Saint George’s Cathedral at the summit.
places_taglines.GR::galissas: A Blue Flag cove with fine sand on the west coast of Syros.
places_taglines.GR::volax: A basket-weaving village surrounded by granite boulders on the plateau.
places_taglines.GR::pyrgos-tinos: The largest village on Tinos, home to sculptors and marble craftsmanship.
places_taglines.GR::tinos: A pilgrimage town dominated by the Church of Panagia Evangelistria.
places_taglines.GR::palaiopoli: The ancient capital of Andros in the Classical period, linked to the road by 1,039 steps.
places_taglines.GR::menites: A village of springs with fountains adorned with lion heads.
places_taglines.GR::apoikia: Home to the Sariza spring and the starting point for the Pythara waterfalls.
places_taglines.GR::ormos-korthiou: A town on the Gulf of Korthi, near Tis Grias to Pidima.
places_taglines.GR::andros: A shipowners’ Chora, with museums, a Venetian castle, and the Tourlitis lighthouse.
places_taglines.GR::rafina: Port in eastern Attica connecting Andros to the mainland.

highlights: Ermoupoli: Ernst Ziller’s town hall on Miaouli Square
Volax: granite boulders and basket makers’ workshops on the Tinos plateau
Kionia: sanctuary of Poseidon and Amphitrite founded in the late 4th century BC
Apoikia: Sariza Spring, built in 1787, and the Pythara waterfalls
Korthi: the 21 m rock at Tis Grias to Pidima
Chora on Andros: Tourlitis Lighthouse, returned to service in 1994

itineraries.title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 5 Days: Castles and Coves
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, travel from the Venetian castles of Kythira to the beaches of Simos and the submerged city of Pavlopetri.
itineraries.notes: Neapoli Voion, where the loop begins, is about 320 km from Athens: drive there and take your car on the ferry to Kythira. In summer, book the Neapoli–Diakofti crossing early; it runs up to three times a day.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May–June or September: on Kythira, average highs rise from 22 °C in May to 26 °C in June and September, with very little rain. July and August bring average highs of 29 °C and fill the ferries and beaches, with Elafonisos receiving more than 3,000 visitors a day. October stays mild (22 °C) but is rainier; when winds blow from the north or east, avoid exposed coves such as Kaladi.

activities.text: In Neapoli Voion, you’ll board the Porfyrousa, the ferry connecting the tip of the Peloponnese to Diakofti, Kythira’s main port. Allow about 1 hour 15 minutes for the 27 km sea crossing, with up to three departures a day depending on the season. In summer, book early if you’re bringing a car: you’ll need it to get around the island.

practical_info.tip: Indicative fares: from €12.50 per adult and about €45 per car.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Neapoli → Diakofti → Kythira Chora
to_next_leg.justification: Ferry de Neapoli au port de Diakofti puis route intérieure vers Chora de Cythère ; hors attente portuaire.

visits.text: Nothing explains Venice’s determination to hold Kythira better than Chora Castle. Perched at an elevation of about 200 m, above Kapsali, it was nicknamed “the eye of Crete”: it commanded the Ionian Sea, the Aegean Sea, and the Sea of Crete. Its current form dates to 1503. Among the cannons from the Venetian, Russo-Ottoman, and British periods, look for the gunpowder magazine and Panagia Myrtidiotissa Church, which remained Catholic until 1806. Head up late in the day: in summer, the site stays open until 8 p.m.; admission is €5.

An Archaic marble lion, carved in the 6th century BCE, presides over the Archaeological Museum of Kythira, 190 m from Chora’s main square. Around it, displays trace the island’s history from the 9th millennium BCE to the 3rd century CE, with finds from the Minoan settlement of Paleopoli and the sanctuaries of Poseidon and Athena. Check the schedule: the museum is closed on Tuesdays and closes at 3:30 p.m. Wednesday through Friday in summer; full-price admission is €10.

activities.text: Sand mixed with pebbles, shallow water, and two crescent-shaped bays beneath the castle: Kapsali, 2.5 km from Chora, serves as the capital’s beach. It was also Kythira’s very first port, and yachts still anchor in the old harbor. Rent a pedal boat to reach Sparagario, a quieter cove, then have a fish lunch at the tavernas lining the back of the beach.

practical_info.tip: Pedal boats are available to rent on the main beach; you can reach Sparagario by pedal boat or by swimming.

activities.text: If the sea is calm in the late afternoon, take a boat from Kapsali harbor to the islet of Chytra. At that hour, sunlight strikes its western face and lights up the sea cave with shifting reflections; the waters below shelter seals. Sempreviva, a yellow flower that made the islet famous, grows on the rock. Bring a snorkeling mask: some trips use a glass-bottom boat.

practical_info.tip: Ask at Kapsali harbor about glass-bottom boat departures for Chytra.

visits.text: For the people of Kythira, Panagia Myrtidiotissa is the island’s protector, celebrated on September 24. Her monastery nestles among the pines on the west coast, 12 km from Chora; according to tradition, a shepherd found the icon there beneath a myrtle tree in the 13th century. Stop on your way to Mylopotamos, wearing clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.

Above its gate, Kato Chora Castle displays a lion of Saint Mark holding his book, with the inscription “PAX TIBI MARCE EVANGELISTA MEUS,” dated 1565. Within the walls, on the edge of Mylopotamos, nine churches stand close together with multistory houses inhabited until the mid-20th century. Admission is free; wear sturdy shoes.

activities.text: A 20 m waterfall that sometimes runs dry: Neraida, also known as Fonissa, depends on rainfall. Trail M41 starts at the square with three plane trees in Mylopotamos and follows the mill ravine on an easy 2.8 km loop, taking about 2 hours. Of the stream’s 22 mills, only one has been restored. Aim for spring.

practical_info.tip: In late summer, the waterfall may dwindle to a trickle or disappear altogether.

activities.text: You’ll end the day at Limnionas, the cove near Mylopotamos: shallow water, sand, pines for shade, and colorful fishermen’s shelters. A fish taverna and a snack bar provide all you need to spend the late afternoon here.

practical_info.tip: Natural shade under the pines, with a snack bar and taverna on-site.

visits.text: Thirteen arches, 110 m long, and 15 m high: completed in 1826 under British administration, Katouni Bridge is reputed to be the largest stone bridge in Greece. It was intended to carry a road to Avlemonas that was never completed; legend claims that engineer John MacPhail built it near his beloved’s house. Photograph it from the side to capture the arches in a row.

to_next_leg.road_type: Road via Potamos, then a dirt track to the site

visits.text: If you’re passing through on a Sunday, stop at the Potamos bazaar, where Kythira’s producers sell farm and livestock products. The island’s largest village is lined with traditional houses and neoclassical facades. Stock up on supplies and refill your water bottles here: nearby Paliochora has only ruins.

Nestled at the fork of two ravines, Paliochora was meant to remain hidden from view; nevertheless, Barbarossa razed this Byzantine capital, then called Agios Dimitrios, in 1537. Among the walls, Agia Varvara Church retains the fine proportions characteristic of Monemvasian architecture. Admission is free, with access via a dirt track: take care near the cliff edges overlooking Kakia Lagada Gorge.

to_next_leg.road_type: Dirt track, then a road toward the northeast coast

visits.text: Agia Pelagia was Kythira’s main port until the mid-1990s, when Diakofti took over. Its quay now serves recreational boats and sea excursions, facing the mountains of the Peloponnese. Have a coffee on the waterfront before heading to Lagada Beach.

activities.text: Fine sand, pebbles, and a small lake at the mouth of a lush ravine: the right-hand section of Lagada Beach, near Agia Pelagia, offers a peaceful setting. The long, sandy main section has a beach bar and a lively atmosphere. Choose your side to suit your mood, and bring water for the undeveloped section.

practical_info.tip: There’s a beach bar on the main section; the right-hand section has no services.

visits.text: It’s worth knowing the history before viewing the small Kastello in Avlemonas. In September 1802, Lord Elgin’s brig Mentor sank in the bay at a depth of 22 m, carrying seventeen crates of antiquities, including pieces from the Parthenon; no one died, and the marbles were recovered as early as 1804. Admire the small Venetian fort from the surrounding area at the end of the harbor.

activities.text: At Avlemonas, you’ll swim from the rocks or the small beach beside the harbor, where fishing caiques bob on very clear water. The taverna tables are just a few steps away. Save this swim for the end of the day, once you’ve settled into the village.

practical_info.tip: Swimming access is mainly from the rocks: water shoes make it easier to enter the sea.

activities.text: If the wind is blowing from neither the north nor the east, head down to Kaladi, not far from Avlemonas: more than a hundred steps lead to three pebble coves. A large rock separates the first two; the third, a small open cave, leads to a tiny beach. There’s just one snack bar, at the top: bring water and something for shade.

practical_info.tip: Avoid in northerly or easterly winds; access is via a dirt track followed by steps.

activities.text: Paleopoli Beach, the longest on Kythira, stretches out a few kilometers from Avlemonas. Sand and fine pebbles, clear, shallow water: children can wade a long way out before it gets deep. Park in the parking lot at the entrance, then walk toward the undeveloped sections for more space.

practical_info.tip: Parking at the entrance; only part of the beach has facilities in summer.

visits.text: A freighter’s bow juts out of the water off Diakofti: it belongs to the Nordland, a Russian ship that ran aground on the islet of Prasonisi on August 29, 2000. Its stern rests at a depth of around 30 m and attracts divers. View the bow from the white-sand beach while waiting for the ferry.

activities.text: From Diakofti, you’ll take the ferry back to Neapoli Voion, a crossing of about 1 hour 15 minutes, then drive 13 km to Pounta, where the ferry reaches Elafonisos in about ten minutes. Bring water and a snack: the snack bar at Diakofti port was not expected to open in summer 2026.

practical_info.tip: Ferries between Pounta and Elafonisos run roughly every half hour, year-round.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Diakofti → Neapoli → Pounta → Elafonisos
to_next_leg.justification: Ferry de Diakofti à Neapoli, route jusqu’à Pounta, puis seconde courte traversée pour Elafonisos.

visits.text: Agios Spyridon Chapel, built in 1858 on a rock linked to the village by a small bridge, welcomes boats at the entrance to Elafonisos, near a ruined mill. Spyridon is the island’s patron saint, celebrated on December 12. Stop by on your way back from Simos, then try kakavia, the local fish soup, at the harbor.

activities.text: The photos don’t lie: at Simos, almost-white sand and shallow water form twin bays, Sarakiniko, with more facilities, and the more unspoiled Fragkos. Dunes and junipers separate them, 4.5 km from the village of Elafonisos. Climb for about twenty minutes to Simos Cave for the view.

practical_info.tip: Lifeguards on duty in summer; arrive early in July and August, when the island receives the most visitors.

to_next_leg.road_type: Local loop to Panagia and Lefki

visits.text: Here, the village is simply called Chora: Elafonisos’s main settlement lines the north coast, facing Pounta. In winter, the island has 300 to 350 residents; in July and August, more than 3,000 visitors arrive each day. Pausanias already described this land as a peninsula shaped like a donkey’s jaw, Onou Gnathos. Stroll between the harbor and Kontogoni Beach, sheltered from southerly winds, then order a tsaiti, a pie from Vatika filled with fresh goat cheese and mint.

activities.text: Dunes, junipers, and four islets offshore: Panagia Beach, near Kato Nisi, 5 km southwest of the village of Elafonisos, offers a different setting from Simos. The area, designated a Natura 2000 site, is home to endemic plants such as the sea daffodil. Expect fine sand, warm, shallow water, and beach umbrellas along only part of the shore. Settle in early and stay until sunset, which is renowned here.

practical_info.tip: Beach umbrellas cover only part of the beach; the rest remains unspoiled.

activities.text: A caique will take you where the road cannot: boat trips from Elafonisos harbor reach the islets facing Panagia, including Xeropoules, Prasonisi, and Kassela, as well as Karandreas Sea Cave. In summer, small boats are also available to rent at the old harbor. Book the day before and allow some flexibility: trips depend on the wind, which is common on the island.

practical_info.tip: Departures depend on the weather: the island is often windy, so have a backup plan on land.

activities.text: When a southerly wind picks up, head to Lefki on Elafonisos’s east coast: it becomes the calmest spot on the island, and small boats come here for shelter. White sand, rocks, and clear water make it a good snorkeling spot to explore in the late morning. Pack your mask and snorkel before setting out.

practical_info.tip: In southerly winds, Lefki and Kontogoni offer the most sheltered swimming.

activities.text: At 276 m, Vardia is the highest point on Elafonisos; one of the island’s six hiking trails climbs to it from Vigla. Along the way, you’ll look down over Sarakiniko Beach. On a clear day, look for Kythira to the south: its Cape Frangos is just 8.5 km from the island. Set out late in the day, the recommended time for this hike, and bring water and a headlamp for the descent.

practical_info.tip: The Elafonisos topoGuide app includes routes for hiking and biking trails.

activities.text: The trip’s most beautiful swim takes you above a city: Pavlopetri, around 5,000 years old, lies beneath 3 to 4 m of water between Pounta Beach and the nearby islet. All you need is a mask and snorkel; underwater signs mark routes above the walls and tombs. Do not touch anything or walk on the remains.

practical_info.tip: Free access from Pounta Beach, next to the ferry to Elafonisos.

activities.text: You’ll get back in the car at Pounta, about 320 km from Athens. If time allows, the medieval town of Monemvasia, 31 km to the north, is worth a detour along the way. Leave promptly after your swim: the drive to the capital takes up a good part of the day.

practical_info.tip: Pounta–Athens: about 320 km; plan breaks on this long drive.

seo.h1_title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 5 Days: Castles and Coves
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day road trip starts in Neapoli Voion, crosses Kythira from Chora to Avlemonas, then continues to Elafonisos on the ferry from Pounta. You’ll alternate between Venetian fortresses, the mills trail, coves reached by stone steps, and swimming above a submerged city.
seo.seo_hook: Kythira and Elafonisos in 5 days: Chora Castle, Mylopotamos waterfall, the ruins of Paliochora, the dunes of Simos, and snorkeling over Pavlopetri.
featured_list: Chora: a Venetian castle nicknamed “the eye of Crete”
Mylopotamos: a 2.8 km loop along the mills ravine
Katouni: a stone bridge with 13 arches, completed in 1826
Paliochora: the former capital razed by Barbarossa in 1537
Avlemonas: the bay where Lord Elgin’s Mentor sank in 1802
Elafonisos: the twin bays of Simos amid dunes and junipers
Pavlopetri: a submerged city beneath 3 to 4 m of water

places_taglines.GR::neapoli-voion: The port where the ferry departs for Kythira, a crossing of 1 hour 15 minutes.
places_taglines.GR::kythira: Chora’s Venetian castle watches over the two bays of Kapsali.
places_taglines.GR::mylopotamos-kythira: Mills, a waterfall, and a castle dating to 1565 on the west coast.
places_taglines.GR::katouni: A stone bridge with 13 arches, completed under British rule in 1826.
places_taglines.GR::paliochora-kythira: The ruins of the Byzantine capital, razed in 1537, overlook a gorge.
places_taglines.GR::agia-pelagia-kythira: The island’s former main port opens onto Lagada Beach.
places_taglines.GR::avlemonas: A fishing port, a Venetian fort, and the bay where the Mentor sank.
places_taglines.GR::diakofti: Kythira’s main port, facing the wreck of the Nordland.
places_taglines.GR::elafonisos: Almost white sand, juniper-covered dunes, and a chapel on its rocky outcrop.
places_taglines.GR::pavlopetri: A submerged city to explore with a snorkel mask, 3 or 4 m below the surface.

highlights: Chora: Venetian castle in its 1503 form and the museum’s Archaic lion
Mylopotamos: mill trail and Kato Chora castle, dated to 1565
Paliochora: Byzantine capital razed by Barbarossa in 1537
Avlemonas: bay where Lord Elgin’s Mentor sank in 1802
Elafonisos: twin bays of Simos and Panagia Beach within a Natura 2000 area
Pavlopetri: snorkeling above a city roughly 5,000 years old

itineraries.title: Drama and Nestos in 6 Days: Philippi, Caves, and Elatia
itineraries.subtitle: In 6 days, travel from Philippi and Drama to Aggitis Cave, Elatia Forest, and the Nestos Delta.
itineraries.notes: Elatia is reached from Drama via the mountain road through Sidironero: the forest day trip starts and ends in Drama, with a fuel stop in Sidironero. From November to March, the Philippi museum opens only Friday through Sunday, and Ktima Kosta Lazaridi welcomes visitors only on weekdays.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May–June or September–October, when average highs in Drama range from about 21 to 30 °C. Avoid July–August, when temperatures exceed 32 °C, making the exposed site of Philippi uncomfortable in full sun. In January, highs drop to around 8 °C: check mountain road conditions before heading up to Elatia.

visits.text: Allow 2 hours rather than a fleeting stop at the archaeological site of Philippi, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016. The theater built under Philip II was converted into a Roman arena, and Basilica B, which travelers nicknamed “direkler,” the pillars, was built shortly after Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Enter as early as 8 a.m., before the sun beats down on the plain.

The Archaeological Museum of Philippi traces the city’s entire history: Neolithic figurines from Dikili Tash and sculptures from the Roman forum on the ground floor, followed upstairs by Christian Philippi through its abandonment in the late 14th century. From November to March, it opens only Friday through Sunday; save it for the end of your visit.

Local tradition identifies her as the first European woman to be baptized: at the Baptistery of Lydia, the church built in 1974 honors the purple-dye merchant from Thyatira whom Paul baptized on the banks of the Zygaktis around 49–50. On the riverbank, a cross-shaped outdoor baptistery marks the presumed spot. Allow 30 minutes, one kilometer from the archaeological site.

Small but exceptionally clear in its presentation, the Archaeological Museum of Drama covers some 50,000 years in three rooms. The oldest tools come from the cave at the Aggitis springs, which you will visit the following day, while a bust of Dionysus attests to the worship of the god of wine in the region. On Tuesdays, opening is delayed until 11 a.m.; full-price admission is €5. The Hellenistic tomb on Troias Street can be visited by appointment through the museum.

The sound of water drowns out the city at Agia Varvara Park, fed by springs that emerge in the heart of Drama. Giant plane trees, small lakes, wooden bridges, and old watermills spread across about six hectares; the Marble House, built in 1875 as a tobacco merchant’s residence, displays photographs of Drama. Return after dark: crayfish can be made out under the underwater lights. Around December 4, the feast of Saint Barbara, candles float on the lake.

Still standing after more than a thousand years, Agia Sofia Church, built in the 10th century, is Drama’s oldest surviving building. Converted into a mosque under Ottoman rule, it retains a bell tower set on the base of the former minaret. Nearby, sections of the Byzantine walls emerge throughout the northern neighborhood, and some still serve as boundaries between private properties. Follow them on foot, looking up as you go.

So inconspicuous that it is easy to miss, the Church of the Taxiarchs on Venizelou Street is worth a detour for its Palaiologan-era frescoes. This single-nave church from the 14th century measures just 7 meters by 3.45; a staircase connects it to the neighboring Byzantine wall. Its age only came to light in 1973, when the porch that concealed it was demolished. Continue to nearby Agia Sofia.

Drama built its late-19th-century prosperity on tobacco. On a 30-minute walk, look for the Portokaloglou (1904), Protopappa (1912), and Spierer warehouses, the last a four-story building designed in 1924 by the Austrian Konrad von Vilas. These warehouses also carry a painful memory: in March 1943, Drama’s Jews were rounded up in tobacco warehouses before being deported, and none of the 589 returned.

If the sky is clear toward the end of the day, head up Korylovos, a hill about 500 m high with Drama spread out at its foot. A 4 km paved road leads to the summit, where the remains of the Byzantine church of Panagia Koryliotissa, dating to around 1050, still stand. On foot, start at the Panorama kiosk, 2.7 km from the center, and follow a marked trail through the pine forest.

activities.text: Leave the city for Adriani, 12 km away, where Ktima Kosta Lazaridi welcomes visitors Monday through Friday. In 1979, its founder planted the region’s first vineyard with trellised rows, earning him the nickname “patriarch” of Drama wines. The tour takes you through the red wine aging cellars and a corridor of marble sculptures before the tasting. Call the day before to arrange a time.

practical_info.tip: The estate offers tours Monday through Friday; on Saturday mornings, head to Ktima Pavlidis in Kokkinogeia for your tasting instead.

visits.text: A steady cool temperature of 15 to 17 °C year-round greets visitors to Alistrati Cave in Petroto, 6 km from town. The entrance chamber measures 100 meters by 60, with stalactites hanging down as much as 15 meters; it takes at least a century for one cubic centimeter of mineral deposits to form. Open daily, with adult admission at €10.

Greece’s only river cave equipped for visitors, Aggitis Cave, also known as Maara, lies at the river’s source. A walkway takes you upstream along the first 500 meters, open to visitors since 2000. In the Wheel Chamber, a waterwheel 8 m in diameter irrigated the plain as far back as the Ottoman period. Bring a sweater, even in August: the water is ice-cold.

activities.text: Then head back down to Kokkinogeia, 10 minutes away, where Ktima Pavlidis harvests its grapes by hand at night to preserve their aromas. The limestone-clad winery, built in 2001, houses two underground cellars where wine matures in barrels, tanks, and ceramic amphorae. Tours are by appointment, Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Saturday until 2 p.m.

practical_info.tip: Contact the estate by phone or email before visiting; it may be closed on public holidays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Drama, then a mountain road via Sidironero

visits.text: Elatia Forest Village, 72 km north of Drama, occupies the former summer camp of Sarakatsani shepherds, known as Kalyvia Koutra. It is surrounded by Greece’s only forest of Norway spruce, a northern European species with some trees exceeding 30 meters. Every July 20, the Sarakatsani of Eastern Macedonia gather here. Fill up in Sidironero: it has the last gas station on the road.

The scent of resin gives way to that of water near Vathyrema, a stream lined with alders and willows. The mountain range reaches its highest point at Tsakalos, at 1,826 m, and a birch forest unique in Greece grows on its western flank at Magoula. Come in the fall, when the deciduous trees turn orange and red among the conifers.

activities.text: If you take just one hike in Elatia, choose the Stravorema Valley, east of the forest village, where the stream meanders through a meadow. The path following it downhill is suitable for hikers but remains rough even for a 4x4; it crosses the Megalo Rema forest road. Save some energy for the climb back up, and bring water, a windbreaker, and a picnic.

practical_info.tip: There are no stores on-site: buy lunch supplies in Sidironero, the last place to stock up along the road.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road, overnight in Drama, then EO14
to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

activities.text: At 175 meters high, Thisavros Dam, in operation since 1997, holds back the Nestos about 20 kilometers from Paranesti. The paved road follows the river beneath oaks and ash trees, passes below the crest of Platanovrysi Dam, then continues through a tunnel and across a metal bridge. Allow 40 minutes each way.

practical_info.tip: Fill up in Paranesti, the last supply center before the mountains.

activities.text: Then head up toward Dipotama, north of Paranesti, to Agia Varvara Waterfall, which is more than 15 meters high. The trail laid out by the forest service is about 1.5 km round-trip and first crosses a small footbridge; at the waterfall, turn left to reach the top. Park along the road by the sign just before the hamlet.

practical_info.tip: Rafting trips start at Platanovrysi Dam and take about 2 hours to reach the outskirts of Paranesti: book with a local operator.

visits.text: Until 1920, it was called Yeni Köy, the “new village.” In Stavroupoli, the Folklore Museum occupies the former tobacco tax office: traditional costumes and a furnished Thracian room are on the ground floor, with everyday objects upstairs, where the antique lamps catch the eye. Since no opening hours are published, call town hall before stopping by.

Stavroupoli may look like a farming town, but it preserves Evangelistria Church, built in 1858, with its carved wooden iconostasis. Traditional houses line the way to the central square, where cafés and pastry shops offer a break before dinner. On Clean Monday, the first day of Orthodox Lent, the square hosts the annual Kamila, or camel, custom.

activities.text: In our view, the Nestos should first be seen from above. Allow for 17 km of paved road from Stavroupoli to the Nestos observation point, a wooden gazebo in the abandoned hamlet of Ano Livera: the river’s meanders unfold between the mountains like a silver ribbon. Feeding stations for birds of prey have been set up nearby; bring binoculars and aim for the late-afternoon light.

practical_info.tip: Allow about 30 minutes to drive there and about 20 minutes to return.

activities.text: You’ll set out from Galani, at the mouth of Nestos Gorge, along the paved trail that railroad workers built above the river in the late 19th century, a section of the E6 European long-distance path. Allow about 2 hours to reach Kromniko Spring and the same amount of time to return. Wild horses graze near this abandoned village. Never enter the railroad tunnels, even with a flashlight.

practical_info.tip: To take to the water instead of the trail, the Class 1–2 canoe route from Stavroupoli to Galani via Toxotes involves about 2 hours of paddling; trips mainly run from May through September with an outfitter.

to_next_leg.road_type: EO2, then the road to Chrysoupoli

visits.text: Keramoti began as a fishing village populated by Greek refugees from Asia Minor. Today, this small resort town has a sandy beach facing Thassos, and ferries to the island leave from its dock. Save the evening for the harbor: Kavala Airport is only about 20 minutes away for your departure the next day.

activities.text: Drive or cycle along the Vassova, Eratinos, and Agiasma lagoons around the Nestos Delta. Listed as a Ramsar site since 1975 and covering 21,930 hectares, the delta hosts up to 50,000 birds in winter; ruddy shelducks, black-winged stilts, and spur-winged lapwings are among its standout species. A spotting scope will come in handy, especially during the spring and fall migrations.

practical_info.tip: No bird blinds are indicated: stay on the paths and avoid disturbing nesting birds in spring.

activities.text: At Keramoti, the sand extends into a long spit pointing out to sea opposite the delta. Walk along it at sunset, when Thassos stands out on the horizon. Upstream, Kotza Orman, the “great forest” along the Nestos, survives only in fragments: it depended on the river’s floods.

practical_info.tip: The riparian forest visitor center in Nea Karya is open by appointment only.

seo.h1_title: Drama and Nestos in 6 Days: Philippi, Caves, and Elatia
seo.intro_paragraph: This 6-day road trip begins at the ancient site of Philippi and includes four nights in Drama, a city of springs and wine. It visits Alistrati Cave and Aggitis Cave and the spruce forest of Elatia, then follows the Nestos from its dams through its gorge to the lagoons of Keramoti.
seo.seo_hook: UNESCO-listed Philippi, Alistrati Cave and Maara Cave, the spruce trees of Elatia, Nestos Gorge, and the Nestos Delta: a 6-day road trip around Drama.
featured_list: Philippi: Philip II’s theater and Basilica B, a UNESCO site since 2016
Drama: Agia Varvara Park, 10th-century Agia Sofia Church, and the vineyards of Adriani
Alistrati Cave and Aggitis Cave: giant cave formations and an underground river
Elatia: forest village and Greece’s only Norway spruce forest
Nestos: Thisavros Dam, Ano Livera viewpoint, and Galani trail
Keramoti: delta lagoons, a Ramsar site since 1975

places_taglines.GR::philippoi: City founded by Philip II, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016.
places_taglines.GR::drama: City of springs, tobacco, and wine at the foot of Mount Falakro.
places_taglines.GR::alistrati-cave: Cave with giant formations, open year-round near Alistrati.
places_taglines.GR::aggitis-cave: Greece’s only river cave developed for visitors, at the sources of the Aggitis.
places_taglines.GR::elatia: Greece’s only spruce forest, in the Rhodope Mountains north of Drama.
places_taglines.GR::paranesti: Village on the Nestos, gateway to Thisavros Dam and Platanovrysi Dam.
places_taglines.GR::stavroupoli: Former tobacco center built facing the Nestos Gorge.
places_taglines.GR::toxotes: Village at the mouth of the Nestos Gorge, a launching point for canoes.
places_taglines.GR::keramoti: Fishing port and sandy beach on the edge of the Nestos Delta.

highlights: Philippi: theater, forum, and basilicas, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016
Drama: Agia Varvara Springs Park and the 10th-century Agia Sofia Church
Aggitis Cave: Greece’s only river cave developed for visitors
Elatia: Greece’s only Norway spruce forest
Nestos Gorge: the railway workers’ trail from Galani to Kromniko
Nestos Delta: a Ramsar site since 1975, with lagoons and waterbirds
