itineraries.title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Ioannina, Arta, and Aromanian Villages
itineraries.subtitle: Complete a 3-day loop from Ioannina via the Bridge of Arta, Plaka Bridge, and the villages of Tzoumerka.
itineraries.notes: Avoid Tuesdays, when most museums in Ioannina and Arta are closed; the Church of the Parigoritissa in Arta remains closed to the public during restoration. In winter, keep snow chains in the trunk: the road to Syrrako is often damaged by severe weather.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with average highs of 21 to 28 °C in Ioannina and cool evenings in villages perched at around 1,200 m. Avoid the mountains from November through March: November and December are Ioannina’s wettest months, and snow can close minor roads. In July–August, expect afternoon temperatures above 30 °C in town.

visits.text: In 1940, residents of Perama looking for shelter from bombing during the Greco-Italian War stumbled upon Perama Cave. Open to the public since 1956, it can be explored on a guided tour lasting about 45 minutes, along a 1,100 m route at a year-round temperature of 18 °C. Teeth and bones from a family of cave bears were found here. Park at the entrance to Perama, beside the lake, 300 m from the cave, and wear sturdy shoes: 163 steps await before the exit.

At the Archaeological Museum of Ioannina, you can read questions posed to the oracle of Zeus at Dodona, inscribed by pilgrims on small lead tablets. Among the known questions, a man named Ermon asks, toward the end of the 6th century BC, which god he should pray to so that his wife will bear him useful children. Aris Konstantinidis’s modernist building stands in Litharitsia Park. The museum is closed on Tuesdays; allow a full hour for the Dodona gallery.

A minaret, but no more call to prayer: since 1933, the Aslan Pasha Mosque has housed the Municipal Ethnographic Museum of Ioannina. Completed in 1618, it replaced the Church of Saint John, razed after the failed revolt of Dionysios the Philosopher in 1611. Its display cases bring together objects from the city’s three communities: Christian, Jewish, and Muslim. Visit on a weekday if possible: on Saturdays and Sundays, admission ends as early as 3:00 p.m.

The bustle of the lower town fades as soon as you pass through the gate of Its Kale, the inner citadel of Ioannina’s kastro. At its highest point stands the Fethiye Mosque, whose name means “of the Conquest”; beside it, an ornate iron cage covers the tomb of Ali Pasha, buried without his head, which was displayed as far away as Constantinople. The neighboring Byzantine Museum brings together sculptures, silverware, and post-Byzantine icons. A single ticket grants admission to the museum and the mosque; both are closed on Tuesdays.

Since 2016, the Silversmithing Museum has occupied the western bastion of Its Kale and the neighboring former kitchens. The first level explains the techniques used by the silversmiths of Epirus; the second displays jewelry, filigree boxes, and silver and gold pieces from the 18th to the 20th century. In the restored kitchen, the sound of hammers recreates the workshop atmosphere. Full-price admission is €8; the museum is closed on Tuesdays and closes at 5:00 p.m. from October 16 through the end of February.

In 1822, Ali Pasha, rebelling against the sultan, was killed by Ottoman forces at Saint Panteleimon Monastery on the island in Lake Pamvotis. The Ali Pasha and Revolutionary Period Museum now occupies the site: objects from his rule (1788–1822) are housed in one building, and memorabilia from the Greek Revolution in another, largely drawn from the collection of Fotis Rapakousis. Save it for the end of the day: its posted opening hours extend to 7:30 p.m.

If you visit only one monastery on the island, choose Philanthropinon Monastery, founded in 1291–1292 by Michael Philanthropenos. Among scenes from the life of Christ, the 16th-century frescoes in its church depict seven sages of ancient Greece: pagan thinkers painted in an Orthodox sanctuary, a sign of the humanist spirit of Ioannina at the time. The island covers just 0.2 km²: walk there from the Ali Pasha Museum.

activities.text: Board a boat at Ioannina’s dock for the island in Lake Pamvotis: the crossing takes no more than about 10 minutes. The car-free village has around 110 slate-roofed houses built of stone and wood, and its cobblestone lanes lead to the monasteries. Tavernas serve lake fish, eels, and frog legs. Boats run throughout the day; check the last departure time posted at the dock before sitting down to eat.

practical_info.tip: Avoid scheduling this day for a Tuesday: the Byzantine Museum, Silversmithing Museum, and Archaeological Museum are closed that day.

visits.text: It is best to begin your visit to Arta with its buried past at the Archaeological Museum, dedicated to Ambracia, a colony founded by Corinth in 625 BC. A reconstructed necropolis, a cenotaph honoring warriors who fell in the 6th century BC, and a life-size house bring the city to life. Open from 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM; closed Tuesdays.

In Greece, an endless construction project still brings to mind the Bridge of Arta: according to the ballad, its foundations collapsed every night until the builder walled his wife into them. The current bridge, about 145 m long, dates from the early 17th century; from 1881 to 1912, its highest arch marked the border with the Ottoman Empire. Walk across, then admire it from the riverbank.

Around 1250, Despot Michael II founded Kato Panagia, reportedly to atone for exiling his wife Theodora. On the banks of the Arachthos, 3 km south of the center, the church preserves 13th-century frescoes and an extensive cycle of paintings from 1715. The monastery is home to nuns: keep shoulders and knees covered.

Climb up to Arta Castle, protected by the Arachthos to the north and east. Its walls enclose about 9 hectares, roughly a dozen soccer fields, and feature 18 towers, repaired by Ali Pasha between 1796 and 1820. A hotel built within the walls in the 1960s erased most of the remains inside. Open from 8:30 AM to 4 PM.

A Doric temple beneath the sidewalk: in central Arta, the foundations of the 44 m-long Temple of Apollo Pythios emerge at street level. Nearby, the small theater of Ambracia, built around 300 BC, retains only five rows of seats; it may have served as a council chamber. Look for both around Vasileos Pyrrou Street.

Finish at Agia Theodora Church, on the corner of Vasileos Pyrrou and Agias Theodoras Streets, decorated with ceramic crosses and suns. Theodora, wife of Michael II, became a nun here and was buried here; she became Arta’s patron saint. Near the south entrance, a cenotaph from 1873 is thought to depict her with her son Nikephoros. A procession takes place every March 11.

to_next_leg.road_type: Valley road followed by a mountain road via Monolithi

visits.text: Plaka Bridge spans the Arachthos with a single arch of about 40 m, built in 1866 by Kostas Bekas of Pramanta. The previous bridge collapsed on its inauguration day in 1863. Swept away by a flood on February 1, 2015, the arch was rebuilt in 2020 using the original techniques, without metal. Come in the late afternoon, when the light falls at a low angle.

activities.text: Head down to the banks of the Arachthos to appreciate the scale of Plaka Bridge’s arch, nearly 18 m high. From 1881 to 1912, the river marked the Greek-Ottoman border; the old customs post still stands near the bridge. In 1944, the Plaka Agreement between resistance movements was signed nearby. Keep well away from the swift current.

practical_info.tip: In season, local outfitters offer rafting and canoeing on the Arachthos, starting from Plaka Bridge; book ahead.

visits.text: Water sings in the Arapis Fountain on Pramanta’s square, shaded by an old plane tree, opposite Agia Paraskevi Church and its stone roof. The largest village in Northern Tzoumerka, Pramanta faces the 2,112 m summit of Strogoula. Arrive before nightfall to enjoy the view from the square.

“Wind hole” is the meaning of Anemotrypa, a cave discovered in 1960 by two young men following a current of cold air. In the cave, 3 km from Pramanta, a 250 m illuminated route runs alongside small underground lakes to a river cascading down a 2 m drop. The ground is slippery: wear shoes with treaded soles and call ahead in the off-season.

If heights make you uneasy, Kipina Monastery will test your nerves: it clings to the entrance to a cave in a cliff in the Kalarrytikos Gorge, and its church has a dome carved from the rock. Sources date its founding to the 13th or 14th century. A wooden bridge, which the monks could remove, guards the entrance; free parking.

Before 1821, Kalarrytes had about 500 families; after Ottoman troops burned the village, only 26 were recorded in 1831. Its silversmiths made it famous, and the family of Sotirios Voulgaris, founder of Bulgari, came from here. Cars are banned from the cobbled lanes: walk up to the square and its stone tiers.

to_next_leg.justification: La route entre Kalarrytes et Syrrako contourne le ravin par les virages ; le faible écart à vol d’oiseau ne reflète pas la route.

visits.text: Syrrako can only be explored on foot: cars stay outside, and you enter over a stone bridge. On July 10, 1821, the Ottomans destroyed the village; only five buildings, including Panagia Church, survived. Busts of local sons Ioannis Kolettis and the poet Zalokostas take pride of place in the square with the statues. It is uphill all the way: wear good shoes.

activities.text: Follow Syrrako’s lanes to the statue of Kostas Krystallis, a poet born here in 1868, then continue to Agios Nikolaos, the village’s largest church, with an iconostasis carved by artisans from Metsovo. The old trail to Kalarrytes, across the ravine, takes 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours: save it for a longer stay.

practical_info.tip: Syrrako’s folklore museum opens only in August or by request; ask in the village.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road via Michalitsi, then Egnatia Odos

activities.text: There’s no better place than Mavili Square to end the tour beside Lake Pamvotis, facing Mount Mitsikeli. It is named after the Corfiot poet Lorentzos Mavilis. At a tsipouradiko in Ioannina, tsipouro comes with a plate of meze. The next day, Ioannina Airport is just 5 km from the center, about a fifteen-minute drive.

practical_info.tip: Bring a jacket for evenings by the lake, even in spring and fall.

seo.h1_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Ioannina, Arta, and Aromanian Villages
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day tour starts in Ioannina, with its Its Kale citadel, island, and museums, then heads down to the Bridge of Arta before climbing into the Tzoumerka mountains. You cross Plaka Bridge, spend the night in Pramanta, and explore the two car-free Aromanian villages of Kalarrytes and Syrrako on foot before returning to Lake Pamvotis.
seo.seo_hook: Its Kale and Ioannina’s island, the Bridge of Arta, Plaka Bridge, Kipina Monastery, Syrrako, and Kalarrytes: a 3-day loop through the Tzoumerka mountains.
featured_list: Ioannina: Ali Pasha’s tomb beneath an iron cage at Its Kale
Ioannina: seven sages of antiquity painted at Philanthropinon Monastery
Arta: a bridge about 145 m long and its ballad of a woman walled in
Plaka: an arch spanning about 40 m, rebuilt in 2020 without metal
Pramanta: Anemotrypa Cave and its underground river
Kalarrytes: the Voulgaris family’s village of origin
Syrrako: a stone village explored on foot

places_taglines.GR::ioannina: Its Kale citadel, the island in Lake Pamvotis, and the Silversmithing Museum.
places_taglines.GR::arta: Ancient Ambracia, a legendary bridge, and a castle beside the Arachthos.
places_taglines.GR::plaka-bridge: A stone arch spanning about 40 m above the Arachthos.
places_taglines.GR::pramanta: A large village in the Tzoumerka mountains, with a plane tree, a fountain, and a cave of the wind.
places_taglines.GR::kalarrytes: A village of Aromanian silversmiths near the cave monastery of Kipina.
places_taglines.GR::syrrako: A car-free stone village, birthplace of the poet Kostas Krystallis.

highlights: Ioannina: Ali Pasha’s tomb at Its Kale and the island in Lake Pamvotis
Ioannina: questions to the oracle of Dodona inscribed on lead
Arta: 17th-century stone bridge, approximately 145 m long
Plaka Bridge: a single arch spanning approximately 40 m, rebuilt in 2020
Pramanta: Anemotrypa Cave, discovered in 1960
Syrrako and Kalarrytes: car-free Aromanian villages

itineraries.title: Evros in 5 Days: Delta, Vultures, and Thracian Silk
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, travel up the Evros from Alexandroupoli to Orestiada, exploring the delta, Dadia’s vultures, and Byzantine ramparts.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Wednesday, between April and October: most museums close on Mondays or Tuesdays, and several sites reduce their opening days in winter. For boat trips in the delta, foreign visitors must apply several weeks in advance for permission to enter the military zone; the last two nights are spent in Didymoteicho, about 90 km from Alexandroupoli and its airport.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with average highs of 20 to 27 °C in Alexandroupoli. Avoid July–August, when temperatures average above 30 °C and wildfires are a risk: the minibus to the Dadia observation hide does not run when the fire risk is very high or temperatures exceed 40 °C. Fall and spring offer the greatest variety of migratory birds in the delta.

visits.text: No place offers a better introduction to Evros than the Archaeological Museum of Alexandroupoli. Opened in 2022, it displays more than 1,000 objects, tracing the coast and then the hinterland as far as the Thracian burial mounds. Look for the spherical anthropomorphic vessel from Toumba of Makri, unmatched in Greece in size and style, made in the second half of the 6th millennium BC. Closed Tuesdays; open only from 1 PM to 8 PM on Saturdays; full-price admission is €10.

Exposed ashlar masonry, an entrance framed by four Tuscan columns, Gothic openings: the facade of the Ethnological Museum of Thrace intrigues you before you even step inside. Built in 1899 for Miltiadis Altinalmazis, this mansion was restored in 1998 by the Giannakidis family, who showcase folk culture from across Thrace here. Come in the morning: the museum is open Tuesday through Saturday from 9 AM to 3 PM and Sunday from 10 AM to 2 PM, and is always closed on Mondays.

If you could keep just one image of Alexandroupoli, it would be its lighthouse, the city’s waterfront landmark. A French company built it in 1880 for the Ottoman lighthouse administration, as the railroad completed in 1870 was increasing port traffic. It still emits three flashes every 15 seconds. Come at sunset.

The Ecclesiastical Museum of the Metropolis of Alexandroupoli holds a direct link to Feres, your stop on the third day: a fragment of the funerary slab of the sebastokrator Isaac Komnenos. Housed in the former Leontarideio School, built in 1909 near Saint Nicholas Cathedral, it brings together more than 400 works of religious art, including portable icons from the 16th–18th centuries. Hours vary: check with the Metropolis before visiting.

Until 1920, the city was called Dedeağaç; that year, it took the name Alexandroupoli in honor of King Alexander, who had come to visit. This recent history is captured in the Historical Museum of Alexandroupoli, which opened in 1995: paintings by regional artists, including a large portion of Hariklia Hadjisavvas-Fotiou’s work, and a collection of photographs, newspapers, and historical objects. Admission is €2, Tuesday through Saturday from 10 AM to 2 PM only.

activities.text: You’ll end the day on Alexandroupoli’s waterfront, between the lighthouse and the port, where ferries leave daily for Samothrace. The municipal beach, steps from the center, has visitor facilities and Blue Flag certification. At dinner, look for local specialties: pies, youfkades (small pasta), dairy products, and fish from the Thracian Sea.

practical_info.tip: The city’s museums close between 2 PM and 3:30 PM: save swimming and strolling for late afternoon.

visits.text: Bulgarian soldiers digging trenches uncovered the archaeological site of Mesimvria-Zone in the early 20th century. Founded in the late 7th century BCE as a colony of Samothrace, Zone paid the highest tribute of all the Samothracian colonies to the Athenian League in the 5th century BCE. Sanctuary of Demeter and Temple of Apollo: open 8:30 AM to 3:30 PM except Tuesdays (€5), Friday through Sunday in winter.

A path leads between old olive trees from Makri’s cemetery to the Cyclops Cave, which opens in a rocky spur above the beach. Tradition places Polyphemus, blinded by Odysseus, here; nearby, the Toumba of Makri was inhabited as early as around 6200 BCE. Access is unrestricted and free: bring a flashlight.

Makri’s Byzantine defensive wall, about 400 m long, dates to the 9th and 10th centuries, when the village was a fortified stop on the Via Egnatia. A four-room Ottoman hammam survives against the northeastern wall, and the Church of Saint Anastasia (1800) preserves a carved wooden iconostasis. Emperor Isaac II Angelos was captured here in 1195. You can see everything on foot in just under 1 hour.

activities.text: You’ll finish the morning on Makri Beach, one of the main beaches in the municipality of Alexandroupoli. The village is surrounded by an olive grove of about 220,000 trees over a century old, whose oil holds European protected designation of origin status. Ask for it at lunch, on a simple piece of bread.

practical_info.tip: Keep an eye on the time: the delta information center in Traianoupoli welcomes visitors until 4 PM.

visits.text: The city founded by Trajan on the Via Egnatia has left behind its baths, while the Evrenos Bey caravanserai, a travelers’ inn built between 1370 and 1390, forms a long building measuring 38.8 m by 13 m.

Next, you’ll visit the Evros Delta Information Center beside the thermal baths. Admission is free, and the center introduces a wetland of about 200 km², protected under the Ramsar Convention since the 1970s, where more than 300 bird species have been recorded. Open daily from 8 AM to 4 PM: ask for details about arrangements for the following day’s boat trip.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Alexandroupoli, then EO51 toward Feres

visits.text: Isaac Komnenos, son of Emperor Alexios I, wanted to live and be laid to rest here: in 1152, he founded a monastery in Feres, of which the Church of Panagia Kosmosoteira survives. Beneath its five domes, military saints bear the features of his relatives, including his father. His typikon provided for 74 monks and barred eunuchs from entering. The church remains active: dress appropriately, and call 25550 22227 if the door is closed.

If you have an extra 30 minutes, head to the Feres aqueduct at the entrance to town, near a former Turkish bath complex. The large Kotza Tsesmes fountain is close by, and a waterfall spills into a pool near the center, beside an old bridge. The aqueduct is illuminated after dark.

activities.text: Endless reeds and still canal waters: a guided trip in a plava, the river’s traditional boat, takes you through the heart of the Evros Delta in two to two and a half hours. Dalmatian pelicans and spoonbills are often spotted around lagoons such as Drana. Expect to pay €10 to €15 per person, and book through the municipal tourist kiosk in Feres.

practical_info.tip: Foreign visitors must obtain permission to enter the military zone: email mdpp.evros-dadia@necca.gov.gr several weeks in advance. Feres Information Center: 25550 24310, 8 AM to 4 PM.

visits.text: Around 1900, Soufli had about 10,000 residents; the 2021 census counted 3,770. In between, silk enjoyed its golden age and then declined, a story told by the Silk Museum in the Kourtidis mansion, built in 1883. Open 10 AM to 6 PM from March to mid-October (5 PM in winter), except Tuesdays; admission €6.

Less solemn than its neighbor, but livelier: at the Art of Silk Museum, live silkworms share the space with working looms. Opened in 2008 by the Tsiakiris family in an 1886 neoclassical building, it follows the thread from cocoon to fabric. Open until 9 PM in season, it’s worth saving for the end of the day; admission €3.

You’ll then stroll past late-19th-century mansions to Soufli’s churches of Saint George and Saint Athanasius, both dating from before the mid-19th century. The Evros River, which marks the border, flows just 500 m from the center. Soufli silk is still sold in town: compare stores before buying a scarf.

Dadia’s bird-of-prey observation hide overlooks the feeding site where rangers leave carcasses for vultures. The park is home to the Balkans’ only natural colony of cinereous vultures, with 36 to 47 pairs according to the Bulgarian Society for the Protection of Birds (BSPB). A 15-seat minibus heads up at 8:30 AM, 10 AM, 11:30 AM, and 1 PM: book at 25540 32209 and aim for the first departure.

The most striking sight in Dadia remains the forest itself: the August 2023 wildfire swept through it for seventeen days and burned a large part of it. Natural regeneration is underway, and the vultures have stayed. The park information center, 800 m from the village square, introduces the park through an exhibition room and documentaries; open daily from 8 AM to 4 PM.

activities.text: You’ll continue the morning on foot along the marked 5 km loop that starts at the Dadia ecotourism center, follows the edge of the protected area, and returns near the village. The route is easy; another trail climbs to Kapsalo for panoramic views of the forest. Set out before the heat and bring water.

practical_info.tip: Cars are not allowed in the protected forest: access is only by minibus or on foot.

visits.text: “The unknown capital of Byzantium”: this is how the Byzantine Museum of Didymoteicho presents the city where Emperors John III Vatatzes and John V Palaiologos were born. The exhibits also explore Plotinopolis, a city founded by Trajan on Agia Petra hill, and end with an illuminated map of the Via Egnatia that visitors can walk across like a game. On Saturdays, it is open from 1 PM to 8 PM; closed Mondays and Tuesdays, admission €5.

Climb to the Kale, Didymoteicho’s citadel, perched on a rocky hill 107 m above the Erythropotamos. Its ramparts have 24 towers; the most famous, Vasilopoula Tower, takes its name from a governor’s daughter who, legend has it, fell from its battlements. At the foot of the hill, cavities carved into the rock served as storerooms and cisterns. Near the Church of Saint Athanasius (1834), a cave is said to have held Charles XII of Sweden captive. Closed-toe shoes are essential.

Small but charming, the Folklore Museum of Didymoteicho is worth a 45-minute visit. Embroidery, woven bedding, traditional jewelry, a raki still, and tools from an old print shop fill the displays; the courtyard is dominated by the giachana, a sesame mill once used to produce oil. Open Tuesday through Saturday from 9 AM to 2 PM and Sunday from 10:30 AM to 1:30 PM.

activities.text: In the evening, the Erythropotamos flows below the ramparts: follow the river, then head into central Didymoteicho, where the Ottoman baths of Oruç Pasha, built in 1398–1399, still stand. In front of these walls in 1352, the Ottomans won their first victory in Europe. View the hammam ruins from the outside, then finish at the central square.

practical_info.tip: The Turkish border is very close: do not photograph military installations.

visits.text: Small but sturdy, Pythio Castle served as a refuge and private treasury for John VI Kantakouzenos, who had it built between 1331 and 1341 to control the Evros crossings. Its two towers have survived, the smaller still standing 20 m tall, but the railroad claimed part of the enclosing wall. View it from the road and do not photograph any military installations along the border.

If a city established in 1923 seems to have no history, step inside the Historical and Folklore Museum of Orestiada. The city was founded by refugees from Karaağaç, a suburb of Edirne awarded to Turkey at Lausanne, and inaugurated on August 12, 1923. Thracian costumes and objects dating from 1800 to 1950 tell the story of their resettlement, just 19 km from the city they lost. Call before visiting (25520 28080).

seo.h1_title: Evros in 5 Days: Delta, Vultures, and Thracian Silk
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day road trip follows the Evros, which forms the border with Turkey, from Alexandroupoli to Orestiada. You’ll visit ancient sites along the coast, take a boat trip in the delta, and visit Dadia’s bird-of-prey observatory, Soufli’s silk museums, and the Byzantine citadel of Didymoteicho.
seo.seo_hook: Evros in 5 days: Alexandroupoli’s museums, a boat trip in the delta, Dadia’s cinereous vultures, Soufli’s silk, and Didymoteicho’s citadel.
featured_list: Alexandroupoli: an archaeological museum with more than 1,000 objects and a lighthouse dating to 1880
Evros Delta: a traditional boat trip lasting two to two and a half hours
Feres: a five-domed church founded in 1152 by Isaac Komnenos
Dadia: a bird-of-prey observatory and the Balkans’ only natural colony of cinereous vultures
Soufli: two silk museums, including one with live silkworms
Didymoteicho: a citadel with 24 towers and a Byzantine museum

itineraries.title: Ikaria in 4 Days: Hot Springs, Seychelles, and Raches
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, cross Ikaria from the hot baths of Agios Kirykos to the hilltop villages of Raches and to Nas.
itineraries.notes: A car is essential: mountain roads are slow, and the meltemi winds in July and August can delay ferries.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May–June or September–October: temperatures range from 15 to 24 °C depending on the month, with the sea warm enough for swimming by late May and still warm in September. These months are also ideal for hiking. July and August bring temperatures of 24–32 °C, with meltemi winds that churn up the north coast and can disrupt ferries. From November through March, many businesses close and ferry services become less frequent.

visits.text: Free to visit and fully renovated, the Archaeological Museum of Agios Kirykos is worth an hour before heading to the beach. It occupies the former gymnasium built in 1925 by Ikarians who had emigrated to America, and displays pottery, tools, and coins from ancient Drakano or shipwrecks.

The angular statue of Icarus on the pier in Agios Kirykos divides visitors, but it recalls the story that the island takes its name from the son of Daedalus, who fell into the sea nearby. Near the harbor, Agios Nikolaos Church, the oldest in the old town, preserves an iconostasis made between 1820 and 1840. Finish with coffee at an outdoor café.

activities.text: At 59 °C where it emerges, the water from the Lefkada hot springs flows toward the sea and fills a pool enclosed by large boulders, 2.5 km west of Agios Kirykos. Baths operated here from the 1950s through the 1970s. Follow the “Hot Springs” sign, then continue along the rocks for about fifty meters.

practical_info.tip: Limit your soak to about twenty minutes and wear sturdy shoes for walking on the rocks.

activities.text: Warm currents suddenly rise beneath your arms near the cave at the southern end of Therma Bay. Saline and rich in radon, these springs, at 45 to 52.8 °C, mix with seawater here in a pool enclosed by rocks. From the small harbor, it is just a thirty-meter swim; do not soak for more than twenty minutes.

practical_info.tip: The Therma hot springs can be enjoyed from May through November; a caique also connects Agios Kirykos with the village.

activities.text: You can walk to Therma in about 15 minutes along the coastal path that starts at the Agios Kirykos police station. Therma Beach, divided by a fishing pier, stretches below the village square and is at its best when the wind blows from the north. Finish on a terrace overlooking the harbor.

practical_info.tip: There are only a few beach umbrellas on one side of the beach: bring your own shade.

visits.text: Drakano Tower watches over Ikaria’s eastern tip: three stories of white marble, about 13 m tall, more than 50 m above the sea. On clear days, Fourni and Samos stand out offshore. Allow 25 minutes for the walk; open from 8:30 a.m. to 3 p.m., except Sundays and Mondays.

activities.text: Local legend places Dionysus’s birth near Iero Beach, and a small sea cave still bears his name. This cove of sand and small pebbles remains uncrowded; a freighter wreck lies to the west. Bring a mask and snorkel, and reach the cove via the airport road or the trail down from Drakano.

practical_info.tip: There are no facilities at Iero Beach: bring water and something for shade.

activities.text: If you’re traveling with young children, Faros Beach, the largest on the south coast, has a shallow rocky pool where the water stays warm. Pebbles alternate with sand, with large, smooth slabs underwater in places. Park for free a few meters from the village center, then have lunch at a seaside taverna.

practical_info.tip: Kayaking, windsurfing, and diving are available from Faros Beach in season.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road via Chrysostomos and the tunnel

visits.text: Giant granite boulders line the road to Manganitis, and the island’s only tunnel, bored in the early 1990s, cuts through them. About 150 residents live around the small fishing harbor, where a taverna overlooks the sea. Park on the jetty at the end of the road and take a dip at Gialos, the small beach nearby.

activities.text: Created by a landslide after the Manganitis tunnel was bored, Seychelles Beach has become Ikaria’s most famous beach. White pebbles, granite cliffs, and turquoise water: rocks serve as diving platforms, and underwater caves can be explored with a mask. Leave your car in the roadside parking lot, then follow the steep trail down in sturdy shoes.

practical_info.tip: This beach has no facilities and gets very crowded in August: arrive early, or come by boat from Manganitis harbor when the service is running.

to_next_leg.road_type: Road toward Kosikia, then an unpaved road for a few kilometers

visits.text: Climb to Koskina Castle, at about 660 m above sea level, for views over much of the island. The Byzantines built it in the 10th century; only sections of its walls remain, and the small, vaulted church of Agios Georgios Dorganas incorporates ancient columns. From Kosikia, an unpaved road runs for a few kilometers before a rugged trail leads to the summit.

to_next_leg.road_type: Unpaved road to Kosikia, then coastal road via Evdilos

activities.text: Easy to access and family-friendly, Livadi Beach at the entrance to Armenistis offers fine golden sand, a small lake formed by a mountain stream, and shade from tamarisk trees. The stream flowing down from the mountain makes the water slightly cooler. Sun loungers, umbrellas, and a snack bar are available in summer; come toward the end of the day, as the beach is very popular.

practical_info.tip: Park along the paved road and walk the rest of the way to the sand.

activities.text: You’ll then follow Messakti Beach, a long stretch of golden sand where the small Myrsonas River forms a wetland before reaching the sea. Shallow water and a lifeguard station make it a good choice for families with children. When the meltemi winds pick up, surfers take over: stay close to shore then.

practical_info.tip: Access is down a few steps from the paved road, where you can park.

visits.text: The Agios Polykarpos Folklore Museum, in a village near Christos Raches, tells the story of everyday life in Raches in years past through a wide range of objects. Admission is free, and a visit takes less than 1 hour. Stop by in the morning: it opens daily from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., well before the mountains come alive in the evening.

“The village that never sleeps” is how Christos Raches is described, perched among pine trees at about 500 m above sea level. Its square paved with Ikarian slate, church with a marble bell tower, and the women’s association’s sweets workshop can be explored on foot, with cars left at the village entrance. Return after 9 p.m., when shops and cafés come alive until midnight.

activities.text: Walk 15 minutes from Christos Raches to Litani Rock, a viewpoint known for its sunsets. The path winds through the pines and oaks surrounding scattered houses, with an old mill hidden beneath the trees. The walk stays cool in the morning; return at dusk if you want the evening light.

practical_info.tip: On August 6, the festival in Christos Raches is one of the island’s largest, with music and dancing until dawn.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: Around the 6th century BC, sailors calling at Nas honored Artemis Tauropolos in a temple overlooking the cove. Only the floor and fragments of marble remain; the rest ended up in a lime kiln. Walk down the steps from the paved road: the site is outdoors and free to enter.

activities.text: Walk upstream from the mouth of the Halaris, behind Nas Beach: a small freshwater lake forms here, surrounded by dense vegetation, before the ravine extends inland toward Raches. This marked trail connects Nas to the village of Christos, passing plane trees and stone bridges. A round-trip walk of 1 hour 30 minutes is enough to enjoy its shade.

practical_info.tip: The mouth of the Halaris is a protected wetland: stay on the trails and wear closed-toe shoes.

activities.text: If the north wind picks up, admire Nas Beach from the sand: treacherous currents and sudden waves give it a reputation for being dangerous, and a rope extending out to sea helps swimmers return to shore. When the sea is calm, the sand and small pebbles invite a swim. Stay afterward to watch the sunset over the open sea.

practical_info.tip: Nudist beach with no facilities; tavernas in neighboring villages.

visits.text: There is no need to look for a large fenced site: in Kampos, the remains of Oinoe, the island’s ancient capital, blend into the present-day village. Ramparts, a late antique odeon with large arches, an aqueduct, and “Palatia,” a civic building from the early Byzantine period, line the walk. The site is free to visit and open daily from 8:30 a.m. to 3 p.m.

Agia Irini in Kampos holds a quiet distinction: it is the oldest church still standing on the island. Rebuilt in the 11th and 12th centuries on the ruins of a 4th-century early Christian basilica, it retains a few frescoes and columns from the original building. In the grounds, walk around the carved marble sarcophagus from late antiquity.

Just one room, but a wealth of finds from Oinoe: the Kampos Archaeological Museum, on Agia Irini hill, brings together vases, statues, and inscribed stones found in the tombs of the ancient necropolis. Other objects come from Frandato, Arethousa, and Petropouli. Access is by steps only.

A slab of rock serves as the roof of Theoskepasti Chapel, tucked into a cavity near the Monastery of Osia Theoktisti in Pigi, above Kampos. The Cretan-inspired frescoes in the main church date to 1688, and no monks live here anymore. A short trail climbs here from Kampos; wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.

activities.text: When the wind stays away, Kampos Beach, a long stretch of sand below Oinoe, offers shallow water for children, and a small delta forms a lagoon. One section remains undeveloped, while the other has lounge chairs and a bar. Take a swim before heading to Evdilos, a few minutes away by car, for the ferry.

practical_info.tip: Waves sometimes build up: watch children closely, even in shallow water.

activities.text: You will leave Ikaria from Evdilos, the island’s second port and its capital from 1834 to 1912, where ferries depart for Piraeus. While you wait, explore the small harbor, its stately homes, and its stepped lanes. Check the departure time the day before: sailings vary by season and can be disrupted by wind.

practical_info.tip: If you are flying out, the airport is at the other end of the island, near Faros: allow plenty of time.

seo.h1_title: Ikaria in 4 Days: Hot Springs, Seychelles, and Raches
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary crosses Ikaria from Agios Kirykos to Evdilos, taking you from the hot springs of Lefkada and Therma to Drakano Tower and Seychelles Beach. You then cross the mountain via Koskina Castle to reach Armenistis, Nas, and Christos Raches, before finishing at the ruins of Oinoe in Kampos.
seo.seo_hook: Ikaria in 4 days: hot spring bathing in the sea at Lefkada and Therma, Seychelles cove, the temple at Nas, and late nights in Christos Raches.
featured_list: Agios Kirykos: free museum and Lefkada hot springs at 59 °C
Therma: hot spring bathing in the sea at the foot of a cave
Faros: Drakano Tower and Iero Beach
Manganitis: Seychelles Beach, formed by a landslide
Koskina Castle: a 10th-century Byzantine fortress
Nas: remains of the sanctuary of Artemis Tauropolos
Christos Raches: the village that comes alive at night
Kampos: remains of Oinoe and Agia Irini Church

Seychelles: a cove formed by a landslide after the Manganitis tunnel was excavated

itineraries.title: Saronic Islands in 3 Days: Aegina, Poros, and Hydra
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel between Aegina, Poros, and Hydra by ferry, from the Temple of Aphaia to Hydra’s car-free trails.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday: Kolona is closed on Tuesdays, the Poros museum on Mondays and Tuesdays, and Hydra’s ecclesiastical museum on Mondays. The direct Aegina–Poros service (Saronic Ferries, 1 hour 20 minutes) runs only once a day in season and only on certain days during the rest of the year: check it before booking the rest of your trip.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May–June or September–October: on Hydra, average highs range from 24 °C in October to 30 °C in June. Avoid July–August, when temperatures are around 33 °C, for climbs to Paleochora or Prophet Elijah in full sun. From November to April, rain returns and ferry services become less frequent, especially between Aegina and Poros.

activities.text: You’ll board at Piraeus, Europe’s fifth-busiest passenger port, from gate E8 on the Akti Poseidonos quay. Aegean Flying Dolphins hydrofoils reach Aegina in 40 minutes, while conventional Saronic Ferries vessels take 1 hour 10 minutes. Choose a departure around 8 a.m. to reach Aphaia before the heat, and arrive 30 to 45 minutes before sailing.

practical_info.tip: Piraeus station, the terminus of the green metro line, is a 15- to 20-minute walk from gate E8.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Piraeus → Aegina port → Aphaia temple
to_next_leg.justification: Traversée du Pirée vers le port d’Égine, puis route terrestre jusqu’au temple d’Aphaïa.

visits.text: The scent of pine and golden limestone: the Temple of Aphaia crowns a 160 m hill in eastern Aegina. Built around 500 BC, this Doric temple retains 24 of its 32 columns, and the Acropolis is visible in the distance on clear days. Most buses to Agia Marina stop here; from April through August, the site opens at 8 a.m. (admission €10).

Aphaia’s pediments are in Munich, yet the site’s scientific collection is well worth half an hour. Removed in 1811, the statues were sold the following year to the future King Ludwig I of Bavaria; here, the reconstructed entablature of the earlier Archaic temple and copies of sculptures put them in context. Included in admission, the collection is closed on Tuesdays.

Saint Nektarios, who died in 1920 and was canonized in 1961, draws thousands of pilgrims to Agios Nektarios Monastery. He restored the complex in 1904 for a community of nuns; you can visit his tomb and small house beside an immense church with two bell towers. The bus to Agia Marina stops outside; dress modestly, as the site remains very popular with worshippers.

Nicknamed the “Mystras of Aegina,” Paleochora became the island’s hilltop inland capital in the 9th century as a refuge from pirates. Barbarossa sacked it in 1537, and its residents abandoned it in the early 19th century. Legend speaks of 365 churches; 38 survive, including Agios Nikolaos Mavrikas with its frescoes from 1330. Admission is free: bring closed-toe shoes, a hat, and water.

Just one column remains standing, yet Kolona tells the whole story of Aegina. It comes from the Doric Temple of Apollo (late 6th century BC), on a hill inhabited since the Neolithic period; the nearby museum, founded in 1829, was the Greek state's first. Allow 15 minutes to walk from the port; open from 10 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

Markellos Tower, probably a Venetian watchtower, housed the government from 1826 to 1828, just before Aegina became the first capital of modern Greece. At the Metropolitan Cathedral, where Kapodistrias took his oath of office, his stall still faces the bishop's throne. Finish at Agios Nikolaos Chapel, at the harbor entrance, at sunset.

activities.text: If you bring back just one souvenir from Aegina, choose “Fistiki Aiginis” pistachios. Physician Nikolaos Peroglou began their systematic cultivation in 1896; their protected designation of origin dates to 1996, and the island reportedly produces some 2,700 tonnes a year. Shop in town on the second morning, before the ferry to Poros.

practical_info.tip: The Saronic Ferries service to Poros departs once a day in season, in the late morning: check the schedule the day before.

visits.text: After stepping off the ferry from Aegina, head straight to the Archaeological Museum of Poros, five minutes from the port: it closes at 3 p.m. The former home of Prime Minister Alexandros Koryzis houses finds from the Sanctuary of Poseidon, where Demosthenes poisoned himself in 322 BC, along with a rich collection of Mycenaean artifacts. Open Wednesday through Sunday, admission €5.

Zoodochos Pigi Monastery, founded in 1720, nestles on a pine-covered hillside, 4 km east of town. Its dome and bell tower watch over Monastiri Bay below. A bus climbs there from the port of Poros; on foot, allow nearly 1 hour along the road.

The finest viewpoint in Poros is reached on foot: the clock tower, built in 1927 at the summit of Sferia, the volcanic part of the island where the town climbs the hillside. A 15-minute climb from the waterfront is all it takes; at the top await views of the bay, Galatas, the Peloponnese, and the lemon grove. Go up at sunset, which the tower faces.

activities.text: Deep, clear water and pines reaching the shore: Monastiri Beach, beside Zoodochos Pigi Monastery, is the place for an afternoon swim. Here Poros reveals its wooded side, far from the bustle of the port. Pack a swimsuit and towel in your day bag, then head back down by bus or taxi before sunset.

practical_info.tip: Return to the port early enough to climb to the clock tower at sunset.

activities.text: Just two hundred meters of sea separate Poros from the Peloponnese, and Galatas seems within shouting distance from the waterfront. In the evening, the quay comes alive: fishing boats and sailboats line up, while fishermen mend their nets in Pounta. Dine overlooking the channel, then turn in early: the hydrofoil to Hydra leaves in the morning.

practical_info.tip: Poros–Hydra hydrofoil: 25 to 35 minutes, with several departures a day in summer and far fewer in the off-season.

to_next_leg.justification: Traversée en hydroptère ou ferry rapide entre les ports de Poros et Hydra, sans attente ni embarquement.

visits.text: If the hydrofoil from Poros drops you off around 10 a.m., start at the Monastery of the Dormition, whose marble bell tower with a clock watches over Hydra's harbor. Built in the mid-17th century and rebuilt by Venetian architects after the earthquake of 1750, it holds the tomb of Lazaros Koundouriotis in its courtyard. Its small ecclesiastical museum, housed in the former prison, displays the icon of the “Unfading Rose” (1774). Open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from April to mid-November, except Mondays.

An admiral's heart rests in a silver urn at the Historical Archives Museum of Hydra: that of Andreas Miaoulis, master of the fireships of the War of Independence. Figureheads, flags, and weapons recall how Hydra outfitted around 150 ships against the Ottomans. On the waterfront, the museum opens daily from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. (€8). In late June, the Miaoulia festivities reenact the burning of an Ottoman fleet at sea, complete with fireworks.

One house is enough to grasp the wealth of Hydra's shipowners: the Historic House of Lazaros Koundouriotis, on the western side of the harbor. Built in the late 18th century, it belonged to the island's richest captain, who gave his entire fortune to the War of Independence; since 2001, it has been a branch of the National Historical Museum. Landscapes by Panayiotis Tetsis hang upstairs, with paintings by the Vyzantios family in the former cellars. Open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., March 25 through October 31 (€10).

activities.text: You’ll follow Hydra's coastal path west, past the cannons of the 18th-century bastions guarding the harbor entrance. There are no cars or motorcycles—the law prohibits them—and not even a bicycle: donkeys and mules pass walkers along the way. Fishing boats line the shore at Kamini; Vlychos, less than 1 hour away on foot, offers gray pebbles and Agia Paraskevi Chapel on its rock. Swim, wait for sunset, then return by water taxi.

practical_info.tip: In summer, water taxis frequently shuttle between Vlychos and the port; bring water and sturdy shoes.

activities.text: A peaceful place of prayer, yet once a hero's prison: Theodoros Kolokotronis was held for four months at the Monastery of Prophet Elijah. Founded in 1813 by thirteen monks from Mount Athos, it overlooks Hydra's harbor at an elevation of around 500 m, reached after an hour and a half of climbing through the pines. Set out at dawn on the last morning and aim for a late-morning or afternoon ferry: the island has no springs, so bring your own water.

practical_info.tip: Allow about 1 hour 30 minutes for the climb from the port, largely in the shade of pines; the summit of Mount Eros (588 m) is another 30 minutes away.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Hydra → Saronic Gulf → Piraeus
to_next_leg.justification: Navigation d’Hydra vers Le Pirée dans le golfe Saronique ; la distance est corrigée au-dessus de la ligne droite.

activities.text: You will dock at Gate E8 in Piraeus after a nonstop crossing of 1 hour 5 minutes from Hydra, or up to 1 hour 50 minutes if the boat makes other stops. The metro's Green Line, which terminates in Piraeus, departs from a station 15 or 20 minutes' walk from the docks. Leave extra time if you have a flight the same day: schedules change with the seasons.

practical_info.tip: Hydra–Piraeus: 1 hour 5 minutes to 1 hour 50 minutes, depending on the company and the number of stops.

seo.h1_title: Saronic Islands in 3 Days: Aegina, Poros, and Hydra
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day trip links three Saronic Islands at a relaxed pace: a day on Aegina exploring the Temple of Aphaia, Paleochora, and Kolona, an afternoon and evening on Poros, then a full day on Hydra. Crossings take from 25 minutes to 1 hour 50 minutes, with an overnight stay on each island.
seo.seo_hook: Saronic Islands in 3 days: the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina, the clock tower on Poros, and Hydra’s museums and coastal trail, linked by short ferry rides.
featured_list: Aegina: Temple of Aphaia, built around 500 BC among pine trees
Paleochora: 38 churches in the abandoned medieval capital
Kolona: a column from the Temple of Apollo and the Greek state’s first museum
Poros: a clock tower built in 1927 facing the Peloponnese
Hydra: Admiral Miaoulis’s heart at the Historical Archives Museum

itineraries.title: Lemnos in 4 Days: Ancient Cities, Flamingos, and Dunes
itineraries.subtitle: Spend 4 days exploring from Myrina, visiting Poliochni, the Kabirion, the dunes of Katalakkos, and the flamingos of Alyki.
itineraries.notes: The museum in Myrina, Poliochni, Hephaistia, and the Kabirion are open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. and closed on Tuesdays: schedule your dune day for Tuesday. A car is essential, and two short dirt roads lead to the dunes of Katalakkos and Faraklo.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May, June, and September, with average highs of 22 to 27 °C. In July and August, highs hover around 29 °C, and the meltemi, a steady summer wind, delights kitesurfers at Keros. Avoid November through January, the rainiest months (66 to 85 mm per month).

visits.text: Lemnos’s finest vantage point takes some effort to reach: a twenty- to twenty-five-minute climb leads to Myrina’s Kastro. Reinforced in the late 12th century by Emperor Andronikos I Komnenos, then expanded by the Venetians, its ramparts feature fourteen towers. The fallow deer grazing within the walls descend from a small group brought from Rhodes in the early 1970s. Head up in the late afternoon: the slope offers little shade, and on clear days the view stretches as far as Mount Athos.

Opened in August 2025, the new exhibition at the Archaeological Museum of Lemnos provides a key to understanding the entire island. The 19th-century building once housed the Ottoman governor’s offices; the second floor brings together the prehistory of Poliochni, Myrina, and Koukonisi, while the third covers the Late Bronze Age through the Byzantine period. Visit before Poliochni to better understand the site: open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. except Tuesdays, with admission costing €10.

Stone facades, carved balconies resting on brackets, and tables at the water’s edge: Romeikos Gialos is best enjoyed at sunset. Under Ottoman rule, the Greek community lived along this shore; its neoclassical homes, built from the mid-19th to the early 20th century, were often commissioned by Lemnians who had made their fortunes in Egypt and were nicknamed the “Egyptians.” A ramp provides access to the water for swimmers with limited mobility.

Less photogenic than its neighbor, Tourkikos Gialos nevertheless shelters Myrina’s fishing harbor. Before the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, the Turkish community lived along this shore, south of the rocky headland; fish tavernas have since taken over around the old harbor. Between the two bays, the Agora is lined with pottery, pasta, honey, and wine shops. Pliny the Elder claimed that the shadow of Athos reached Myrina’s square at the summer solstice. Stroll through the Agora toward the end of the day, then choose a table facing the boats.

activities.text: You won’t need a car for your first swim: Riha Nera Beach lies right in Myrina. Its name means “shallow waters,” and its sandy shore slopes gently into the sea beneath a Blue Flag. Lounge chairs, umbrellas, beach bars, and water sports make it easy to unwind; come in the early afternoon after the museum, and save the end of the day for the castle.

practical_info.tip: Within walking distance of central Myrina; lounge chairs and umbrellas available on-site.

activities.text: Lemnians call their handmade pasta flomaria: look for it on the menus of Tourkikos Gialos’s tavernas. Add kalathaki Limnou, the island’s PDO cheese, followed by a glass of local wine: Muscat of Alexandria, brought from Egypt in the early 20th century, has two PDO designations here, one for dry wine and the other for sweet, while the old Limnio grape variety has enjoyed a revival over the past twenty years or so. Finish with samsades, sesame pastries.

practical_info.tip: Ask for wines by the glass to compare dry Muscat and red Limnio.

visits.text: Kontias’s stone houses rise in tiers among pines and cypresses beneath a row of windmills. The Church of Saint John the Baptist, the oldest in the village, has the look of a fortress with its battlements and cannons. Walk up to the windmills early in the morning: the low-angle light bathes the stone and the bay below in gold.

If you visit between June and September, step inside the Gallery of Contemporary Balkan Art in Kontias. Established in 2007 following the symposiums of 1999 and 2001, it houses works donated by Greek, Albanian, Bulgarian, Romanian, Serbian, and Turkish artists, often focusing on Lemnos. It is open from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., except Tuesdays, with evening hours in July and August.

Rows of white headstones, quiet countryside, and a road named Anzac Street: Portianos Military Cemetery is an unexpected sight in this small village. Opened in August 1915 for soldiers who died of wounds or illness after Gallipoli, it remained in use until August 1920 and contains some 350 Commonwealth graves. The cemetery is accessible at all hours; follow the CWGC signs in the village.

Founded in 1995 by the association of people originally from Portianou, the Folklore Museum occupies the Vagiakos residence, a protected example of Lemnian vernacular architecture. Across approximately 225 m², household objects, farming tools, and traditional costumes tell the story of life in the past, from farmwork to family customs. Arrive before noon: the museum is open from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., except Tuesdays.

Surprisingly monumental for a town of barely 900 residents, the Church of Evangelistria towers over Moudros with its twin bell towers. Built in 1903, this three-aisled basilica was not inaugurated until 1919, when Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis presented it with its epitaphios. Enter the courtyard through the carved stone gateway and wear clothing that provides adequate coverage.

On October 30, 1918, the Armistice of Mudros was signed aboard HMS Agamemnon in this roadstead. Near the town, East Mudros Military Cemetery contains 885 Commonwealth graves from World War I; a plaque also commemorates 29 Russians who died during the evacuation of Novorossiisk in 1921. Open at all hours: follow signs toward Kaminia, then the CWGC signs.

Next, step inside the Moudros History and Naval Tradition Information Center, housed in a 19th-century stone building that served first as a school and then as a courthouse. Documents, screenings, and interactive activities explain the roadstead’s role during the Balkan Wars and the Gallipoli campaign. Hours vary by season: check locally before having lunch at the port.

Not a column or a temple in sight: Poliochni impresses with its streets. Inhabited from around 3500 to 2000 BC, the city left behind wells, paved squares, and a bouleuterion with tiered stone seating, considered one of the oldest known assembly halls. Its hoard of gold jewelry is displayed in Athens. Admission is €5, with opening hours from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays: arrive before 2 p.m.

activities.text: You can then wash off the dust of Poliochni at Kokkinovrachos, a beach whose name means “red rock,” about 3 km from the village of Kaminia. Discover Greece specifically recommends it after visiting the excavations. Allow 1 hour for swimming, followed by about 40 minutes of driving to return to Myrina.

practical_info.tip: Bring water and a towel: the day ends at the beach, far from Myrina.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Myrina, then take the northern route to Kotsinas

visits.text: Cool underground air is guaranteed: some sixty steps beneath a vaulted ceiling lead into the heart of Kotsinas hill, down to the sacred spring of Zoodochos Pigi. The current church dates from the 1950s, but the Venetian builders of the castle had already preserved this well. On the Friday after Easter, a major celebration fills the courtyard: come another day for peace and quiet.

In Kotsinas, the first story you will hear is Maroula’s. According to legend, during the Ottoman siege of 1478, this young woman picked up her mortally wounded father’s sword to lead the garrison; her statue has watched over the site of the former castle since 1969. Walk around the mound: with no natural elevation available, the builders raised it to a height of around twenty meters.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: In 2010, Oedipus Rex rang out in the theater of Hephaistia for the first time in approximately 2,500 years. Carved into the slope in the late Classical period, it was restored between 2000 and 2004 and once again hosts festivals and concerts. Admission is €5, with opening hours from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays; last entry is 20 minutes before closing.

Hephaistia is named after the blacksmith god, and Aeschylus placed the first appearance of fire here, before Prometheus’s act. Around the theater, the sanctuary of the Great Goddess, the agora, pottery workshops, and thermal baths from the 4th century BC recall a busy port connecting Thrace, Macedonia, and the Hellespont. Allow 1 hour to walk between these remains and the theater.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: If you visit only one sanctuary on Lemnos, choose the Kabirion, set on two terraces above the sea. Each year, mystery rites open to both free men and slaves were celebrated here after sunset for nine days. The Hellenistic initiation hall had twelve Doric columns. Admission is €5, with opening hours from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

activities.text: The Cave of Philoctetes opens beneath the Kabirion, at the end of a narrow path leading down to the shore. According to myth, the Greeks abandoned the wounded hero here on their way to Troy, leaving him to suffer for ten years before they returned. A wide opening lets the sea enter the cave: wear shoes with good traction for the descent.

practical_info.tip: Narrow path: descend in dry weather and wear sturdy shoes.

activities.text: In the height of summer, Lake Alyki is reduced to a salt crust, yet this is where Greece’s largest seasonal concentration of greater flamingos gathers. In spring, more than 4,000 birds may congregate in this wetland protected by Natura 2000. There are no bird blinds: bring binoculars and stay on the paths.

practical_info.tip: Watch from the paths with binoculars or a spotting scope; in summer, the water evaporates.

activities.text: You’ll spot the colorful wings before the sand: Keros Bay, about 3 km wide, gets steady meltemi winds over shallow water. Surf Club Keros, Greece’s first certified wing foiling center, offers lessons here. For swimming, seek out calm spots; the last 100 meters of the road are unpaved.

practical_info.tip: Lessons and rentals available on-site; the last 100 meters of the access road are unpaved.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Myrina, then the road to Katalakkos

activities.text: The Pachies Ammoudies cover about seven hectares north of Katalakkos, roughly the size of ten soccer fields. The northeast wind deposits sand worn from nearby rocks here, and white lilies grow right in the dunes. Come in the morning with a hat and water, and walk around the vegetation that holds the sand in place.

practical_info.tip: Access is via a dirt road from Katalakkos; bring a hat and water.

activities.text: The real reward after the dunes is Gomati, about 4 km from Katalakkos along a partly unpaved road. Fine sand, shallow water, and a beachfront taverna offer a chance to recharge before Faraklo. When the wind picks up, kitesurfers take over; save swimming for calmer hours.

practical_info.tip: Taverna and snack bar on the beach; swimming is more pleasant in calm weather.

to_next_leg.road_type: Dirt roads at Katalakkos and beyond Propouli

activities.text: Yellow and red spheres, as smooth as giant pebbles, descend to the sea at Faraklo, on Cape Falakro. Locals call them “frangokefala,” or Franks’ heads; some see lava cooled by contact with water, others sandstone sculpted by erosion. From Propouli, a signposted dirt road leads to the parking lot, then a trail continues to the rocks.

practical_info.tip: Passable dirt road from Propouli; wear closed-toe shoes to walk on the rocks.

to_next_leg.road_type: Dirt road to Propouli, then a paved road

visits.text: Inhabited since the late 11th or early 12th century, Kaspakas is among the oldest villages on Lemnos. Its name is thought to come from a Byzantine admiral, and Emperor Alexios Mourtzouphlos is said to have taken refuge here in April 1204; the nearby cape is still called Mourtzouflos. Look for the stone basins of the old communal washhouse, reminders of a once-abundant water supply.

activities.text: Next, head down to Agios Ioannis Beach below Kaspakas, where enormous volcanic boulders dot the sand and pebbles. The small Agios Ioannis Church, built before 1858, clings to the rocky slopes along the shore. These shallow waters have earned Blue Flag status; have lunch at a waterfront fish taverna before heading to Kakaviotissa.

practical_info.tip: Lounge chairs, beach umbrellas, and tavernas available on-site; shallow water.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Myrina, then a narrow road to the parking lot

visits.text: A church with no roof, yet sheltered: at Panagia Kakaviotissa, the rock of Mount Kakavos forms the vault. Affiliated with the Great Lavra of Mount Athos since 1305, the cave was converted into a church by monks from Agios Efstratios; its walls are no more than 1.30 m high. On the Tuesday after Easter, the icon is carried back up here in a procession: expect crowds.

activities.text: If you arrive one hour before sunset, the Kakaviotissa trail will reward you with golden light over the sea. From the parking lot at the end of a narrow, signposted road east of Myrina, allow about 15 minutes for the roughly 900 m walk: steep steps, a plateau of sculpted rocks, then the final climb. Bring a flashlight for the descent.

practical_info.tip: About 900 m from the parking lot; a flashlight and closed-toe shoes are recommended.

activities.text: Myrina’s port, at the foot of the Kastro, is your departure point if you’re leaving by ferry: routes include Piraeus, Lavrio, and Thessaloniki, with more frequent departures in summer. Lemnos International Airport is 18 km east of town. Allow extra time to return the car and board without rushing.

practical_info.tip: Check ferry schedules the day before: departures are less frequent outside peak season.

seo.h1_title: Lemnos in 4 Days: Ancient Cities, Flamingos, and Dunes
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary makes Myrina, the capital of Lemnos, your base for exploring the island by car. You visit the prehistoric city of Poliochni, the theater at Hephaistia, the sanctuary of Kabirion, and the Gallipoli cemeteries in Moudros and Portianou. The final day takes you to the dunes of Katalakkos, the rocks of Faraklo, and the roofless chapel of Kakaviotissa.
seo.seo_hook: Lemnos in 4 days from Myrina: a castle with fallow deer, Poliochni, Hephaistia, Kabirion, the dunes of Pachies Ammoudies, and flamingos at Lake Alyki.

Poliochni: a bouleuterion among the oldest known assembly halls
Moudros: the roadstead where the armistice was signed on October 30, 1918
Hephaistia: Oedipus Rex performed again in 2010 in the restored theater
Kabirion: mysteries celebrated for nine days above the cave of Philoctetes
Lake Alyki: more than 4,000 flamingos in spring
Pachies Ammoudies: about seven hectares of dunes in the north of the island
Panagia Kakaviotissa: a roofless chapel affiliated with Mount Athos as early as 1305

itineraries.title: Serres and Lake Kerkini in 4 Days: Amphipolis and Pelicans
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, connect the Lion of Amphipolis and Alistrati Cave with the acropolis of Serres and the pelicans of Lake Kerkini.
itineraries.notes: Arrive and depart through Thessaloniki Airport: Amphipolis is on the highway toward Kavala, and Kerkini is about 95 km from Thessaloniki. Leave early on the third day, as Rupel Fort can only be visited from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
itineraries.climate: Aim for April through June or September–October: in Serres, average highs range from about 20 to 30 °C in spring and from 28 to 21 °C in fall, and spring is the best season for birds. Avoid July–August on the plain, when average highs exceed 32 °C and temperatures can soar above 40 °C. January–February remains cold (8 to 11 °C in the afternoon, with a thin layer of ice possible on the lake) but offers the most photogenic Dalmatian pelicans.

visits.text: It is best to start with the Archaeological Museum of Amphipolis: without it, the site’s foundations reveal little. Founded by the Athenians in 437 BC, the city was the birthplace of admirals Nearchus and Androsthenes; exhibits include coin displays, the stele of Amyntas, and a gold stater of Alexander the Great. Full-price admission is €10; from November through March, the museum closes at 3:30 p.m.

Few walls remain standing, but the archaeological site of Amphipolis holds so much history! Brasidas and Cleon fell here in 422 BC, Roxana and Alexander IV were murdered here in 311 BC, and excavations have uncovered four early Christian basilicas with mosaic floors. The site is about 1 km from the museum: get back in the car.

Over 8 m tall including its pedestal, the Lion of Amphipolis, carved in the 4th century BC, is more massive than the lion at Chaeronea. Its blocks were recovered from the mud of the Strymon beginning in 1912, but were not reassembled until 1937. It stands about 2 km south of the ancient site; 15 minutes with your camera is enough.

Feel the immediate coolness beneath the vaults of Alistrati Cave, which opened to the public in 1998. The entrance chamber stretches for about a hundred meters, stalactites reach nearly 15 m, and in 2021 a robot named Persephone even guided the first part of the tour in 33 languages. Open daily, €10, about 1 hour: bring a light sweater.

Serres residents simply call the pine-covered hill crowned by the acropolis “Koulas.” The 9th-century Byzantine ramparts stand on a fortress dating to the 7th century BC; of the four towers mentioned in historical texts, only the Tower of Orestes, about 20 m tall and built around 1350, has survived. Look on its western face for the brick inscription “tower of King Andronikos, built by Orestes.” Head up in the late afternoon for views over the city and the Strymon plain.

Agios Nikolaos Church nestles on the wooded slopes of Koulas, below the Tower of Orestes. Built on a cross-in-square plan, it retains a 12th-century exonarthex and was restored in the mid-1930s. Stop here on your way down to the center: even with the door closed, you can appreciate its Byzantine forms from the forecourt, in the shade of the pines.

Almost completely destroyed in 1913 during the Second Balkan War, the Old Metropolitan Church of Saints Theodore was rebuilt between 1938 and 1959. This three-aisled Byzantine basilica, 24 m long, was famous for its mosaics; its northern annexes now house a small museum of sculptures and inscriptions from the church and surrounding area. The church remains an active place of worship: visit outside service times, with your shoulders covered.

Footsteps echo beneath the six domes of the Bezesteni, an Ottoman covered market measuring 21 m by 31 m, built around 1493–1494. Home to the Serres Archaeological Museum since 1970, it displays a Neolithic vase from Promachonas, the inscription identifying ancient Sirris with the present-day city, and the 12th-century mosaic of the Apostle Andrew rescued from the Old Metropolitan Church. Come in the morning, before the heat bears down on Eleftherias Square.

If an exhibition is on, step inside Zincirli Mosque to see its finely carved marble minbar. Built in the late 16th century near Emporiou Square, it blends Ottoman architecture with Byzantine influences and now hosts cultural events. Otherwise, take a ten-minute walk around it: its facades are easy to appreciate from the street.

Serres’ most endearing museum tells the story of a people of nomadic shepherds: the Sarakatsani Folklore Museum. Opened in 1979 and housed since 1997 in a building designed for it, the museum recreates the tsiatoura, a shelter used on the move, and woven huts on the ground floor; upstairs are looms, flokati rugs, and costumes. The municipality highlights its 1987 European award. Hours vary: call before you go.

Leave the city for a ravine on Mount Menikio, 12 km to the northeast, where Timios Prodromos Monastery lies hidden. Founded in the 1270s by the monk Ioannikios, it preserves a 14th-century katholikon and the tomb of Gennadios Scholarios, the first ecumenical patriarch after the fall of Constantinople, who died here in 1472. Nuns have lived here since 1986: wear clothing that covers your body, and avoid the August 29 feast day if you are seeking peace and quiet.

activities.text: Eleftherias Square, the heart of Serres and surrounded by pedestrian streets, is the ideal place to try akanes, a local sweet similar to Turkish delight but made with fresh butter and well-toasted almonds. In the morning, enjoy Serres bougatsa, renowned for its flaky pastry, at the foot of the statue of Emmanuel Papas, a local native who led the 1821 uprising. Buy a box of akanes for the drive to the lake.

practical_info.tip: Bougatsa for breakfast, akanes with afternoon coffee: the square is ideal for both.

activities.text: End the day in the Agioi Anargyroi Valley, Serres’ green lung close to the center, which the municipality lists among its sights to see. Century-old plane trees, flowing water, sports facilities, cafés, and tavernas: the valley is especially lively in summer, when the heat subsides. Save it for dinner after the climb up Koulas, and allow 1 hour for a leisurely stroll.

practical_info.tip: In summer, bring insect repellent for evenings by the water.

to_next_leg.road_type: A25 to Rupel Fort, then Sidirokastro

visits.text: With 4,251 m of tunnels beneath the mountain, Rupel Fort, the largest of the Metaxas Line’s 21 forts, held out for three days against the German attack of April 1941. Military personnel lead free tours daily from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., covering the memorial, observation post, museum, and central tunnel. Never photograph the personnel.

The view alone justifies the climb to Isari Castle, which gave Sidirokastro its name, meaning “iron castle.” Built in the 6th century and modified through the 14th, the fortress retains stretches of ramparts, semicircular towers, and a cistern. Admission is free, with access by dirt road or trail and views over the Strymon plain and Lake Kerkini.

activities.text: Have lunch in the shade of the plane trees in the valley of the Krousovitis, the river that runs along the northeastern side of Sidirokastro before joining the Strymon. Tavernas and cafés overlook the water; right next door, the spring-fed swimming pools, in operation since 1979, open to the public in summer. An hour is enough before heading to the thermal baths.

practical_info.tip: The valley’s swimming pools open only in summer; the tavernas serve food year-round.

activities.text: If your legs need a break after Rupel, head to the Sidirokastro thermal baths in Loutra, just north of town near the railway bridge over the Strymon. The spring, known since Byzantine times, exceeds 40 °C; the building houses an indoor pool and private hydromassage baths. Check the hours: call before you leave.

practical_info.tip: Keep a swimsuit and towel in the trunk; afterward, allow 35 minutes to drive to Kerkini.

visits.text: Kerkini’s small harbor makes a fine lookout for your first evening by the lake, with one of the national park’s five wooden observation towers. The paradox here is that this reservoir, created in 1932 by damming the Strymon to irrigate the Serres plain, has become a Ramsar wetland where more than 300 bird species have been recorded. In hot weather, mosquitoes are especially active between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m.: repellent is essential.

Stop by the Kerkini Wetland Information Center in the village before choosing your observation spots. It falls under NECCA, the public agency that manages the national park established in 2006. According to the agency, the lake and Porto Lagos together form Europe’s main wintering site for Dalmatian pelicans, and the area has the largest number of water buffalo in Greece. Ask about the current rules: each area of the park has its own.

From Kerkini, it is about 17 km, or a 25-minute drive, to Lithotopos. Built in 1932 and replaced by a new structure in 1982 after silt from the Strymon had reduced the lake’s capacity, Lithotopos Dam is the key to understanding the entire landscape. A paved road leads up to it; in Lithotopos, the Ecotourism Promotion Center displays taxidermy specimens of birds, plants, and local products. Lithotopos also has a small harbor and woods ideal for walking: allow 1 hour, and check the center’s hours locally.

activities.text: The silence of dawn gives way to the heavy rustle of wings above the plava, the flat-bottomed boat used by Lake Kerkini’s fishermen. The boat skirts the flooded forest and its heronry, then approaches the Dalmatian pelican colony as far as a yellow buoy marking the permitted limit; the birds nest on wooden platforms installed for them. Book the day before at the harbor or through your accommodations, and allow about 2 hours on the water.

practical_info.tip: January and February offer Dalmatian pelicans at their most photogenic; from April to June, the flooded forest and waterbird colonies take center stage. In winter, dress warmly: a thin layer of ice can form on the lake.

activities.text: From Kerkini, first drive to the Megalochori triangle on the opposite shore of the lake. Then follow the dirt road along Lake Kerkini’s eastern dike by car, keeping the lake on your right, as far as Chrysochorafa or Lithotopos. This flat dirt road is ideal for birdwatching from your car: Dalmatian pelicans, glossy ibises, night herons, and birds of prey appear depending on the season, while water buffalo often wade in the shallows. Drive at walking speed, turn off the engine at every stop, and bring a spotting scope.

practical_info.tip: The dirt road is flat and unpaved; depending on the season, the lower part of the route may be dry. Ask at the information center.

activities.text: If you prefer paddling, head out in a canoe on Lake Kerkini: these boats hold up to three people, and guided outings are available for less experienced paddlers. Vast carpets of water lilies cover part of the lake, and numerous stork nests dot the surrounding area. Keep your distance from the colonies and preferably go with a local guide who knows which areas are open to boating.

practical_info.tip: In summer, save canoeing for late afternoon, when temperatures are milder than at midday.

activities.text: Head uphill for dinner in Ano Poroia, at the foot of Mount Beles. Fifteen minutes from Kerkini, it is the most developed of the upland villages, with cafés and tavernas. Local specialties include buffalo meat products, buffalo milk yogurt, and kazan dipi, a regional caramelized dessert, along with eels and carp from the lake. Save room for dessert, and ask which products come from the herds around the lake.

practical_info.tip: In winter, some accommodations in the region close: check before booking.

seo.h1_title: Serres and Lake Kerkini in 4 Days: Amphipolis and Pelicans
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary starts in Amphipolis, a city founded by the Athenians in 437 BC, passes through Alistrati Cave, and includes two nights in Serres, between its Byzantine acropolis and Ottoman Bezesteni. It then heads up the Strymon Valley via Rupel Fort and Sidirokastro, ending at Lake Kerkini, a national park where Dalmatian pelicans spend the winter.
seo.seo_hook: Serres and Lake Kerkini in 4 days: the Amphipolis museum, Alistrati Cave, Rupel Fort, and a boat trip among Dalmatian pelicans.
featured_list: Amphipolis: a lion standing over 8 m tall including its pedestal
Alistrati Cave: an entrance chamber measuring around 100 meters
Serres: the Tower of Orestes, built around 1350 on Koulas Hill
Timios Prodromos Monastery: a 14th-century katholikon
Rupel Fort: the largest of the Metaxas Line’s 21 forts
Lake Kerkini: over 300 bird species recorded

places_taglines.GR::amphipolis: An Athenian city founded in 437 BC, a museum with extensive collections, and a monumental lion.
places_taglines.GR::alistrati-cave: A cave opened to the public in 1998, with stalactites reaching nearly 15 m.
places_taglines.GR::serres: A Byzantine acropolis, an Ottoman Bezesteni, and the tomb of Patriarch Gennadios Scholarios.
places_taglines.GR::sidirokastro: Byzantine Isari Castle, Rupel Fort, and hot springs.
places_taglines.GR::kerkini: A reservoir turned national park, home to Dalmatian pelicans and buffalo.

highlights: Amphipolis: museum of the city founded by the Athenians in 437 BC
Alistrati Cave: stalactites nearly 15 m long, a tour lasting about 1 hour
Serres: Tower of Orestes dating to around 1350 and the Ottoman Bezesteni with its six domes
Timios Prodromos: tomb of Patriarch Gennadios Scholarios, who died in 1472
Rupel: 4,251 m of tunnels, free guided tour in the morning
Lake Kerkini: a plava boat trip to the Dalmatian pelican colony
