itineraries.title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena in 3 Days: Mansions and Fossils
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, connect Kozani’s library, Aiani’s museum, Siatista’s mansions, and Grevena’s bridges.
itineraries.notes: Museums and mansions are mainly open in the morning (until 2 p.m. at Kozani’s folklore museum and 3:30 p.m. in Aiani and Siatista): save late afternoons and evenings for the squares and tavernas. The Koventareios Library is open only on weekdays, while the Milia museum and Dolgiras Mansion can be visited by appointment.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with average highs of 19 to 27 °C in Kozani. Avoid the depths of winter if you dislike the cold (average lows near -1 °C in January), and bear in mind that November is the rainiest month; in July, expect around 30 °C in the afternoon. To see the saffron fields around Krokos in bloom, come from mid-October to early November.

visits.text: Agios Nikolaos Church in Kozani began life half underground: built in 1664 below ground level to avoid provoking the Ottoman authorities, it was rebuilt on a larger scale in 1721. Frescoes painted in 1730 by two brothers from Ioannina cover the entire interior, facing a carved wooden iconostasis. Beside it, the 26 m bell tower, built in 1855, houses the clock donated in 1939 by Konstantinos Mamatsios, whose nickname it still bears. Come in the morning, when Nikis Square comes alive.

Our loveliest surprise in Kozani: the Koventareios Library, the successor to a library founded in 1668 and now home to more than 153,000 documents. Its museum section displays an original copy of Rigas Feraios’s Charta, the large map printed in 1796–1797, along with editions dating back to 1494. Admission is free, but the library is open only on weekdays: set aside a morning from Monday through Friday.

Make your way from the basement to the top floor of Kozani’s Historical, Folklore, and Natural History Museum, spread over six levels. Downstairs, rocks and fossils trace the region’s geological history; above, costumes, tools, furniture, and works of art cover the 17th through 20th centuries. At the very top, a recreated Kozani home interior illustrates everyday life from the Ottoman era through the late 1950s. Open daily from 8:30 a.m. to 2 p.m.: start your day here.

Some twenty years after the 1995 earthquake, the Archaeological Collection of Kozani reopened in December 2016. It occupies a two-story neoclassical house from the early 20th century: five rooms display finds from across the region, from prehistory to Roman times, while statues and votive stelae stand outside. Hours vary: check with the Ephorate of Antiquities of Kozani before visiting.

If your visit falls on a Wednesday evening or Sunday morning, add the Nikos Kalogeropoulos Museum of Contemporary Local History. Archival photographs, period newspapers, uniforms, and equipment trace the years 1940 to 1947, from World War II to the Greek Civil War. Admission is free, with opening hours on Wednesdays from 5:30 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.; on other days, visits are by appointment only.

activities.text: An everyday savory pie, Kozani’s kichi nevertheless looks like a festive pastry: rolls of phyllo dough filled with leek and feta, coiled into a spiral like a snail shell. Try it at lunch with yaprakia, stuffed cabbage leaves that the city serves each year shortly after Christmas in Nikis Square, accompanied by local wine. Choose a downtown taverna a short walk from the museums.

practical_info.tip: During the eleven days of Kozani’s carnival, from Fat Thursday to Clean Monday, a different neighborhood lights its large bonfire, the fanos, each evening and offers visitors kichi and meatballs.

visits.text: A firm favorite of ours is the Archaeological Museum of Aiani, which the national tourism board ranks among the most important in northern Greece. Its galleries tell the story of the capital of ancient Elimeia: painted vases from the 14th century BC, a gold fibula, and a kore figurine from the 6th century BC. Open daily from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.: arrive as soon as it opens.

Next, climb Megali Rachi hill, the site of ancient Aiani. Excavations have uncovered large public buildings, a portico that may have served as a market, a circular cistern cut into the rock, and several Hellenistic houses. The site has its own parking lot; wear sturdy shoes.

Beneath your feet at the royal necropolis of Aiani lay the kings of Elimeia. Twelve large chamber tombs, the largest measuring 11 m by 11 m, were built here from the Archaic through the Hellenistic period, and a marble lion stood guard over the complex. The site is open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.: save it for late morning, after the museum.

activities.text: About 150,000 flowers for one kilo of stigmas: that is what it takes to produce saffron in Krokos, a village 5 km south of Kozani on the road to Aiani. The flowers bloom from mid-October to early November and are picked by hand. The growers’ cooperative, founded in 1971, offers guided tours only to groups of more than 20 people, by reservation.

practical_info.tip: If you are visiting independently, enjoy the purple fields along the roadside during the October and November harvest, and look for the Krokos Kozanis PDO label on the packets.

visits.text: Colorful stained glass, wooden ceilings carved with rosettes, and ships and arabesques painted on the walls: the Poulkos mansion in the Gerania neighborhood is a feast for the eyes. An inscription above the entrance dates its construction to the mid-18th century, and a view of Constantinople appears among the decorations. Open daily from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.; admission €5.

Our favorite in Siatista is still the Maliogas mansion, built in 1759 and decorated in 1844. Rigas Feraios appears alongside King Otto and Tsar Nicholas I, while a fresco depicts Frankfurt based on an engraving by Johann Balthasar Probst: a German city painted in the heart of Macedonia. Opening hours are the same as at the Poulkos mansion: visit both on the same morning, starting at 8:30 a.m.

Aristotle, Plato, and Solon in a church: they appear in the women’s gallery of Agia Paraskevi, Siatista’s oldest surviving church, dated to 1677. Its frescoes date to 1679, and its hexagonal bell tower, funded by the residents of Gerania, to 1862. It overlooks Gerania Square; if the door is closed, ask at the municipal tourist office.

With a day’s notice, the Dolgiras mansion in the Chora neighborhood will open its folk museum to you. The house dates to 1700–1730 and its murals to around 1840; each room displays objects, often more than 200 years old, donated by people from Siatista living around the world. Visits by appointment only; admission €3.

Stop at the Siatista Paleontological Collection to see the prehistoric elephant from Kaloneri: a partial skull with intact tusks, about 125,000 years old, discovered in 2006. It all began in 1902 with a tusk found in the Aliakmon Valley. Admission is free, with weekday opening hours until 3 p.m. and weekend hours from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.; call before stopping by.

activities.text: Siatista unfolds on two levels: Gerania, the lower neighborhood, and Chora, perched at the top of town, each once with its own church and school committees. Around thirty mansions dating from the mid-18th through the 19th century survive between the two. Walk uphill from one to the other in the late afternoon: at an elevation of about 920 m, views open up over the mountains of Western Macedonia.

practical_info.tip: On December 23, for the Klatharies festivities, each neighborhood builds conical bonfires 3 to 6 m high and lights them at nightfall as a brass band passes by.

activities.text: On August 15, so the story goes in Siatista, wine flows freely, even for the horses the men bring back from the chapel on the plain. The most highly regarded local wine is Liasto Siatistas, a sweet wine made from xinomavro and moschomavro grapes and aged for many years in oak barrels. On the edge of town, Dio Fili winery offers tastings and tours by appointment: call the day before.

practical_info.tip: On August 15, Siatista’s horsemen bring back the icon of the Panagia and dance on their horses’ backs: book your room well in advance.

visits.text: 5.02 m: that is the length of the mastodon tusks on display at the Milia Natural History Museum, longer than a car and listed in Guinness World Records in 2009. They belonged to a Mammut borsoni dating back about 3 million years, excavated in 2007, and are displayed alongside more than 2,000 fossils: rhinoceroses, hipparions, and saber-toothed cats. Admission is free; call before visiting, as tours are by appointment.

Legend has it that Aziz Aga threatened to have his master builder beheaded if the central arch collapsed a third time. Aziz Aga Bridge has stood firm: more than 70 m long, with three arches, one spanning 28 m, it rises 15 m above the Venetikos and was dated to 1727 by an inscription now lost. Only pedestrians and visitors use it today: bring walking shoes.

Head back toward Grevena via Spanos Bridge, about 16 km southwest of town, between Kosmati and Kipourio. Its five arches cross the Venetikos over roughly 85 m; one bears the date 1846, and cars still cross it. Stop before crossing to take in all five arches at once; the Egnatia highway runs just a few meters away.

Grevena centers on two squares: the square by the Clock Tower, a downtown landmark, and Aimilianou Square, linked by a broad pedestrian street. At an elevation of about 530 m beside the Grevenitis River, the town has held the title of “City of Mushrooms” since 2007. Take a stroll in the late afternoon before sitting down to dinner.

Mushrooms everywhere, all made of wood: at Grevena Mushroom Park, on the northeastern edge of town along the road to Kozani, sculptures of local species line the paths. Every August, the park hosts the Panhellenic Mushroom Festival. Popular with families, it takes just under 1 hour to visit.

activities.text: Sit down for dinner at a taverna in Grevena: almost every dish features mushrooms, whether in pies, soups, pilaf, trahanas, or even a spoon sweet. More than 2,500 species have been recorded in the regional district, but only about ten make it onto plates. Ask for seasonal species; spring and fall are the best times for mushroom picking.

practical_info.tip: Never pick mushrooms on your own unless you can identify the species with certainty: the region’s alternative tourism offices organize guided outings to Valia Calda or Mount Orliakas.

activities.text: Our pick for the region’s most original souvenir: the mushroom products sold in Grevena. Producers’ stalls are filled with pickled, oil-packed, or dried mushrooms, liqueur, loukoumi, and even mushroom and truffle chocolates. Buy them on your last evening: a jar travels much better than a tray of fresh mushrooms.

practical_info.tip: Tuck glass jars between your clothes in the center of your suitcase for the trip home.

activities.text: Take the Egnatia Highway to Kozani, just under half an hour from Grevena, to catch your flight or continue by road. Filippos Airport, 3 or 4 km from the city, connects it to Athens, and the Egnatia passes just north of Kozani toward Thessaloniki. Allow time for one last coffee in Nikis Square before returning your rental car.

practical_info.tip: Check flight schedules to Athens before setting your departure date.

seo.h1_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena in 3 Days: Mansions and Fossils
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts in Kozani, with its Agios Nikolaos Church and Koventareios Library, then takes you through the saffron fields of Krokos and the museum in Aiani. You stay overnight in Siatista, a town of painted 18th-century mansions, before heading to the mastodon tusks of Milia, the stone bridges over the Venetikos, and Grevena, the town of mushrooms.
seo.seo_hook: Aiani’s museum, Siatista’s painted mansions, Milia’s mastodon tusks, and Grevena’s bridges: Western Macedonia in 3 days.

itineraries.title: Mount Olympus in 3 Days: Dion, Litochoro, and Larissa
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from the sanctuary of Dion to the trails of Mount Olympus, Platamon Castle, and Larissa.
itineraries.notes: Do not schedule the third day on a Tuesday, when Platamon Castle and the Schwartz Mansion are closed, or the first day on a Tuesday or Wednesday from November through March, when the Dion site and museum are closed. In the Vale of Tempe, the footbridge leading to the chapel of Agia Paraskevi, swept away by Storm Daniel, was still being rebuilt in July 2026.
itineraries.climate: Best times: May–June and September–October, with average highs of 22 to 31 °C in Larissa, and the Spilios Agapitos Refuge open from May through October. Avoid July–August on the Plain of Thessaly (an average of 33 °C in July, with peaks around 40 °C every summer) and winter for hiking: snow, avalanche risk, and a closed refuge. Bring a warm layer, as the air gets considerably colder at higher elevations.

visits.text: Water from the springs of Mount Olympus still flows between the columns of the Dion archaeological park; it helped preserve the mosaics. Here, Alexander the Great sacrificed to Zeus before marching against the Persians, and the sanctuary of Isis retains a canal representing the Nile. In season, the park opens at 8 a.m.: explore it before the heat sets in.

The real showstopper at the Archaeological Museum of Dion awaits upstairs: the hydraulis, a water organ unearthed in 1992 and presented as the oldest known example. In the neighboring Archaiothiki, you can admire the 100 m² Dionysus mosaic—the size of a large apartment—from a gallery. From April through October, the museum opens at 11 a.m.: visit the ruins first.

Litochoro’s story unfolds along its cobbled lanes, between Macedonian-style houses with wooden balconies and a brick bell tower. This hamlet, founded in the 14th century, long made its living from the sea and its textile workshops, known as skoutia. Save this stroll for late afternoon, after Dion, and walk up to Agios Nikolaos Church in the center of town.

A maritime museum at the foot of Greece’s highest peak: the Maritime Museum of Litochoro recalls the town’s past as a hub for shipowners and sailors. Sextants, scale models, and a replica of a cargo ship’s bridge surround a model of the torpedo boat that sank a Turkish ship off Thessaloniki in 1912. The entrance is one floor above ground level in the municipal building on Agiou Nikolaou Street.

activities.text: You’ll head to Katounia Park, a pine grove facing the Enipeas Gorge, then to Myloi, at around 400 m above sea level, where the E4 trail begins. A few switchbacks bring you alongside a mountain stream whose water stays close to 0 °C. Turn back before the footbridges: the Spilios Agapitos Refuge reports damaged bridges on the lower section of the route.

practical_info.tip: Hiking shoes recommended; the trail becomes slippery after rain.

map_keywords: Old Monastery of Agios Dionysios Olympus

visits.text: It is called Palaia Moni, the old monastery, to distinguish it from the monastery rebuilt farther down after 1943. Founded in 1542 by Saint Dionysios at around 850 m above sea level, Agios Dionysios was burned by the Ottomans in 1828, then blown up by the German army in April 1943 on suspicion that it sheltered resistance fighters. Stop on your way down, 3 km from the Prionia parking lot.

activities.text: If you were to make just one ascent on Mount Olympus, it would be the hike from Prionia to the Spilios Agapitos Refuge. The E4 trail climbs nearly 1,000 m through black pines and beeches before emerging onto a bare, sunny slope: allow 2 hours 30 minutes to 3 hours. Higher up, Mytikas (2,918 m) was first reached in 1913; from the refuge, at around 2,100 m, reaching it remains a full-fledged mountaineering undertaking. Set out before 9 a.m., with water and a windbreaker.

practical_info.tip: The Spilios Agapitos Refuge is open from May to October; from November to April, snow and avalanche risk mean the ascent is only for properly equipped hikers. Fill your water bottles at the Prionia fountain, as the spring halfway up often runs dry in summer.

activities.text: Water barely above freezing fills the pool beneath the Enipeas waterfall, whose main drop measures 38 m. A downhill trail leads there in 10 to 15 minutes from a parking lot 500 m before the Old Monastery. Few dare to swim here: save your breath for the climb back up.

practical_info.tip: The Old Monastery of Agios Dionysios is open from April to October; the waterfall trail is slippery after rain.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Litochoro, then south on the A1 highway

visits.text: In April 1941, a New Zealand battalion held the ridge at Platamon Castle against a German armored division. Built by Crusaders between 1204 and 1222, the fortress guards the exit from the Vale of Tempe; its walls rise to 9.50 m. Arrive when it opens at 8:30 a.m. to walk along the ramparts in the cool morning air, facing the Aegean Sea.

to_next_leg.road_type: A1 through the Tempe tunnels, then a mountain road

visits.text: Schwartz Mansion alone is worth the climb to Ampelakia. Its builder, Georgios Mavros, adopted the name Schwartz in Germany: both names mean “black” in their respective languages. Completed in 1798, the house features carved wooden ceilings and walls painted with views of Constantinople. Come in the morning: admission ends at 3:30 p.m.

activities.text: You’ll then stroll through Ampelakia’s square beneath the plane trees, among stone houses with red roofs. In 1778, the village’s dyers founded a joint company, often described as one of the earliest cooperatives: their red thread was exported to Austria and Germany. Below lies the Vale of Tempe, a 10 km corridor between Mount Olympus and Mount Ossa.

practical_info.tip: Schwartz Mansion is closed on Tuesdays and national holidays; admission costs €6.

to_next_leg.road_type: Descent to the A1, then across the Thessalian Plain

visits.text: If you arrive in Larissa in the early afternoon, head straight to the Diachronic Museum on Mezourlo Hill, a 15-minute drive from downtown. Opened in 2015, it traces Thessaly’s history from the Paleolithic period to the 19th century in eleven sections, from a Bronze Age menhir to two Persian gold darics. From November to March, arrive before 3 p.m.

Ten thousand seats squeezed between apartment buildings: the First Ancient Theater of Larissa lay hidden for years beneath houses, a street opened in 1910, and a clock tower. Built in the 3rd century BC and converted into an arena by the Romans, it has regained its marble seating. Walk around it along the neighboring streets, then head up to Frourio.

Frourio Hill, the ancient acropolis, reveals several layers of Larissa’s history. At the top stand the walls of the Bezesteni, a late-15th-century Ottoman covered market with 19 shops that became a gunpowder magazine in the 19th century; the Basilica of Agios Achillios was uncovered in 1978 above vaulted tombs. Head down the back way: Pappas Mill dates to 1883.

activities.text: You’ll then head down to Alcazar Park, a long green lung stretching along the banks of the Pineios River. Legend traces the city’s name to the nymph Larissa, who drowned in the river, and a monument to Hippocrates, who is said to have died here, faces the park. Come in the late afternoon and follow the riverbank on foot or by bike.

practical_info.tip: You can explore the banks of the Pineios River on foot or by bike; allow 1 hour for the loop.

activities.text: Larissa is nicknamed the “city of coffee,” and its pedestrian streets live up to the name. In the evening, order meze with a tsipouro, the spirit that neighboring Tyrnavos has made its specialty, followed by halva from Farsala, made with butter and almonds. Save a box for the next day’s journey.

practical_info.tip: For your onward journey, Larissa station has InterCity train service to Thessaloniki and Athens.

seo.h1_title: Mount Olympus in 3 Days: Dion, Litochoro, and Larissa
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts at the Macedonian sanctuary of Dion, uses Litochoro as a base, and devotes a full day to the trails of Mount Olympus, Greece’s first national park. On the third day, it descends via Platamon Castle and Schwartz Mansion in Ampelakia to Larissa, its ancient theater, and its Diachronic Museum.
seo.seo_hook: Explore Mount Olympus in 3 days: the ruins of Dion, the ascent to Spilios Agapitos Refuge, Platamon Castle, the mansion in Ampelakia, and the theater in Larissa.
featured_list: Dion: the hydraulis, presented as the oldest known organ
Litochoro: a maritime museum at the foot of Mount Olympus
Prionia: nearly 1,000 m of elevation gain to Spilios Agapitos Refuge
Platamon: a castle built by Crusaders between 1204 and 1222
Ampelakia: Schwartz Mansion, completed in 1798
Larissa: a 10,000-seat ancient theater in the heart of the city

places_taglines.GR::litochoro: Once a town of sailors, Litochoro serves as a base for Mount Olympus.
places_taglines.GR::prionia: The road ends at 1,100 m, at the start of the E4 trail.
places_taglines.GR::platamonas: A Crusader castle watches over the exit from the Vale of Tempe.
places_taglines.GR::ampelakia: The village of red-yarn dyers overlooks the Vale of Tempe.
places_taglines.GR::larissa: The ancient theater and the Frourio overlook the city center, near the Pineios River.

highlights: Dion: sanctuary of Olympian Zeus and hydraulis at the museum
Mount Olympus: hike from Prionia to the Spilios Agapitos Refuge, at around 2,100 m
Platamon: castle built by Crusaders between 1204 and 1222
Ampelakia: Schwartz Mansion and the legacy of the company founded in 1778
Larissa: ancient theater with 10,000 seats and the Diachronic Museum

itineraries.title: Northern Pindus in 4 Days: Metsovo, Zagori, and Vikos Gorge
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from Metsovo to the Valia Kalda valley, then hike through Vikos Gorge in Zagori.
itineraries.notes: Book a taxi in advance to take you back from the village of Vikos to Monodendri after hiking through the gorge. From November to March, snow can intermittently block mountain roads, especially those leading to Vovousa, Vradeto, and Papingo.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through October: in Metsovo (1,160 m), average highs range from 17 °C in May to 25 °C in August, with nighttime temperatures between 8 and 15 °C. May, September, and October remain rainy (more than 130 mm per month in Metsovo): keep a waterproof jacket and a warm layer handy, even in summer. Avoid November through March, when snow intermittently closes the roads to Vradeto and Papingo, as well as the road from Lake Aoos toward Vovousa.

activities.text: You’ll land at Ioannina National Airport “King Pyrrhus,” 4 km from downtown, served by scheduled flights from Athens. Pick up your rental car there: Metsovo is only about 50 minutes away via the A2 highway, Egnatia Odos. Stock up on groceries in Ioannina before heading into the mountains.

practical_info.tip: Choose a car that handles narrow roads well: several mountain roads in the Pindus and Zagori are winding and snowy in winter.

map_keywords: Tositsa Mansion Folk Art Museum Metsovo

visits.text: Few mountain villages display a collection of Greek paintings of this caliber, and the Averoff Gallery alone makes Metsovo worth a stop. Evangelos Averoff-Tossizza opened it in 1988 in a purpose-built, three-story building, with around 200 works by Greek artists from the 19th and 20th centuries. The museum closes at 4 p.m.: visit as soon as you arrive, before strolling through the village.

Wooden chests, antique textiles, and subdued lighting: the Metsovo Folk Art Museum occupies Tositsa Mansion, built in 1661 and open to the public since 1955. Costumes, looms, copperware, weapons from the 1821 War of Independence, and 66 icons remain arranged in the original rooms. Visits are guided, with tours departing every half hour from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., except on Thursdays; admission costs €3.

Metsovo’s central square serves as the town’s living room. The town is the main center of Aromanian (Vlach) culture in Greece and is called Aminciu in that language. Agia Paraskevi Church, on the square, houses a carved wooden iconostasis and silver chandeliers. Then sit down to try metsovone, a smoked stretched-curd cheese with protected designation of origin (PDO) status since 1996, and take a piece with you for picnics over the following days.

activities.text: Walk down to Agios Nikolaos Monastery, nestled on the slope below the village. Left in ruins, it was restored thanks to Evangelos Averoff and funding from the Tositsa Foundation; its 17th-century iconostasis, the work of the monk Ioannikios, is worth the descent alone. The trail is steep and rocky: allow about 30 minutes to walk down and 1 hour to climb back up.

practical_info.tip: Wear sturdy shoes and bring water for the climb back up, and avoid the trail in rainy weather.

activities.text: In the late 1950s, Evangelos Averoff planted some of Greece’s first Cabernet Sauvignon vines on the slopes of the Pindus: the Katogi Averoff estate grew out of this high-altitude gamble. The tour of the historic cellars takes about 30 minutes, following an aisle between rows of oak barrels and then a glass walkway above hundreds of bottles. Visit between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.

practical_info.tip: Tours that include a tasting must be booked in advance; choose a designated driver for the evening.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road via the Profitis Ilias ski resort

visits.text: Man-made, yet strikingly wild in its beauty, Aoos Springs Lake lies at an elevation of about 1,350 m, between Valia Kalda and Vikos-Aoos national parks. Greece’s public electricity company created it by damming the Aoos near its source; it covers about 11.5 km². Follow the road around the lake past its viewpoints to the dam.

activities.text: If you have 1 hour, walk through the meadows and along the forest trails bordering Lake Aoos; wild daffodils bloom here in spring. Black storks and kingfishers frequent the shores. Flocks often graze nearby, guarded by large shepherd dogs: keep your distance and avoid provoking them.

practical_info.tip: In winter, drive only as far as the dam: beyond it, the road to Vovousa receives heavy snowfall.

to_next_leg.road_type: Narrow mountain road with heavy snow in winter

visits.text: Vovousa Bridge spans the Aoos with a single arch in the heart of the village and has linked its two banks since 1748. Alexis Mitsios, a merchant from Zagori, funded its construction with a donation. Walk across it, then head down to the riverbank to see the arch in profile, more elegant when viewed from below.

Băiasa is the Aromanian name for Vovousa, a Vlach village built at an elevation of around 1,000 m, with the river dividing it into two neighborhoods. Barely more than a hundred people live here, surrounded by beech and fir trees. Stop by Agios Georgios Church, which dates to 1814, and return in midsummer for the village festival, which combines music, theater, and hikes.

activities.text: Valia Kalda has a misleading name: “warm valley” in Aromanian, yet it is one of the coldest and wettest areas in the region. A national park since 1966, this basin of black pines and beeches is home to brown bears, wolves, and chamois. From the Valia Kalda refuge near Vovousa, follow the E6 European long-distance trail toward the heart of the park, then retrace your steps.

practical_info.tip: E6 trail markings can be intermittent: bring a GPS track and turn back halfway through your allotted time. To reach the valley floor without a 4x4, guided jeep tours depart from Krania and Perivoli from March to November.

visits.text: Plakida Bridge, also known as Kalogeriko, spans 56 m on three stone arches near Kipoi. In 1814, Abbot Seraphim of the Prophet Elijah Monastery in Vitsa had it built to replace a wooden bridge. Park on the shoulder of the road between Dilofo and Kipoi: it is just a few minutes’ walk along a flat path.

A single gray stone arch, more than 13 m high, leaps over the rocky riverbed: this is Kokkoros Bridge, also known as Noutsos Bridge, built around 1750. It is one of more than 160 arch bridges built in the Zagori region. The best view is from the riverbank below; allow about 20 minutes.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: Until a road opened in the 1970s, the Vradeto Steps, a mule route with around a thousand steps, remained the village’s only link to the outside world. At 1,340 m, Vradeto is the highest village in Zagori. Take in the switchbacks from above before heading toward Beloi.

activities.text: Walk from Vradeto’s square to the Beloi viewpoint on the eastern rim of Vikos Gorge: a nearly level 2.8 km round trip. At the end of the trail, the plateau drops away abruptly and the canyon opens beneath your feet. Allow 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes, depending on your photo stops, including the gentle climb on the way back.

practical_info.tip: From November to March, snow can intermittently block the road to Vradeto: check conditions the day before.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: Agia Paraskevi Monastery clings to the rim of Vikos Gorge, a 15-minute walk from Monodendri along a paved path. The voivode Michael Therianos had it built around 1413–1414; it is now uninhabited.

If you choose just one sunset to remember from this trip, make it the Oxya viewpoint, a natural platform above the deepest part of Vikos Gorge. The narrow road climbs 8 km from Monodendri through Petrino Dasos, the “stone forest.” Arrive in the late afternoon: the low-angle light brings out the contours of the canyon walls across a 270° panorama.

Monodendri deserves more than a stop to park before your hike. This stone village perched at 1,060 m was the birthplace of Manthos and Georgios Rizaris, who founded the Rizareios Foundation in Athens in 1841; their bequests are still evident here. Save your stroll for the evening, after Oxya, and have dinner on the square.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot: Monodendri → Vikos gorge hiking trail
to_next_leg.justification: Le point de la gorge est distant de cinq kilomètres à vol d’oiseau ; une randonnée sur sentier et un dénivelé important sont nécessaires, non une marche de 1 km.

visits.text: Icy turquoise water emerges in the final section of the gorge: these are the springs of the Voidomatis, a river that flows on to join the Aoos. In April, its temperature is around 7 to 10 °C. Dip your feet in to soothe your legs before the final climb to the village of Vikos, which is steep and exposed to the sun.

activities.text: Leave Monodendri early to hike through Vikos Gorge, ranked by Guinness World Records as the world’s deepest canyon relative to its width. The trail descends steeply to the bed of the Voidomatis, follows the wooded canyon floor, then climbs to the village of Vikos: roughly 12 kilometers and 5 to 7 hours of hiking. Carry two liters of water per person.

practical_info.tip: There is only one spring along the route, halfway through. Book a taxi in advance to take you from the village of Vikos back to Monodendri, a drive of nearly an hour. The full hike can be done from April to November; if you are less fit, hike down into the gorge for one hour, then turn back.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road with switchbacks to Papingo
to_next_leg.justification: Les gorges de Vikos ne peuvent pas être franchies directement en voiture : les voies routières font un détour réel par les villages.

visits.text: Megalo Papingo and Mikro Papingo, two stone villages at around 950 m beneath the peaks of Astraka, mark the edge of Zagori north of Vikos Gorge. Written records mention the site as early as 1325. Park at the entrance to Megalo Papingo, then stop at the Northern Pindus National Park information center in Mikro Papingo to ask about the trails.

activities.text: Walk down from Mikro Papingo to the Ovires of Rogovo, the “kolymbithres,” pools carved into the limestone by the Rogovo stream. Tradition has it that Ali Pasha, ruler of Ioannina, used to bathe here. The trail is 1.8 km round-trip with 80 m of elevation change, taking about one hour; the water is suitable for swimming only during the hottest months.

practical_info.tip: Come in the morning to enjoy the pools in peace, and wear shoes with soles that grip the polished rock.

activities.text: Just 4 km from downtown Ioannina, “King Pyrrhus” National Airport is a little over an hour’s drive from Papingo. Return your rental car before your flight to Athens or one of the seasonal flights to Scandinavia. Allow plenty of extra time: travel is slow on Zagori’s mountain roads.

practical_info.tip: The day before, check the car return time specified in your rental agreement.

seo.h1_title: Northern Pindus in 4 Days: Metsovo, Zagori, and Vikos Gorge
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip leaves Ioannina for Metsovo, Greece’s main center of Aromanian culture, then follows Lake Aoos to Vovousa, gateway to the Valia Kalda valley. It then heads to Zagori, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2023, for its stone bridges, viewpoints, and hike through Vikos Gorge, before a final morning in Papingo.
seo.seo_hook: Metsovo’s museums, Lake Aoos, the forests of Valia Kalda, Zagori’s bridges, and a hike through Vikos Gorge: Northern Pindus in 4 days.
featured_list: Metsovo: Averoff Gallery and Tositsa Mansion, dating from 1661
Valia Kalda: a national park since 1966, with black pines and brown bears
Kipoi: Plakida Bridge, three stone arches built in 1814
Vikos Gorge: hike from Monodendri to Vikos in 5 to 7 hours
Papingo: Rogovo rock pools at the foot of Astraka

itineraries.title: Samos in 4 Days: Heraion, Manolates, and Potami Waterfalls
itineraries.subtitle: Explore Samos in 4 days, from the Tunnel of Eupalinos to hilltop villages and Potami Waterfalls.
itineraries.notes: Plan to arrive on a Tuesday or Saturday if possible: the Tunnel of Eupalinos and the archaeological museums are closed on Tuesdays, the museums in Mytilinii and the Wine Museum on Mondays, and the Tannery Museum on weekends. A car is essential, as buses generally allow you to visit only one village per day.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May–June or September: average highs range from 24 to 30 °C, with almost no rain. July–August approach 33 °C, so set out early for hikes to Seitani or Potami Waterfalls. From November to February, rainfall exceeds 100 mm per month, and the museum in Mytilinii opens by appointment only.

visits.text: You have to walk through the Tunnel of Eupalinos, helmet on, to appreciate the audacity of its construction. Excavated in the 6th century BC by two teams starting from opposite sides, it runs through the mountain for 1,036 m; Herodotus ranked it among the three greatest engineering works of the Greek world. The short route covers less than 200 m, at a temperature of 16.5 °C even in August. Children under 14 are not admitted, and it is closed on Tuesdays: aim for the first departure, around 8:40 a.m.

A tithe levied on piracy: that is what the inscription proclaims on the seated statue of Aiakes, dedicated to Hera around 540 BC and displayed at the Pythagoreio Archaeological Museum. Opened in 2010, the museum also features a 2.71 m statue of Trajan and portraits of Augustus and Claudius. Allow 1 hour 15 minutes; it opens at 8:30 a.m. and is closed on Tuesdays, making it an ideal stop right after the tunnel.

“Christ saved Samos on August 6, 1824”: Lykourgos Logothetis, leader of the Samian uprising, commissioned this inscription to commemorate the naval victory over the Ottoman fleet in the Strait of Mycale. His tower, built between 1824 and 1827 partly with ancient stone blocks, stands beside the Church of the Transfiguration, completed in 1853. Visit on August 6 if you can: candles illuminate the castle after nightfall.

The dim light and cool air of a cave: 95 steps lead down to the chapel of Panagia Spiliani Monastery, set inside a cavern above Pythagoreio. A spring of holy water flows behind the church. On the same hill, the ancient Roman-era theater has had its seating and orchestra restored on a wooden structure, providing a setting for summer festivals. Head up in the late afternoon: the view stretches all the way to the coast of Asia Minor.

Pythagoreio’s harbor hides its history underwater: the ancient breakwater, built in the time of Polycrates, lies beneath the present-day ferry pier. On the eastern pier, the statue of Pythagoras recalls that the town, long known as Tigani, only took the mathematician’s name in 1955. Come at dusk, when the waterfront tavernas light up alongside the colorful fishing boats.

activities.text: End the day with your feet in the water at Remataki, a small beach right beside the eastern breakwater of Pythagoreio’s harbor. Around 150 m of pebbles mixed with sand, a gently sloping entry, and usually calm, clear water make it ideal for a swim after sightseeing. Showers, lounge chairs, and cafés are available, and the taxi stand is 200 m away.

practical_info.tip: Seaweed washes ashore on some days: take a look from the waterfront before settling in.

map_keywords: Natural History Museum of the Aegean Mytilinii

visits.text: If Samos means only temples to you, the Natural History Museum of the Aegean in Mytilinii puts things on a different timescale: its local fossils are between 8 and 10 million years old. You will also encounter Kaplani, a wild cat that arrived from Asia Minor around 130 years ago. Open from May to October, closed on Mondays, and open only in the morning: visit before 2 p.m.

Underfoot are the pebbles of Agia Matrona’s courtyard; all around, the houses of Mytilinii rise in an amphitheater-like arrangement from the valley floor. The village has six churches and the Efthimiada School, built in 1893. Park near the museum and explore the central square on foot before heading to Vathy.

Nothing prepares you for coming face-to-face with the Samos kouros: more than five meters of marble, dedicated around 580 BC by a certain Isches and discovered in 1980 beneath the Sacred Way of the Heraion, with its head only resurfacing in 1984. The Samos Archaeological Museum displays it alongside the Geneleos votive group. Allow 2 hours; the museum is closed on Tuesdays. A modernization project has been announced, so check the hours before visiting.

A Boeotian lion stands guard over an Ionian harbor: the statue in Pythagoras Square in Samos is a copy of the Lion of Chaeronea. Unveiled on August 6, 1921, for the centennial of independence, this Pentelic marble sculpture still bears the scars of a 1943 bombing. Have a coffee in the square when you arrive—it is the heart of the lower town.

Head up to Ano Vathy in the late afternoon, when the lanes of the old quarter perched above the harbor begin to cool down. Designated a “traditional settlement,” it preserves the post-Byzantine church of Agios Giannakis at its highest point, where Samos joined the War of Independence on April 20, 1821. Allow 1 to 2 hours and wear sturdy shoes; the slopes are steep.

The scent of oak and sweet wine fills the air: in Malagari, the Samos Wine Museum occupies a former wine cellar where the cooperative stored its wines and made its barrels. The largest wooden vat holds 80 tonnes, and the manual wine presses date from 1910. The €5 ticket includes a tasting of Muscat, the sole grape variety of the Samos appellation, established in 1970. Closed on Mondays.

Kokkari sits on a small peninsula, with the fishing harbor on one side and the pebble beach on the other. Founded in the early 19th century by families from Mytilinii, the village retains its flower-lined lanes and the church of Agios Nikolaos, a domed basilica begun in 1902 and completed in 1963. Have dinner by the harbor, then stroll along the beach, home to a windsurfing school.

activities.text: Walk west from Kokkari to reach Lemonakia in 20 to 25 minutes. Tsamadou, about a kilometer farther on, is named after the hero Anastasios Tsamados and draws fewer visitors than its neighbor; its far end serves as an unofficial nudist beach. Both beaches have tavernas and lounge chairs. In summer, arrive before 11 a.m., as Lemonakia fills up quickly.

practical_info.tip: For snorkeling, continue to Tsambou, about 5 km from Kokkari: its rocks are ideal, especially on the left side of the beach.

activities.text: If the wind stirs up too many waves, head uphill to Plaka instead, about 2 km southwest of Kokkari. Water flows abundantly beneath tall plane trees, and the ruins of a temple dedicated to Asclepius lie hidden in the greenery. This is a shady walk for the hottest hours of the day; bring water and sturdy shoes.

practical_info.tip: Visit Plaka in the late morning, then head back down to the sea for lunch.

visits.text: Two fires, in 1999 and 2020, failed to destroy Vrontiani Monastery, rebuilt in 1566 on the site of an earlier monastery and counted among the island’s oldest. Perched at about 450 m, roughly 2 km southeast of Vourliotes, it preserves a carved wooden iconostasis embellished with gold. Cover your shoulders and knees; the monastery’s feast day falls on September 8.

Vourliotes takes its name from Vourla, ancient Clazomenae in Asia Minor, where its founders came from in the late 16th century. On the square, tavernas serve wine from the Muscat vineyards surrounding the village: ask to taste the local wine. Head up for lunch, then wander the lanes lined with restored Samian houses.

activities.text: Continue to Pnaka Spring, 1.6 km from the Vourliotes turnoff, for shade, cool water, and a taverna. It is a simple stop to break up the day before the drive to Manolates; 30 minutes is enough, or longer if you have lunch there.

practical_info.tip: Save Pnaka for the middle of the day, when the shade matters most.

to_next_leg.road_type: Descent to the coast, then ascent via Platanakia
to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: The most charming hilltop village in the north? Manolates makes a strong case, with car-free cobbled lanes, stone houses, and pottery workshops in the foothills of Mount Ampelos, at about 360 m above sea level. The village had just 79 residents in 2011, compared with 375 in 1961. Park at the entrance and visit early or late in the day to avoid the midday tour buses.

activities.text: Samians call it Kakorema, the “bad stream,” yet its waters sustain the old plane trees of Platanakia and the valley of Aidonia, the valley of nightingales, below Manolates. From the coastal road, at kilometer 18 between Samos and Karlovasi, the road to Manolates runs through the shade for 1.5 km to Aidonia; marked trails also lead down from the village to the valley.

practical_info.tip: Come in spring for the rushing water; in summer, the valley remains the best refuge from the heat. Fires and camping are prohibited.

visits.text: More than fifty tanneries and some 300 workers: between 1880 and 1930, Karlovasi made its living from leather, which accounted for as much as 24% of Samos’s exports in 1888. The Tannery Museum, in the Tambakika district, displays tools, machinery, photographs, and a map of the vanished workshops. Admission is free; its 2023 opening hours were weekdays from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., so call before stopping by.

Paleo Karlovasi was built on high ground far from the shore to protect it from pirates, and that distance has preserved its tranquility. The city's oldest district, founded in the mid-16th century, rises in tiers across several hills topped with small churches where metal votive offerings are hung. Walk up from the port along trail No. 4, then head to the small park overlooking the old village.

You will first pass the Byzantine Church of the Transfiguration, which guards the entrance to the Potami Waterfalls trail; it is thought to date to the 11th century. The remains of a Genoese castle stand on the hill above. Leave your car on the road, as the path is not accessible to vehicles, and allow a few minutes to walk around the church.

activities.text: Modest in size but wonderfully refreshing, Potami Waterfalls take some effort to reach. A trail of about 1 km follows the river upstream beneath plane trees and ferns to a pool that you must swim across to reach the first waterfall, about 2 m high. The second, larger waterfall is 400 m farther upstream, reached by wooden steps. Access is free.

practical_info.tip: Shoes suitable for wearing in water are essential; to reach the second waterfall, take the wooden steps instead of climbing the rock walls.

activities.text: Pebbles tumble in the waves, and the water is clear and cold: Potami Beach stretches for 730 m west of Karlovasi. The sea is often rough, and the shore drops off fairly steeply; when the swell is strong, stay at the water's edge. There are lounge chairs, showers, and tavernas on site, and parking is free: save it for late afternoon, on your way back from Seitani.

practical_info.tip: On days when the sea is rough, swim in the waterfall pool.

activities.text: “The Devil's Port”: the Ottomans are said to have named Seitani using the Turkish word for Satan. Beyond Potami Beach, a 1.3 km track followed by a walk of about 1 km leads to Mikro Seitani, a sandy and pebbly cove about 60 m long. The area, designated a Natura 2000 site, is home to the Mediterranean monk seal. No road leads down to it: bring water and closed-toe shoes.

practical_info.tip: Experienced hikers continue to Megalo Seitani, a 470 m beach about 3 km from the end of the track.

to_next_leg.road_type: Drive across the island from northwest to southeast

visits.text: Only one column remains standing, yet the Heraion of Samos is still staggering: the great temple begun under Polycrates measured 55 m by 108 m, with a peristyle of 155 columns around 20 m tall. The Byzantines quarried the rest for stone, sparing this shaft, probably as a landmark for sailors. Arrive at opening time, before the heat; hours vary by season, so check them the day before.

activities.text: You will then head back down to Ireo, a seaside village one kilometer from the sanctuary, where former fishermen's huts now house tavernas and cafés. Enjoy one last swim and lunch overlooking the water; Samos Airport is just a few kilometers away, between Ireo and Pythagoreio. Allow plenty of time before check-in.

practical_info.tip: In August, the Ireo rock festival brings the village to life for three days.

seo.h1_title: Samos in 4 Days: Heraion, Manolates, and Potami Waterfalls
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary circles Samos from Pythagoreio, taking you from the Tunnel of Eupalinos to the Archaeological Museum of Vathy, where a kouros more than five meters tall stands. You then climb to Vourliotes and Manolates on the slopes of Mount Ampelos before visiting Potami Waterfalls and the coves of Seitani, then complete the loop at the Heraion, just a short distance from the airport.
seo.seo_hook: Samos in 4 days: the Tunnel of Eupalinos, the UNESCO-listed Heraion, the hilltop villages of Manolates and Vourliotes, and the waterfalls and coves of Potami.
featured_list: Pythagoreio: the Tunnel of Eupalinos, 1,036 m dug beneath the mountain
Vathy: a marble kouros more than five meters tall
Manolates: car-free lanes and pottery workshops
Potami: a waterfall reached by swimming beneath plane trees
Heraion: the last standing column of Polycrates’ temple

places_taglines.GR::mytilinii: A village arranged like an amphitheater and fossils dating back 8 to 10 million years.
places_taglines.GR::vathy: The island’s capital, a giant kouros, a marble lion, and the Wine Museum.
places_taglines.GR::kokkari: A fishing harbor on a peninsula and the pebble beaches of Lemonakia.
places_taglines.GR::vourliotes: A winegrowers’ village founded by people from Vourla, near Vrontiani.
places_taglines.GR::manolates: A car-free village, pottery workshops, and a valley of nightingales.
places_taglines.GR::karlovasi: A former tannery town, a hilltop old quarter, and a leather museum.
places_taglines.GR::potami: Waterfalls beneath plane trees, a pebble beach, and the coves of Seitani.

highlights: Tunnel of Eupalinos: 1,036 m excavated in the 6th century BC by two teams starting from opposite sides of the mountain
Samos Archaeological Museum: a kouros over five meters tall, discovered at the Heraion in 1980
Manolates: a mountain village with car-free lanes on the slopes of Mount Ampelos
Potami: waterfalls beneath plane trees and the coves of Seitani, frequented by monk seals
Heraion: a single standing column from a temple 108 m long, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1992

itineraries.title: Thermopylae and Phocis in 3 Days: Delphi, Hosios Loukas
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Lamia and Thermopylae to the sanctuary at Delphi, then to the monastery of Hosios Loukas.
itineraries.notes: The sanctuary of Athena Pronaia and its Tholos, the Castalian Spring, and the gymnasium at Delphi are not included in the itinerary: these areas have been closed in recent years for construction work or following rockfalls, so check locally. Hosios Loukas no longer admits visitors after 3:10 p.m., which is why the visit is scheduled for late morning on the third day.
itineraries.climate: Aim for April–May or September–October: average highs in Lamia and Amfissa range from about 20 to 30 °C during these months. Avoid July–August, when they exceed 33 °C, making the climb through the Delphi site uncomfortable in full sun. In winter, Arachova, at nearly 1,000 m, follows the rhythm of the ski slopes on Mount Parnassus, and ancient sites close as early as 3:30 p.m.

visits.text: For an at-a-glance understanding of Central Greece’s geography, nothing beats the ramparts of Lamia Castle. Its triangular enclosure, with a perimeter of about 600 m, preserves polygonal walls from the late 5th century BC that rise 13 m on the northwest side. Head up in the morning: the view opens onto the Sperchios Valley and the Malian Gulf.

In 1871, a gunpowder magazine explosion destroyed the castle’s barracks; restored, the building has housed the Archaeological Museum of Lamia since 1994, though it is currently closed for construction work. Its collections from Phthiotis, spanning the Neolithic period to the Roman era, are inaccessible, including the votive relief of Artemis Eileithyia carved around 400 BC in the style of Praxiteles. View the barracks from outside and explore the castle enclosure, which remains open.

“I was born Greek, I will die Greek”: the reply attributed to Athanasios Diakos hangs over Diakou Square in Lamia. Refusing to convert to Islam, he was impaled on April 24, 1821; his statue has stood watch here since 1903. Continue to Laou Square, where a statue of Aris Velouchiotis, leader of ELAS, stands: you will encounter his name again at Gorgopotamos.

Famous for having been blown up, the Gorgopotamos viaduct has seen no trains since 2018. On the night of November 25–26, 1942, Greek resistance fighters and British saboteurs brought down its spans; rebuilt in 1948, it measures 211 m long and 30 m high. Access is free, but there is no parking: park in the village.

The Leonidas Monument marks the spot where the final phase of the battle of 480 BC unfolded. The bronze statue of the Spartan king, created by Vasos Falireas and erected in 1955, is flanked by two marble figures representing the Eurotas River and Mount Taygetus. Come early in summer: in July, average highs on the plain exceed 33 °C.

Climb Kolonos Hill, opposite the monument, where the last defenders are said to have fallen. On the battlefield, a stone lion bore the epigram by Simonides: “Stranger, go tell the Lacedaemonians that we lie here, obeying their orders.” Turn toward the sea: in 480 BC, it bordered the pass; today, a plain about 5 km wide separates the two.

If the landscape makes the battle difficult to picture, the Thermopylae Historical Information Center puts the armies back in position. Opened in 2010, this 850 m² building shaped like a spearhead takes you through a film, digital tables, and a 3D projection. Allow 1 hour and €3; the time of the last screening varies by day.

activities.text: A sulfur smell hangs at the foot of Kallidromo: the hot springs of Thermopylae, opposite the monument, gave the “Hot Gates” pass its name. Legend has Heracles bathing here after being poisoned by the tunic of the centaur Nessus. Access is free, with no facilities: bring a towel and sandals, and test the water near the spring before settling in.

practical_info.tip: There are no changing rooms, restrooms, or showers on site: come during daylight hours and keep a change of clothes in the car.

visits.text: Climb to Salona Castle above Amfissa for sweeping views of the Crisa plain and its sea of olive trees. The Frankish lords of Autremencourt built it after the conquest of 1205 on the ancient acropolis, whose massive stone blocks can still be seen to the southwest and southeast. Access is free at all hours: aim for late afternoon, when temperatures are milder.

Harmaina, Amfissa’s old quarter, unfolds along cobblestone lanes around former tanneries, where some restored workshops tell the story of leatherworking. On your way back down, look for local olive oil: Visit Greece describes the olive grove stretching from Amfissa to the Gulf of Corinth as the largest continuous olive grove in Greece, with more than a million trees. Leave the car behind and explore these lanes on foot.

If its doors are open, step inside Amfissa’s Cathedral of the Annunciation: its murals are the work of painter Spyros Papaloukas. An early Christian baptistery stands right beside the building. Wear clothing that provides adequate coverage and be discreet during services.

to_next_leg.road_type: EO48 along the edge of the olive grove

visits.text: It is best to climb the Sacred Way at Delphi slowly, like the pilgrims who came to consult the Pythia. Lined with offerings and treasuries, it passes the Treasury of the Athenians, built from Parian marble with the spoils of Marathon (490 BC) and reassembled by the French School at Athens between 1903 and 1906; its metopes are copies, with the originals in the museum. The €20 ticket covers both the site and the museum: buy it at tickets.hh.gr to save time.

The “navel of the world”: the Greeks placed the omphalos at Delphi, a stone marking the spot determined, according to legend, by two eagles released by Zeus. On its terrace, the Temple of Apollo whose remains you see dates to the 4th century BC; the Pythia delivered her oracles there from a tripod in the adyton. Bring water and a hat: the sanctuary rises in tiers up the southwestern slope of Mount Parnassus.

Continue uphill to the theater of Delphi, built in the 4th century BC for some 4,500 spectators: from above, the Temple of Apollo stands out against the valley. One more climb brings you to the stadium at the highest point of the site, with its roughly 177 m track and seating for 6,500 people; you can admire it from the edge. Wear shoes with treaded soles for the steps.

Inlaid glass eyes gaze at you across nearly 2,500 years: the Charioteer of Delphi retains a remarkably lifelike gaze. This life-size bronze, about 1.80 m tall, was dedicated around 470 BC by Polyzalos, tyrant of Gela, after a chariot race victory and was unearthed in 1896. At the Delphi Archaeological Museum, take time to view it from several angles: it is one of the few Greek bronzes to have survived with its glass eyes intact.

Around 560 BC, the Naxians erected a 2.22 m sphinx atop a 10 m column near Delphi’s most sacred spot. It now presides over the Archaeological Museum, not far from Kleobis and Biton, two kouroi carved in Argos around 600 BC. Allow at least 1 hour for the fourteen galleries spread across two levels, and save the museum for the hot hours of the day.

activities.text: The village of Delphi seems to have stood here forever, yet it owes its existence to a relocation. The houses covering the sanctuary were moved to allow excavations, and the modern town was built away from the ruins. In the evening, once the tour buses have left, stroll along its main street and choose a terrace overlooking the valley for dinner.

practical_info.tip: The village is your base for two nights: ask for a room facing the valley to enjoy the view.

visits.text: Expect more than 250 steps to reach Agios Georgios Church at the top of Arachova. Built in 1676, it celebrates Saint George and the 1826 victory over the Ottomans on April 23, or on Orthodox Easter Monday when April 23 falls before Easter or on Easter Sunday. Climb early: from the forecourt, the view stretches from the slopes of Mount Parnassus across the landscape of Delphi to the shores of the Peloponnese.

Arachova’s clock has crowned a rocky spur since the early 18th century. In a curious piece of local history, this rock once served as a natural refrigerator for storing cheese. A spiral staircase leads to the top; right next door, the former school houses the Ethnographic Museum, which you can save for a longer stay.

activities.text: If you are packing a picnic for the drive to Hosios Loukas, include some formaela, a cheese from Mount Parnassus with European protected designation of origin status, often served grilled. Around Lakka Square, shops also sell Arachova’s woven textiles, whose weavers inspired painter Théodore Ralli in 1877. Save a bottle of brousko, the local wine, for the evening.

practical_info.tip: Formaela is easy to find in the village; ask for it grilled if you sit down for a meal.

visits.text: On June 10, 1944, a Waffen-SS unit massacred more than two hundred residents of Distomo, including many women, children, and elderly people. On the hill, the memorial comprises a chapel, an ossuary, and a marble wall engraved with the victims’ names and ages. Dress respectfully and speak quietly: this remains a burial place.

Next, head to D. Gamvrili Square, where the Distomo Archaeological Collection occupies a former elementary school. From Classical and Hellenistic funerary stelae to vases dating from Mycenaean through Roman times, the objects come from ancient Ambrossos, beneath the present-day village, as well as Medeon and Antikyra. Admission is €5, with opening hours from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., except Tuesdays.

Austere outside, radiant within: the katholikon of Hosios Loukas reveals its colored marble and mosaics to those who step inside. Built around 1011 to house the relics of the hermit Luke, who died in 953, this domed octagonal church became a model for others; its mosaics are among the best preserved from the Macedonian Renaissance, despite the loss of the dome’s Pantocrator. Arrive before noon: last admission is at 3:10 p.m.

The Church of the Theotokos, next to the katholikon, is the older of the two, dating to the second half of the 10th century. The Thebes Museum identifies it as Greece’s first four-column cross-in-square church, with a richly decorated brick facade. In the narthex, look for the Archangel Michael appearing to Joshua: the monastery’s oldest wall painting.

Cool air and dim light greet visitors descending into the crypt of Hosios Loukas, beneath the katholikon. The saint’s original tomb rests against the north wall; surrounding it, 11th-century frescoes display some forty medallion portraits, cleaned in the 1960s. Let your eyes adjust for a few moments before looking for the faces.

Finish at the former refectory of Hosios Loukas, restored to house a collection of Byzantine sculptures that has been on display since 1993. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990 alongside Daphni and Nea Moni of Chios, the monastery was nevertheless damaged and looted during World War II. Allow €10 for full-price admission, and take time to look at the complex’s bell tower, monastic cells, and towers.

If your legs are still up to it, climb to Livadia Castle, above the springs. Built mainly by the Catalan Company in the 14th century, it is one of Greece’s four Catalan fortresses; its enclosure contains the churches of Agia Varvara and Agia Sofia. The walking trail starts in Krya: head back down before dark.

activities.text: It is hard to imagine a more refreshing stop than the Krya Springs in the heart of Livadia. The Erkyna rises here beneath tall plane trees, amid restored stone bridges and a 19th-century watermill. According to Pausanias, before consulting the oracle of Trophonios, visitors drank from the spring of Lethe to forget, then from that of Mnemosyne to remember. Nothing remains of the oracle: enjoy the riverbanks.

practical_info.tip: If you are leaving by train, Livadia station is about 5 km from the center.

seo.h1_title: Thermopylae and Phocis in 3 Days: Delphi, Hosios Loukas
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day road trip starts in Lamia, passes the Gorgopotamos viaduct and the pass at Thermopylae, then heads through the mountains to Amfissa and Delphi. A full day is devoted to the Sanctuary of Apollo and its museum, followed by Arachova, the Distomo memorial, Hosios Loukas Monastery, and the springs of Livadia.
seo.seo_hook: Thermopylae and Phocis in 3 days: the Leonidas Monument, the sanctuary and Charioteer of Delphi, the mosaics of Hosios Loukas, and Amfissa Castle.
featured_list: Lamia: castle with polygonal walls
Gorgopotamos: viaduct rebuilt in 1948 after the 1942 sabotage
Thermopylae: statue of Leonidas by Vasos Falireas and Kolonos Hill
Amfissa: Salona Castle and the narrow streets of the Harmaina neighborhood
Delphi: Sacred Way, Temple of Apollo, and the Charioteer in the museum
Arachova: Agios Georgios Church, built in 1676 above the village
Hosios Loukas: katholikon dating to 1011 and crypt with medallion portraits
Livadia: Krya Springs at the foot of a Catalan castle

places_taglines.GR::lamia: Ancient and medieval castle, archaeological museum, and remembrance of Diakos.
places_taglines.GR::gorgopotamos: 211 m railway viaduct sabotaged by the Resistance in 1942.
places_taglines.GR::thermopylae: Leonidas’s pass, between hot springs and Kolonos Hill.
places_taglines.GR::amfissa: Frankish castle, tanners’ quarter, and olive grove on the plain of Crisa.
places_taglines.GR::delphi: Sanctuary of Apollo, Sacred Way, and bronze Charioteer in the museum.
places_taglines.GR::arachova: Village on Mount Parnassus, hilltop church, and formaela cheese with protected status.
places_taglines.GR::distomo: Memorial to the victims of the June 10, 1944 massacre.
places_taglines.GR::livadeia: Krya Springs, memories of Trophonios, and a Catalan castle.

highlights: Delphi: the Charioteer, a life-size bronze dedicated around 470 BC
Hosios Loukas: katholikon dating to 1011 and mosaics, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990
Thermopylae: the Leonidas Monument (1955), facing Kolonos Hill
Gorgopotamos: a 211 m viaduct sabotaged by the Resistance in November 1942
Amfissa: Salona Castle, built after the Frankish conquest of 1205
Livadia: the Krya Springs and a 14th-century Catalan castle

itineraries.title: Greek Thrace in 5 Days: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini
itineraries.subtitle: Travel from Xanthi to Komotini in 5 days via the Nestos Gorge, Abdera, the Vistonida lagoons, and Maroneia.
itineraries.notes: The Xanthi Folklore Museum is closed on Mondays, and the Archaeological Museum of Abdera is closed on Tuesdays: plan these visits accordingly. Winter remains the best season for watching lagoon birds; for hiking in the Nestos Gorge, choose spring or fall.
itineraries.climate: Favor May–June and September–October: on the Thracian coast (Alexandroupoli weather station), average highs range from about 20 °C in October to 27 °C in June. Avoid midday walks in July and August, when average highs exceed 30 °C. November and December are the rainiest months, each receiving more than 80 mm of rain.

visits.text: Polished cobblestones, projecting wooden upper stories, and colorful facades: keep your eyes up as you explore Xanthi’s Palia Poli. Rebuilt after the earthquakes of 1829 and protected since 1976, the old town covers about 38 hectares, the equivalent of around fifty soccer fields, with neoclassical mansions and Ottoman houses. Follow Orfeos Street uphill to Mitropoleos Square and the Church of Saint John the Baptist, wearing comfortable shoes: the cobbled lanes are unforgiving on smooth soles.

In 1860, two brothers from the Kougioumtzoglou family, both tobacco merchants, had a double mansion built: today it houses the Xanthi Folklore and History Museum. Painted ceilings, carved woodwork, and two domed hammams in the rear courtyard speak to the fortune made from tobacco leaves. The displays draw on a collection of more than 10,000 objects, from costumes of Thrace and Pontus to jewelry. Visit in the morning, Tuesday through Sunday; admission costs €5.

More moving than monumental, the Grand Maison on Venizelou Street preserves the memory of Manos Hadjidakis, born in Xanthi on October 23, 1925, and an Oscar winner for the music of “Never on Sunday,” specifically the song “Never on Sunday.” The composer spent at least part of his childhood here. Today, the mansion houses a space for art and ideas, with photographs, musical scores, and personal belongings upstairs. Opening hours depend on the event schedule: check them when you arrive in the old town.

Locally, it is simply called the “Π”: the tobacco warehouse takes its nickname from the Greek letter formed by its buildings. The Ottoman monopoly, which controlled the region until 1912, stored tobacco leaves here; the Foundation for Thracian Art and Tradition now occupies the site. Continue your walk through the warehouse district, southeast of the old town, where facades from the late 19th and early 20th centuries tell the story of tobacco’s golden age.

Head up to the Monastery of Panagia Archangeliotissa toward the end of the day, when the Xanthi plain spreads out below its wooded slopes. Rebuilt in 1841 after the earthquakes of 1829, it preserves a small 16th-century icon depicting the Virgin between the archangels Gabriel and Michael. On August 15, thousands of pilgrims from across Thrace gather here: choose another day for a quiet visit, and cover your shoulders and knees.

activities.text: If your stay falls on a Saturday, save the morning for the Xanthi bazaar, a weekly market with Ottoman roots held in Emboriou Square. Renowned throughout the region, it invites a leisurely stroll from stall to stall. Then head uphill toward Dimokratias Square, laid out in 1870 and dominated by the clock tower. On other days, its outdoor cafés are enough for a break between the modern city and the old town.

practical_info.tip: The bazaar takes place only on Saturdays. In February, the Xanthi Carnival also brings the city and its neighborhoods to life.

visits.text: Drive uphill from Toxotes toward Imera and Achladas: about ten kilometers of paved switchbacks lead to the Nestos viewpoint, a wooden gazebo perched above the river’s meanders. On clear days, the view stretches as far as Thasos, and sometimes Limnos. Bring binoculars for birds of prey and take your time on the curves.

activities.text: Easy, but worth taking seriously: the Nestos Gorge trail starts in Galani and follows the east bank along an old railway workers’ path, a branch of the E6 European long-distance trail. The first 3.5 kilometers follow the river; Kromniko Spring is about 2 hours away. Never enter the railway tunnels on foot.

practical_info.tip: Park in Galani, where a snack bar serves coffee and snacks. A round trip along the riverside section takes about three hours, including breaks. Canoeing and kayaking can be booked through local operators; in summer, you can swim along the sandy banks.

to_next_leg.road_type: Mountain road via Imera and the viewpoint
to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: Designated a traditional village by the Greek Ministry of Culture, Stavroupoli still bore its Ottoman name, Yeni Köy, until 1920. Two-story stone houses with balconies supported by wooden beams line the streets around the town hall. Then climb Prophet Elijah Hill for one last view of the Nestos River’s meanders.

Unassuming from the outside, the Stavroupoli Folklore Museum occupies the former tobacco tax office, a nod to the crop that once sustained the valley. Costumes, farming tools, musical instruments, and everyday objects were brought together here at the initiative of Stavros Karampatzakis. No opening hours are published: call the Stavroupoli municipal office before visiting.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Xanthi, then take the road to Avdira

visits.text: It is best to start at the Archaeological Museum of Abdera, in the village of Avdira, before tackling the ruins. Opened in 2000, it covers nearly two thousand years, from the 7th century BC to the 13th century AD, and reconstructs burials with clay sarcophagi and funerary offerings. Note that it is closed on Tuesdays.

Head down to Cape Bouloustra, about ten kilometers south, following in the footsteps of Democritus and Protagoras, both born in Abdera. Founded in the 7th century BC by settlers from Clazomenae and refounded by settlers from Teos around 544 BC, the city retains its defensive walls, a sanctuary of Demeter and Kore, and a quay now buried in sand. Check seasonal opening hours.

Salty air rises to the promontory of Polystylon, the Byzantine acropolis of Abdera, whose name recalls the columns that adorned its buildings. On the western side of the present-day anchorage, look for granite blocks from the ancient harbor. Save this sea view for the end of your visit before taking the road to Porto Lagos.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via the ancient site at Cape Bouloustra

visits.text: Set on an islet in the lagoon, the Agios Nikolaos Monastery in Porto Lagos seems to float on the water. This dependency of Vatopedi Monastery on Mount Athos is reached by a wooden footbridge, as is the chapel of Panagia Pantanassa, which houses a copy of the Vatopedi icon. Clothing that covers the body is required; on December 6, the Feast of Saint Nicholas draws crowds.

activities.text: If you see a patch of pink moving on the water in the distance, those are flamingos feeding in the lagoons around Porto Lagos. Lake Vistonida, Greece’s fourth-largest lake at 4,500 hectares, and its marshes are home to more than two hundred bird species, including Dalmatian pelicans. Winter is the best season; bring binoculars and a spotting scope.

practical_info.tip: Access to the lagoon east of Porto Lagos is not signposted: locate it on a map before setting out.

activities.text: Fanari deserves more than just a swim at the end of the day. This fishing village has five beaches, known for their Blue Flag status, and an old harbor lined with fish tavernas. Skala Beach, across from the promenade, is suitable for children and offers wide-open sunset views. Return in late October for the arrival of migratory birds.

practical_info.tip: Fanari borders part of Lake Vistonida: combine beach time with birdwatching before heading to Komotini.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Komotini, then take the road to Pagouria

activities.text: Locals still call it “limni Mitrikou”: ask for it by that name if you are looking for Lake Ismarida, which is hidden from the road. Shallow, averaging barely one meter deep, it is protected under the Ramsar Convention and hosts more than 200 bird species. Bring water and a hat for the walk to the bird observatory: the terrain is flat and sandy, with little shade.

practical_info.tip: The tracks around the lake are partly unpaved but passable. A spotting scope is very helpful at the observation point.

visits.text: Homer places Maron, the priest of Apollo whose wine Odysseus used to get the Cyclops drunk, in the Ismaros area. Built in the early Hellenistic period, the theater of Maroneia seated 1,200 to 1,300 spectators facing the sea and Samothrace, near the sanctuary attributed to Dionysus. You can explore the site freely; in summer, come early.

An enormous plane tree shades Maroneia’s small square, near a stone fountain. Clinging to the slopes of Ismaros, the village has about ten churches and chapels, including two basilicas with timber roof structures dating from the late 18th century. Leave the car and walk uphill: the narrow streets twist and turn constantly.

activities.text: Head down for lunch at the harbor of Agios Charalampos, a few minutes’ drive from the village. This small fishing harbor occupies the site of Maroneia’s ancient and Byzantine port: defensive walls with towers and wine presses have been uncovered here, and remains surface even in the courtyards of the tavernas. Order the fish of the day.

practical_info.tip: In winter, few restaurants stay open in Maroneia: have lunch at the harbor and spend the night in Komotini.

visits.text: The Archaeological Museum of Komotini is worth a stop for its gold bust alone. Found in 1965 in Didymoteicho, ancient Plotinopolis, this portrait of Septimius Severus weighs about 980 grams and is made of 23-karat gold. The building, designed by architect Aris Konstantinidis, also houses a sarcophagus carved with the twelve labors of Heracles and three milestones from the Via Egnatia found in town. Arrive early: the museum opens at 8:30 a.m. and closes in midafternoon.

Small but still discernible in the urban fabric, Komotini’s Byzantine fortress enclosed about 1.45 hectares, equivalent to two soccer fields, within a 472-meter defensive wall. Tradition attributes it to Theodosius I; some researchers suggest the 12th century instead. In the southeast corner, step inside the Metropolitan Church of the Dormition, built in 1800, then look for the ruins of an 18th-century synagogue against the western side.

In the 1360s, just after the conquest, Gazi Evrenos had the Imaret of Komotini built, one of the oldest Ottoman civic buildings in the Balkans. An unexpected detail: under Bulgarian occupation, it became a power station and remained one until 1973. Since 1999, it has housed the Ecclesiastical Museum, with icons and liturgical objects dating from the 16th to the early 20th century. Check opening hours before visiting.

Beneath the 25-meter clock tower donated by Sultan Abdülhamid II in 1884–1885, Komotini’s Yeni Mosque holds an understated treasure: it is the only building in Greece decorated with Iznik tiles from the 1580s. Founded in the late 16th century, it gained a large prayer hall in the 19th century. This is an active mosque: ask before entering, visit outside prayer times, and cover your shoulders and legs.

If you enjoyed the museum in Xanthi, compare it with the Folklore Museum of Komotini, housed since 1989 in the Peidis mansion, built around 1870. Costumes, embroidery, copperware, and silverware from Thrace and Asia Minor sit alongside personal mementos of Chrysanthos, the archbishop of Trebizond who was born in Komotini. Since no opening hours are published, call before visiting on Agiou Georgiou Street.

activities.text: Weave through Komotini’s old bazaar, between Yeni Mosque and Eski Mosque: this designated historic district preserves shops that have disappeared elsewhere, such as the teneketzidika, or tinsmiths’ workshops. In the 17th century, Ottoman traveler Evliya Çelebi already counted 400 shops in town. Bring cash for small purchases.

practical_info.tip: Continue to Yeni Mosque and the clock tower, just steps from the shops.

activities.text: The scent of resin and views stretching to Lake Vistonida: the Nymfaia pine forest, 3 km north of Komotini, serves as the city’s green lung. Planted in the 1930s, it has trails, tables, and gazebos spread across about 450 hectares; a paved road leads through it to Nymfaia Fort, part of the Metaxas Line. Head up in the late afternoon, when the Rhodope plain takes on a softer appearance.

practical_info.tip: The Nymfaia snack bar offers a sweeping view over the plain, Lake Vistonida, and the Thracian Sea.

seo.h1_title: Greek Thrace in 5 Days: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day itinerary through Greek Thrace starts in Xanthi’s old town, heads up Nestos Gorge, then follows the coast through Abdera, Porto Lagos, and Lake Vistonida. It ends in Komotini, with a day in Maroneia taking in an ancient theater, a village on Ismaros, and a fishing harbor.
seo.seo_hook: Xanthi’s old town, Nestos Gorge, Abdera, Porto Lagos Monastery, and Komotini’s gold bust: 5 days in Greek Thrace.
featured_list: Xanthi: an old town covering about 38 hectares, protected since 1976
Galani: the Nestos Gorge trail follows an old railway workers’ path
Stavroupoli: a designated traditional village on the edge of the Nestos Valley
Abdera: a museum spanning the 7th century BC to the 13th century
Porto Lagos: flamingos and Dalmatian pelicans on the Vistonida lagoons
Lake Ismarida: more than 200 bird species around an observation hide
Maroneia: an ancient theater facing the sea and Samothrace
Komotini: a 14th-century imaret turned ecclesiastical museum

places_taglines.GR::xanthi: An old town of tobacco mansions at the foot of the Rhodope Mountains.
places_taglines.GR::galani: The village is the gateway to the Nestos Gorge trail.
places_taglines.GR::stavroupoli: A designated traditional village with a museum in the former tobacco office.
places_taglines.GR::avdira: A museum and ruins in the birthplace of Democritus.
places_taglines.GR::porto-lagos: A monastery on an islet between Lake Vistonida and the Thracian Sea.
places_taglines.GR::limni-ismarida: A shallow lake protected under the Ramsar Convention, rich in waterbirds.
places_taglines.GR::maroneia: A village on Ismaros above a Hellenistic theater.
places_taglines.GR::komotini: A Byzantine fortress, a bazaar, and a gold bust of Septimius Severus.

highlights: Xanthi: old town protected since 1976 and the Kougioumtzoglou mansion dating to 1860
Nestos Gorge: Galani trail, a branch of the E6 European long-distance trail
Abdera: birthplace of Democritus and Protagoras, at Cape Bouloustra
Porto Lagos: Agios Nikolaos Monastery on its islet, a dependency of Vatopedi Monastery
Maroneia: Hellenistic theater seating 1,200 to 1,300, facing Samothrace
Komotini: gold bust of Septimius Severus and Iznik tiles in the Yeni Mosque
