itineraries.title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Sounion to Eleusis
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from the mines of Lavrio and Cape Sounion to Marathon, Rhamnous, and Eleusis, all the way to the ports of Piraeus.
itineraries.notes: Ideally, start on a Wednesday: almost all sites close on Tuesdays, the Lavrio Mineralogical Museum opens only on Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday mornings, and the maritime museum in Piraeus opens Tuesday through Saturday. Brauron, Marathon, and Rhamnous close at 3:30 p.m. year-round, so get an early start on the second day.
itineraries.climate: Aim for April–May or September–October: in Athens, average highs rise from 21 °C in April to nearly 27 °C in May, and fall from 30 °C in September to 24 °C in October (1991–2020 climate normals). Avoid July–August, when temperatures hover around 34 °C, at sites without shade such as Sounion, Rhamnous, or the Marathon Dam. In winter, most sites close at 3:30 p.m.: set out early each morning.

visits.text: Waste turned into display pieces: at the Lavrio Mineralogical Museum, slag from the smelters has produced minerals found nowhere else, such as nealite and georgiadesite. Display cases hold 740 specimens of 220 mineral species in a former ore-washing workshop dating from the late 19th century. Open Wednesday, Saturday, and Sunday, from 10 a.m. to noon only: make this your first stop.

The Lavrio Archaeological Museum holds a piece of Sounion: slabs from the frieze of the Temple of Poseidon, carved in the mid-5th century BC, depicting battles between centaurs, giants, and gods. Nearby, Neolithic objects from Kitsos Cave and inscriptions from the mines tell the story of Athens’ silver. Admission €5, open 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. except Tuesdays: visit before heading to the cape to fully appreciate the frieze in context.

In 1875, J.-B. Serpieri founded the French Mining Company of Lavrion, whose complex did not cease all operations until 1989. The Lavrio Technological and Cultural Park, entrusted to the National Technical University of Athens, has restored 17 of its 42 buildings, which were built between 1876 and 1898. The grounds are open on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on weekends by appointment; continue on foot to Kyprianos, the neighborhood built for the company’s employees.

Unexpected, and that is its charm: the ancient theater of Thorikos is nothing like a semicircle. On Velatouri Hill, 2.5 km north of Lavrio, its seating tiers surround an almost rectangular orchestra measuring about 16 m by 30 m, and construction began between 525 and 480 BC. Admission is free: wear walking shoes to explore this minimally developed site, with views of Attica’s southern coast.

activities.text: Sit down along Lavrio’s waterfront at one of the fish tavernas that have earned the port its reputation. Fish, grilled or fried, is often presented on marble slabs, and ferries to the Cyclades depart from the same port, Attica’s third-largest. Ask the price before choosing your fish, then head toward Cape Sounion in the early afternoon.

practical_info.tip: The mineralogical museum is open only from 10 a.m. to noon: visit before sitting down to eat.

visits.text: If you experience just one sunset in Attica, make it the one at the Temple of Poseidon on Cape Sounion, perched nearly 60 m above the sea. Built between 444 and 440 BC from Agrileza marble, it has columns with 16 flutes instead of 20, and Lord Byron carved his name into one of them. Admission €20, open from 9:30 a.m. until sunset: arrive 1 hour 30 minutes beforehand; last admission is 20 minutes before closing.

In 413 BC, Athens fortified Cape Sounion to protect its grain supply. From the temple, look for the remains of this fortress, then, a few hundred meters away, the ruins of the sanctuary of Athena, which were reused as early as antiquity. Take this walk in the late afternoon before choosing your spot facing the sunset.

activities.text: Deep, clear water beneath the columns: Sounio Beach, 1.5 km from the temple, is the only beach within walking distance of the site. The Temple of Poseidon towers above swimmers; for a quieter spot, drive from Sounion to the KAPE coast, then walk down a staircase, while the more family-friendly Legrena awaits 5 km away. Expect an extra charge for lounge chairs on beaches with facilities.

practical_info.tip: Go swimming in the afternoon, then head back up to the temple 1 hour 30 minutes before sunset.

visits.text: “Little she-bears”: at Brauron, the Athenians used the name arktoi for young girls dedicated to Artemis before marriage, who danced and ran in saffron-colored clothing. The sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia features a stoa with re-erected columns and a stone bridge, the only known example of a Classical-period bridge in Greece. Admission €5, open 8:30 AM–3:30 PM except Tuesdays: arrive at opening time to continue on to Marathon and Rhamnous.

Few museums have so much to say about childhood: Brauron’s museum displays statues of children, toys, vases, and figurines offered to Artemis, along with fragments of her cult statue. Look for the “relief of the gods,” which illustrates the founding myth: Iphigenia and Orestes bringing back the goddess’s statue from Tauris. Separate admission of €5; the museum is a five-minute walk from the sanctuary.

The Greeks call it Soros, “the coffin”: this burial mound on the plain of Marathon holds the ashes of the 192 Athenians who fell fighting the Persians in 490 BC. In 1890, archaeologist Valérios Staïs uncovered the funeral pyre here, with charred bones and black-figure pottery. Admission €5, open 8:30 AM–3:30 PM except Tuesdays; a modern statue of Miltiades, the Athenian general, stands nearby.

The Archaeological Museum of Marathon holds an Egyptian surprise: colossal Egyptian-style statues from the sanctuary that Herodes Atticus dedicated to the gods of Egypt at Brexiza. You can also see original fragments of the victory trophy and, just steps away, the so-called Mound of the Plataeans and the Bronze Age tombs of Vrana. Separate admission of €5: allow a full hour.

In 1896, the marathon at the first modern Olympic Games started in this town, and the medal won by its victor, Spyros Louis, is on display at the Marathon Run Museum. The town’s former school houses more than 4,000 objects, including memorabilia from Stelios Kyriakidis, who won in Boston in 1946. Open Tuesday through Friday, 9 AM–3 PM, and weekends, 10 AM–2 PM: stop by when you arrive from Brauron.

A hydraulic structure clad like a temple: Marathon Dam, 8 km west of town, is faced with the same Pentelic marble as the Parthenon. Built from 1926 to 1929 by the American firm Ulen to supply Athens with water, it measures 54 m high and 285 m long, with a replica of the Treasury of the Athenians at Delphi at its base. The road crosses the crest: stop for a short walk above the lake, or even a picnic on its shores.

activities.text: End the day at Schinias Beach, southeast of Marathon, on the edge of Schinias-Marathon National Park, where sea, pine forest, wetlands, and dunes meet. The nearby body of water hosted rowing at the 2004 Olympic Games, and the wind draws windsurfers here. Come after Rhamnous, in the late afternoon, once you have visited the ancient sites.

practical_info.tip: The sites at Brauron, Marathon, and Rhamnous close at 3:30 PM year-round: save the beach for the end of the day.

visits.text: A secluded cove below, the Gulf of Euboea on the horizon: reaching the sanctuary of Nemesis at Rhamnous takes some effort. Its great temple, begun around 460–450 BC, housed a statue by Agoracritus, a pupil of Phidias, carved, legend has it, from marble brought by the Persians for their trophy; the traveler William Leake already considered the story a fable. Admission €5, open 8:30 AM–3:30 PM except Tuesdays.

Next, follow the ancient road through Rhamnous, lined with funerary enclosures belonging to wealthy families of the Classical period, to the fortress crowning the hill. Its roughly 800 m circuit of walls overlooked two small harbors and the passage through the Gulf of Euboea, guarded by a garrison of Athenian ephebes. It is a long walk: athletic shoes and water are essential, especially in summer.

to_next_leg.road_type: A6 Attiki Odos highway to Eleusis

visits.text: Eleusis calls for imagination, and that is its whole appeal: initiates were forbidden to reveal a word about the Mysteries celebrated here for nearly a millennium. Pass through the Greater and then the Lesser Propylaea and continue to the Telesterion, a columned hall whose foundations survive, designed by Ictinus, the architect of the Parthenon. Admission €10 including the museum; open except Tuesdays, 8:30 AM–3:30 PM in winter and until 8 PM from April through August.

If the Telesterion left you wanting more, the Archaeological Museum of Eleusis, in the heart of the site, puts faces to the cult. Built in 1889, it is among Greece’s earliest archaeological museums and displays large statues of Demeter and Asclepius in sections devoted to “the city around the sanctuary” and “the Great Mysteries.” Save it for the end of your visit, when the sun beats down on the ruins.

activities.text: Next, walk along the Eleusis waterfront, past Palaio Elaiourgeio, a former factory that hosted performances during the Aischylia Festival. Since 1975, this festival has honored Aeschylus, who was born in Eleusis, and the city was a European Capital of Culture in 2023, amid an oil refinery and ancient remains. If you visit from late August through September, check the festival program for performance venues.

practical_info.tip: Save this walk for late morning, before driving to Daphni Monastery.

visits.text: The stern gaze of the Pantocrator looks down from the dome of Daphni Monastery, on the ancient Sacred Way that led to Eleusis. Its gold-background mosaics, dating to around 1100, have survived many changes in the monastery’s use: a Cistercian presence until 1458, a gunpowder magazine during the revolution of 1821, and later a psychiatric hospital. UNESCO listed the monastery in 1990. Admission is free, every day except Tuesday, until 3:30 PM in winter and 5 PM in summer.

In July 1959, the ancient port of Piraeus yielded three bronzes at once—an Apollo, an Athena, and an Artemis—now brought together at the Archaeological Museum of Piraeus. Long considered Archaic, the Apollo is now regarded by some scholars as a Hellenistic work imitating that style. Admission €10, open except Tuesdays until 3:30 PM in winter and 5 PM in summer; take a look at the Hellenistic theater of Zea, which the building surrounds.

The Hellenic Maritime Museum, at the entrance to Zea Marina, incorporates a section of Conon’s Long Walls into its ground floor. More than 2,500 objects trace the history of Greek seafaring, from anchors dating to the time of Navarino to models and paintings, while the conning tower of the submarine Papanikolis takes pride of place in the courtyard. Open Tuesday through Saturday from 9 AM to 2 PM: visit before the archaeological museum.

A balcony overlooking Athens, right in Piraeus: from Kastella Hill, the view stretches from Mikrolimano to the Acropolis, Mount Lycabettus, and Mount Hymettus. The Veakeio Theater, at an elevation of 87 m, hosts performances only in summer, and the Church of the Prophet Elijah, destroyed in 1944, took on its current form in 1995. Climb the stairs from Papanastasiou Avenue in the late afternoon, with binoculars in your pocket.

activities.text: Walk along Akti Themistokleous, the waterfront road around the Piraeus peninsula: 2.5 km along the water between the naval cadet school, with its neoclassical touches by Ernst Ziller, and Zea Marina. Remains of Conon’s wall, dating to the 4th century BC, emerge among the rocks, and Freattyda Beach offers a place to swim right in the city. Set out an hour before sunset, when the western sky lights up.

practical_info.tip: You can walk the route in either direction: start at Zea Marina to walk toward the sunset.

activities.text: Tourkolimano to some, Mikrolimano to others: the smallest of Piraeus’s three natural harbors, ancient Munichia, has restaurants and cafés lining a broad esplanade at the foot of Kastella. Redeveloped in 2022, it evokes an Aegean island harbor right in the city. Reserve a table for dinner, especially on weekends, and end your third day here.

practical_info.tip: The broad, child-friendly esplanade is ideal for an after-dinner stroll.

seo.h1_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Sounion to Eleusis
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day road trip explores Attica without entering Athens: the silver mines of Lavrio, the Temple of Poseidon at Sounion, the sanctuaries of Brauron and Rhamnous, and the plain of Marathon. The final day follows the ancient Sacred Way from Eleusis to Daphni Monastery, then ends at the harbors of Piraeus.
seo.seo_hook: The Temple of Poseidon at Sounion, the burial mound at Marathon, Rhamnous, Brauron, the Eleusinian Mysteries, and the mosaics of Daphni: Attica beyond Athens in 3 days.
featured_list: Lavrio: 740 mineral specimens in a 19th-century mining workshop
Sounion: columns with 16 flutes and Lord Byron’s signature
Brauron: reconstructed stoa and Classical-period stone bridge
Marathon: burial mound of the 192 Athenians and a dam built of Pentelic marble
Rhamnous: funerary road and fortress with 800 m of perimeter walls
Eleusis: Telesterion designed by Ictinus, the architect of the Parthenon
Daphni: mosaic of Christ Pantocrator at the crown of the dome
Piraeus: three ancient bronzes recovered from the harbor in 1959

places_taglines.GR::lavrio: Ancient silver mines, French smelting works, and minerals formed from slag.
places_taglines.GR::sounion: The Temple of Poseidon overlooks the sea from a height of nearly 60 m.
places_taglines.GR::brauron: Sanctuary of Artemis, reconstructed stoa, and Classical-period stone bridge.
places_taglines.GR::marathon: Burial mound of the 192 Athenians, marathon race museum, and marble dam.
places_taglines.GR::rhamnous: Temple of Nemesis and ancient fortress overlooking the Gulf of Euboea.
places_taglines.GR::elefsina: The sanctuary of the Mysteries of Demeter in the heart of an industrial city.
places_taglines.GR::daphni-monastery: Byzantine mosaics on gold backgrounds beside the ancient Sacred Way.
places_taglines.GR::piraeus: Ancient bronzes, a maritime museum, and the small harbor of Mikrolimano.

highlights: Sounion: Temple of Poseidon, built between 444 and 440 BC, nearly 60 m above the sea
Marathon: the Soros, the burial mound of the 192 Athenians who fell in 490 BC
Brauron: the only known Classical-period bridge in Greece, at the foot of the sanctuary of Artemis
Rhamnous: Temple of Nemesis and fortress overlooking the Gulf of Euboea
Eleusis: the Telesterion designed by Ictinus, the heart of the Mysteries for nearly a millennium
Daphni: Byzantine mosaics with gold backgrounds, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1990

itineraries.title: The Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Parga, Acheron, and Nicopolis
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, follow the Epirus coast from Igoumenitsa to Preveza, taking in Sivota’s coves, Parga, the Acheron, and Nicopolis.
itineraries.notes: Opening hours at the Necromanteion and Kassope vary by season, and both may close in the middle of the afternoon: visit in the morning. For walking in the Acheron, bring water shoes and a dry bag, and avoid winter, when the current grows stronger.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May, June, and September, with average highs of 23 to 27 °C in Preveza. July and August reach around 30 °C: swim early and save the ancient sites for the morning. Avoid the rainy season, from October to February, when the Acheron becomes too turbulent for river walking.

visits.text: A better introduction than a harborside café, the Archaeological Museum of Igoumenitsa puts Thesprotia in perspective as soon as you step off the ferry. Opened in late 2009, it brings together more than 1,600 objects, from the Middle Paleolithic to the Roman era, with an emphasis on the Hellenistic period. Allow 1 hour: it is a 30-minute walk from the new port terminal and is closed on Tuesdays.

Pines, old walls, and the city’s rooftops at your feet: Igoumenitsa Castle crowns a low hill southwest of the center. Its earliest defenses probably date back to Roman times; the Venetian admiral Morosini partly destroyed it in 1685, and Ali Pasha repaired it in 1798. Allow 30 minutes for the south wall facing the harbor, the best-preserved section with its cannon embrasures.

In 433 BC, around 270 ships from Corinth, Corcyra, and Athens clashed in these waters, with the Corcyrean fleet based in the Sybota islands. From Sivota’s harbor, the bay looks peaceful today, guarded by four uninhabited islets. Stroll along the waterfront and negotiate your water taxi fare: expect around ten euros per person, depending on the distance.

activities.text: You can reach Bella Vraka in 15 minutes on foot from central Sivota, then wade across the sandbar stretching toward the islet of Megalo Mourtemeno. The shallow water comes up to your knees, making it ideal for families. There is no café on-site: bring water and snacks, and arrive early in the height of summer.

practical_info.tip: The beach is very popular in peak season; water sandals make it easier to cross the sandy, pebbly bottom.

activities.text: Pisina, nicknamed Blue Lagoon, looks like an emerald pool nestled between Sivota’s islets. Water taxis and small rental boats head there daily from the harbor, making it possible to combine several coves. Bring a mask and snorkel: the neighboring inlets lend themselves to kayaking and leisurely exploration.

practical_info.tip: A small motorboat for five to six people can be rented without a boating license, starting at around €50 for 6 hours.

activities.text: If you prefer to stay on dry land, Megali Ammos offers Sivota’s well-equipped beach experience: golden sand, deep, clear water, and water sports. Its neighbor Mikri Ammos offers much the same on a smaller scale. Save this swim for the afternoon, before driving to Parga.

practical_info.tip: Both beaches are accessible by a paved road from the village; amenities and water sports are available in season.

visits.text: Nothing beats Parga Castle for taking in the town at a glance, an eight-minute climb along a cobbled path from the harbor. The Venetians rebuilt it several times after Barbarossa burned it in 1537; Ali Pasha added a hammam, and the winged lion of Saint Mark still watches over the gate. Admission is free from April through October, with a café in the former barracks: head up at sunset.

You will walk back down from the castle through Parga’s sloping lanes to the waterfront at Kryoneri, the town beach facing the islet of Panagia. In the middle of the bay, the tall rock of Skorda completes the scene. Take a seat on a terrace at dusk, when the ramparts light up above you.

Built to capture Parga, Ali Pasha’s castle in Anthousa lost its purpose five years later, when the town was ceded to him in 1819. Built in 1814 on a hill 5 km to the northwest, it overlooks the entire bay from its eastern tower, approximately 15 m high. Admission is free and the site is unstaffed: closed-toe shoes are essential.

activities.text: The islet of Panagia, just off Parga’s harbor, takes its name from its small church. The boat crossing is short; once ashore, you’ll find vegetation covering the islet and can walk around it at a leisurely pace. Go in the morning, before the heat, and allow just under 1 hour, including the round-trip crossing.

practical_info.tip: Boats leave from Parga’s harbor; check the time of the last return crossing before boarding.

activities.text: White sand mixed with smooth pebbles and deep blue water: Valtos Beach stretches for 3 km, a 20-minute walk northwest of Parga. Developed for tourism, with tavernas, pedal boats, and canoes, it faces the back of the castle. Go in the late afternoon, when the low sun lights up the ramparts.

practical_info.tip: The little tourist train departing from Parga Beach also climbs to Anthousa Castle—a handy option if you leave the car behind.

visits.text: Descend into the crypt of the Necromanteion of Acheron, carved into the rock beneath the hall where the dead were supposedly summoned: fifteen arches support it at a height of 3.25 m. Pilgrims swore secrecy on pain of death, and the Romans burned the sanctuary in 167 BC. Above it, the Church of Saint John the Baptist, built over the ruins in the 16th century, preserves frescoes from 1740. Arrive at opening time and scan the QR code for the audio guide.

The main spring of the Acheron gushes out approximately 300 m from the Glyki parking lot, at the end of a trail following the river beneath plane trees. The ancients saw this as an entrance to the Underworld; today, white-throated dippers and wagtails are the main visitors to its clear waters. Arrive early: the site gets very busy on some summer days.

activities.text: The icy water grips your calves as soon as you leave the bank: in the Acheron Gorge, you walk upstream, with a few short stretches to swim. The classic round trip, approximately 1.9 km with around 100 m of elevation gain, takes you close to Skala Tzavelaina, where the walls narrow. Water shoes and a dry bag are essential.

practical_info.tip: In winter, the current becomes much stronger: save river walking for summer. Rafting, kayaking, and horseback riding are also available on-site.

activities.text: Until 1928, Ammoudia was called Splantza; this small fishing port grew up right at the mouth of the Acheron. Boats head upriver daily on guided tours, and you can also rent a kayak to paddle upstream. Choose a late-afternoon outing, when the northwesterly wind dies down.

practical_info.tip: Boat and kayak trips depart from the river quays; the wind often picks up around 11 a.m. in summer.

activities.text: You will end the afternoon on Ammoudia’s large sandy beach, where the shallow water suits young children. Farther upstream, the Acheron’s water stays cold and very clear, offering a bracing dip. The riverside tavernas serve the day’s catch, so you can have dinner here before heading to Parga.

practical_info.tip: Parga is only about fifteen kilometers away, so dinner in Ammoudia barely extends your evening.

to_next_leg.road_type: Overnight in Parga, then drive to Kamarina

visits.text: Few ruins in Epirus offer such a vantage point: Kassope, perched on a plateau on Mount Zalongo, commands views of the Ionian Sea and the Ambracian Gulf. Founded around the middle of the 4th century BC, the capital of the Kassopaeans was ravaged by the Romans in 167 BC; its katagogeion, an inn with a peristyle courtyard, remains its best-preserved public building. Come in the morning, as the site may close by midafternoon.

The 13 m-high Zalongo Monument stands atop the cliff near Kassope. It commemorates the roughly sixty Souliot women who, cornered by Ottoman troops in December 1803, chose death over captivity. Expect approximately 400 steps from the Monastery of Agios Dimitrios; climb before the heat sets in.

Start at the Archaeological Museum of Nicopolis to bring the ruins you will explore afterward to life. Opened in 2009, it holds more than 10,000 objects, with around 1,100 on display, including a bust of General Agrippa. Admission is €10; from April through October, it is open from 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. except Tuesdays, and in winter until 3:30 p.m.

The Basilica of Doumetios reveals Nicopolis at its most refined: its early Christian mosaics have just been restored. Founded by Octavian in 29 BC, two years after his naval victory at Actium, the city had six basilicas from around 460 onward, and the Byzantine walls enclosed only one-sixth of its former area. An accessible path now runs alongside Basilica IV.

Compact and easy to interpret, the Odeon of Nicopolis helps you picture public life in the Roman capital, where it was used from the late 1st century to the late 3rd century. Nearby, the House of Georgios Ekdikos has gained 36 more rooms following the latest excavations, and the small nymphaeum preserves the site’s only wall mosaic. A hat and water are essential in summer.

At least 36 bronze rams taken from Antony and Cleopatra’s galleys once adorned the Monument of Augustus on Michalitsi Hill, north of Nicopolis. Only the anchor-shaped sockets remain, arranged by size in the retaining wall, but they are enough to convey the scale of the fleet defeated in 31 BC. Contact the Ephorate of Antiquities before visiting. Drive there: the hill is some distance from the main ruins.

“Seitan Bazaar!”—the devil’s bazaar: according to a story told in Preveza, an Ottoman officer uttered this curse as he slipped on this cobbled lane, which residents had greased. Farther along, the Venetian clock tower of 1752 stands beside the Church of Agios Charalambos with its gilded iconostasis. Come for a predinner drink, when the ouzeris come alive, and order grilled sardines.

A French colonel designed a pasha’s fortress: Pantokrator Castle, built under Ali Pasha beginning in 1807, bears the signature of Guillaume de Vaudoncourt. High buttressed walls, a dry moat to the south, and a water-filled moat to the north form an almost perfect rectangle facing the entrance to the gulf. Aim for a summer evening: the fortress hosts cultural events.

Next, you will follow the perimeter walls of Agios Andreas Fort, an elongated quadrilateral with four corner bastions that controlled Preveza’s harbor. Built by the Ottomans in the early 18th century and expanded by the Venetians and later Ali Pasha, it served as a military base for many years.

activities.text: Masts clink softly along Preveza’s waterfront as the sun sinks over the roughly 700 m-wide Aktio Strait. Since 2002, an underwater road tunnel has linked the two shores of the Ambracian Gulf, previously crossed only by ferry. Choose a harbor taverna for the fish of the day.

practical_info.tip: The Ambracian Gulf is a wetland protected under the Ramsar Convention; dolphins and sea turtles are regularly spotted here.

activities.text: If you have an hour before dinner, you can walk from central Preveza to Kyani Akti Beach beneath large shade trees. Above it, Agios Georgios Castle, dating to 1718, rounds out the city’s series of forts. For a wilder beach, Monolithi borders a forest a few minutes away by car.

practical_info.tip: Aktion National Airport, very close to Preveza, lets you fly out the next morning.

seo.h1_title: The Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Parga, Acheron, and Nicopolis
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day road trip follows the Epirus coast from the port of Igoumenitsa to Preveza. You will explore the coves of Sivota and Parga Castle, walk through the Acheron Gorge, and visit the oracle of the dead, followed by Kassope and Nicopolis, the city founded by Octavian after Actium.
seo.seo_hook: Sivota’s coves, Parga Castle, the Acheron Gorge, the Necromanteion, and the ruins of Nicopolis: 3 days along the Epirus coast to Preveza.
featured_list: Sivota: Bella Vraka’s sand spit leading to the islet of Megalo Mourtemeno
Parga: castle rebuilt by the Venetians, with the lion of Saint Mark on the gate
Acheron Springs: approximately 1.9 km round-trip through the riverbed
Necromanteion: rock-cut crypt beneath the Hall of Apparitions
Kassope and Zalongo: a 4th-century BC city and a 13 m monument
Nicopolis: city founded by Octavian in 29 BC after Actium

places_taglines.GR::igoumenitsa: Port for ferries from Italy, the Thesprotia museum, and a hilltop castle.
places_taglines.GR::sivota: Four uninhabited islets, Pisina lagoon, and the sandy ford at Bella Vraka.
places_taglines.GR::parga: Venetian castle on its rocky outcrop, Panagia islet, and Valtos Beach.
places_taglines.GR::necromanteion-of-acheron: Hellenistic oracle of the dead, with a fifteen-arch crypt beneath the sanctuary.
places_taglines.GR::acheron-springs: An icy spring and a walk through the Acheron gorges near Glyki.
places_taglines.GR::ammoudia: Fishing village at the mouth of the Acheron, with a large sandy beach.
places_taglines.GR::kassope: City of the Kassopaeans perched overlooking the gulf, with the Zalongo monument nearby.
places_taglines.GR::nicopolis: Octavian’s city of victory, basilicas with mosaics, and a museum.
places_taglines.GR::preveza: Seitan Bazaar alley, Ali Pasha’s forts, and the strait of the Ambracian Gulf.

highlights: Sivota: wade across to the islet of Megalo Mourtemeno
Parga: castle with free admission from April to October, café in the former barracks
Acheron: walk in the river to the area near Skala Tzavelaina
Necromanteion: a 3.25 m-high crypt supported by fifteen arches
Nicopolis: sockets for at least 36 naval rams on the Monument of Augustus
Preveza: Venetian clock tower dating from 1752 and Seitan Bazaar

itineraries.title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Mytilene, Molyvos and the Petrified Forest
itineraries.subtitle: Complete a circuit of Lesbos in 4 days via Mytilene, Molyvos, Sigri and Plomari, exploring castles, fossils and ouzo.
itineraries.notes: Start the circuit on a Wednesday, Thursday or Friday: Mytilene Castle and Archaeological Museum, Molyvos Castle, the Vareltzidaina Mansion and the Eresos collection are closed on Tuesdays. These sites close at 3:30 p.m. and the Petrified Forest parks at 4 p.m., so set out early each day.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May, June, September or October: average highs in Mytilene then range from 22 to 29 °C, with little rain. July and August average over 30 °C and draw crowds to the coastal villages. From November through February, expect between 96 and 139 mm of rain per month, making both beaches and mountain roads less appealing.

visits.text: No site on the island tells the story of as many successive rulers as Mytilene Castle, set between the sea and a pine grove. Originally Byzantine, it owes its outline to the Genoese Gattilusi family (1355–1462), followed by the Ottomans, who added mosques, a hammam and a gunpowder magazine; look for the Byzantine cistern and the Princess’s Tower. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., closed Tuesdays, admission €5: arrive at opening time, while the ramparts are still cool.

Orpheus charms wild beasts on a tessellated floor, near a bust of the muse Thalia and a portrait of the poet Menander: this mosaic takes pride of place in the New Archaeological Museum of Mytilene. Dating from the second half of the 3rd century, it is displayed alongside floors from the House of Telephus and wall paintings from wealthy Roman homes. Admission is €10, and the museum closes at 3:30 p.m. and on Tuesdays: visit in the late morning.

Baroque, neoclassical, Gothic: Agios Therapon Church blends all these styles, yet its dome commands Mytilene’s entire harbor. Begun in the early 19th century and only completed in 1935, it is the work of Argyris Adalis, a Lesbos native who trained under architect Ernst Ziller. Wear clothing that provides modest coverage when entering, and look up at the dome, visible from all along the waterfront.

Established from a small collection rediscovered in 1958 by Metropolitan Iakovos, the Byzantine Ecclesiastical Museum of Mytilene faces the entrance to Agios Therapon. Its oldest icons date to the 13th century; among the liturgical vestments, manuscripts and woodwork, look for an Assumption painted by Theophilos, the naive painter from Lesbos. Allow forty minutes, combining it with a visit to the church on foot.

The ancient theater of Mytilene served as a model for Rome: according to Plutarch, Pompey copied its layout for the theater he had built in 55 BC. On Agia Kyriaki Hill, its horseshoe-shaped cavea held around 10,000 spectators; what remains is mainly the slope, the orchestra and remnants of the later stage. While work is underway, visits require prior approval from the Ephorate of Antiquities of Lesbos: arrange your visit before heading up.

Seventeen arches rise in the countryside around Moria: the Roman aqueduct is a surprising sight just a few kilometers from Mytilene’s harbor. Dating from the late 2nd or early 3rd century, it carried water to the city from the springs of Olympos, some 26 km away; the surviving section measures 170 m. Drive there late in the day, when the low light picks out each pier.

activities.text: If you walk just one street, make it Ermou Street, a narrow pedestrian thoroughfare running from Agios Therapon toward Pano Skala, the former Turkish quarter. It was originally a channel separating the castle islet from the rest of the island, filled in by alluvial deposits after the 6th century. To the north stands Yeni Tzami, built in 1825 and roofless since 1951; along the way, stock up on aged cheeses and spices at the local shops.

practical_info.tip: The street is entirely pedestrian: leave your car near the harbor and return along the waterfront.

activities.text: End the day on the waterfront, where Mytilene’s Statue of Liberty watches over the harbor. Standing 15 m tall including its marble pedestal, cast in Germany in 1922 and unveiled in 1930, it is the work of sculptor Grigorios Zevgolis, based on a drawing by painter Georgios Iakovidis. Afterward, enjoy an ouzo and a few fish meze dishes at a waterfront taverna.

practical_info.tip: The statue can be viewed freely from the quay at any hour; sunset is the best time for a stroll.

visits.text: An icon molded from mud and blood: this is the tradition associated with the Taxiarchis Monastery in Mantamados. After a pirate raid, a single novice is said to have survived and shaped the archangel Michael from earth soaked in his brothers’ blood, resulting in an oversized head. The current church dates to 1879; cover your shoulders and knees, and preferably come in the morning.

activities.text: You will find Mantamados pottery right at the village entrance on the Mytilene side, in the Stamatis family’s workshop: the father throws cups and pitchers on the wheel, while his wife and daughter paint them by hand. Only two or three workshops remain in the village. Try the local cheese and yogurt, too, both sources of local pride.

practical_info.tip: The Stamatis workshop stands beside the road from Mytilene, at the village entrance: stop when you arrive.

visits.text: Panagia Gorgona Chapel seems perched on the rock at the end of the jetty in Skala Sykamias. It inspired Stratis Myrivilis’s novel “The Mermaid Madonna,” published in 1949, which shares the chapel’s name in Greek. Avoid August 15, its feast day, if you are looking for peace and quiet.

activities.text: For lunch, head three kilometers uphill to Sykamia, the birthplace of Stratis Myrivilis, known for its elegant homes and ouzo taverns, many of them a century old. Order hahles, little cups made from trahanas and filled with tomato, feta, and olive oil, the local specialty. Finish with almond candies before taking the road to Molyvos.

practical_info.tip: Sykamia is 3 km uphill from the harbor, on the road that continues to Molyvos.

visits.text: Small but sturdy, Molyvos Castle has crowned the village since the Middle Ages, on the ancient acropolis of Mithymna. The Genoese Francesco Gattilusio remodeled it in 1373, before the Ottomans captured it in 1462. Allow seven minutes for the climb along the marked route and €3 for admission; it is closed on Tuesdays and closes at 3:30 p.m., so sunset visits are never possible.

Painted hulls, stacked nets, the smell of food grilling: the little harbor of Molyvos still shelters its fishing caiques at the edge of the village. The waterfront taverns serve fish overlooking the boats that bring it in. Reserve a table for dinner, when the illuminated castle stands out above the rooftops.

activities.text: You will then head down toward the harbor through the cobblestone lanes of Molyvos, shaded by wisteria and bougainvillea. The loop suggested by the Greek tourism office is about 2.2 km long and takes 1 to 2 hours, depending on your stops. Wear shoes with good soles: all the streets are cobbled, and the village slopes uphill without ever becoming steep.

practical_info.tip: Wisteria blooms in April; in summer, walk the loop before 11 a.m. or after 6 p.m.

activities.text: If the heat gets oppressive, Molyvos Beach is about ten minutes on foot from the harbor. Dark pebbles line the shore, giving way to a sandy bottom once the water reaches your thighs: you can wade a long way before reaching deep water, and snorkeling is enjoyable here. Watch out for sea urchins near the rocks and arrive early, as the beach fills up quickly.

practical_info.tip: An equipped section offers lounge chairs, a shower, and a changing cabin; it gets quieter farther south.

visits.text: One hundred fourteen steps cut into the rock: that is the price of the view from Panagia Glykofilousa in Petra. The church crowns a rocky pinnacle about 40 m high that gave the village its name (petra means rock), and houses Byzantine icons and a carved wooden bishop’s throne. Climb early, before the heat, wearing modest clothing.

Less conspicuous than the church, the Vareltzidaina mansion holds Petra’s loveliest surprise. Above an almost fortified stone ground floor, this house from the late Ottoman era conceals carved wooden ceilings and murals depicting port cities and garlands. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. except Tuesdays; admission is €5.

activities.text: Stock up at the Petra women farmers’ association, which sells its local products and prepares home-cooked dishes daily. Facing the village’s large beach, the islets of Ai Giorgis, Glaronisi, and Myrmigi form a protected area for birds. Bring your lunch: the day continues toward the island’s volcanic west.

practical_info.tip: On August 15, the feast of Glykofilousa draws pilgrims from across the island to the village.

visits.text: Ochre plains, bare rock, the sea in the distance: from the walls of Ypsilou Monastery, the volcanic west of Lesbos spreads out like a map. Founded around the year 800 atop Ordymnos, at 511 m, it preserves old icons and Byzantine manuscripts in a small museum. Wear modest clothing and allow forty minutes, then head back down toward the Petrified Forest.

to_next_leg.road_type: 5 km paved road from the road to Sigri

visits.text: Standing 7.02 m tall and turned to stone, an ancestor of the sequoia still stands in Bali Alonia Petrified Forest Park: according to the museum, no standing fossil trunk in Europe is taller. Eruptions 17 to 20 million years ago also preserved a fallen trunk more than 20 m long here. Three themed trails wind through the park: arrive before 2 p.m., as it closes at 4 p.m.

map_keywords: Natural History Museum of the Lesvos Petrified Forest Sigri

visits.text: The Natural History Museum of the Lesbos Petrified Forest, in the upper part of Sigri, finally puts what you have just seen into perspective. Its main hall, redesigned in 2021, displays previously unexhibited fossils and tells the story of the forest’s formation and the geological history of the Aegean. Open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.; the €10 ticket also covers Bali Alonia and the neighboring parks, so keep it.

Continue to Sigri Park, laid out on the museum’s own grounds, where roots and standing trunks are remarkably well preserved. The easy trail is suitable for children and older visitors alike. Access is through the museum, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m.: if you arrive around 3 p.m., start with the park before visiting the galleries.

Built in the 18th century to defend against pirates, Sigri’s Ottoman fortress watches over the largest natural harbor on Lesbos. It faces the island of Nisiopi, a long barrier that shelters the bay from prevailing winds. A walk around the walls takes 20 minutes; save it for late afternoon, when the light fades over the bay.

activities.text: If you have 1 hour to spare, head to Plaka Park, 500 m from Sigri along the road to Eresos. More than thirty fossil trunks of conifers and fruit trees emerge from the ground between land and sea; the largest standing trunk measures 13.7 m in circumference. The museum manages the parks in summer: outside the season, call before visiting.

practical_info.tip: Museum and parks: 22530 54434. On-site parking at Plaka.

activities.text: Gray volcanic sand, a gentle slope, calm water: Sigri Beach forms an almost complete arc around the bay. Children can wade a long way out, but the breeze quickly carries off inflatable rings and air mattresses, so secure them. If you have an extra morning, the glass-bottom boat to Nisiopi Marine Park leaves the harbor at 10:30 a.m.; reserve through the museum.

practical_info.tip: Nisiopi boat: €15, daily trips weather permitting.

visits.text: Strabo already described Eresos as perched on a hill beside the sea, and its acropolis still overlooks the harbor of Skala Eresou. The visit takes in pre-Classical walls, the ruins of a medieval castle, and the fifth-century Agios Andreas Church with its mosaic floor. Admission is free: climb up in the morning, before the sun heats the hillside.

Housed in a former stone schoolhouse, the Archaeological Collection of Eresos stands beside St. Andrew’s Basilica. A rare statuette of Cybele, a terracotta larnax, and Ionic and Doric capitals tell the story of Sappho’s city, from the Late Bronze Age to the early Christians. Open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., closed Tuesdays; admission is €5.

activities.text: Sappho’s hometown, Skala Eresou nevertheless revolves above all around its beach: nearly 3 km of Blue Flag dark sand stretching from the small harbor to the western cape. Since the 1980s, lesbian travelers have made it one of their favorite destinations, and cafés and beach bars line the waterfront. Swim in the late morning before the long drive to Kalloni.

practical_info.tip: Use the parking lots on the edge of the village: explore the center on foot.

activities.text: If you visit in spring or fall, stop at the Kalloni salt pans, southeast of town: flamingos gather here during migration. The gulf and its wetlands host more than 250 bird species. A bird blind lets you watch without disturbing them; bring binoculars, as the field south of the road is difficult to walk through.

practical_info.tip: Flat terrain with little shade: bring a hat and water, especially around midday.

activities.text: Sometimes nicknamed “Lesbos sushi,” the Kalloni sardine, or papalina, is salted just a few hours after being caught. Caught in the gulf from May to October, it tastes best in August. Order it in Skala Kallonis with an ouzo as a lunchtime meze dish before heading toward Olympos.

practical_info.tip: Fresh sardine season runs from May to October, with peak flavor in August.

visits.text: The Church of Panagia in Agiasos houses the icon that gave the village its name, Agia Sion, which tradition attributes to St. Luke. The current sanctuary, dating from 1815, is the third on these foundations; a copy made around 1453 concealed the original until its rediscovery in 1838. Avoid August 15 if you dislike crowds: pilgrims walk up from all over the island.

Founded in 1894, when the island was still under Ottoman rule, the Anagnostirio of Agiasos welcomes visitors at the village entrance. This cultural center brings together a library of more than 25,000 volumes, a cinema and theater auditorium, and a folk museum. Stop here when you arrive, then walk down through the lanes to the church.

activities.text: Then stroll through the lanes of Agiasos, among colorful stone houses largely rebuilt after the fire of 1877. Pottery workshops and woodcarving shops line the center, and the Museum of Traditional Trades, created by sculptor Dimitris Kamaros, recreates a market from bygone days. Favor a piece signed by a village artisan when shopping.

practical_info.tip: Park at the lower entrance to the village, its main access point, and explore the center on foot.

activities.text: Grounds at the bottom of the cup, preserves served by the spoonful: the century-old cafés on Agiasos’s market square, above the church, set an unhurried pace. Perched more than 450 m up the slopes of Olympos, the village also makes a living from chestnuts, at their best in October. Order a Greek coffee with a glyko tou koutaliou and take your time before heading down to Plomari.

practical_info.tip: In October, a trail leads from the Apesos neighborhood up toward Megalochori through the chestnut trees.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: A still older than the distillery: at the Barbayanni Ouzo Museum, the family’s first still was made in Constantinople in 1858, two years before Efstathios Barbayannis settled in Plomari. Bottling and labeling machines tell the story of five generations of distillers. The museum stands beside the road to Mytilene: visit on your way out, allow 30 minutes to 1 hour, with tastings offered free or for €2.

activities.text: Plomari, the second-largest town on Lesbos, is a place to savor at aperitif time, between its harbor and the Basilica of Saint Nicholas, surrounded by stone houses. This is the home of ouzo: in the 19th century, merchant families from Asia Minor brought their stills here, and the July festival brings together more than 40 brands. Drop an ice cube into your glass: the ouzo turns cloudy at once.

practical_info.tip: Ammoudeli Beach, close to the center, is a good spot for a swim before dinner.

visits.text: Unexpected, almost incongruous: lithographs by Matisse, Chagall, Picasso, and Léger await in an olive grove in Varia, at the Tériade Museum, 4 km south of Mytilene. Opened in 1979, it showcases the publishing work of Stratis Eleftheriadis, a native of Lesbos who became known as Tériade: the 26 issues of Verve magazine (1937–1960) and his 26 illustrated “Great Books.” Opening hours are not published online: call the museum the day before.

activities.text: You will then head to Odysseas Elytis Airport, a few kilometers south of Varia, or to the port of Mytilene if you are leaving by sea. Daily flights connect to Athens year-round, while conventional ferries take about 11 to 13 hours to reach Piraeus. Return your rental car at the airport or port counter, according to your rental agreement.

practical_info.tip: Tériade Museum: 22510 23372. Allow an extra hour before check-in.

seo.h1_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Mytilene, Molyvos and the Petrified Forest
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day loop begins with a full day in Mytilene, exploring its Genoese castle, Roman mosaics, and Ermou Street. It then heads north to Mantamados, Molyvos, and Petra, crosses the volcanic west to the Petrified Forest of Sigri, and loops back down through Eresos, Kalloni, and Agiasos to the ouzo distilleries of Plomari.
seo.seo_hook: Mytilene Castle, the lanes of Molyvos, the Petrified Forest of Sigri, and Plomari’s ouzo: explore Lesbos in 4 days on a loop from the capital.
featured_list: Mytilene: the Gattilusi castle and the mosaic from the House of Menander
Molyvos: castle remodeled in 1373 on the acropolis of Mithymna
Bali Alonia: standing petrified trunk measuring 7.02 m
Plomari: the first Barbayanni still, made in 1858

itineraries.title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, explore Thessaloniki from the White Tower to Ano Poli, then head to Pella and the tombs of Vergina.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Wednesday or Thursday: most museums and sites close on Tuesdays, and Kapani Market closes on Sundays. For Pella and Vergina, rent a car for the day, as traveling by bus requires going through Veria, then completing the journey by local bus or taxi.
itineraries.climate: Aim for April–May and September–October, when average highs range from about 20 to 28 °C. Avoid July and August, when daytime temperatures hover around 32 °C, making the climb through Ano Poli tough. In winter (around 11 °C in January), sites close as early as 3:30 p.m., so start early.

visits.text: The White Tower is the best place to begin your stay: its museum traces Thessaloniki’s history from its founding in 316–315 BC, with a different theme on each floor. Standing about 34 m tall, the tower was called Kanlı Kule, the “Tower of Blood,” when it served as a prison under the Ottomans; rebellious Janissaries were massacred there in 1826. Climb to the roof for views over the gulf. In winter, it opens from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.; admission is €8.

A golden gleam without a gram of gold: the Derveni Krater owes its brilliance to bronze containing about 15% tin. At the Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki, this 90.5 cm, 40 kg vessel, found in a tomb at Derveni in 1962, depicts Dionysus and Ariadne among satyrs and maenads. Allow 1 hour for the permanent exhibition “The Gold of Macedon,” drawn from eight necropolises in the region. Open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Tuesdays; admission is €10.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Archaeological Museum Of Thessaloniki to Museum Of Byzantine Culture
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Awarded the Council of Europe Museum Prize in 2005, the Museum of Byzantine Culture reveals what the city’s churches no longer show: daily life, funerary rites, and trade. Designed by Kyriakos Krokos and opened in 1994, it features eleven permanent galleries covering 3,430 m², almost half the area of a soccer field. Arrive before 1:30 p.m.: in winter, it closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays. Admission is €10.

activities.text: You’ll then walk along Nea Paralia, the new waterfront, starting at the statue of Alexander the Great on Bucephalus, a work by Evangelos Moustakas. Completed in December 2013 and designed by Prodromos Nikiforidis and Bernard Cuomo, the promenade features seven themed gardens, from the sculpture garden to the Mediterranean garden planted with thyme, oregano, and lavender. Set out 1 hour before sunset, facing the Thermaic Gulf.

practical_info.tip: The promenade is free to access and lit by streetlights in the evening, so you can keep walking after sunset.

visits.text: Ordinary buildings all around, an imperial palace in the middle: the Palace of Galerius sits below street level in Navarinou Square. Galerius made Thessaloniki his residence in 299; you can still make out the colonnaded courtyard, the baths, and, to the southwest, the Octagon, probably a throne room. Go as soon as it opens: in winter, the site opens from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., is closed on Tuesdays year-round, and costs €5 to enter.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Palace Of Galerius Thessaloniki to Arch Of Galerius
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Locals simply call it “Kamara” and meet up here. Around 300, the Arch of Galerius celebrated Galerius’s victory over the Persian king Narses; only three of its original eight pillars are still standing. Look closely at the marble panels: you can make out Galerius on horseback charging at Narses, the imperial family, camels, and elephants. The arch is freely accessible at the intersection of Egnatia Street and Dimitriou Gounari Street.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Arch Of Galerius to Rotunda Thessaloniki
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: The Rotunda has been a temple or mausoleum, a church, a mosque, and then a church again, known as Saint George since 1912. Built under Galerius around 306, it retains its Ottoman-era minaret and, beneath its dome, early Byzantine mosaics, including a charcoal sketch near the top. Its 6.30 m thick walls have helped it withstand earthquakes. Admission €10; closed Tuesdays, open until 3:30 p.m. in winter.

More modest than its larger counterpart in Constantinople, Hagia Sophia in Thessaloniki saves its finest sight for the dome. The current church dates to the 7th century; high above, a 9th-century mosaic of the Ascension depicts Christ surrounded by the Virgin, two angels, and the twelve apostles. A mosque from 1430 to 1912, it later returned to Orthodox worship. Visit between services with your shoulders and knees covered, and keep your binoculars handy for the dome.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Hagia Sophia Thessaloniki to Acheiropoietos Thessaloniki
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Built around 450–470, the Church of the Acheiropoietos has stood for more than fifteen centuries. Its name means “not made by human hands,” after a miraculous icon of the Virgin it once housed; in 1430, it became the first church converted into a mosque, by Sultan Murad II himself. Inside, look for fragments of 5th-century decorative mosaics and the green marble columns from Thessaly. It is a few minutes from Hagia Sophia.

If you see only one church, choose Saint Demetrios, dedicated to the city’s patron saint. Rebuilt as a five-aisled basilica in 629–634, nearly destroyed by the great fire of 1917, and reconsecrated in 1949, it retains six ancient mosaic panels. Head down into the crypt, a former Roman bath where the saint is said to have been martyred in 303. The church is open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.; the crypt is closed Tuesdays and closes at 3 p.m. in winter (1 p.m. on Fridays).

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Hagios Demetrios Thessaloniki to Roman Forum Thessaloniki
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: The finest sculptures from Thessaloniki’s Roman Forum are in the Louvre: the mythological reliefs from the Stoa of the Idols were taken there. The central square, an underground cryptoporticus, and an odeon that still hosts performances remain on site; in 1966, these remains led to plans for a courthouse being abandoned. The site is closed Tuesdays and open from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. in winter; admission €10.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Roman Forum Thessaloniki to Panagia Chalkeon
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Built entirely of brick, Panagia Chalkeon lives up to its nickname, the “red church.” Its foundation inscription dates it to 1028; it takes its name from the neighborhood’s coppersmiths, and the Ottomans turned it into the Mosque of the Cauldron Merchants. In the apse, the Virgin stands in prayer between two archangels. As you leave, follow Egnatia Street east to see Bey Hamam, the city’s first Ottoman bath, built in 1444 and open during exhibitions.

activities.text: You’ll end the day in Ladadika, the former olive oil merchants’ district, whose shops gave it its name. Before World War I, it was the red-light district; granted protected status by the Ministry of Culture in 1985, it has retained its 19th-century architecture, and its former warehouses house tavernas, ouzo bars, and bars all the way to Morichovou Square. Order mezze to share and reserve a table on weekends.

practical_info.tip: The neighborhood is pedestrian-only; Aristotelous Square is less than a 10-minute walk away.

visits.text: The name is misleading: the Heptapyrgion, the “fortress of seven towers,” has ten at the top of Ano Poli. The Ottomans called it Yedi Kule; converted into a prison in 1890, it held inmates until 1989, and rebetiko songs refer to it as Yedi Koule. Take bus 23 to the Eptapyrgio stop to arrive when it opens, at 8:30 a.m. in winter. Closed Tuesdays; admission €10, free on the first and third Sundays from November through March.

activities.text: You’ll then walk downhill along the acropolis walls to Trigonion Tower, at the northeastern corner of the city walls. It was the last refuge of the city’s Byzantine defenders, then served as an arsenal and artillery post after the Ottoman conquest. From the nearby walls, the view takes in the rooftops of the lower city and the gulf: this is the best place to get a sense of Thessaloniki’s sloping terrain.

practical_info.tip: The tower’s interior can be visited on Fridays by appointment at +30 2313 310400 (admission €5); you can walk freely along the walls.

visits.text: Ano Poli’s finest balcony may belong to monks: Vlatades Monastery offers a view over the entire city. Founded in the 14th century by the brothers Dorotheos and Markos Vlattis, it remains Thessaloniki’s only active Byzantine monastery and has housed the Patriarchal Institute for Patristic Studies since 1965. Speak softly in the courtyard, as this is a place of prayer, and save your camera for the overlook.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Vlatadon Monastery to Hosios David Thessaloniki
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: A beardless Christ, rare for the period, fills the apse of Hosios David, the former church of Latomou Monastery. This late 5th-century mosaic, known as the Vision of Ezekiel, surrounds him with the prophets Ezekiel and Habakkuk; legend has it that it lay hidden beneath plaster and an oxhide until an earthquake revealed it. The visit is short: set aside ten minutes facing the apse. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Mustafa Kemal, the future Atatürk and founder of modern Turkey, is said to have been born in 1881 in this pink house on Apostolou Pavlou Street. The Atatürk Museum now stands within the grounds of the Turkish consulate: family furniture, his mother Zübeyde Hanım’s bedroom, clothing, and rare photographs are displayed across two floors. Allow 30 minutes; admission is free, Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

If one visit can change how you see the city, it is the Jewish Museum of Thessaloniki on Agiou Mina Street. Opened in 2001 in a 1904 building designed by Vitaliano Poselli, it displays gravestones from the destroyed old Jewish cemetery and dedicates a room to victims of the Holocaust: some 49,000 of the city’s Jews were deported to Auschwitz and Bergen-Belsen. Check the museum’s website for opening hours before visiting.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Jewish Museum Of Thessaloniki to Kapani Market Thessaloniki
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: Olives, spices, fish, and loukoumi vie for space on the stalls of Kapani, the city’s oldest open-air market, officially called Agora Vlali. Its name comes from the Turkish Un Kapan, meaning flour market; it dates back to the late 15th century, and many shops have been passed down through two or three generations. Preferably come in the morning, and before 4 p.m. on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays.

practical_info.tip: Closed Sunday; on Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday, the market stays open into the evening, until around 9 PM, according to the hours published online.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Kapani Market Thessaloniki to Modiano Market Thessaloniki
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: You will have dinner at Modiano Market, a covered market hall whose construction began in 1922 on the site of the former Talmud Torah synagogue. Eli Modiano, a member of a local Sephardic family who trained in Paris, modeled it on certain Parisian market halls; following restoration, it reopened in December 2022. Shop for cheeses and olives on the street side, then settle into a tavern inside for ouzo and meze.

practical_info.tip: The stalls are best browsed in the morning or late afternoon; the market hall’s taverns and bars take over in the evening.

visits.text: Pella was the birthplace of Alexander the Great, and its broad streets, laid out in a regular grid, still reflect the ambition of its kings. Archelaus moved the Macedonian capital here from Aigai in the late 5th century BC; under Philip II, the city gained an agora described as the largest square marketplace in the ancient Greek world. Arrive as early as 8:30 a.m.: in winter, the site closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

The Archaeological Museum of Pella alone is worth the trip from Thessaloniki. Opened in 2009, it displays mosaic floors from the Houses of Dionysus and the Abduction of Helen, a stag hunt dating to around 300 BC, and a marble head believed to be a portrait of Alexander. Look for the first object on display: a tile marked “Pellis,” which helped identify the city. Admission €10, closed Tuesday.

map_keywords: Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai Vergina

visits.text: Eleven kilograms of gold: that is the weight of the larnax adorned with the Vergina Sun at the Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai. Buried beneath an earthen mound resembling a tumulus, the museum protects the tombs excavated by Manolis Andronikos beginning in 1977, including the one attributed to Philip II, with its frescoes and gold wreath. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996; in winter, it opens from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., except on Tuesdays.

You will then walk about 750 m to the Palace of Aigai, which reopened in January 2024 after sixteen years of restoration. Built under Philip II, it covers 15,000 m², three times the area of the Parthenon according to the regional tourism office; Alexander was proclaimed king here, and Philip II was assassinated in 336 BC in the nearby theater. The €20 combined ticket covers the palace, tombs, and central museum: enter before 4:40 p.m.

activities.text: French on paper, Greek in everyday life: Aristotelous Square, Thessaloniki’s main square, originated in Ernest Hébrard’s 1918 plans following the great fire of 1917, but was largely built in the 1950s. The twelve buildings lining it have been protected since 1950, and the square opens directly onto the waterfront. Stroll along the water after nightfall, then dine in the small taverns of nearby Athonos Square.

practical_info.tip: Pedestrian square with free access; Athonos Square is a two-minute walk away.

seo.h1_title: Thessaloniki in 4 Days: City Walls, Mosaics, and Vergina
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day stay explores Thessaloniki on foot, from the waterfront museums to the UNESCO-listed Byzantine churches, then from the city walls of Ano Poli to Kapani and Modiano Markets. A full day then takes you to Pella, the birthplace of Alexander the Great, and the royal tombs of Aigai in Vergina.
seo.seo_hook: White Tower, Rotunda, Saint Demetrios, Ano Poli, and markets: Thessaloniki in 4 days, with a day trip to Pella and the royal tombs of Vergina.
featured_list: White Tower: 34 m tall, with a museum on the city’s history
Rotunda: built under Galerius around 306, with walls 6.30 m thick
Saint Demetrios: a crypt in the Roman bath where the martyrdom took place in 303
Vergina: an 11 kg gold larnax at the Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai

places_taglines.GR::archaeological-museum-of-thessalonik: The Derveni Krater and Macedonian gold, from prehistory to Roman times.
places_taglines.GR::museum-of-byzantine-culture: Eleven galleries on Byzantine daily life, art, and faith.
places_taglines.GR::nea-paralia-thessaloniki: Waterfront completed in 2013, lined with seven themed gardens.
places_taglines.GR::palace-of-galerius-thessaloniki: Remains of the Palace of Galerius and its Octagon in Navarinou Square.
places_taglines.GR::arch-of-galerius: Galerius’s triumphal arch, nicknamed Kamara, with marble reliefs.
places_taglines.GR::rotunda-thessaloniki: Galerius’s Rotunda, dating to around 306, with 6.30 m walls and mosaics.
places_taglines.GR::hagia-sophia-thessaloniki: A 7th-century church with an Ascension mosaic in its dome.
places_taglines.GR::acheiropoietos-thessaloniki: A basilica dating to 450–470, the first church converted into a mosque in 1430.
places_taglines.GR::hagios-demetrios-thessaloniki: The patron saint’s basilica, with six mosaic panels and a Roman crypt.
places_taglines.GR::roman-forum-thessaloniki: Roman forum with an odeon, a cryptoporticus, and a small underground museum.
places_taglines.GR::panagia-chalkeon: The red church of the coppersmiths, dated to 1028 by its inscription.
places_taglines.GR::ladadika-thessaloniki: Former olive oil district, designated a protected area in 1985, with lively tavernas.
places_taglines.GR::heptapyrgion-thessaloniki: A ten-towered fortress in Ano Poli, used as a prison until 1989.
places_taglines.GR::trigonion-tower-thessaloniki: A corner tower of the Byzantine city walls and a viewpoint overlooking the city.
places_taglines.GR::vlatadon-monastery: Thessaloniki’s only Byzantine monastery still in use, with panoramic views.
places_taglines.GR::hosios-david-thessaloniki: A small 5th-century church with a mosaic of a beardless Christ.
places_taglines.GR::ataturk-museum-thessaloniki: The pink house where Mustafa Kemal Atatürk is believed to have been born in 1881.
places_taglines.GR::jewish-museum-of-thessaloniki: The city’s Sephardic heritage and a room commemorating Holocaust victims.
places_taglines.GR::kapani-market-thessaloniki: The city’s oldest open-air market, established in the 15th century.
places_taglines.GR::modiano-market-thessaloniki: Eli Modiano’s covered market, reopened in December 2022 after restoration.
places_taglines.GR::pella: Macedonian capital where Alexander was born, with mosaics and a museum opened in 2009.
places_taglines.GR::vergina: Royal tombs of Aigai and Philip II’s restored palace, UNESCO-listed in 1996.
places_taglines.GR::aristotelous-square-thessaloniki: Grand square designed by Ernest Hébrard in 1918, opening onto the sea.

highlights: White Tower: a different theme on each floor covering the city’s history, plus views from the roof
Rotunda and Arch of Galerius: Galerius’s capital around AD 300
Saint Demetrios, Hagia Sophia, and Hosios David: mosaic-adorned churches inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1988
Ano Poli: the ten towers of the Heptapyrgion, a prison until 1989
Kapani and Modiano: two markets spanning the 15th century to the 1920s
Vergina: an 11 kg gold larnax and the Palace of Aigai, reopened in 2024
