itineraries.title: Kastoria, Prespes, and Nymfaio in 5 Days: Icons and Bears
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, travel from Kastoria’s frescoes to Prespa’s hermitages, then on to the bears of Nymfaio.
itineraries.notes: Ideally, start on a Wednesday: the Byzantine Museum of Kastoria is closed on Tuesdays, the Dragon’s Cave on Mondays, and the Arcturos sanctuaries on Wednesdays. The bear sanctuary also closes during hibernation, generally from early January to early March. Kastoria has an airport with flights to Athens, and Amyntaio station, about twenty kilometers from Nymfaio, has been served by Florina–Thessaloniki trains again since May 2026.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September, with highs of 23 to 28 °C in Kastoria; October remains pleasant at around 20 °C. Avoid January and February: overnight frosts, Lake Orestiada sometimes frozen over for several weeks, and bear sanctuaries closed during hibernation. In July–August, expect afternoon temperatures of 30 to 31 °C in Kastoria, and bring a jacket for evenings in Nymfaio, at 1,350 m.

visits.text: Nothing offers a better introduction to the city’s churches than the Byzantine Museum of Kastoria, on Dexamenis Square at the highest point of the peninsula. Its collections include around 700 icons from Kastoria’s churches; the selection on display spans the 12th to the 17th century, grouped by period and workshop. The museum is closed on Tuesdays (€10 in summer, €5 in winter): ask at the front desk about visiting the churches, which requires an appointment arranged through the museum.

Its name comes from the Turkish kubbe, meaning dome: Panagia Koumbelidiki was long Kastoria’s only domed church. This 11th-century sanctuary lost much of its dome in a bombing raid in 1940; the dome was restored in 1949. Walk around the exterior to find the Dance of Salome, dated 1496, painted over an older Deesis. The interior, with its rare depiction of the Holy Trinity, opens by appointment through the Byzantine Museum.

Kastorian notables gaze out at you from the walls: the Church of the Taxiarchs of the Metropolis, a few steps from the cathedral, dates to the 10th century. Its frescoes were painted in two phases, the more recent in the 14th century, including funerary portraits. It also houses the remains of Pavlos Melas, a figure in the Macedonian Struggle. Arrange access through the Byzantine Museum, then look for his name again at the Museum of the Macedonian Struggle.

If you want to see the face of a Byzantine patron, head to Agios Nikolaos tou Kasnitzi on Omonoia Square. In the narthex of this 12th-century church, Nikephoros Kasnitzis and his wife Anna present the building to Saint Nicholas. The decoration forms a cohesive whole: the Platytera in the apse, and scenes from the lives of Christ and the saint on the walls. Include it with the other churches when requesting an appointment at the Byzantine Museum.

Agios Stefanos, a 9th-century basilica with a nave and two side aisles, stands on a hill between the Apozari and Doltso neighborhoods. Repainted in the 13th and 14th centuries, it retains a two-story narthex with a women’s gallery, where a small chapel dedicated to Saint Anne is tucked away. The regional tourist office identifies its depiction of the Last Judgment as the oldest in Greece. Walk up from Doltso, wearing shoes suited to cobblestones.

Fragments of 11th-century faces still emerge in the narthex of Agioi Anargyroi, one of Kastoria’s oldest churches. The nave is covered with 12th-century frescoes whose figures grow more expressive: Byzantine art takes on new life before your eyes. The church is near the old Apozari neighborhood; follow your visit with a walk through its narrow streets, and include the church in your combined appointment to visit the churches.

Step inside the Nerantzis Aivazis Mansion in Doltso: the Folklore Museum of Kastoria recreates the life of a wealthy 18th-century family. A kitchen, well, and wooden boat occupy the courtyard; the mezzanine has winter and summer bedrooms, followed upstairs by a formal reception room and a kiosk with colorful stained-glass windows. One detail captures the city’s character: the fur workshop preserves Kastoria’s first sewing machine for pelts. Open mornings only, except Mondays; admission is €2.

Limited hours, a rare collection: the Costume Museum of Kastoria occupies the Emmanouil brothers’ mansion in the Doltso neighborhood. The second floor brings together costumes from across Greece; the third displays Kastorian dress, including fezzes with gold tassels for women and black tassels for men. Leave time for the silk clothing for children and infants. Outside Sunday mornings, visits must be booked by phone; admission is €3.

The Museum of the Macedonian Struggle occupies the Picheon Mansion, near Emmanouil Brothers Square. Uniforms, photographs, and relics donated by descendants of the fighters trace the beginnings and then the height of the Struggle; the map room displays a map from 1550, and the library holds more than 2,500 titles. Come before 2 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday (Sunday hours are 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.; admission is €3), after your visit to the Church of the Taxiarchs.

activities.text: From the deck of the municipal boat Olympia, you can finally take in Kastoria at a glance: the peninsula, the mansions of Doltso, then the Dragon’s Cave and the Monastery of Mavriotissa right by the water. The cruise lasts around 45 minutes and departs from the northern lakefront. Lake Orestiada covers 28 km², and the peninsula divides it into two basins. Board in the late afternoon, when the light turns the facades golden.

practical_info.tip: Departures vary with the season and weather: check at the northern dock when you arrive.

to_next_leg.road_type: Road along the shore of Lake Orestiada

visits.text: Discovered in the 1940s during construction of the lakeside road, the Dragon’s Cave did not open to the public until 2009. Its 300 m route passes through ten chambers and alongside seven underground freshwater lakes; cave bear bones dating back around 10,000 years were found here. Visits are guided, tickets cost €6, and the cave is closed on Mondays: visit in the morning, before nearby Mavriotissa.

The most moving stop on the loop? The waterfront Monastery of Panagia Mavriotissa, about 4 km from central Kastoria. Founded in the 11th century, it features one of the oldest surviving Trees of Jesse on its facade, along with two imperial portraits attributed to Alexios I Komnenos and Michael VIII Palaiologos. The Chapel of St. John the Theologian preserves frescoes from 1552. Open daily from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m.; keep your shoulders covered.

The reconstruction feels a little like a school exhibit, but the history is staggering: the open-air museum at Dispilio, 7 km from Kastoria on the southern shore, recreates a lakeside village from around 7,500 years ago. The site’s wooden piles emerged in 1932, when the water level fell. In 1993, excavations by Aristotle University uncovered a wooden tablet engraved with symbols, radiocarbon-dated to between 5324 and 5079 BC; a replica is on display. Open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., admission €5.

activities.text: Circle the peninsula along the lakeside road, a roughly 6 km route lined with plane and beech trees. More than 200 bird species have been recorded on Lake Orestiada, which hosts Greece’s largest breeding colony of mute swans; pelicans and swans often approach walkers. Set out early, on foot or on a rented bike: driving spoils the outing, and both the Dragon’s Cave and Mavriotissa lie along the route.

practical_info.tip: Keep binoculars handy and follow the loop in whichever direction gets you to the Dragon’s Cave in the morning.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, set aside an hour and a half for the summit of Agios Athanasios, at 870 m, linked to Kastoria by marked trails. The lake spreads out 240 m below, its kidney-shaped outline divided in two by the peninsula. In the distance, the Grammos and Vitsi mountains frame the basin. Bring sturdy shoes and water, and head up in the late afternoon for the light.

practical_info.tip: Kastoria’s municipal tourist office (tel. 2467026777) can point you to the trailheads.

visits.text: Mikrolimni is the only village on Lesser Prespa built right at the water’s edge, around a dock facing the islet of Vidronisi. This uninhabited islet is a refuge for birds, and no one is allowed to land there. The village was called Lagka until 1928. Bring binoculars: from the dock, you can watch cormorants without disturbing them.

activities.text: Head up to the Mikrolimni bird observatory on the shore of Lesser Prespa: in spring, up to six species of herons may appear here. The Prespa basin also hosts the world’s largest breeding colony of Dalmatian pelicans. Come early in the morning, with a spotting scope if possible, and keep quiet near the reed beds.

practical_info.tip: Spring is the best season for herons; keep your distance from the colonies.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: Around 986–990, Tsar Samuel had the Basilica of Agios Achilleios built on the islet to house the relics of St. Achilleios. Its nave and two aisles covered an area of about 20 m by 47 m, and Samuel was buried there after his death in 1014. Its frescoes, removed in 1976, are now in the Archaeological Museum of Florina: you will see them farther along the route.

activities.text: Cross Lesser Prespa on the floating footbridge stretching more than 600 m between the island of Agios Achilleios and the shore. Before it was built, you had to call for a boat. The island trail passes Agios Georgios, the 15th-century Monastery of Panagia Porfyra, and the ruins of Agios Dimitrios and the Twelve Apostles. Climb to the highest point for the view.

practical_info.tip: A waterfront taverna on the island lets you have lunch without crossing back over the footbridge.

activities.text: Krina Hill, above the path to Agios Achilleios, offers the best vantage point over the footbridge. From here, the geography becomes clear: the strip of land at Koula separates Lesser Prespa from Great Prespa, once joined as a single lake. Head up with binoculars, preferably early in the morning.

practical_info.tip: The hill also serves as a birdwatching spot: stay on the paths.

visits.text: With just seventy-three residents in 2021, Psarades nevertheless made history: on June 17, 2018, the Greek and Macedonian prime ministers signed the Prespa Agreement here. It is the only Greek village on the shore of Great Prespa and is designated a traditional settlement. Look for old water-level marks on the rocks, well above the current surface.

activities.text: Board at Psarades harbor: boat operators wait at the lakefront kiosk for a trip lasting about an hour. The boat passes icons painted on the rock in the 14th and 15th centuries, then docks below the Hermitage of Panagia Eleousa, with its frescoes from 1409–1410, reached by steps. Out on the lake, a buoy marks the meeting point of three borders.

practical_info.tip: A shorter trip of about 20 minutes is available; the 1 hour trip allows time for the hermitages.

activities.text: Low-angle light and still water: Cape Roti, an easy one-hour walk from Psarades, offers a sunset viewpoint. Another trail reaches the 13th-century Hermitage of the Transfiguration in about an hour, without taking a boat. Bring a headlamp for the return after dark; vegetation is dense in places.

practical_info.tip: Hiking shoes are recommended: the trail passes through dense vegetation.

activities.text: Coated in oil and then sun-dried, tsironi, a fish from Great Prespa, accompanies aperitifs in the tavernas of Psarades. Round out your meal with Prespes giant beans, grown above 900 m and protected by a geographical indication, served in soup or baked. Reserve a lakeside table for dinner.

practical_info.tip: Tsironi is eaten fresh or salted; ask about the day’s catch.

visits.text: The Church of Agios Germanos, built in the early 11th century, gave the village its name. Its walls bear frescoes from three periods: the 11th century, the 12th–13th centuries, and 1743, with a Pantocrator in the dome and a cycle of the Twelve Great Feasts. Look up at the dome first, then find the Virgin Deomeni on the sanctuary arch.

More charming than it first appears, the Agios Germanos watermill, built in 1930, is a survivor of some twenty mills in the area. It was used to grind grain, wash woven textiles, and full wool. Visits are free and must be booked through the Society for the Protection of Prespa.

activities.text: Stop at the Prespa National Park information center on the square in Agios Germanos. Protected since 1974, the area covers 32,700 ha, and more than 275 bird species have been recorded here. Ask for a trail map: the Society for the Protection of Prespa has marked about ten trails, plus three cycling routes.

practical_info.tip: Call the information center (23850 51870) to check that day’s hours.

activities.text: Large restored stone houses and grocery stores stocked with beans: Agios Germanos, a protected traditional village, rewards an unhurried stroll. In the past, the ground floor was used for storage, while the family lived upstairs. Buy your Prespes beans here, giant or flat, before crossing the mountain toward Florina.

practical_info.tip: The village grocery stores also sell lake fish, depending on deliveries.

activities.text: If the road is clear, stop at the Vigla-Pisoderi ski resort, at around 1,600 m, on the way to Florina. The view takes in Florina, the village of Pisoderi, and the mountains around Prespes. In winter, come equipped for snow: allow for a round trip from Agios Germanos for this stop.

practical_info.tip: The resort has nine ski runs in winter; the rest of the year, it mainly serves as a viewpoint.

visits.text: Agios Panteleimon Hill, above Florina, preserves the remains of a Hellenistic city founded in the 4th century BC and destroyed by fire in the early 1st century BC. You can make out house foundations, jars, hearths, and ironworking workshops. The site closes at 4 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays: make it your first stop.

The frescoes removed from Agios Achilleios in 1976 await you at the Archaeological Museum of Florina, near the train station. The displays span the Neolithic period at Armenochori through the Byzantine era, and the exhibition “Prespes: Monuments and Art” covers the 10th–18th centuries. Open from 8 AM to 7 PM except Tuesdays; admission is €5.

Chagall on the banks of the Sakoulevas, who would have thought? Founded in 1977, the Museum of Contemporary Art of Florina brings together more than 700 works, from Moralis and Tsoklis to foreign artists such as Chagall. Admission is free, but the hours are unusual: on weekdays, it opens only late in the day, and never on Mondays.

activities.text: Stroll along the Sakoulevas, the river that runs through Florina between neoclassical houses and cafés. Theo Angelopoulos shot several films in the city, including Ulysses’ Gaze and The Beekeeper; its gray riverbanks evoke something of his long takes. Finish at an outdoor table by the water while waiting for the Museum of Contemporary Art to open.

practical_info.tip: On Sundays, the Museum of Contemporary Art is open only from 11 AM to 1 PM: adjust the order of your visits accordingly.

visits.text: The Agios Panteleimonas windmill, built in the mid-18th century and designated a historic monument, stands on a rise in the village. It recalls a time when wind powered the local economy. Make it your first stop for a photo before a tasting at the nearby winery.

activities.text: This tasting room overlooking Lake Vegoritida is a lovely surprise: the Kir-Yianni estate of Amyndeon, in Agios Panteleimonas, offers cellar tours and shows how its sparkling wines are made, including riddling. The Amyntaio area produces appellation wines made from xinomavro. Reservations are required; the estate is closed on Mondays and opens at 11 AM on weekends.

practical_info.tip: Choose a designated driver: the route continues toward the Arcturos sanctuaries.

activities.text: Old maps call it “Lake Ostrovo”: Vegoritida, one of the largest natural lakes in northern Greece, covers 54 km² at an elevation of 540 m. Its falling water level in the late 1990s even sparked a land dispute with the neighboring village of Vegora. Follow the shore before getting back on the road.

practical_info.tip: The village celebrates tsipouro during the rakokazana festivities in the last week of November.

activities.text: Less well known than the bear sanctuary, the Arcturos wolf and lynx sanctuary near Agrapidies is well worth a visit. Established in 1993, it protects 7 ha of natural oak woodland at an elevation of 650 m, explored on guided tours. The same ticket includes admission to the bear sanctuary in Nymfaio; the sanctuary is closed on Wednesdays, and pets and flash photography are prohibited.

practical_info.tip: Tours depart at set times between 10 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.: combine your visit with Nymfaio, a 15-minute drive away.

to_next_leg.justification: La distance et la durée actuellement indiquées sont cohérentes avec le cheminement réel ; le routeur automobile ne doit pas les remplacer.

visits.text: In 1928, tobacco merchant Ioannis Zan Nikos donated the Nikeios School to Nymfaio, a three-story stone building topped by a clock tower, built from plans brought back from Sweden. Students left in 1980; since 1993, it has housed the Arcturos brown bear information center. The center opens only on weekends, from 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Wedding crowns, belt buckles, snuffboxes: since 2000, the Museum of Silversmithing, Folklore, and History has occupied the House of Nymfaio, a three-story mansion. Silversmithing has supported the village since the 18th century, and its pieces circulated as far as Central Europe. One room preserves original letters by Pavlos Melas. Open seasonally: call ahead.

Few villages are as well cared for as Nymfaio, founded around 1385 by Vlachs at an elevation of 1,350 m. Cobblestone lanes, stone mansions, sheet-metal roofs that shed the snow; at the entrance, an arched wooden bridge connects two homes. Agios Nikolaos Church, rebuilt in 2000, stands on a site that has been consecrated since 1385. Wear shoes with good traction.

activities.text: Put on your hiking shoes: the guided tour of the Arcturos bear sanctuary, 1.5 km from Nymfaio, follows a trail through beech woodland. Opened in 1993, the 5 ha enclosure houses bears rescued from captivity, including former dancing bears. Tours depart hourly from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., with a final departure at 4:30 p.m., except on Wednesdays.

practical_info.tip: The sanctuary is closed to visitors while the bears hibernate, generally from early January to early March.

activities.text: The scent of moss and green light: Nymfaio’s marked trails wind through the beech woodland surrounding the village. Choose a short loop in the late afternoon, after visiting the bears. Horseback riders will find an equestrian center, and mountain bikes are available to rent locally for the forest trails.

practical_info.tip: After rain, ask in the village which trails are still passable.

seo.h1_title: Kastoria, Prespes, and Nymfaio in 5 Days: Icons and Bears
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day itinerary starts in Kastoria, with its Byzantine churches and lake, then heads to the Prespa lakes, Florina, and the mountain village of Nymfaio. You alternate between frescoes, boat trips to hermitages, museums, and Arcturos sanctuaries, with drives that never exceed an hour.
seo.seo_hook: Kastoria’s Byzantine churches, the Agios Achilleios footbridge, the hermitages of Psarades, and the bears of Nymfaio: 5 days among the lakes of Western Macedonia.
featured_list: Kastoria: around 700 icons at the Byzantine Museum of Kastoria, at the top of the peninsula
Dispilio: a reconstructed Neolithic lakeside village dating back around 7,500 years
Agios Achilleios: floating footbridge and Tsar Samuel’s basilica
Psarades: boat trip to 14th- and 15th-century frescoes on rock faces
Agios Germanos: 11th-century church and watermill dating to 1930
Florina: frescoes from Agios Achilleios and more than 700 works of contemporary art
Agios Panteleimonas: tasting overlooking Lake Vegoritida
Nymfaio: Arcturos bear sanctuary at 1,350 m

Dispilio: a Neolithic lakeside village dating back around 7,500 years, reconstructed on the lakeshore
Agios Achilleios: floating footbridge and Tsar Samuel’s basilica, circa 986–990
Psarades: a boat trip to 14th- and 15th-century frescoes painted on rock faces
Florina: frescoes from Agios Achilleios at the museum and contemporary art along the Sakoulevas River
